paragraphs.text: THE COMPLETE EXTANT WORKS OF OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS, JOHN CHRYSOSTOM, ARCHBISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE. [I] ON PSALM 3. A psalm of David, when he fled from the face of Absalom his son. Lord, why have those who afflict me multiplied? Kings set up victory statues to generals who have won, and rulers raise triumphal images and pillars to charioteers and athletes, and with the inscription, as with a mouth, they make the very material a herald of the victory. Others again write the praises of victors in books and documents, wanting to show that their own power in praising is greater than that of the men they praise. Speech-writers and painters, bronze-smiths and sculptors, peoples and rulers, cities and countries all admire the victors. But no one has ever drawn a portrait of a man who fled and did not fight, as David does now. For it says, "A psalm of David, when he fled from the face of Absalom his son." When is a runaway worthy of praise? When does a fugitive deserve an inscription? Runaways are hunted down with written notices, not admired in inscriptions. But learn the reason for the title, brother, and make your soul secure. Let the story become for you a correction of life; let the persecution of the righteous man be for you a strengthening of mind. Learn why David was pursued by Absalom, so that, having found the matter as a foundation, you may build upon it with the word [?] of God. For as a building without a foundation is unsound, so Scripture is of no benefit unless its purpose is found. Blessed David's purpose in the present psalm was to instruct and discipline our life, so that we never do evil or despise the laws of God, lest the one who sins suffer such things as he himself suffered. David fled from his son because he had fled from chastity; he fled from his son because he had outraged a chaste marriage; he fled from his son because he had fled from the law of God that says, You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery. For since he brought another man's ewe-lamb into his own house and killed its shepherd, the lamb from his own house butted the shepherd. He made war on another man's house, and war rose up against him from his own house. The thought is not mine; the saying is God's. And where God is the interpreter, [?]

[?] even if the wife who strikes and the husband who is struck do not know the cause of the blow, God, like a physician, knows what is beneficial. That a wicked wife is a blow for sins, divine Scripture testifies. Hear what it says: A wicked wife will be given to a sinful man. She will be given to him like a bitter antidote, consuming the humours of his sins. That being besieged by one's children is also a torment for sins, David is witness: he was warred against by his son Absalom because of the unlawful bed, as our discourse has shown. That brothers too have made war on brothers because of sins, the book of Judges is witness. For when the men of the tribe of Benjamin committed fornication against the traveller's concubine, and she, unable to bear the boundless outrage, died, the eleven tribes made war on the one. And since the eleven tribes had departed from God and gone whoring after idols, the eleven were defeated by the one tribe; and after being defeated many times by the one, they defeated it once. And brothers made war on brothers, since God, because of their sins, took away the dividing wall of sin. For since the one tribe committed fornication against the woman, and the eleven tribes went whoring after idols, both the one and the others were destroyed by God, as it is written: You have destroyed everyone who goes whoring away from you. So brothers made war on brothers because of sins. When you are warred against by your brothers, do not groan against them so much as call yourself to account, and examine yourself, asking for what sins your brothers have become your enemies. Not that everyone who is warred against by brothers suffers it because of sins: Joseph too was warred against by his brothers, and not at all because of sins; Job too was plotted against by his wife, and not at all because of sins. But most of us human beings have enemies in our own households because of sins. Sometimes friends too turn into enemies because of sins, and those who once loved come to hate and turn away, God casting in such hatred for reasons he knows. For so it is written in the hundred and fourth psalm about the Egyptians: He turned their heart to hate his people. Hatred would not have been given by God had they not first been friends in a wicked way. For those to whom friendship brings destruction, hatred becomes an occasion of virtue. And even the bodies of slaves and subjects have often risen up against their masters because of sins. Look at Adam: before he had sinned, he had the beasts as slaves and subjects, and gave them names as one does to slaves. But when he stained his face with sin, the beasts no longer recognized him, and the slaves became enemies against him. Just as the dog in the house serves the one who feeds it, fears him and stands in awe of him, but if it suddenly sees him with his face blackened with soot, or wearing a strange mask over his face, it attacks him as a stranger and wants to tear him apart; so with Adam: as long as he kept pure the face made in the image of God, the beasts were subject to him as slaves, but when he stained that face by disobedience, they no longer recognized their master and were hostile to him as to a stranger. So the rebellion of slaves too is a requital for sins. Daniel was righteous, and the lions recognized his mastery: they saw one who had not tasted sin, and they let him go with no share in punishment. A prophet sinned by lying [?] [Note: some manuscripts read "those who once longed" (?)]

[?] the earth turned away from him, refusing to be defiled by the steps of a parricide. For if it swallowed Dathan for speaking against Moses, and opened its mouth against the one who had wickedly opened his mouth, how could it bear feet that ran against a parent? So, as he hung high in the tree, Joab the commander-in-chief came upon him and drove three darts into the heart of that heartless man, striking him in the very place where lawlessness was stored. And as he hung high in the tree, David sang a fitting epitaph over him: I saw the ungodly exalted and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and behold, he was not. "A psalm of David, when he fled from the face of Absalom his son." He fled, not out of cowardice, but because he was wary of killing his son. He himself would have spared him as his child, but those with him would not have spared him as a rebel. So David, pursued by his son and reviled by Shimei on his son's account, was himself patient. But many took offence at him, especially those siding with Absalom, and they rose up against him as one abandoned by providence, saying: "David is now deserted, utterly without help. God has now departed from him, as he once departed from Saul. For just as he then departed from Saul and was with David, so now he has departed from David and is with Absalom. Let us rise up and attack; there is no salvation for him in God." Since they said these things, David, grieved more by them than by his son's insolent capers, asks God: Lord, why have those who afflict me multiplied? "I am fenced in by trials, hemmed in by torrents of evils. The perilous rain has come down, the rivers of enemies have come, the winds of evil spirits have blown and dashed against my house, wanting to move my soul away from you. But since I am founded on the rock of faith, I do not fall; rather I fall down before you, so that I may learn: Lord, why have those who afflict me multiplied? The one who came from me is against me, but you are for me. My own flesh and blood wars against me; my people follow Absalom; my army arms itself against me. My sheep have become wolves, the lambs lions, the lambs rabid dogs, the rams goring bulls. I do not grieve for myself; I lament their destruction."

EXPOSITION OF PSALM 4. When I called, the God of my righteousness heard me. 1. The Prophet says this not merely so that we may learn that he was heard, but so that we may be taught how we too, when we call upon God, may be heard quickly and receive our request even before our prayer is finished. For he did not say, "After I called, he heard me," but, "While I was calling." For indeed [?] [Note: some manuscripts end the preceding psalm: "I lament their destruction, and to you, my Saviour, I give thanks. For to you belong glory and might, now and always, etc."]

[?] one who wants to take what belongs to others and is not content with his own. So too we call a man arrogant when he demands more from his neighbour than is owed him, when someone places himself in every honour but dishonours another. This comes from nowhere else than from injustice. That it is injustice, consider from this: God made both you and him, and gave you everything in common and on equal terms with him. How then can you cast him out and rob him of the honour that God gave him, and not let him be a sharer, but by making the whole your own, make him poor not only in money but also in esteem? God granted both of you one nature; he deemed you worthy of the same rank, of equal formation. For "Let us make man" is common to the whole race. How then can you cast him out of his ancestral estate, bringing him down to the utmost cheapness, and appropriate what is common? But the blessed Prophet was not like that, and so he said with boldness: He heard my righteousness. So too Paul often brings himself forward, not exalting himself or puffing himself up, but making himself an example to others, as when he says, I wish all people to be as I myself am, in self-control. So too David, when the occasion called for it, brought forward his own courage, which came from God's help, saying that he had strangled bears and grappled with lions; he too was not exalting himself, God forbid, but thereby securing credibility for himself. "And if I have righteousness," someone may perhaps say, "what need is there of prayer, when the deed is enough to set everything right, and the one who is to give knows what we need?" Because prayer is no small bond of love toward God: it makes us familiar with conversing with him and leads us to the life of wisdom. For if someone who spends time with an admirable man reaps much from his company, how much more one who converses with God continually! But we do not know the gain of prayer as we should, since we neither attend to it carefully nor use it according to God's laws. When we are about to speak with men above us, we arrange our bearing, our gait, our dress and everything else as is proper, and only then do we speak; but when we approach God we yawn, we scratch ourselves, we turn this way and that, we are slack: our knees lie on the ground, while we wander about the marketplace. If we approached with fitting reverence, as people about to converse with God, then we would know, even before receiving what we asked, how great a gain we reap. For a man taught to converse with God, as is natural [?] has made it his own [?], has done this. Let us too, then, practise approaching God;

let us learn how this petition ought to be made. You do not need to go off to a school, or spend money, or hire tutors, rhetoricians and sophists, or spend a long time learning this rhetoric. It is enough merely to will it, and the art is complete. And you will be able to plead in this court not only for yourself but for many others too. And what does this art of pleading aim at? The right manner of prayer: to approach him with a sober mind, a contrite soul, with fountains of tears; to ask for nothing of this life; to long for the things to come; to make petition for spiritual things; not to pray against enemies; to bear no one a grudge; to cast every passion out of the soul; to approach with a broken heart; to be humble; to practise great gentleness and turn the tongue to words of blessing; to take part in no evil dealings; to have nothing in common with the common enemy of the world, I mean the devil. For even the laws of the outside world punish a man who pleads with the king on behalf of others while conferring with the king's enemies. So you too, if you wish to plead both for yourself and for others, achieve this above all: to have nothing in common with the common enemy of the world. In this way you will be righteous, and being righteous you will be heard, having such an advocate. In affliction you have enlarged me. He did not say, "You removed the afflictions," nor "[?] the trials," but, "You let them stand, and enlarged me." For God's resourcefulness and abundance are shown most of all here: not only in removing afflictions, but in granting great ease while they remain. This both displays God's strength and makes those who fall into afflictions wiser, when there is a spaciousness to comfort the afflicted soul, and yet the affliction is not removed, but keeps the soul tight when it grows slack and frees it from all negligence. "And how," someone asks, "could there be enlargement in affliction?" As in the furnace of the three youths, as in the lions' den. He did not quench the flame and then set them in a spacious place, nor kill the lions and then set Daniel in safety; but there, while the furnace blazed fiercely, and here, while the beasts remained, the righteous enjoyed great ease. One can also speak of spaciousness in another way: when the soul, afflicted by trials, is set free from its passions and its many diseases; for then above all it enjoys spaciousness. Many who live in prosperity have the most absurd loves that afflict their souls, for money, for bodies, and for other such absurdities; but when they fall into affliction they are freed from all of them and come into a spacious place. And just as people with fevers, so long as they indulge their untimely desires, I mean a laden table, neat wine and the like, are all the more distressed, but if they were willing to afflict themselves a little

We must therefore also know the right manner of prayer. And what is the manner of prayer? Learn it from the tax collector, and do not be ashamed to take him as your teacher, for he succeeded at it so well that he accomplished everything with bare words. Because his mind was well prepared, a single word was enough to open heaven for him. And how was it prepared? He called himself wretched, he beat his breast, he did not dare even to look up to heaven. If you too will pray in this way, you will make your prayer lighter than a feather. For if the sinner became righteous through prayer, consider how great the righteous man will become if he learns to offer such a petition. That is why here too he does not simply put himself forward, but his prayer: above he spoke of righteousness, here of prayer: Have mercy on me and hear my prayer. So too Cornelius was heard, since he had this as his advocate: Your prayers and your alms, it says, have gone up before God. And rightly [?]; for it is works that are heard, and good deeds; and not simply prayers, but prayers made according to God's law. And which are these? Those that ask for what it befits God to give, those that do not urge him to do things contrary to his laws. "And who," someone says, "is so bold as to ask God to act against his own laws?" The one who calls on him against his enemies; for this is contrary to the law he himself laid down. For he says, Forgive your debtors. And do you call upon the very one who commands you to forgive, against your enemies? What could be worse than such folly? The one who prays must have the bearing, the disposition and the mind of a suppliant. Why then do you put on another mask, that of the accuser? How will you be able to obtain pardon for your own sins, when you ask God to be the avenger of offences committed by others? Let prayer, then, be gentle and calm, with a gracious and tender face. Such is prayer made with meekness and not against enemies; the opposite kind is like a drunken, raving woman, swinish and savage. That is why heaven is closed to it. But prayer made with meekness is not like that: it has something clear and sweet-voiced, pleasing, worthy of royal ears, delightful, perfectly harmonious and tuneful. That is why it is not thrown out of the theatre, but departs crowned; for it has a golden lyre and a golden robe. That is why it delights the judge with its bearing, its look and its voice. For this reason no one drives it from the vaults of heaven, for it brings that whole theatre to its feet with joy. This is the prayer worthy of heaven; this is the tongue of angels, when it utters nothing bitter but everything gentle. When it comes making supplication for those who wrong and abuse it, then the angels stand by and listen in deep silence, and after it has ended they do not cease applauding it, praising it, marvelling at it. Let us too offer such a prayer, and we shall surely be heard. And when we approach God, let us not think that the theatre is of an ordinary kind, but that it is gathered from the whole world, or rather from the peoples of heaven above, with the King in the midst [?] [Notes: one manuscript reads "to give to laws"; one manuscript reads "and on behalf of enemies"; one manuscript reads "impiety".]

[?] and all sons of the Most High. But you die like men. And see the Prophet's understanding. Having first shown God's strength, his abundance, his resourcefulness, his kindness and his love for humankind, that he enlarges us in affliction and graciously consents in mercy, he then considers the wickedness spread abroad among men and the tyranny of impiety, and, as though choking with despondency, he turns his words to those who live in wickedness, all but saying: "Having such a God, so kind, so loving, so powerful, how could you turn aside to impiety?" And see how full his exhortation is of gentleness as well as anger, how full of wisdom. What does he say? Sons of men, how long will you be heavy-hearted? Here he rebukes them sharply from the length of time too. For if failing to perceive God's kindness from the beginning is a fault, what pardon can there be for staying blind to the truth for so long? And what does "heavy-hearted" mean? Dull of heart, carnal, nailed to the earth, pursuing vice, practising wickedness, rotting in luxuries; for such is the carnal man. And in condemning their way of life he shows the source of their impiety, making it clear that this above all is what keeps them from the lofty doctrines. For nothing makes the heart so heavy as evil desire, attachment to the things of this life, and being nailed to the earth. One would not be wrong to call such a heart a heart of clay; that is why he called it heavy. And he said that this is the cause of evils because, though it holds the place of a charioteer, not only does it fail to restrain the horse with the reins, but it is itself dragged down and carried away; and when it ought to give wings to the flesh, lift it up and lead it to heaven, it is instead dragged down along with that heaviest burden of diseases. When the charioteer or the helmsman is like this, what hope of safety is there? As when he says, If the light in you is darkness, how great is the darkness! When the helmsman is drunk and imitates the disorder of the waves and winds, how will the ship be saved? 6. What, then, can make the soul light? An admirable life: gaping after nothing here, and not tying to one's feet things that sink and drag down. For some bodies naturally move downward, such as stones, wood and everything of that kind, and others upward, such as fire, air and light feathers. If, then, you tie something that sinks to something light, the feathers and the air are of no use, since the weight upsets the balance, overpowers and prevails. So too if someone has feet weighed down, whether by an evil humour flowing into them or by some other disease, it does him no good that the rest of his body is light. If this is so with bodies, much more is it so with the heart. Let us not make it heavy, then, lest, like ships carrying much sand, it be sunk. For this lies in our power: the heart is not such by nature, but [?] Jacob [?] others, those in Mesopotamia.

Do you see that the whole world was being taught by the saints, if only people had been willing? Even before these, the flood and the confusion of tongues were enough to rouse their minds. So that the event would not be forgotten over time, the place takes its name from it: it is called Babylon because of the confusion of tongues. In this way the hearer, guided by the name, may go back to the origin of what happened and learn the power of God. So too all who lived in the West learned everything through their dealings with the Egyptians in trade. Besides, at the beginning, in the earliest times, there were not many nations in that part of the world; the great mass of the human population was gathered in the regions of the East. Adam came out from there, the descendants of Noah lived there, and after the tower they were there and lived for the most part in the East. Yet in every generation God appointed teachers for them: Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Melchizedek. That is why this prophet also leads those who live in wickedness back by means of what happened to the saints, saying: "Know that the Lord has made his holy one wonderful." What does "made wonderful" mean? He made the one devoted to him wonderful, distinguished, brilliant, renowned. So learn the power of the Master from the servant and from what happened to him. He did not say only "He has given good things," but "He has made wonderful," showing that he gave with great wonder and with many marvels. So it was with Abraham. Not only did God give him back his wife untouched, he also made him wonderful, so that the gift to him lay not only in suffering no harm but also in becoming illustrious in Egypt. The first, his suffering nothing unpleasant, happened because of his righteousness; the second, his returning from there with marvels, happened for the benefit of the Egyptians. This happened with the three young men, this happened with the lions, this happened with the sea monster and Jonah. Everywhere he saves with wonder, not everyone indiscriminately, but the holy one. 7. Do you see how, along with the knowledge of God, he also introduces [?] an exhortation to a strict life, teaching us to place our hopes of salvation not only in God's goodness but also in our own virtue? "The Lord will hear me when I cry to him." Having said that he "made wonderful," he does not stop there but speaks of another kind of blessing. What is it? Having God always as ally and helper, standing by us everywhere. He does this not once, or twice, or three times, he says, but always, if we call on him. And notice the speed here again. Just as he said above, "When I called, the God of my righteousness heard me," so here too: "When I cry to

How is it, then, that many are not heard? Because they ask for things that do no good. Here not being heard is better than being heard. So even if we are heard, let us not rejoice for that reason; and when we are not heard, let us give glory for that too. Either we ask for things that do no good and are not heard, and we gain by not receiving them [?] [Reg.: and an exhortation to a life of providence [?], a hindrance to strictness [?]...] Paul said.

[?] being angry without cause. For it is also possible to be angry justly: Paul was angry with Elymas, and Peter with Sapphira. But I would not call this simply anger; I would call it wisdom, care and wise management. A father too is angry with his son, but out of care for him. The one who is angry without cause is the one who avenges himself. The one who corrects other people's faults is the gentlest of all. When God is said to be angry, he is not angry to defend himself but to correct us. So let us imitate him too. To proceed in this way is divine; to proceed otherwise is human. Yet God differs from us not only in being angry justly [?], but also in that anger is not a passion in God at all. So let us not be angry without cause either. Anger was implanted in us for this reason: not so that we might sin, but so that we might stop others from sinning; not so that it might become a passion and a disease, but a remedy for the passions. 8. Consider, then, the height of wickedness, when the remedy becomes a poison, when the very thing with which we ought to heal other people's wounds is what we use to inflict wounds. It is as if someone took a knife to cut away other people's rotting flesh and then slashed himself for no reason, making sores all over his body; or as if a helmsman sank the ship with the very rudder by which he ought to break the force of the unruly winds. Anger is something like this. It is a useful tool for waking us from our drowsiness, putting vigor into the soul, making us more vehement in our indignation on behalf of those who are wronged, and making us avengers against those who plot evil. That is why he says, "Be angry, and do not sin." If this were not possible, he would not have commanded it, for no one commands what is impossible. So, introducing an apostolic law and the wisdom of the Gospel, and saying the same things Christ said, he adds a further exhortation: "What you say in your hearts, be pierced with remorse for it on your beds." What does this mean? It seems obscure. At the time after supper, he says, when you go off to sleep, when you are about to lie down and no one is with you, when there is deep quiet and profound calm and nothing disturbs you, then convene the court of your conscience and demand an account from it. Whatever wicked things you planned during the day, whether weaving deceits, or tripping up your neighbor, or entertaining corrupt desires, bring all of it out into the open in that time of quiet. Set your conscience over these wicked thoughts, rake them over, demand satisfaction, put the sinful mind on the rack. That is what "be pierced with remorse" means. It stands for: "Prick and sting the things you said in your hearts during the day." In other words, the wicked plans you devised, punish them on your beds in that time of quiet and exact the penalty for them. When no friend disturbs you, no servant provokes you, no crowd of business presses on you, then give an account of how you have lived during the day. And why did he not speak of words and deeds, but of wicked thoughts? He is teaching us all the more by this. If we must punish wicked plans so that they do not turn into action, how much more must we chasten the soul for deeds and words. Let this be done every day, and do not fall asleep, O man, until you have [?] [?].

9. For this reason the Prophet, having led them away from wickedness through remorse, made them better suited to the practice of virtue and softened the hardness of the mind, making it tender [?]. He brings in a word [?] and says: "Offer a sacrifice of righteousness, and hope in the Lord." What does "Offer a sacrifice of righteousness" mean? Pursue righteousness, offer righteousness. This is the greatest gift to God, this is an acceptable sacrifice, this is an offering that pleases him greatly: not sacrificing sheep and calves, but doing what is just. Do you see the way of life of the Church sketched out long beforehand, and spiritual things required in place of those material ones? By righteousness here, as I said before, he does not mean a particular virtue but virtue as a whole, just as we call a man righteous who has all virtue in himself. This sacrifice needs no money, no knife, no altar, no fire. It does not dissolve into smoke and ash and the smell of burnt fat; the intention of the one who offers it is enough. Poverty is no hindrance to it, destitution no obstacle, nor place, nor anything else of the kind. Wherever you are, you will be able to offer it, becoming yourself priest, altar, knife and victim. Such are the things of the mind and the spirit: they are much easier, since they need no external labor. "And hope in the Lord." Another translator says: "And trust in the Lord." For the one who has made God gracious and kindly toward him through a righteous way of life has the greatest alliance, an invincible help, and great support from that quarter. Do you see the fruit of the sacrifice right at the door? Do you see the treasure of good things springing up at once? For whom will the one who has God as his ally fear from then on? No one. And this is no small virtue: to take courage in him and trust in him. Along with righteousness he also requires this virtue of us: to trust in him, to hope in him, to rely on nothing in this life, but to withdraw from everything and fix our minds there. For the affairs of this present life are like dreams and shadows, and even feebler than these. They appear and fly away at the same moment, and even while they are present they bring a great deal of trouble on those who have them. But hope in God is immortal, unchanging, immovable. It admits no alteration, it sets us in complete security, and it makes invincible the one who uses it carefully and with the right disposition. "Many say, Who will show us good things? The light of your face has been stamped upon us, O Lord." Having completed his exhortation about conduct, having led them to the knowledge of God, having tried every means that could rouse the minds of those who had gone astray, and having shown God's care above all through those devoted to him and through his providence toward them, he sets down an objection raised by the weaker and coarser sort and says: "Many say, Who will show us good things?" It is not the few, the genuine and approved who know how to live wisely, who say this, but the scattered crowd, the undiscerning, the [?] [Reg.: ...by your goodness you have given us wings.]

showing that gladness does not lie in external things: not in slaves, nor in gold and silver, nor in clothes, nor in a crowded table, nor in great power, nor in the size of a house. That kind of gladness belongs not to the heart but only to the eyes. At any rate, many of those who possess these things think life is not worth living and carry a furnace of despondency in their souls, swamped by the mass of their worries and crushed by constant fears. "But my gladness," he says, "does not lie in these things, but in the spiritual heart, in the bodiless mind that pictures bodiless things." So if present things gladden you and you learn God's providence from them, learn it much more from the things to come, since those are better, more lasting, and cannot be taken away. If being rich and prosperous persuades you that God's providence exists, much more should being rich in heaven lead you to that conviction. And if you say, "Why are these things stored up in hope, and why are they unseen?" I would answer that we believers consider the things we hope for more evident than these visible things; such is the full assurance of faith. And if you ask again, "Why do we not receive the rewards here?" I would answer that this is the time of the training ground and the contests, and that is the time of the crowns and the prizes. This too was the work of God's care: to allot the toils and the sweat to this short and perishable life, and to extend the prizes and crowns into the immortal and ageless age. Besides, when most people were in a weaker condition, he gave them these material goods as well. Indeed he led the people of the Jews by just such a way of life. Wealth flowed to them, their life stretched into old age, every disease was kept away; the destruction of enemies, deep peace, trophies and victories, good children and many children, and all such things were theirs as long as they obeyed God. But when our Lord Jesus Christ came, calling us to heaven, persuading us to despise the things here, implanting in us the love of those things above and separating us from the affairs of this life, these things were naturally curtailed, and all our wealth lies in those things above, since we have become mature. The same happens with children: while they are still small, fathers give them such things as shoes and clothes, gold ornaments and bracelets; but when they grow up, they take these away and give them other, greater things: distinction on the speaker's platform, eminence in the city, freedom of speech in the royal courts, offices and positions of power, drawing them away from all childish ambition. God has done the same: drawing us away from those small and childish things, he has promised the things of heaven. So do not be dazzled by these things that flow away and pass by, and do not be faint-hearted. He has not left you without a share in these either. Since we are clothed in flesh and bound up with a body, and we could not do without these things, he supplies them to us abundantly as well. For this reason the Prophet too, setting in motion that kind of providence [?] [Reg.: you want God's providence to be. Reg.: and why these things are stored up for all, where (?). Reg.: of your body. Reg.: to accept him even as an adulterer and corrupter of boys.]

[?] if you run to allegories, I will ask you this: what is Zeus? "The boiling substance," they say, "the region above the air, which they call ether, from boiling and burning." In that case Zeus is not a rational and discerning substance but an irrational one. That the nature of the air has neither reason nor reasoning is plain to everyone; everyone knows it, even someone more senseless than stones. So Zeus has been done away with for now, and his substance has vanished. For if Zeus is air, and the air [?] [?] the myth will [?]. And if he is air, he did not become anyone's father, nor did he beget any substance [?] [?] the sun, which they also call Apollo and say is his son. For the sun has no reasoning, nor understanding and mind [?] a work driven and carried around by the living being [?] [?] the beginning for him [?] [?] of the ether, but of the clouds [?] water, or from the sea [?] [?] the heaven [?], as the prophets said. And if you do not believe the prophets, we offer clear and evident signs, which show most of all [?] [?] foretold to us [?] said by them. [?] more harshly, and it usually does more damage. This holds for everything. A worm bred inside wood destroys it more, and diseases that spring up within ruin the body's strength and health more than those that grow on the outside. Cities too are brought down not so much by wars from outside as by civil wars. So too the soul is ruined not so much by schemes that come at it from outside as by the diseases bred within it. But if someone who has the fear of God carefully strangles those many-colored beasts of wicked thoughts and does not let them make their dens in him, he will enjoy a pure, heavenly and most profound peace. This is the peace that Christ came and bestowed. This is the peace Paul prayed for the faithful to have, saying in every letter: "Grace to you and peace from God our Father." For the one who has this peace fears not only barbarians and enemies, but not even the devil himself; rather, [he is above] the whole [?] of demons. [?] and the outcome has become plain to all [?]; and the things concerning Christ [?] [?] both Scriptures being divine. And if Scripture is divine, then everything said in it about God is true. So do not doubt God's providence. Instead, marvel at his care, that although there are both wicked and good people, he has given the world and the sun to all, and he sends the rains. If he lets some live in poverty and need, he does so to correct their souls, making their minds wiser. You know, you know well, that wealth serves wickedness in those who are not careful, while poverty is the mother of wisdom. Events prove this every day. How many of the poor are more sensible and wiser than the rich, and healthier in body too, because poverty sets right both their flesh and their soul? "In peace I will lie down together and sleep, for you alone, O Lord, have made me dwell in hope." Here is another kind of providence, and no small one: those devoted to God enjoy peace. "Great peace have those who love your law, and nothing makes them stumble." Nothing creates peace like the knowledge of God and the acquisition of virtue. It drives out the war of the passions within and does not let a person be at strife with himself. So if someone does not enjoy this peace, even if there is the deepest peace outside, even if no enemy strikes at him, he is more wretched than all who are warred upon by the whole world. [Reg.: and the sight to all.]

suffering no such unpleasantness. That is why the Prophet, enjoying this providence, said: "In peace I will lie down together and sleep." He shows that for the one who does not have this peace, not even the harbor common to all, the harbor of sleep and night, lies open; it too is silted up. These passions destroy even the respite that nature gives, thrusting aside the tyranny of sleep altogether with another, harsher tyranny. The envious, the spiteful, the greedy and the rapacious carry this war around with them everywhere and have the enemy lying in wait inside them. Wherever they go they cannot escape the battle. Even if they stay at home, even if they lie on their beds, they endure clouds of arrows, uproars more violent than the waves, slaughter, shouts, wailing, and other things far worse than what happens in war. But the righteous man is not like this. Even when awake he lives in delight, and at night he welcomes sleep with great pleasure. What does "together" mean? "Gathered into myself," he says, "collected, not split among countless worries, not anxious about the affairs of this man or that, not cut up into pieces by cares about the whole world, but thinking about my own affairs, the things that concern me, and what is most fitting for a human being." "For you alone, O Lord, have made me dwell in hope." What he means is something like this: "By the hope of things to come and by my expectation in you, I have calmed all my passions." As Paul too says: "For our momentary light affliction is producing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure, as we look not at the things that are seen but at the things that are unseen." There is nothing burdensome that does not become very easy through the hope of winning approval with God. That is why he says, "You have made me dwell in hope." And "alone" also contains no small value as teaching. 13. What does "alone" mean? Apart from the wicked. "I have achieved this peace with you," he says, "and I live alone, fleeing the corrupt." And with good reason. Just as bodies often perish from the contagion of corrupted air, so the soul has often been harmed by the company of the wicked. And just as a healthy eye is affected when it sees a diseased one, and someone covered with scabies passes it on to the healthy, so it often happens with the company of wicked people. That is why Christ urged us not only to flee such people but even to cut them off, saying: "If your right eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and throw it away from you." He was not speaking about the eye, for what harm could an eye do when the mind is healthy? He laid down this law about close friends who are like these members of ours and who harm us, commanding us to disregard the friendship of such people so as to make our own salvation more secure. That is why he himself says again further on: "I have not sat with a council of vanity, and I will not go in with lawbreakers." Jeremiah too calls blessed the one who sits alone and bears the yoke from his youth. And Proverbs, at length, on behalf of [?] [Colb.: a harbor that lies open to all.]

…and falls to us; and then the time at which it is given. And it is surely absurd that when a will concerning money is announced to you, as if the inheritance belonged to us, we take great pains and fuss over it, hunt out the documents, pay out money, go to the papers, copy what is written in them, and show every kind of eagerness; but here, when spiritual testaments are set out for all to see and all the books lie open, we are careless and lie back at our ease, and this when the inheritance is not one of the things of sense. Let us approach, then, and open the documents, and pore over what is written in them, and see on what terms this inheritance has been left to us, and what kind of inheritance it is. For he did not leave us the inheritance unconditionally, but on a certain condition. What condition is that? "He who loves me," he says, "will keep my commandments." And again: "Whoever does not take up his cross and follow after me"; and many other things that are written in the Testament. Let us learn also the time at which we are to receive these things. It is not the present time but the time to come; or rather, both the present and the time to come. For "Seek the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you"; but the whole of it is given then. Since the present life is perishable and we are still in a rather imperfect state, God does what the lawgivers outside do, who hand over the father's estate to those who have come of age. When we attain to the perfect man and the measure of stature, and pass over to the undefiled life, then he puts that inheritance into our hands. Meanwhile he has made his testament and left us the documents, and has told us what we must do to obtain the inheritance, so that we may not lose it or be disinherited. If it troubles anyone that we are not yet perfect, and he is suspicious of what has been said, let such people hear Paul saying: "When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I thought as a child, I reasoned as a child; but when I became a man, I put away the things of the child." Here he is speaking of the present age and the age to come. And again: "Until we all attain to the perfect man, to the measure of stature." For in the present life, he means, we are brought up by this creation as by a nurse; but when we are about to be led into the Master's house, we strip off the garments of corruption, put on incorruption, and pass over to another lot. This testament has also threatened to disinherit many, if they prove unworthy of the conditions written in it. But let us see, then, what the inheritance is. "What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man." How then could we have received the use of these things in the present life, when even the knowledge of them surpasses our understanding? That is why it has been stored up for us there. And see how great his care is. He allotted the labors to the present life, so that with the shortness of the time [?] … the documents. [?] Reg. reads ἀποκληρονόμους ("disinherited"), with the same sense.

[?] Exposition … he called her bride, but because he wants all to be one body and one soul in virtue and in love; and because, just as the bride does everything to please her husband, so we too must be like this throughout our whole life. As the bride on that day sits in the bridal chamber, anxious about one thing only, how she may please the bridegroom, so let us too, seated as we are in this life, look to one thing, the bridegroom's pleasure, and keep the bride's good order. [51] David too speaks of this bride, saying: "The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in raiment woven with gold, adorned with golden fringes." Do you want to see her sandals as well? Hear Paul, who escorts the bride, saying: "Having shod your feet with the readiness of the gospel of peace." Do you want to see her girdle too, and how it is made of truth? The same will teach you: "Having girded your loins with truth." Do you want to see her beauty? You will learn this too from him: "Having no spot or wrinkle." Hear also what the Ecclesiast says about her: "You are all fair, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you." Do you want to see her feet too? "How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news of peace, who bring good news of good things!" And what is marvelous and full of astonishment is this: having adorned her in this way, he did not come displaying his glory, lest he stun her with the excess of his beauty and drive her out of her mind. Instead he comes clothed in a garment, as the bride is; for he shares in blood and flesh just as she does. And he does not call her up above; he himself comes to her, keeping here too the bridegroom's law, which leads him to the bride. Moses said this too: "For this reason a man shall leave his father and his mother and cleave to his wife." And Paul: "This mystery is great; but I speak with reference to Christ and the Church." So he came to her lodging, and finding her filthy, unkempt, naked, smeared with blood, he washed her, anointed her, fed her, and clothed her in a garment whose like is not to be found. He himself became her covering, and taking her, he leads her up in this way. For her the inheritance has been prepared. What then does the Prophet say on her behalf? Much; for he is her advocate, and he foretold and proclaimed in advance most of what would happen to her: about the bridegroom, about the bridal procession, about the good things that would come to her. For this reason here too he speaks on her behalf, and at the outset, like these advocates, the orators in the law courts, he states on whose behalf he is pleading: "For her who inherits." And let us hear what she who inherits asks. "Give ear to my words, O Lord." She calls the bridegroom Lord; for this is what a grateful bride does. For if among those of the same nature it happens that the wife calls her husband lord, much more is this so with the Church and Christ, where he is Lord by nature. So she calls him Lord not only as bridegroom but also as Master, and draws him to hear her petition. For since an inheritance [?] … [Note:] "Let us look to the bridegroom's virtue, and the": so Reg., Coisl. and Savile; Morel and Montfaucon read "let us look … of the bridegroom." [?] Reg. reads "let us array."

…but from the very beginning of the day he offered the first fruits to God. For, it says, "One must rise before the sun to give you thanks, and meet with you before the dawn of light." In the presence of a king you would not put up with someone of lower rank getting in ahead of you to do him homage; yet now, while the sun is worshiping, you sleep, and yield precedence to the creation, and you do not rise before [55] the whole creation that was made for your sake, nor render thanks to him. Instead, when you get up you wash your face and hands, but leave your soul unclean? Do you not know that just as the body is cleansed by water, so the soul is cleansed by prayer? Wash your soul, then, before your body. Many specks of vice cling to it; let us put them off through prayer. For if we fortify our mouth in this way, we shall lay a good foundation for the day's work. "In the morning I will stand before you, and I will look." I will stand before you, he means, not in place but in deeds. For such a one can come near to God. Nearness and distance come about in this way, since God is everywhere. "I will stand before you and I will look, for you are not a God who wills lawlessness." Another translator says: "And I will consider that you are not a God who wills lawlessness." "Nor shall the evildoer dwell beside you." Here he hints at the idols, because they delighted in these, and in every kind of lawlessness, and in the other works of wickedness. "Nor shall the evildoer dwell beside you." He will not be your friend, he means, he will not be near you. "Nor shall the lawless remain before your eyes." Here he shows God's hatred of evil, teaching those who come near him to make themselves like this, since there is no other way to come near. For if no one could come near a good man while differing from him in character, much more is this true of God. That the wicked cannot come near virtuous men, hear what they say about the righteous man: "He is grievous to us even to look at." So too John, while living in prison and not even being seen, grieved Herodias, although the woman was so far removed from him; and after his death he shook the conscience of the tyrant of that day as well. Let no one, then, who lives in virtue think he is suffering anything terrible, even if he is plotted against by the wicked. For those who suffer harm are the ones who do it. "You have hated all who work lawlessness; you will destroy all who speak falsehood. The Lord abhors a man of blood and deceit." These things are said not that we may merely hear them, but that by hearing them continually we may be trained both to conform ourselves to the bridegroom's ways and to come near him. If this does not happen, we are deprived of help from above, and nothing could be worse than that. 4. "You have hated all who work lawlessness": whether he is a slave, he means, or free, or a king, or anyone at all. For God is accustomed to choose his friends not by rank but by virtue. But since many of the duller sort think hatred is nothing, hear how he added the fear of punishment as well, saying: "You will destroy all who speak falsehood," shifting the discourse to the grosser sins. For not as far as [?] … [Note:] … "and you yield to the precedence of the creation." [?] Reg. reads "and let us learn."

…[?] to be saved he brought in; he turned her away from vice, guided her by the hand toward virtue, and held out good hopes even to those who live in wickedness, if they are willing to change, as people who can obtain mercy. Then he turns the discourse at last to petition, saying: "Lord, lead me in your righteousness." By this he teaches the hearer first to offer hymns to God and give thanks for the benefits he has received, then to ask for whatever he wishes, and then again to give thanks for whatever he receives. But let us see what it is she asks for. Something worldly? Something perishable? Something of the things that slip away? Is she speaking about wealth? About glory? About power? About vengeance on enemies? None of these. What then? "Lord, lead me in your righteousness because of my enemies." Do you see how she asks for nothing perishable, and how she needs alliance from above? For those who travel this road need that help most of all. By righteousness here he means virtue in general. And he did well to say "in your righteousness." For there is also a righteousness of men, which comes from the laws outside; but it is a paltry thing, lacking what is perfect and complete, and put together out of human reasonings. "But I ask for your righteousness, which has been brought down from you and leads by the hand to heaven, and for your alliance, so that I may draw this righteousness to myself." 5. And he did well also to say "Lead." For the present life is a road, and needs guidance from above. If, when we are about to enter a city, we need someone to show us the way, much more, when we are about to journey to heaven, do we need help from above, to show us, to steady us, and to guide us by the hand; for there are many paths that turn aside. That is why we should cling to God's right hand. "Because of my enemies." Many enemies have risen up, he says, wanting to turn my steps aside, to lead me astray, and to bring me onto another road. Since, then, such are the plots and such the assaults, lead me yourself. For I need alliance from you. Being led is his doing; but being worthy to be held by that hand must be the fruit of our own effort. For if you are unclean, that hand does not hold you; nor if you are greedy, or have some other stain. "Make my way straight before you"; that is, make it plain to me, clear, known; cut it straight for me. Another translator said: "Make your way level before me"; that is, make it easy and smooth. "For there is no truth in their mouth; their heart is vain." It seems to me that he says this both about those who live in error, censuring their mouth, [56] and their mind as empty of all good, and about those who live in wickedness. "Their throat is an open grave." Here he means either their murderousness, or their offering of dead and foul-smelling doctrines. Nor would one be wrong to call the mouths of those who utter shameful words an open grave as well. For much [?] … [Note:] Reg. [?] "to draw the guard." And [?]. Reg. reads προφέρειν ("to bring forth"); others read προσφέρειν ("to offer"). Patrol. Gr. LV.

…"Rejoice and rejoice with me." With those who take delight in this way God dwells. That is why he says: "They shall exult forever, and you shall dwell among them." Christ too was showing this very thing, and pointing to the indestructibility of that joy, when he said: "I will see you again, and no one takes your joy from you." And Paul again: "Rejoice always, pray without ceasing." "And those who love your name shall boast in you." For in these things alone above all is it right to boast, in these to rejoice, in these to be glad; since one who prides himself on worldly things is no different from people feasting in a dream. 6. For tell me, what is there among human things that can give grounds for boasting? Bodily strength? But that achievement does not come from free choice, and so it gives no ground for boasting. Besides, it withers and fails quickly, and often it has harmed its possessor when he did not use it as he should. The same can be said of youthful bloom and good looks, of wealth, of power, of luxury, and of all worldly things. But to boast in God and in love for him is an adornment greater than all, and a splendor surpassing countless diadems, even if the one who boasts is a prisoner. This adornment is not cut short by disease, by old age, by adverse circumstances, by the changes of the times, not even by death itself; rather, even then it shines out more brightly. "For you will bless the righteous." Since many who are so disposed are reviled and mocked by men, and especially those who pursue virtue, he wants none of the duller sort to fall away because of this; so see how he lifts up their minds by saying: "For you have blessed the righteous." For what harm is there if men, even the whole inhabited world, despise us, when the Master of the angels praises and proclaims us? Just as, if he does not bless us, there is no profit even if all who dwell on land and sea praise us. So let us look to this everywhere, that he may proclaim us, that he may crown us. If this is so, we are higher than all, [38] even if we are in poverty, even in sickness, even in the worst of misfortunes. For blessed Job too, though he sat on the dung heap, ulcerated with the pus of his wounds, teeming with countless springs of worms, suffering those incurable afflictions, spat upon by his servants, plotted against by friends and enemies and his wife, and brought down to poverty and hunger and that incurable sickness, was the most blessed of all. How so? Because God blessed him, saying: "A man blameless, righteous, true, God-fearing, keeping himself from every evil thing." "Lord, you have crowned us as with a shield of good pleasure." Again he has ended in thanksgiving, offering hymns of thanks to God. What is a "shield of good pleasure"? The best shield, a shield in keeping with God's will, a most beautiful shield. What he means is this [?] … [Note:] Symmachus [?] … "This is not so clear" [?] … [?] to God. These are grievous darts against the devil, this is a mortal blow against the demon; then above all [?] shine…

…the crowns are bright. For in the case of blessed Job too (nothing prevents us from taking refuge in him again), this above all made him illustrious, this proclaimed his name, this crowned him: that in the time of trial, sickness and poverty his resolve was seen to be unswerving and his mind unshaken, and that he offered words of thanksgiving to God, that spiritual sacrifice. For his words were a sacrifice, the words he spoke: "The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it seemed good to the Lord, so it has come to pass; blessed be the name of the Lord forever." Let us too always do the same: in trials, in hardships, in the face of plots, glorifying God and blessing him continually; for to him be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

ON PSALM 6

"Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor chasten me in your wrath."

1. When you hear of anger and wrath in God, do not suspect anything human; for these words are spoken out of condescension. The Divine is free of all such things. He speaks this way in order to reach the minds of the duller sort. We too, when we speak with barbarians, use their language; and when we talk to a child, we lisp along with it, and however wise we may be, we come down to its lowly level. And what wonder if we do this in words, when we do it even in deeds, biting our hands and pretending to be angry, in order to correct the child? So God too, wishing to reach the duller sort, uses words of this kind. [39] For he was not concerned to speak in a manner befitting his own dignity, but for the benefit of his hearers. Elsewhere, showing that he is free of anger, he said: "Is it me they provoke, and not themselves?" How would you have had him speak to the Jews? Saying that he is not angry, and does not hate the wicked, since hatred is a passion? Nor that he looks upon human affairs, since seeing is a notion taken from bodies? Nor that he hears, since this too comes from the flesh? But from this another evil doctrine would have been brought in, that all things are without providence; and many people of that time, shrinking from hearing such things about God, would not even have known that God exists at all. And had this been unknown, all would have been lost; whereas once that other doctrine was brought in, correction would soon follow. For one who is persuaded that God exists, even if he does not have a worthy conception of him but imagines something grosser, will in time be persuaded that there is nothing of that kind in God. But one who is persuaded that God exercises no providence, does not care about what exists, and does not even exist, what will he gain from the doctrine of impassibility? For this reason he first spoke to them in that way, and once he had implanted in them the belief that he exists, he purifies them again little by little, leading them up to this doctrine, saying loftier things about himself and introducing the teaching of his impassibility. For another prophet says: "Not [?] …" [Note:] Reg. and Savile read ἐσπούδακεν ("he has been concerned"). … For those in the New [Testament] also sin; … [?]

…both pay the same penalty, but these pay a harsher one. Paul made this clear when he said: "Anyone who has set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses. How much worse a punishment, do you think, will he deserve who has trampled the Son of God underfoot and regarded the blood of the covenant as common?" When he says, "How much worse a punishment, do you think, will he deserve," he shows that the punishment is heightened. Those before the law sinned, and so did those under the law. Here again the former pay a milder penalty. He made this clear when he said: "For all who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law." "Without the law" means not more harshly but more mildly. "And all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law." Why is that? Because the former have nature as their accuser, while the latter have the law as well as nature; and the more teaching they have enjoyed, the greater the punishment they will undergo. Again, one can see the same thing happening with rank, and it is clear from the sacrifice. When the whole people sinned, as great a sacrifice was offered for them as for the priest alone [?]. Scripture shows that the greater the rank, the harsher the punishment for the sins people commit. This is why a woman who simply committed fornication was put to death, but the priest's daughter was burned. From another angle too one can see pardon and heightened punishment at work: for example, when one person who has sinned pays the penalty here, while another enjoys a life of luxury. The latter will undergo a greater punishment there, and the former a lesser one, unless he has discharged it all here. Christ makes this clear when he brings in Abraham saying to the rich man: "You received your good things, and he his bad things; and now he is comforted here, and you are in anguish." But Lazarus laid aside his punishment completely because of the evils he suffered; others lay it aside not completely but in part, and so they are punished more mildly. One can also see a difference of punishment that arises from greater understanding and from simplicity, when he says: "The servant who knew his master's will and did not do it will receive many blows; but the one who did not know, and did not do it, will receive few." And one could find many other things that make for a difference in punishment, and a difference in mercy and kindness. Consider the first-formed man as well. Eve sinned, Adam sinned too, and the sin was one, for both ate from the tree; yet they did not both pay the same penalty. Cain killed, and Lamech killed; and one was shown mercy while the other was punished. A man gathered wood on the Sabbath and received no pardon; David committed murder and adultery, and enjoyed kindness. So let us spend some time on this question, for it is far better to investigate these things than to be glued to the idle talk and gatherings in the marketplaces. Not only finding the answers to such questions but even seeking them is a great gain, even if we do not find them. For we will be compelled to occupy ourselves with them and to spend all our time on them. Why then (for we must go back to our earlier discussion), when all the Jews made the calf, were some punished and others not… [Coisl.: "pay the punishment." Morel.: "and enjoyed salvation."]

…this; but if you stay with the physician, the wound will certainly be healed. For this is not a human art, which might be at a loss, but a divine power, which prevails over natures and diseases, over wickedness and every [44] vice. That is why David too came to God as to a physician and lamented, saying: "Heal me, Lord, for my bones are troubled." Some say that here he means the trouble that comes from sin. When violent winds fall on the open sea, they stir everything up: the sand from the depths is carried to the surface, and those sailing are in danger. In the same way the soul in us is troubled, the body is shaken, everything is filled with the storm, and from then on our vessel is full of turmoil. There is deep darkness, everything leaves its proper place and is swept away, and the confusion is great. This tends to happen above all with the desires of lust, but also with anger and with misfortunes. All these trouble both soul and bones; the pupils of the eyes are distorted, and the eyes do not even see properly. Just as horses run wild when the charioteer is thrown into confusion, so when reason is thrown into turmoil everything is confused, everything is distorted and loses its proper path. It is also necessary to say how this trouble arises. It does not come about in the soul as it does at sea, through the onslaught of winds, by some unexpected circumstance; it comes about through our own negligence. For we are the cause both of its happening and of its not happening. What I mean is this: when desire is aroused, the furnace does not burn unless you kindle the flame, unless you supply fuel to the material. The furnace is not lit unless you pry curiously into beautiful faces, unless you busy yourself with other kinds of beauty, unless you go up to the theaters of lawlessness. If you do not fatten the flesh with luxury, if you do not drown your reason in wine, the flame does not rise, the furnace is not lit, the beast does not grow fiercer, and the purity of the mind is not torn apart as if by savage winds. "Are these things enough, then," someone says, "to escape the flame of sin?" These things alone are not enough; others must be added as well: constant prayers, the company of holy people, moderate fasting, a simple diet, necessary occupations, and before everything else the fear of God, the coming judgment, the unbearable punishments, and the promises of good things. Through all of these you can bridle raging desire and calm the surging sea. "And you, Lord, how long? Turn, Lord, rescue my soul; save me for the sake of your mercy." He keeps putting in "Lord," as though putting forward a claim to pardon and grace. For this is our greatest hope: his unspeakable love for humankind, and the fact that he is so ready to pardon. And "How long?" is not the cry of someone who is resentful or indignant, but of someone in pain and anguish who cannot bear the weight of his trials. [Reg.: "we are masters"; "when desire is kindled; but if you do not [kindle] the flame [?] … do not supply fuel to the material … not the beauty of others"; Colb. [?]: "we are masters … it does not rise."]

…4. "…you have received your consolation." [46] Let those who have silver beds hear what the king's bed was like: not set with precious stones, not sprinkled with gold, but washed with tears. His nights were not nights of rest but of laments and wailing. Because many cares distracted him during the day, he made the time that everyone else uses for relaxation a time of confession, lamenting all the more fervently then. Weeping is always good, but especially at night, when no one interrupts this wonderful pleasure and anyone who wishes can take his fill of it in complete freedom. Those who have experienced what I am talking about know how much joy these fountains of tears hold. These tears can quench the unquenchable fire, that river which flows before the judgment seat. That is why Paul too wept night and day for three years, setting right the passions of others. We, though, do not weep even over our own; instead we give ourselves up to laughter and luxury and bury ourselves at night in deep stupor. Some are fastened to a sleep that resembles death, while others keep a vigil harsher than death, reckoning up at that hour interest and loans and their schemes against other people. Not so the sober; they cultivate their own souls, using these tears like rain and making the seeds of virtue grow. A bed that receives such tears is closed to every vice and every lust. Whoever sheds such tears considers the things of earth as nothing; he frees his soul from every siege and makes his mind brighter than the sun. And do not think that I am saying this only to monks. The exhortation is also for people living in the world, and for them even more than for the monks, since they are the ones who most need the medicines of repentance. Whoever laments like this will rise with his soul in a better state than a calm harbor, having driven out all the passions. Filled with great joy, such a person will go to the house of God with confidence and will talk with his neighbor with pleasure. For no anger lurks within him, no desire inflames him, no love of money, no envy, nothing else of the kind. That groaning in the night and those tears have made all these things, which lurk in their dens like wild beasts, slink away. "My eye is troubled by wrath." Do you see a crushed soul? Having spoken of repentance, he speaks again of the sufferings: the turmoil in the mind and the fear that arises from God's anger. 5. By "eye" he here means the eye of the soul, that faculty of discernment and reason which the thought of one's own sins tends to trouble. Since he always kept his offenses before his eyes and reflected on God's anger, he lived in fear; he did not live without feeling, as most people do, but in anguish and trembling. Such trouble is the [47] mother of calm; such fear is the foundation of security. Whoever is troubled in this way drives out every storm; whoever does not have such a soul will undergo a severe tempest. Just as an unballasted ship given over to the force of savage winds quickly sinks, so too a soul that lives without feeling, by countless… [Reg.: "distracted." Reg.: "Whoever groans over such things."]

…"the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping." He did not simply say, "He has heard my voice," but "the voice of my weeping." Do you see how generously he presents his own part as well, both the voice and the weeping? By "voice" he means here not the loudness of the cry but the disposition of the mind, and by "weeping" not only the weeping of the eyes but also that of the soul. For whoever offers repentance and is heard by God can easily achieve this good thing too: driving off the company of the wicked. "Let all my enemies be ashamed and troubled; let them be turned back and be put to shame very swiftly." This prayer brings the greatest benefit, namely their being ashamed and turning back. For those who are running a wicked course, if they are put to shame and turn back, will stop in their wickedness. When we see a man rushing toward a precipice, we check him from going any further, saying, "Man, where are you rushing to? There is a cliff ahead of you"; in the same way David asks that the wicked run back again. So too with a maddened horse: unless someone pulls it back quickly, it will soon perish. So too physicians, when the venom of some serpent is often spreading through the whole body, stop it from advancing any further with great speed, cutting off its harm. Let us do the same, and check the evil within us with great speed, so that it does not advance and make the disease worse. For when neglected, the wounds of sin grow larger; the disease and sickness do not stop at wounds but even give birth to the deathless death. In the same way, if we remove even the small things from the beginning, the great ones will not follow. Consider this: whoever has practiced not insulting others will not know how to fight either; whoever does not know how to fight will also succeed in loving; whoever has succeeded in loving will have no enemy; and whoever has no enemy but shows love will achieve all virtue. So let us not neglect the first steps, so that evils do not grow larger. If Judas had curbed his love of money, he would not have come to sacrilege; if he had checked that, he would not have leapt to the summit of evils. That is why Christ restrains not only fornication and adultery but even the licentious look, pulling the root up from below, so that it is easier to overcome wickedness. He did this with the Jews too, more crudely and as if in riddles, since he was speaking to people of a more fleshly mind; but he did it all the same. [49] How, and in what way? He did not permit any mating among cattle of different kinds, he did not permit eating the blood of animals, he did not permit keeping pledges after evening. By these he restrained great evils: by the first, sodomy; by the second, murders; by the third, cruelty and inhumanity. But now everything is done without restraint and with great shamelessness, and that is why everything has been turned upside down. So when you admit a small passion, do not look at the fact that it is small, but consider that, once it is fed, it gives birth to the greatest evils. When we see a little tow catch fire in a house, we are alarmed and upset, for we do not attend to its beginning… [Reg.: "to occur among seeds," in the same sense, of course. "Of an Ethiopian," he says. [?]]

…he ought to have [revered him] as an old man; and if he disregarded his grey hair, he ought to have been ashamed before him as his benefactor; and if not even that, then as one who had done him no wrong. But the lust for power drove out all this sense of shame and made the man a beast. While that blessed man, who had begotten him and brought him up, wandered through the desert as a vagrant and a fugitive, like an exile in a foreign land, oppressed by the evils that came from this, Absalom revelled in his father's good things. Such was the state of affairs: the armies were ranged on Absalom's side and the cities were under the tyrant. But a certain Hushai, a decent man and a friend of David, stayed true to his friendship with him in this change of fortune. When he suddenly saw David wandering through the desert, he tore his tunic, sprinkled ashes on himself, and wailed bitterly and piteously; and since he could do nothing else, he offered the consolation of his tears. For he was not a friend of the times, nor of power, but of virtue; and so when the kingdom changed hands, he did not change his friendship. When David saw him doing this, he said to him: "This is what a friend does, one who is truly devoted to us; but it will not help us at all. We must make some plan and consider how the terrors that have overtaken us may be ended and how we might find some deliverance from our misfortunes." Having said this, he put forward this plan to him: "Go to my son, put on the mask of a friend, scatter his counsels for me, and make Ahithophel's counsel void." This Ahithophel then held sway over the tyrant. He was skilled in matters of war, and skilled too at leading an army in war and battle; that is why David feared him more than the tyrant himself, so skilled was the man in giving counsel. When Hushai heard this, he obeyed. He had no faint-hearted or cowardly thought, nor did he [51] say: "What if I am caught? What if my mask is uncovered? What if the drama of my pretense is detected? Ahithophel is clever; perhaps he will expose this too and bring it to light, and I shall die for nothing and in vain." Thinking nothing of the kind, he leapt into the tyrant's camp, casting everything on God, and threw himself into the midst of the dangers. I have said this not only so that we may praise him, but so that we may learn both the painful things and all that David suffered, and may bring into the open whatever other benefits can be gained from the story. For here we can find the answer to the question most people keep asking: why the righteous are afflicted while the wicked are at ease. The righteous man was in misfortune, while the abominable parricide, the enemy and foe of nature itself, was prospering in royal courts. Yet Absalom gained nothing from this, and this holy man was not harmed. Instead, the one became liable to greater afflictions, while the other shone more brightly, like gold in a furnace, purer through affliction…

2. Learn this first, then, from this story: not to be troubled in such misfortunes when you see… [One codex: "an exile in a foreign land and punished by the evils that came from this." [?]: "he cried out." Reg.: "terrors, and they might find some way out of their misfortunes, and."]

"Ahithophel," he says, "has never gone wrong." Do you see the man's shrewdness? He does not reject Ahithophel's counsel straight away, but with praise. First he admires him for having given timely advice in times past, and only then does he find fault with the present counsel. What he is saying amounts to this: "I am amazed that he has gone wrong now, for this reasoning does not seem to me to be advantageous. If we attack now, your father will be like a raging bear, full of fury, despairing of his own life, fighting while his anger is at its height. He will take no account of his own safety and will fall on us with great violence. But if we hold back a little, we will attack with more preparation and greater security, and without toil and with complete ease we will catch him as in a net and bring him back." Absalom praised this counsel and said it was more profitable for him. Hushai said this because he wanted to give David time to stop for a while, catch his breath, and gather an army. So, having thrown out Ahithophel's counsel, he sent word [55] through some men in hiding and reported everything to David, including the fact that the tyrant had ratified his own counsel, the one that would bring David victory. And that is exactly what happened. Because Absalom held back a little, David made his preparations, attacked, and set up a trophy of victory. Ahithophel, with his great shrewdness and skill, saw this coming and understood the outcome already from that point: this counsel would be Absalom's ruin. Unable to bear the insult it brought him, he went away, tied a noose, hanged himself, and so ended his life. 3. When David learned all this, he wrote the psalm, offering hymns of thanksgiving to God and attributing the whole stratagem to him. That is why at the beginning he says something like this: "Lord my God, in you I have hoped; save me." Not in Hushai, not in human wisdom, not in his shrewdness, not in my own counsel, but "in you." Let us do this too. Even if some success comes to us through human beings, let us give thanks to God for it, both for the benefits that come to us through ourselves and for those that come through others. If we do this, nothing will be difficult or crooked. This is just what David did, as if he were saying: "I did not rest my hope of safety on Hushai's words, but on your help." And see with what deep feeling he speaks, as he usually does. He did not say, "Lord God," but "Lord my God"; and elsewhere, "O God, my God, I rise early to seek you." For he needed him along with everyone else, but in a special way too, because of the intensity of his longing. God also does this with the righteous: though he is the common God of all, he calls himself in a special way the God of the righteous: "I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." And see his wise disposition. Having said, "Lord my God, in you I have hoped," he did not say, "Punish my foe, destroy my enemy." What then? He asks only for what concerns himself, and says, "Save me," that is, "Do not let me suffer harm from all who persecute me, and rescue me." See how even while suffering harm he does not mention the parricide by name. Even in misfortune he recognizes the bond of nature, even in war he sees his son, and even in dangers he does not forget his own flesh and blood. So loving a father was he, so full of affection; or rather… [One codex: "having been prepared." Patrol. [Gr.] LV. [?]]

[?]…a prayer that can most readily be heard. He showed this in the prayer before this one too: he did not simply ask to be heard, but [?] not even among wild beasts would one see [?] if there is injustice in [?]… but he also brought his own part. And what was that? “Every night I will wash my bed; I will drench my couch with my tears”; and “[?] injustice.” He says these things not to boast, but because he was forced to tell of his own good deeds. [?] “I am weary with my groaning”; “Depart from me, all you who work iniquity”; “My eye is troubled with anger.” 4. All of these are enough to draw God to us: laments, tears, groans, running away from the wicked, and fearing and trembling at his verdict. And elsewhere he said, “The God of my righteousness heard me; in distress you set me free.” For this is how we come to be heard: first, by being worthy to receive; second, by praying according to God’s laws; third, by praying constantly; fourth, by asking for nothing worldly; fifth, by seeking what is good for us; sixth, by contributing everything we can on our own part. You can see many who were heard in this way: Cornelius for his way of life; the Syrophoenician woman for her persistence; Solomon for the way he asked, for God says, “Because you did not ask for wealth, nor for the lives of your enemies”; the tax collector for his humility; and others for other reasons. Just as being heard comes from these things, so not being heard comes from other things, even when those who ask are righteous. For who was more righteous than Paul?
