Yet because he asked for what was not good for him, he was not heard. “Three times,” he says, “I begged the Lord about this, and he said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you.’” And again, who was more righteous than Moses? Yet he was not heard either, for God said, “Let it suffice you.” He asked to enter the land of promise, but that was not good for him, so God did not allow it. Besides these, there is something else that keeps us from being heard: when we pray while persisting in our sins. This is what God said to Jeremiah about the Jews: “Do not pray for this people. Do you not see what they are doing?” They have not turned from their ungodliness, he says, and you offer petitions for them? “I will not hear you.” Again, when we pray against our enemies, not only are we not heard, we even provoke him. Prayer is a medicine, but if we do not know how the medicine should be applied, we do not reap its benefit. Let us see, then, what this man says as he prays: “O Lord my God, if I have done this.” What does “if I have done this” mean? He means: if I have done what I am suffering; if I rose up against a father; if I broke the law in this way. Even here he cannot bring himself to name the one who wronged him; he is ashamed and blushes for his son. It is as when a noble man who sees his wife committing adultery will not bring himself to name the sin in public. So it is with this man: he did not say, “If I rose up against the one who begot me, if I became a parricide,” but, “If I have done this.” And why do I say this, he says [?]. [Note d: Others read “nor its power.”]

[?]…he shows [the punishment] of those who sinned under the law, saying: “Anyone who has set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses. How much worse a punishment, do you think, will he deserve who has trampled underfoot the Son of God and counted the blood of the covenant common?” And again, showing that those who lived before the law deserve a lighter punishment than those who transgressed under the law, he says, “All who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law.” That is, more mildly, since they have nature alone as their accuser and not the law. “And all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law.” That is, more severely, since besides nature they have the law [57] as their accuser as well. “Then may I fall away empty before my enemies. Then let the enemy pursue my soul and overtake it, and trample my life into the ground, and lay my glory in the dust.” Do you see the boldness of a righteous man, and his excellent conscience? If he had not been very sure of himself, he would not have said such things. What he means is this: if I did wrong, if I took revenge, may I suffer this and that. He pronounces the verdict against himself. He does not ask to be judged by due measure, but to pay a penalty far beyond what he deserves, and he makes himself liable to a punishment from which the law exempts him. And see what sort of punishment it is: “May I fall away empty before my enemies. Then let the enemy pursue my soul and overtake it, and trample my life into the ground, and lay my glory in the dust.” That is: may he destroy me without honor and without a name; along with my life, may he ruin my glory too. What does “and lay my glory in the dust” mean? May he humble me, may he trample me; may I become an easy prey for my enemies, he says. What could be more wicked than Absalom? He pursued his father, and such a father, so gentle and reasonable, while he himself was licentious, unbridled and insolent. Well then? Did David repay those who paid him back with evil, or bear a grudge? Not at all. And if you examine the story of Saul, you will see this saying shine out most of all. Saul wronged him after countless benefits, after the trophies and the victories; he plotted against him and wanted to kill him every day. Yet when David had him in his hands, once, twice and many times, asleep, shut in as if in a prison, with no guards, while many urged him to slay and kill him, he spared him and mastered his anger. And he did so knowing that if he let him escape, he would be leaving himself a foe and an implacable enemy. Still, neither the memory of the past, nor fear of the future, nor anything else of the kind drove him to that slaughter. Instead he showed true wisdom: he restrained his hand, bridled his rage, and chose rather to be in danger and plotted against, and even to be driven from his homeland and his freedom, than [to kill] the enemy who without cause and to no purpose [?] him. And he mastered his desire. [Note: a better reading seems to be: ?] …someone is an enemy, or out of vainglory. But if

we rise above these things, we will also rise above being caught by enmity. So if someone insults you, bear it nobly, for he has insulted himself, not you. If he strikes you, do not raise your right hand against him [59], for he is the one who is struck: he strikes you with his hand, but himself with his rage, and earns a bad name with everyone. If this seems hard to you, consider this: if someone in a fit of madness tore your cloak, who would you say was being harmed, you who suffered it or he who did it? Clearly he was. Now, where a cloak is torn, the one who did it has suffered worse than the one who suffered it. Where the heart is torn, and rage does exactly that, will you not think that he has suffered greater harm than you, who have suffered nothing at all? Do not say that he tore your cloak; say rather that he first tore his own heart. Jaundice does not arise unless the bile bursts out and passes its proper bounds, and in the same way rage beyond measure does not arise unless the heart bursts. If you saw someone in the grip of jaundice, you would not choose to bring the disease on yourself, even if he did countless terrible things. So it is with rage. Do not envy or imitate wickedness. Pity the one who does not bridle the beast within him, but harms and ruins himself first. That such people harm themselves you can hear from the many who break up fights of this kind and advise them: “Spare yourself; you are wronging yourself.” For this is what wickedness is like: it harms only the one who gives birth to it, turning everything upside down. So let us not, in wanting to avenge ourselves on others, fall out of the harbor ourselves. If someone who was about to be shipwrecked and go under insulted you while you sat on land, you would not be hurt, nor would you leave the land to share his shipwreck. Reckon it like this, then: the man who insults you and rages at you is sinking as if in a fit of giddiness or a squall; he goes under, having run into the shipwreck of rage. But you, bearing it nobly, take your ease in harbor and on the shore. If you are carried away into the same passion as he, you have sunk not him but yourself. “Arise, O Lord, in your anger; be exalted in the borders of your enemies.” He put it this way to show that God can also arise not in anger, as when he says, “Arise, O Lord, save me, O my God.” When you hear “Arise,” do not suspect anything bodily. Sitting is not said of God in a bodily sense, and neither is this. For he says, “You are seated forever.” What, then, does he hint at by the sitting? The settledness, fixity and stability of his nature, its permanence, which he also made clear by contrast. Having said, “You are seated forever,” he added, “But you perish forever.” So just as the sitting is not bodily, neither is the rising. There it means settledness; here it means punishment and destruction. And there are places where sitting means also [?]… [?] [One codex: “forever; and who is the one who is continually seated? what” [?]. One reads: “where sitting also signifies royalty, and the” [?]. Below, the same: “and there are places where it also signifies royalty, as”]

[?]…others say that he promised to be an enemy to his enemies. “And an assembly of peoples will surround you.” Here too, suspect nothing human. The words may be of that kind, but the meaning befits God. What, then, does “will surround you” mean? It means: will sing to you, will hymn you, will offer you much praise. They did this in choirs, standing round in a circle in the temple and at the altar, and so offered their thanksgivings, and he hinted at the praise from the way they stood. What he means is this: Go forth, help. This will make you exalted even among your enemies, and will bring you much praise from your people. See how he seeks not his own interest but God’s. He wants him to be glorified everywhere, among his enemies and among his own. “And for its sake return on high.” For the sake of what? Of the assembly, he says. That is, because of it, “return on high”: exalt us, lift us up, make our affairs high, make the assembly more brilliant and renowned, restore it to its former prosperity. Notice how everywhere he mixes teaching with his supplications. Earlier, having said, “Have mercy on me and hear me,” he turns his words to counsel, saying, “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?” And here, having said, “Return on high, O Lord,” he adds, “The Lord will judge the peoples.” Another translator says, “The Lord will try the case.” He teaches those who think that everything happens at random and by chance that a providence presides over affairs and demands an account of what is done. By judgment here he means both the judgment to come and the present one. There it will be universal and plain; but even here he exacts penalties in part, rousing the careless and drawing the unbelieving to the thought of a providence over all things. “Judge me, O Lord, according to my righteousness.” Another: “According to my just cause.” “And according to my innocence that is in me. Let the wickedness of sinners come to an end.” Another says, “Let evil be brought to completion against the ungodly.” “And you will guide the righteous.” Another: “And you will establish the righteous.” How can the one who says elsewhere, “Do not enter into judgment with your servant,” say here, “Judge me according to my righteousness”? Because the one is a different thing from the other. There, saying “Do not enter into judgment with your servant,” he means: do not be judged against me yourself, and do not examine my life by comparing it with the benefits I have received from you. That is why he added, “For no one living will be justified before you,” that is, when judged against you. [62] But here he does not say this. He wants to be judged not against God, but against himself. That is why he said, “According to my righteousness,” that is, my own righteousness. By righteousness here he means not having started an unjust attack, which is what he said above: “If I have done this,” and what follows. “According to my innocence” shows the same thing: by this, he says, I want to be judged. [Note: Two manuscripts: “will bring you much praise among your people.” Reg. and Colb.: “concerning the Lord” [?].]

[?]…you, those who are in chastisement and punishment. Have you not heard Christ saying, “In the world you will have tribulation”? Why, then, do you look for relief when he has said this? Have you not heard him saying, “The world will rejoice, but you will always grieve”? The more foolish might have had reason to be scandalized if the opposite of what he said had happened. But if everything is going as it should, why are you scandalized? “And why,” someone says, “did God arrange things this way?” Do not inquire and do not pry. “The thing formed will not say to the one who formed it, ‘Why did you make me like this?’” This is why the prophet rebuked the Jews: full of countless evils, they were busying themselves about God’s ways. He said, “They desire to know my ways, as if they were a people that had done righteousness and had not forsaken the judgment of its God.” They were behaving like a servant who has given offense and is liable to countless charges, and who, instead of appeasing his master’s anger, demands that he account for why he did this or that. Do not ask these things and give up weeping and lamenting and washing away your own evils. I say this not because I am at a loss for an answer, but because I want to turn you from this curiosity to care for your own salvation. Why, then, did he ordain it so? To spare the human race. He allotted toil to this life, where life is short, and stored up the crowns for the future, where the age is ageless and endless. This toil quickly ends and passes away, but those rewards remain undying and never come to an end. Besides, he also trains souls in the love of virtue. When the soul chooses virtue even with toil, though it never receives a prize here, it learns to devote itself to virtue with great care. And when it flees vice even though vice brings pleasure, though it never suffers punishment here, it is trained to hate vice and turn away from it. From this it will acquire a settled habit of hatred for wickedness and love for virtue. There is another reason too. What is it? That affliction, more than anything, trains us for true wisdom and makes us stronger. And besides this there is yet another. What is it? He wants to teach us to look down on present things and not be nailed or bound to them. That is why he allotted us affliction and toil, and made even the good and bright things themselves easily undone. “Let the wickedness [64] of sinners come to an end, and you will guide the righteous.” What does “let it come to an end” mean? Bring punishment, he says, and you will stop them from their wickedness. Just as festering sores give way to bitter medicines, to burning and cutting, so wickedness too is checked by punishment. 9. Knowing this, then, we should weep not for those who are punished or chastised, but for those who sin and go unpunished. The first evil is to sin; the second is for those who sin to receive no treatment. Or rather, one might rightly call this the first, and by far the worst. Being sick is not the hard thing; the hard thing is for the sick person not to be treated. We do not simply lament a man with a festering sore, but a man who has one and lies neglected and does not come under the physicians’ hands. As for the man who is being cut and cauterized, we would say that he is on the road to health, looking not at the pain of the cutting but at the [?] from

…my steps [?], for I was envious of the lawless.” Another says again, “Why does the way of the ungodly prosper?” And Job too asked many questions like this. But in those days people were less advanced, and so those who said such things said them and those who asked asked. Now, though, the one who is troubled by these things deserves no pardon, since he has learned such great wisdom, has received such teachings about the future, has been taught more clearly about Gehenna and the kingdom, and knows that each person will receive there what he deserves. “God who tests hearts and reins [?]… my help is from God who saves the upright in heart.” Another: “The examiner of hearts and reins, God, is just, my shield.” And another: “God is just.” The Seventy, however, put it this way: “God tests hearts and reins. Just is my help from God.” He has said that God will judge the world; next he tells how he will judge. He said that God needs no witnesses, no proofs, no demonstrations, no documents, nothing of the kind, because he himself is the one who knows what is hidden. So let no fool say, “And how will he judge the world, when it is so vast?” He who made it when it did not exist will also judge it now that it exists. By “reins” here he means the hidden things of the mind, the innermost and deepest parts, hinting at this by where that organ lies in the body. 10. What does “testing” mean? What the other translator said: “proving.” The words may be human, but the meaning befits God. When Paul says, “He who searches the hearts,” he uses “searching” for knowing clearly, and in the same way this writer uses “testing” for knowing exactly. To examine thoroughly is to lay bare, which belongs to exact knowledge and understanding, as Paul also says: “All things are naked and laid open before his eyes.” “Just is my help.” Another: “Just is my shield.” What does “Just is my help from God” mean? It would be just, he says, for help to come to me from God, for I ask nothing unjust. So if we are to enjoy help from above, we must ask for things that are just, so that by the very nature of our request we may draw his favor. “Who saves the upright in heart.” This is his work, this is his custom. Since I too did not start an unjust attack, and do not desire to take revenge, my help from God would therefore be just. Knowing this, then, let us ask for nothing that hinders the gift. When you pray against your enemies, your help is not just, for that is contrary to the law of the giver. The same is true if you ask for wealth, or beauty, or anything else of this worldly kind, which is fleeting and contrary to the soul’s true wisdom. So let us ask in such a way that we also receive. “God is a just judge, strong and long-suffering, not bringing wrath every day.” Another says, “Threatening every day.” And the other [?] says, “God is just; my help is from God.” And the Seventy…

…who has looked at women with licentious eyes? Who has not envied? Who has not been vainglorious? Who has not uttered an idle word? Yet all these things are liable to punishment. If we were not earnest about worldly affairs and not earnest about spiritual ones either, we might deserve pardon. As it is, we are deprived even of this defense, for in worldly things we are wide awake, while in spiritual things we lie slack. So that we would not grow more careless on hearing that he is longsuffering, he added: "If you do not turn back, he will polish his sword." Another version says, "He will sharpen his sword." "He has bent his bow and made it ready." Another says, "He will stretch [?]." "And on it he has prepared the instruments of death; he has fashioned his arrows for those who are burning." Another says, "for burning." 11. What will they say here, those who claim that God has human form because he is said to have hands and feet and eyes? Are there bows up above, then, and arrows, and a whetstone, and a sword, and a quiver? And indeed another says: "When you look, the mountains will be troubled before you." And this same prophet says: "He who looks upon the earth and makes it tremble." If he melts even the nature of stones merely by looking at the earth, he can do this all the more to human beings. Why, then, is he said to have a sword and a bow, when he can overturn the world merely by looking at it, or rather merely by willing it? (For it is plain that he who made it by his will alone can also destroy it by his will alone.) [68] For "in his hand are the ends of the earth, and those who dwell in it are like locusts," and "all the nations will be reckoned as a drop from a bucket and as the tipping of a scale." His angel went out and in a brief moment of time slew one hundred and eighty-five thousand. Why do I say an angel? Flies and caterpillars and worms destroyed the army of the Egyptians. What need is there of a bow there? What need of a sword? Why, then, were these things said? Because of the dullness of the hearers, and so that he might shake their minds with the names of the weapons they were used to. He in whose hand is the breath of us all, and before whose cold no one at all can stand, how does he need weapons? But, as I said before, these things are said in this way because of the dullness and insensibility of the hearers. And what does "and he will polish" mean? "He will sharpen." Is there need of a whetstone, then? And of rust on the sword? Who with any sense would bear to take these things as they are stated? But, as I said before, he sketches the punishment by every means and goes on to the grosser images, so that even the very foolish may understand that one must not sit beside the bare words, but draw from them thoughts worthy of God. So if anyone is puzzled why wrath and anger are spoken of God, he will be far more puzzled about these things. And if these are not to be taken as they are stated, yet they do their work and frighten, much more so in the case of God [?]. Nor is it the mark of an ordinary love for mankind to frighten through words and to magnify the punishment, so that [?] those being punished [?]. Then is fire not enough, but there is need of arrows as well? You see [?]…

…not come to the actual experience of these things. This is why he bent the bow, why he made it ready, why he set the arrows on it, why he prepares himself for punishment: so that he may not come to punishment. 15. And he amplifies his language. By "he will polish" he shows the vehemence and keenness of the punishment; by "he has bent" its nearness; by "he has made ready" that it will certainly happen unless they change; by "for those who are burning" he points out the guilty. So, taught by all these things, they might check their wickedness. If these things came from wrath and anger, he would not have announced them in advance to those he was about to attack. Wrath does not put up with this. It does the very opposite, especially when it is at its height, in the act of punishing and preparing the penalty. Enemies, at any rate, when they want to inflict punishment, not only say nothing but even attack from hiding, so that those about to be punished may not find out and guard themselves. But God does not act so. He does the very opposite: he forewarns, he delays, he frightens through words, and he does everything so as not to inflict what he threatens. He did this with the Ninevites too. There as well he bent the bow, polished the sword, made ready the arrows, and did not strike the blow. Or do the prophet's words not seem to you a bow, an arrow and a sharpened sword when he says, "Yet three days, and Nineveh will be overthrown"? But he did not let the arrow fly. It had not been made ready to be shot, but to be laid away. Soldiers arm themselves in order to punish. [70] God does not, but arms himself so that, having made people more sober through fear, he may hold back the hand of punishment. Let us not be alarmed, then. The fear in the words comes from great love for mankind, and the more terrible the things he says, the greater the gentleness they are spoken from. Fathers, too, when they do not want to punish their children, vent their anger in words. So he too, since he does not want to punish, magnifies the fear through words. He says he has prepared Gehenna so that he may not cast anyone into Gehenna. This is also why so many sayings about punishment are stored up in the Gospels, more than those about the kingdom. With the more insensible, the promise of good things does not draw them to virtue and lead them away from vice as much as the fear of painful things does. For this reason he dwells on these at greater length and sets them forth continually. Let us not be pained, then, when we hear harsh words, for they bring great profit. Rather, considering both his longsuffering and his just judgment, let us neither despair of salvation, for he is longsuffering, nor grow slack [?], for he is just. Here he shows great longsuffering; there he hands over to the experience of punishment those who have gained nothing from this life. So that this may not happen, let us ward off the punishment already, here and now. "Behold, he has travailed with injustice." The Hebrew, instead of "travailed," has "Iebal" [?]. "He conceived toil." Another: "And having conceived." "And he brought forth lawlessness." Another: "a lie." "He dug a pit and hollowed it out, and he will fall into the hole that he made." Another: "into corruption" [?]…

…[?] Here he hints at two things, the unbearable and the unexpected. Hezekiah, too, says, "For the pang has come upon her who is giving birth, but she has no strength to bring forth," showing through the birth pang his unbearable fear and pain. So also the prophet here. Though someone be wicked ten thousand times over, the tribunal of conscience is not corrupted. It is natural, implanted in us by God from the beginning. However much we fight against it, it stands over us crying out, punishing, condemning. There is no one living in wickedness who does not endure endless anguish, both while plotting evil and while carrying the plan into action. What was more wicked than Ahab? Yet think how much anguish he had when he coveted the vineyard. Though he was king and ruled over all, and had no one to oppose him, he could not bear the verdict of his conscience. He went in sullen, bowed down and confounded, with a heavy cloud on his face, proclaiming on his countenance the proof of his conscience's condemnation, unable to hide the anguish his dejection had bred in him. That is how even his wife found him out. The traitor, too, who had run aground on such great wickedness, could not bear the anguish that came from the tribunal [72] of conscience; he tied a noose and so ended his life. Just as the one living in wickedness suffers so much, so the one living in virtue enjoys calm and an untroubled mind. Consider this. If someone wants to take revenge on another, or to strike the first unjust blow, see how many terrible things he suffers. He is filled with rage, torn apart by anger. He stirs up countless waves of thoughts and tries countless paths. Fear comes upon him, and anguish, and trembling, as rage tears at him and fear shakes him over how to succeed and how to carry it through. Before the one he means to wrong is harmed, he destroys himself. But the one who casts out anger is rid of all these things, and very rightly so. Of this he himself is master, and he has accomplished the whole. Of the other he is master no longer. There is need of opportunity, and place, and deceit, and villainy, and weapons, and devices, and quarrels [?], and flattery, and servility, and hypocrisy. Do you see how easy virtue is, and how hard vice? How the one is untroubled, while the other is full of tumult? It was this that the Prophet was describing when he said: "Behold, he has travailed with injustice, he has conceived toil, and brought forth lawlessness." This shows that injustice is not natural to us but something foreign. That is why it weighs us down and wraps us in birth pangs until we are rid of it. While the embryo is still being formed, it lies in the womb according to nature, and so it stays there and causes no pain. But once it is complete, if it stays inside, its sojourn there is against nature, and that is why birth pangs arise. Nature, troubled, strains to push it out, since it has done all its work and completed it and can no longer bear it. There, however, conception comes first and then labor. Here he first travailed, and then conceived and bore. What, then, are we to say? That there the labor comes at the time of birth, while here the labor is there from the beginning. As soon as someone plots something wicked, even before he has fixed it in his mind, there is tumult and turmoil in his mind. In…

…to make away with [?] the infant. [And Pharaoh's daughter took the basket out of the river, found the infant and raised him.] And he, when he had grown up, destroyed them all. Here especially God's skill in devising shines out: it brings great correction to the wicked, and joy to those who escape. So it was with the all-beautiful Joseph as well. His brothers cast him into slavery and suffered what they suffered. They did him no harm at all, but even benefited him, while they themselves endured that whole tragedy. Many such things could be told, but consider the other cases too. Has someone defrauded another? He has destroyed himself. The one defrauded he has often even benefited, but he has betrayed his own soul. Has someone done wrong? He has run himself through with the sword. Not suffering evil but doing evil: this above all is what it means to suffer evil. That is why Paul urged us rather to be wronged than to do wrong, and Christ urged us to be struck and not strike back, and even to offer ourselves up to suffering. This is a mark of the greatest strength. This produces endurance, this makes the soul strong, [74] this lifts it above the passions. The man who wrongs another, or strikes or insults him, has first been overpowered by passion himself and taken captive, and only then does he seem to wrong his neighbor. He himself has suffered worse, having served the utmost slavery. "His toil will return upon his head, and his injustice will come down upon his crown." They say this was spoken of Ahithophel and Absalom, for the heads of both went down to punishment. The one used a noose and so ended his life. The other went under the tree, was caught up by his hair, and hung there a long time. So too Judas ended his life with a noose, knowing that he had done everything to the ruin of his own head. Ahithophel, realizing that David would surely prevail, went off and hanged himself. Absalom hung there against his will and was not killed at once. As in a law court, he was first strung up and fastened to the wood, and while God delivered the verdict from above, he hung there a long time, scourged now by his conscience. For he had longed to plunge his right hand into his father's throat, while his father urged the soldiers to spare him even so. So it was not out of vainglory, as is said, that he mourned him even after death. And so that you may learn that what happened was not the work of human effort, but that the tribunal was wholly divine: hair and wood bound him, and a brute beast handed him over. Instead of a rope there was his hair, instead of a gibbet the tree, and instead of a soldier the mule brought him there. And see how extraordinary it was. While he suffered this, none of his own people dared come near and take him down, though there was so much time to do it. God arranged this too, so that he would be neither taken down nor carried off bound to his father, since the father's heart was showing a forbearance beyond all measure. What is more wonderful still, the very man who had reconciled his father to him was the one who killed him… being scourged. The editions read "being whipped." Two manuscripts read: "showed an untimely sparing beyond measure."

How did he not reflect that, even if he won, he would live a life more wretched than anyone's, accursed and unclean, even from the trophy itself? 16. Where now are those who lament their poverty? How much harsher than poverty are these things! Than what disease! Than what pain! Yet he said nothing of the kind to himself. He did not chafe, nor did he lament, saying: "Fine rewards I am getting, I who meditate on his law day and night! I who held such high rank have become lowlier than all! I who spared my enemies have been handed over to a licentious son!" He said nothing of the kind and thought nothing of the kind. He bore everything with true philosophy, having one consolation in what was happening: that these things happened with God's knowledge. So the three young men also said: "And if not, be it known to you, O king, that we do not serve your gods, [76] and we do not worship the golden image that you have set up." If someone had said to them, "With what hope are you dying? What do you expect, what do you hope for after death, after the fire?" (for there was not yet any expectation of the resurrection), he would have heard: "This is our greatest recompense: to die for God." So David too held this to be his greatest consolation, that God, who knew these things, did not prevent them. A lover would choose ten thousand times over to be slaughtered for his beloved, though he expects nothing from her after death. So we too must suffer everything, not in expectation of the kingdom or in hope of any other of the good things to come, but for God himself. Yet many are so slack and sluggish that they do not strive for virtue even with a reward. God, who even promises a kingdom, is not listened to, while the devil, who procures Gehenna, is loved. What is worse than this madness? And why do I speak of Gehenna? Even before Gehenna, he brings pain here, and disgrace, and ridicule, and countless punishments, and still he has many running to him. Think of the adulterer, how he lives more wretchedly than anyone. Even before Gehenna he suspects everything, trembles at shadows, looks no one in the face with free eyes, but fears everyone, those who know and those who do not. He sees swords sharpened, deaths hanging over him, executioners, courts. What is there like this in chastity, even if it involves countless labors? Is not the chaste man always in pleasure, and the adulterer always in pain and in darkness? You can see the same with the others too: with those who are overcome by anger and those who master it, with those who seize what belongs to others and those who give, or rather freely lavish, their own for God's sake. The latter sit in harbor; the former, swept out into the strait of present evils, are tossed about every day. Besides this, when the man who lives with greed finds his age advancing and his licentiousness no longer enough for his enjoyment… Three manuscripts and Savile read: "sharpened, the executioners hanging over him." Two manuscripts read: "overcome by anger." [?] and hymns, and thousands of thousands; and this [?]

…and the conquered nations also say this, calling them sackers of cities, conquerors of barbarians, and the like. Some such song this blessed man also sings. He tells of a victory and a trophy and an end of wars, not wars of that kind, but far harder ones. And see how he begins: "O Lord, our Lord." Of the others, who do not believe in him, he is Lord in one way; of us, in two: both because he made us out of nothing, and because he has become known to us. [78] And see how from the very opening he sets down the sum of his benefaction. If you learn how he became your Lord, how he took to himself and brought to life people who were estranged, dead and deadened, you will see clearly that this is the sum of his benefaction. Struck with wonder at this, the Prophet says: "How wonderful is your name!" That is, exceedingly wonderful. How wonderful, he did not say, for he could not measure it. He only conveyed its intensity and its surpassing greatness. Where are those who pry into the essence of God? If he so marveled on speaking only of God's name that he was astounded, what pardon could they have who claim to know his essence, when the Prophet could not even learn how wonderful his name is? "How wonderful is your name!" For in this name death was undone, demons were bound, heaven was opened, the gates of paradise were flung wide, the Spirit was sent down. Slaves became free, enemies became sons, strangers became heirs, men became angels. Why do I say angels? God became man, and man became God. Heaven received the nature that came from earth; earth received him who sits upon the Cherubim with the angelic host. The dividing wall was removed, the fence was taken down, what was separated was united, darkness was quenched, light shone forth, death was swallowed up. Reflecting on all these things and more, the Prophet cried out: "How wonderful is your name in all the earth!" Where now are the children of the Jews, who are shameless in the face of the truth? I would gladly ask them of whom these things are said. "Of the Almighty," they will say. But his name was not wonderful in all the earth. Isaiah bears witness, saying: "Because of you my name is blasphemed among the nations." If those who served him became the cause of his being blasphemed, where was it wonderful? That it is wonderful by nature is clear. Among men at that time, however, it was not wonderful to most, but even contemptible. Now it is not so. Since the only-begotten Son came, his name is wonderful everywhere along with Christ's. "From the rising of the sun," it says… One manuscript reads: "the conquered, calling them destroyers on land" [?]. [?] … invincible, from the untimely age that speaks clearly for that doxology; for … [?]

…and the deaf, the seeing and the blind? And again: "Giving clear tongues to stammerers." And again: "The Lord gives me a tongue of instruction, to know when I must speak a word." And at the beginning he says: "Come, let us go down and confuse their tongues." Great and strong, then, is the proof. In the other cases, though without reason, they shamelessly suspected something. Here they had nothing to say, since nature itself, bare and unaided, was contending. This is why he did not simply say "of infants," lest anyone think he meant the innocent and simple. [80] He added "and of sucklings," marking their age by naming their food. He does not simply say "of infants," but of those at the breast, who had never yet tasted solid food. And the wonder is not only that they uttered a sound, and a clear one, but that it was full of countless good things. What the apostles did not yet know, these children were singing in their hymns. By this he also hints at something else: that those who come to the doctrines must become children in mind. "For unless one receives the kingdom of heaven like a child," he says, "he cannot enter it." "Because of your enemies." He also states the reason this wonder took place. The other wonders did not happen because of enemies, but so that those who came might enjoy his benefaction and others might be taught. This one happened not only for that reason, but also so that the enemies might be silenced. Another translator, pointing them out more precisely, calls them "those who bind you." For they were the ones who bound him when he was led to the cross. "To destroy the enemy and the avenger." Another: "So as to put a stop to the enemy and the one who avenges himself." Here he means the Jewish people. They hounded Christ as an enemy, but pretended to be doing it to avenge the Father. That is why, depriving them of this excuse, he said: "He who hates me hates my Father also"; and again: "He who believes in me believes in him who sent me." Again and again he joins the Father to the honor and the insult shown to himself. And see the precision of the Prophet. He did not say "to punish," but "to destroy," which the other translator shows more clearly when he says "to put a stop to": that is, to do away with their shamelessness, not to teach them, for their sickness was beyond cure. At any rate, seeing such a wonder and having nothing to say against it, they turned to him and said: "Do you not hear what these are saying?" When they ought then to have worshiped and marveled, they were at a complete loss. And when each of them ought to have said to his neighbor, "Do you not hear what these are saying?", they passed over one another and said it to Christ. And why was this not brought about by the voice of angels? Because that would have seemed… One manuscript reads: "they were shameless, suspecting some hypocrisy" [?] … "to obtain the promised good things" … another [?]. [?] … "shamelessness" [?] … there is added "from the use" [?] … "when we say these things, they say."

[?] tell me. Surely this is not the first time you have sinned? In fact, you have now even become better behaved. But leave that aside for now. This is what I would ask you: why is it that before, though you were always sinning, you used to receive lovingkindness from God, but now no longer do? And, stranger still, why now, when your sins are fewer? Back then you were initiated into the rites of Baal of Peor, you worshipped a calf, you slaughtered your sons [82] and killed your daughters, and you did all this while enjoying signs. Now you do not see the sea split or the rock broken open, prophets do not come to you, and you do not enjoy the providence you were used to, yet you show greater moderation. Why, then, when your sins are fewer and your self-control greater, is the punishment and retribution greater? Is it not plain even to the utterly foolish that it is because the present sin is greater? As long as you sinned against the servants, killing and stoning prophets, you obtained pardon. But once you stretched out your hands against the Master, the wound became incurable from then on. That is why four hundred years have now passed since the very ground of the city was wiped out, the priesthood abolished, the kingdom dissolved, the tribes thrown into confusion, and all those august and splendid things obliterated, so that not even a trace of them remains among you. This had never happened before. In the beginning, even when the temple had been torn down, the prophets remained, and the gifts of the Spirit, and miracles. But now, so that you may learn clearly that God has turned away from you for good, these too have been taken away. Slavery, captivity and the loss of everything have overtaken you, and, harshest of all, abandonment by God. 4. God has done just what a man might do with an ungrateful slave who has been whipped many times and not reformed: he strips him of his clothes and lets him go wandering, naked, destitute, a vagrant, begging and driven off everywhere. Your situation was not like this before. You had prophets among you in Egypt, in Babylon and in the wilderness: Moses in Egypt, Daniel and Ezekiel in Babylon, Jeremiah in Egypt again. There were miracles upon miracles, and the nation grew more glorious, as the captives among you became loftier than kings. But now all that is gone, and the punishment is harsher than the earlier ones, not only in its length but also in the depth of the abandonment. Tell me, then: why, when you sinned more, did you enjoy so much providence, and when, as you claim, you were zealous for the law, you suffered worse? By this you convict God of injustice, as though he honored you when you sinned and dishonored you when you did right. If you killed a deceiver, as you say, and acted rightly, then, if God is just, as indeed he is, he ought to have honored you, not punished you. But if he punishes you, it is plain that your present sins are harsher. And if you neither act impiously now nor sacrifice children as you did before, what other sin [?] …

… you did, he says. So were these, who were worse than the Gentiles, the ones he sent as teachers? Tell me! And who could bear their bloodshed? [84] For they slaughtered sons and daughters to the demons and burned them. David shows this too, when he says: "And they slaughtered their sons and their daughters to the demons." Was it for this, then, that he sent them, so that human nature might learn that sons and daughters must be slaughtered? Are you not ashamed, do you not hide your faces, when you make up such nonsense? Another prophet says: "They mingle blood upon blood; cursing and lying and theft and murder and adultery are poured out over the land." Another: "You had the face of a harlot; you became shameless toward all." Another again: "Your rulers are like wolves of Arabia." And another: "There is none who understands, none who seeks God. All have turned aside; together they have become worthless." 5. Is this, then, what you went out to teach: shamelessness, folly, fornication, adulteries, murders, every kind of wickedness? Will you not stop forcing us to parade your evils in public? You are the ones who were carried from the womb and taught until old age; you are the blind who throw one another into the pit. "For if the blind lead the blind," it says, "both will fall into the pit." You enjoyed the prophets every day and never became any better, and you were going to be teachers of others? Will you not stop talking such nonsense and recognize your own wickedness? This is what has always ruined you: your refusal to know even the cause of your sins. So God does what judges do. They order men to follow those being flogged, shouting out the reasons for the lashes: "Do not be thieves! Do not be robbers!" In the same way God, parading you everywhere, has ordered the prophets to follow you and proclaim the reason for the punishment. They are bound to you all over the world, and even now they are crying out against you. If you go into the synagogues, you will hear them saying these words over and over. David, describing that bandits' court of Caiaphas, says that this is why you have perished. For after saying, "Let us burst their bonds and cast their yoke from us," he went on: "Then he will speak to them in his anger, and in his wrath he will throw them into confusion." Isaiah, after saying, "He was led like a sheep to the slaughter," went on: "And I will give the wicked for his burial and the rich for his death." And again elsewhere, speaking of the vineyard: "I waited for it to do justice, but it did lawlessness; not righteousness, but a cry." What cry? "Crucify him, crucify him!" And he goes on: "Therefore I will tear down its hedge, and it will be trampled; and I will command the clouds not to rain on it." So it was not for that reason that you were scattered, but for what was dared at the cross, and this is plain from the prophets. And so that you may learn Christ's [?] … [?] … even though they constantly mingled good things with the punishments

and set times. [86] Jeremiah fixed seventy years, and Daniel likewise three and a half weeks; and in Egypt it was said that they would be slaves for four hundred and thirty years. But for this captivity no time is laid down anywhere, and no end. Instead, "your house is left desolate," and every day your affairs go from bad to worse. 6. If you reckon all this carefully among yourselves and develop the argument from it (for "give a wise man an opportunity, and he will be wiser"), you will be able to refute their shamelessness and ingratitude. "For I will see the heavens, the works of your fingers." Another version: "For I see the heavens." "The moon and the stars, which you founded." Another: "which you prepared." Another: "which you established." Having said, "You destroyed the enemies," he also supplies the proof of this splendid victory. "You," he says, "the crucified, the slain, have been revealed as the creator of the world." That is why he says, "I will see the heavens," showing that before, not many knew this, but later everyone will know it. And why did he not go through every part of the world? Because once he had gone through the most important of the visible things, there was no need to teach about the rest. So completely, then, were the enemies destroyed that the one they hounded and killed was revealed as the creator of all visible things. And why did he not say "of your hands" but "of your fingers"? To show that the visible world is the work of the slightest exertion, and to show the marvel of the creation: the stars hang there and do not fall. And yet it is not the nature of foundations to hang above; they naturally lie below. But the supremely skilled Craftsman, who works marvels, made most of the things we see beyond the order of nature. And why does he say nothing about the incorporeal powers and show his creative work from them? Because for the time being the aim was for them to learn about the visible things. That is why his Father too, speaking to the Jews again and again, does not say, "I made the angels and the cherubim," but, "I stretched out the heaven; my hand founded the earth; my right hand [?]." He always spends his whole discourse on visible things, arranging everything for the salvation of his hearers. Being rather dull, they were led more by what is seen than by what is unseen. That is why Paul too, whenever he went in to address the people, began from the visible creation, saying, "God, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and all that is in them"; and he always drew his argument from the yearly rains and from the human race. If I say that he made the cherubim, I need a double proof: that there are cherubim, and that he made them. But with visible things I need only prove that he made them. [87] So the argument is easier, for it has sight to bear witness to what is said. The hearer sees the size, the beauty, the usefulness, the position and the harmony. So I have only one task: to show that God made it. And why did he not mention the sun, but the moon and the stars? Above all, having said this, [?] [?] your house is left [?]. [?]

"… and let the dread of you and the fear of you be upon all the beasts of the earth." And: "Let them rule over the fish of the sea." And after this: "You will tread upon snakes and scorpions." But he leaves these aside and weaves his argument from humbler things, leaving those to be perceived by people able to see more sharply. For the greater glory and honor is what has come about under the New Covenant: when man has Christ as his head, when he is counted into his body, when he becomes his brother and joint heir and conformed to his body, when he receives a glory greater than that of Moses. Paul made this clear when he showed that we do not put on a veil as Moses did, but "we all, with unveiled face, behold as in a mirror the glory of God." That is why he also says, "For what was glorified has not been glorified in this respect, because of the glory that surpasses it." This, then, is the glory the Prophet is speaking of, in the higher sense. For what could equal it, when we dance in chorus with angels, when we are brought into adoption as sons, when he does not spare even the Only-begotten for our sake? What purple robe, what diadem is not outshone by these things, when we laugh at death, when we are carried over into the freedom from passion of the incorporeal powers, we who before were dishonored, inglorious and loathsome? Adam, having done neither evil nor good, was honored as soon as he came into being. For how could someone who did not yet exist have done anything? But we, who had done countless terrible things, have enjoyed far greater honor. "No longer," he says, "do I call you servants, for you are my friends." Angels are no longer ashamed of us; they even minister for our salvation. An angel came to Philip, and to many others, and they brought good news to men. We are not heirs on earth; we are sharers in the heavenly goods, partakers of Christ, and we are called into fellowship with the Only-begotten. All this he hints at with "glory and honor." That is why he said, "With glory and honor you will crown him," announcing the future in advance. "And you set him over the works of your hands." Another version: "You gave him authority over the works of your hands." "You put all things under his feet: sheep and all oxen, and the beasts of the field as well." Another: "the wild animals [?]." "The birds of the sky and the fish of the sea, that pass along the paths of the seas. O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth!" When he spoke about creation, he did not touch only on the powers above [89] but brought the discourse down to the things of the senses. In the same way, when he teaches about the honor given to human beings, after hinting at those ineffable and incorporeal things which he listed, he now dwells more on the things of the senses, which were clearer than those to the duller. What were these? The rule over the earth that was given to man. And the wonderful thing, which he especially hinted at, is that God, having honored him before the transgression, did not cast him out of that honor even after the sin. "For you made him a little lower than the angels," he says; that is, you condemned him to death when he sinned. Yet although you condemned him to death, you did not strip him of the gift. [?] … do more terrible damage than beasts, if we do not restrain and bridle them. And why do I speak of anger and wrath,

when even our eye has entangled us in passions worse than beasts, piercing us through with bitter lust? Yet we will not say on that account, "Why did these things come about?" Rather, we will thank the Master for everything. For what the strap is to a child, the wild beast is to human beings. If most people rise to such madness while hemmed in by so many dangers, think how far wickedness would advance if you took away this bridle too. For the same reason our body has been made as it is, prone to sickness, subject to suffering, besieged by countless ills; the earth yields its produce only with toil; and all of life is full of sweat. The present life is a school of discipline, and ease and leisure ruin most people, so he mixed work and toil into our lives, so that the mind's restlessness might be checked as if by bridles. And consider the creatures that swim through the depths of the waters and those that rise into the heights: the Master has made them subject to you through skill. And why did he not go through all visible things, plants and seeds and trees? From a part he hinted at the whole, and left the discussion of these things to those who love learning. And again he ends at the very point from which he began, "O Lord, our Lord," setting the same words both before the proof and after it. Let us too, then, keep on saying the same words, marveling at his care, amazed at his wisdom, his love for humankind and his providence on our behalf. So much we have said by way of interpretation. But if you wish, let us also handle the argument more combatively and ask the Jews: Where did children sing out? Where did such a voice destroy an enemy? When did his name become wonderful? They could name no other occasion than this one, which shows the power of the truth more clearly than the sun. That is why he says, "I will see the heavens, the works of your fingers," although Moses had already said, "In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth." [91] Against the Jews, then, this is enough, together with what was said earlier. But there are also those who, without circumcision, imitate and emulate the Jews' ways: the followers of Paul of Samosata, who say that Christ has existed only from the time he came forth from Mary. Let us ask them too: if Christ existed only from then, how did he create the heavens? For the Prophet says that the one who here perfected praise from the mouth of infants and nursing babies is the same one who made the heavens. And if he is the creator of the heavens, he must be prior to the heavens, and he did not take his beginning from Mary but existed even before Mary. And observe the Prophet's wisdom. He does not simply present him as creator, but as creating with great ease. That is why he says, "I will see the heavens, the works of your fingers": not that God has fingers, but [to show] that visible things are [the work] of the slightest exertion. [?] lets out a voice. Not badly. [?] had existence. Reg.: showing the smallest exertion. [?] … inferior to that essence, and of condescension

it is. For what do you mean to say? That God is great? But that is a small thing to say of God, for what is great, however great it may be, is limited, whereas God is infinite. And even this is a small thing to say of God. I know that he has no limit, but I do not know what he is, or where. Even if you call him wise, even if you call him good, and call these infinite, you have said nothing worthy of that essence; a meaning befitting God must go with the word. If, then, even such great terms do not convey his dignity, what pardon could they deserve who try to cut these down as well? Let us flee their assemblies, then. We have learned of the Only-begotten's existence before the ages, his creative power, his sovereign authority, his exact likeness to the Father, the condescension of the dispensation, and the manifold providence of his care for us; for all this, and more, the treasure laid up in the psalm teaches those who pay careful attention. So let us keep our doctrines exact and show a way of life worthy of them, so that we may also attain the good things to come. May we all be counted worthy of them, by the grace and lovingkindness of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, be honor and glory to the ages of ages. Amen.

ON PSALM 9. [95]

For the end; concerning the hidden things of the son; a psalm of David. Another version: A victory song concerning the death of the son; a song of David. Another: Of the youth of the son.

"I will give thanks to you, O Lord, with my whole heart; I will recount all your wonders."

1. This psalm is long. That too is part of the Spirit's wisdom. He did not make all the psalms short, nor stretch them all out at length, but varied the book in length as well, rousing us from sluggishness with length and relieving our weariness with brevity. "I will give thanks to you, O Lord, with my whole heart; I will recount all your wonders." There are two kinds of confession: either the condemnation of one's own sins, or thanksgiving to God. Here it means thanksgiving. What does "with my whole heart" mean? "With all eagerness, with zeal," he means: not only in prosperity, but also in adversity. For this above all is the mark of a grateful soul, of a philosophic soul: to give thanks even in painful circumstances, to glorify God for everything, not only for his benefits but also for his punishments. This brings a greater reward. When you give thanks for good things, you have paid a debt; but when you give thanks for bad things, you have made God your debtor. The one who has been treated well and is grateful has paid back what he owed; but the one who has been treated badly and still glorifies God has created a debt. So in return for this thanksgiving God gives back many other good things. [Note: In Colb., "those deprived" is missing.]

… recounting the wonders of God that happen every day, private and public, those done for everyone and those done for each individual. For life is full of these stories, and wherever you begin, you will see the opening spring forth all the more brilliantly, whether you start from heaven, or from the earth, or from the air, or from the irrational animals, or from seeds, or from plants. Whether you want to recount the ancient gifts, those before the law, those under the law, those in the age of grace, those after our departure from here, or those in death itself, you will find countless oceans of such stories. What folly would it not be, then, when we have so much to recount, things that bring pleasure and gain and benefit to the soul, to smear our thoughts in the mire by telling stories about greed and robbery? 2. And if you wish, let us leave aside the things above and talk about the earth: its size, its position, its usefulness, its nature, its continual birth-pangs, the varied and diverse things it produces, its seeds, herbs, plants, flowers, meadows and gardens. From these, again, let us single out in our discussion each tree's shape, position, height, fragrance, fruit, season and service, reckoning up everything else, and also the fruitful and the barren parts of the earth itself, for none of it is useless. One part has yielded iron, another bronze, another gold, another silver; another spices, another medicines of every varied kind. What could one say of the usefulness of the waters, both fresh and salt, of the usefulness of the mountains, the quarries of many-colored marbles, the springs in them, the trees suitable for roofs and building? All these are the fruit of the wilderness, and it also feeds animals and all the wild beasts. What could one say of the lakes, the springs, the rivers? Just as women who have given birth pour out a spring of milk and so feed their offspring, so the earth, stretching out its rivers and springs like breasts to gardens and orchards, provides abundant water. But with women, the infant has to come to the breast, while here the earth herself extends her breasts everywhere, bringing them down from on high. The wilderness has another use too. It is better for bodily health, offering purer air to breathe, the chance to survey the whole inhabited world from on high, to practice philosophy in solitude, and to breathe a little from the cares of life. What could one say of the songbirds, or of the way of life of the animals that can be caught? The wilderness has yet another use. It has often served countries as walls, with its mountains stretching up to the heights, its ravines and its cliffs. What could one say of the herbs that grow there, which do great service to sick bodies? If deserts and mountains are so useful and supply so many good things, then think, if you come to the arable land and the level plains, how many springs of stories you will see. For just as in our body some [?] … [Note: "reckoning up" [?] in Colb.]

…back, they will grow weak and perish before your face. Another version: When my enemies are turned back, stumbling and perishing from your presence. This is especially the mark of one who loves: to speak of the benefits he has received all the time, and to glory in them. It comes from affection, and in turn it kindles affection. One would not be wrong to say that here he also means spiritual enemies. These too turn back when they meet a noble soul. A spear that strikes a shield cuts through it if the shield is soft, but does nothing to one that is hard and resistant; its point is bent back and it falls away. So it is with the soul. If the darts the devil sends find it soft and slack, they sink into its depths. But if they find it hard and strong, the devil goes away having achieved nothing, and he has done it no harm. Two gains follow, or rather three: he did not harm the soul, he made it stronger, and he himself became weaker as a result. See how he proclaims God's strength: They will grow weak, he says, and perish before your face. Again, when you hear "face," do not suspect anything bodily. Here it means his working, his appearing, the ease with which his strength acts. As he says elsewhere: He who looks upon the earth and [?]. His gaze alone is enough to destroy the wicked. If the presence of the saints weakens the strength of demons, how much more the presence of God! If his lightning astounds everyone when it appears, consider how that indestructible power astounds, how it destroys the wicked. Do you see this kind of hymn, this manner of doxology, and how he tells of God's power? Here too he teaches no small doctrine of the philosophic life, by saying: I will sing to your name, O Most High, when my enemy is turned back. What doctrine is this? That he kept sober not only in afflictions but also in times of ease. Many people become more earnest when evils humble them, but more careless and slack when good things come. He says this about the Jews further on: When he slew them, then they sought him. But David was not like that. Even in prosperity he is sober and wide awake. This is no small contribution to the philosophic life [?]. For you have upheld my judgment and my cause. Another version: You have pleaded my cause. You sat on the throne, you who judge righteousness. You rebuked the nations, and the ungodly man perished. Another version: You destroyed. You blotted out his name forever and ever. See again the man's philosophy. He does not avenge himself on his enemies, but leaves the judgment to God, keeping the apostle's command: Do not avenge yourselves. And that is not all we can see here. We also see that he suffered these things unjustly. If he had not suffered unjustly, God would not have intervened. You sat on the throne, you who judge righteousness. He speaks in rather human terms when he mentions a throne and a seat. But the words "who judge righteousness" express what is habitual to God and peculiar to his essence. This cannot be said of human beings. They do not always judge righteously, even if they are ten thousand times just, because sometimes through ignorance and sometimes through carelessness they fail to know what is just. But God is free of all these things, and knowing [?]. [Colbert manuscript: "the opponents."]

[?] …but in every case one must accept both the text itself and what follows from it [?]. Another version: To the afflicted [?]. …as is constantly made clear, as with the words: Just as Moses lifted up the serpent. We must believe both that this happened (for it did happen) and what follows from it, that it was a type of Christ. He calls himself both needy and poor, even though he lived in a palace. So too elsewhere: But I am poor. So here too one would not be wrong to apply these words to the affairs of the Jews. You sat on the throne, you who judge righteousness. You rebuked the nations, and the ungodly man perished; you blotted out his name forever, and forever and ever. The swords of the enemy have failed utterly, and you have torn down cities. His memory has perished with a crash. The calamity of those who crucified Christ is plain to see throughout the whole world. Their cities were torn down, and the devil's schemes failed once Christ's care had taken hold of all things. But let us leave it to the studious to work this out, and keep to the matter before us. He has prepared his throne for judgment. Another version: He has set it firm for judgment. And he himself will judge the world in righteousness; he will judge the peoples with uprightness. Do you see how he raises the discourse little by little? Since he mentioned a throne, he shows what the throne is made of: not wood or any other material, but righteousness. In righteousness, he says, it is set. He will judge the world in righteousness. He foretells both present and future things. The universal judgment is stored up for the world to come, but a partial judgment also takes place here. God does a great deal even now, so that the senseless will not think the world is without providence. If not everyone receives crowns here, do not be surprised. He has appointed a day on which he will judge the world. The present is a stadium, a contest, a series of wrestling bouts. That is why not everyone receives what they deserve here. For those who succeed, the gifts are stored up there, and for those who fall, the punishments. Here there is forbearance and long-suffering, so that we may wash away our sins through repentance, but not there. A murderer, as long as he is still on the road, is free to change and escape punishment. But once he comes under the judge's sentence, what remains is the sword, the executioner, and the pit. So it is here. As long as we are in this present life, we can escape punishment by changing. But once we have departed there, we shall lament to no purpose. For he has prepared his throne for judgment. If anyone takes "prepared" in the sense just given, he will not be wrong. Everything has been made ready: the punishments, the crowns, the verdict. With God there is no delay, no lapse of time, no slowness, when the living will not go ahead of those who have fallen asleep. As Paul says: We who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord, will by no means go ahead of those who have fallen asleep. He will judge the peoples with uprightness. See the Prophet's wisdom, how he speaks of the present and how of the future. Of the present: You rebuked the nations, and the ungodly man perished. Of the future: He has prepared his throne for judgment, and he himself will judge the world in righteousness. He does this so that those who do not believe the future things may take proof from the present ones. And the Lord became a refuge for the poor. Another version: For the [?]. [Colbert manuscript: "…is the mother, and will rescue man from death, and of God." …"and will rescue man from death."]

…to be. For the one who helps gives his help to someone who is working. So we must not lie back, but bring our own supplication, our almsgiving, and everything we can contribute. Allies help those who fight, not those who lie back and do nothing. If you want to enjoy God's alliance, then, never fail to do your own part. That is how Job was helped: standing and fighting it out. So were the apostles, because they were active. And let those who know your name hope in you. Another version: And they will trust. The Prophet does this constantly. He turns his discourse from prayer to exhortation, being the common teacher of the whole world, and he sets the treasure of the philosophic life before everyone. He put it well: Let those who know your name hope in you. Those who know you, he says, and know your support and alliance, have their hope in you as a sufficient anchor, a sufficient ally, and an unbreakable tower. This hope not only promises release from troubles; it does not even let a person be shaken while the troubles are still present. Whoever is free of human supports and hangs his whole self on the hope from above not only brings on a very swift release from his troubles, but is not even disturbed or agitated while he is in them, because the hope of that anchor helps him. So the three youths were not only delivered from the furnace; even while they were in the furnace they were not disturbed. They knew the help that came from God. That is why another translator says, And they will trust, meaning "they will take courage." The security that comes from hope in God is far greater than release from troubles [?]. The one is human; the other is divine and unconquerable. Having said that God became a helper and a refuge, he shows how this comes about. How does it come about? When we keep hoping in him continually. And if he does not end the troubles at once, this too is for your testing. Though he could keep troubles from coming, he lets them come, in order to make you firmer. In the same way, though he could end them at the very start, he delays and puts it off again. He is stretching your endurance, training your hope, and making your love for him more earnest. He does not let us be afflicted all the time, so that we will not grow weary, nor be at ease all the time, so that we will not grow slack. For you have not forsaken those who seek you, Lord. Another version: For you did not forsake. So too another writer says: Look at the generations of old and see: who ever hoped in the Lord and was put to shame? Or who called on him, and he forsook him? Someone asks: "And how is God sought, when he is everywhere?" With zeal and eagerness, and by being freed from all the cares of this life. We fail to notice many things we have before our eyes and in our hands. We often go around looking for what we are already holding, when our mind is turned to something else. How, then, is it possible to seek God? When we strain our mind toward him, when we are freed from the cares of this life. For the one who seeks, having cast everything out of his soul, [?]. By saying "He did not forget," he showed that continually each [?]. [Colbert manuscript: "but rather to the meek." The reading of the printed edition above…]

…those men were calling, and did not obtain it at the outset. What, then, are you saying? Do not think that God forgot, and that this is why he did not intervene. It is his own nature to look into such matters even when no one appeals to him, and much more so when people appeal to him and are lowly. Have mercy on me, Lord; see my humiliation at the hands of my enemies, you who lift me up from the gates of death, so that I may declare all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion. Another version: Your hymns. Another: Your praises. See how he stays fixed on prayer all the time. Even after being freed from his troubles and reaching safety, he does not stop praying again. He says, Have mercy on me, and appeals to God about the future too. We always need God's providence, but especially when we have been freed from evils. Another war follows, harder than the first: the war of slackness and of arrogance. At that point the devil blows more violently. So it is above all after being freed from evils that we need that help from God's hand, so that we may bear our prosperity well. Even the Jews, once freed from the Egyptians, were in a hard war, against arrogance and slackness. In fact that was when most of them died, because they could not command themselves well. They did not stand firm and noble against gluttony or faint-heartedness, but copied the passions of the Egyptians, and this destroyed them. David too, once freed from the troubles Saul caused him and from his other enemies, faced a harder war when he came to enjoy ease: the war of licentious desire, which punished him more severely. That is why we must be most afraid when we have been freed from our troubles. 7. We do not fear a wild beast that is tied up as much as one that has been let loose. In the same way, we need not fear vice so much in affliction, because then it is bound by despondency and other bonds. It is after ease comes that we must fear it. That is why you will often see good fortune doing more harm than evils do. So Hezekiah, after his victory, was about to perish. This is why David says elsewhere: It is good for me that you humbled me. And after his release he seeks mercy again, putting forward his sufferings as his claim to mercy: See my humiliation at the hands of my enemies. And another claim: You who lift me up from the gates of death. "I flee to my protector and guardian, who always holds out his hand to me." Do you see how, while asking for things to come, he gives thanks for what is past, and speaks of a double benefit? He did not say, "who frees me from the gates of death," but "who lifts me up." God's kindness did not stop at ending their troubles; it made them admired, glorious, more illustrious, exalted. And he did not say "from the gate" but "from the gates," pointing to the great number of dangers. So that I may declare all your praises in the gates [?]. …executing judgments. Another version: Judgment was made known [?]. That is: punishing, avenging, prosecuting. Do you see another kind of benefit, the kind that comes from punishment? For not only… [Colbert manuscript: "were calling at the outset." Patrologia Graeca 55.]

…he says, does it make those who are punished more earnest; it also makes the knowledge of God shine out. One can see that God turns people to himself more by this means. When he let the herd of pigs rush down the cliffs and be drowned in the sea, that was when people were most astonished. And in the Old Testament, the Jews: When he slew them, then they sought him, as the Prophet says. Then why does he not do this more often? Because he wants virtue to be achieved by free choice rather than by force, and by people receiving his kindness rather than his punishment. Someone asks: "But how much better is it to be good by necessity than evil by choice?" It is not possible to be good by necessity. Someone who becomes good because he is in chains will not stay good; once released from necessity, he will go back to vice. But someone trained to become good by choice stays firm once he has become so. In the works of his own hands the sinner was caught. He did not say "of God's hands," but "of the sinner's hands." 8. Do you see how he varies his discourse, presenting the punishment that comes from above and adding the penalty that comes from vice itself? Where is the punishment from above? The Lord is known, he says, executing judgments. Where is the penalty from vice? The nations are stuck fast in the destruction they made. And again the penalty from wickedness: In the works of his own hands the sinner was caught. He does not speak only of the punishment from God, since God often delays and is slow to act. Nor does he speak only of the penalty from vice, since many people even enjoy lingering in it. Instead he secures his argument on both sides. So he says: In the works of his own hands he was caught. Another version: Of his [?]. So do not think that you are building traps for someone else when you plot against him. You are weaving the nets for yourself. Song; diapsalma. Another version: Sound forever. Another: Melody forever. The Hebrew: Higgaion selah. Let the sinners be turned back into Hades, all the nations that forget God. Another version: They will return. Again he dwells on the same point, showing that punishment comes allotted together with vice, that ungodliness gives birth to death, and sin to dangers. For the poor man will not be forgotten to the end; the endurance of the needy will not perish to the end. Another translator says: For the expectation of the meek will not be forgotten to the end. He rightly said "to the end," showing that one should not seek ease all the time. Where would endurance be shown, if there were always going to be ease? What he means is this: the wicked will pay the penalty and suffer the worst. God will not allow the wronged to be beset by plots forever. In this way he both consoles the one group and frightens the other, and he shows God's love for humanity: God's delay makes some people more tested and proven, and draws others to repentance. [?] again the poor being held in honor; not simply the poor, but those broken in heart. These… [?: "…fits."]

…in prosperity. But if you punish them now, they will have their fear at its height and the memory of the troubles that befell them; then even if they come into prosperity, they will know their own nature. 9. Do you see how he prays on their behalf and asks that their madness be cured? Not to know oneself is worse than the most extreme madness and frenzy. Madness is a disease that comes by necessity; self-ignorance comes from a corrupted will. Why, Lord, do you stand far off? Why do you look away in times of need, in afflictions? The Prophet says this speaking in the person of the afflicted. He is appealing and begging, not accusing. God forbid! Many of the afflicted, because of their pain, ask for judgment before the proper time. In the same way, people undergoing surgery beg the doctor to take his hand away before the cutting is finished. The favor they ask for would harm them, but they ask it because they cannot bear the pain. They often cry out to their doctors, "You have tortured me, you have destroyed me, you have killed me!" These words come not from their mind but from their pain. So too many faint-hearted people talk like this in their afflictions, because they cannot bear the hardships. Zephaniah also takes up an argument of this kind. But these things belong to the Old Testament, when the contests were of moderate size; such words are far from the philosophy of the New. While the ungodly man is arrogant, the poor man is set on fire; they are caught in the schemes they devise. Another version: Let them be caught. For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wrongdoer is blessed. The sinner has provoked the Lord. The Prophet takes on the role of a suppliant. Appealing for the wronged, he also speaks of the feelings they suffer, which come from human weakness: before the punishment and retribution arrive, the wronged person is in pain, unable to bear the prosperity of the wicked. And this is no small punishment in itself. Then he asks that the wicked pay the penalty and that their plots be turned back on themselves, and he names a form of vice that is unbearable. What is it? That the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul. For the very things that should make him hide his face, the very things, he says, that should make him ashamed, he is admired and praised. How could this be cured any longer, when vice is praised? This happens even now. So-and-so is admired as a powerful man; so-and-so for taking revenge on his enemies; so-and-so as shrewd, because he has gathered everyone's property into his hands. And when he ruins himself, they say, "He has found himself." Others say other things, and they have nothing to say about spiritual matters. Nowhere is the man who keeps clear of business quickly praised, or the lover of poverty. It is the moneymaker, the huckster, the flatterer, the one who submits to slavish services for nothing of any use.
