This is what the Prophet laments: that vice has gained such power that it even glories in itself and speaks boldly. Worse still, it is not ashamed. It not only praises itself for what it does, but also has others to praise it. What could be worse than this madness? The sinner has provoked the Lord. Another translator says: For the lawless man boasted according to the desire of his soul, and the covetous man [?]. [Colbert manuscript: "of the blow." Colbert manuscript, in the text: "when he will destroy him." Savile, in the margin: "cutting"; "when he destroyed him."]

…he says this about the man who had committed fornication: "And you are puffed up, and did you not rather mourn?" A sinner ought to be mourned deeply, not praised. Do you see how perverse wickedness is, that it is not only not accused but even applauded? From this, from his own folly and from the praises, he intensified his wickedness and forgot the fear of God and his judgments. From this he forgot even his own nature. For the one who forgets the judgments of God in time comes to ignore even himself. See, then, how he reasons: "I shall not be shaken from generation to generation; I shall be free from harm." What could be more senseless than this thought? He is a human being, perishable, tangled up in passing affairs and subject to countless changes, and he imagines such things! Where does this come from? From folly. When a foolish man enjoys great prosperity, overpowers his enemies, and is praised and admired, he becomes the most wretched of all. Because he does not expect any change, he does not bear his prosperity with moderation, and when he falls into adversity, untrained and unpracticed as he is, he is thrown into turmoil and confusion. But Job was not like this. Even in prosperity he expected adversity every day, and so he said: "For the fear that I feared has come upon me, and what I dreaded has met me. I was not at peace, I was not quiet, I had no rest, and wrath came upon me." That is why another also said: "Remember the time of famine in the time of plenty, poverty and want in the day of wealth." But this man, corrupted once for all, gives no thought to the human condition. Because of his good fortune he thinks his affairs cannot be moved, and this is the ground of utter folly and corruption and the occasion of ruin. So do not call the rich blessed, or those who get the better of their enemies, or those who are praised for these things. For to the unwary these are great pits and precipices, which hurl them down to the very bottom of impiety. "His mouth is full of cursing and bitterness and deceit; under his tongue are trouble and toil." Another version: "Uselessness." "He sits in ambush with the rich in secret places, to kill the innocent." Another: "Lying in ambush by the courtyards." "His eyes are fixed on the poor. He lies in ambush in secret like a lion in his den." Another: "As in his enclosure." "He lies in wait to seize the poor, to seize the poor when he drags him off." Another: "[?] in his [?]." "In his snare he will humble him." Another: "In the dragnet." "[?] and he will fall when he has lorded it over the poor." Another: "And the crushed one will be bowed down, when he falls with his mighty ones upon the…"

Do you see that he has even become a wild beast? The Prophet speaks of him as if he were sketching a wild beast, putting his deceits, his ambushes and his plots on display. What could be more wretched than this man, what poorer, when he needs the money of the poor? Tell me, then, shall we call him rich? Then we must call the thief and the housebreaker rich too. "Away with that," someone says. For even if he does not break through [?] law courts [?]. For what does it matter if he does not come by night, when by deceit he puts out the judge's light? For what does it matter if not while they are sleeping [?] to him. [?]

…the poor man has been left; you were the orphan's helper. Another version: "You became." Another: "You will be." What he means is this: this is your work, your special task. And he would not have neglected what was his own, or betrayed it. Building belongs to the craftsman, steering the ship to the helmsman, and giving light to the sun; in the same way it is yours to protect orphans and to stretch out a hand to the poor. No one else is their protector like this; only you are. That is what "has been left" shows. No one else, he says, but you alone are the protector of orphans and the poor. "Break the arm of the sinner and the wicked man; [?] his sin will be sought out, and it will not be found because of it." Another: "Let his impiety be sought out, so that he himself may not be found." He does not simply ask that the sinner be crushed. He asks that his strength be crushed, his power, the fuel of his wickedness. Then he asks that he be called to account and give a reckoning for what he has done. And to show how great the injustice is, he says: if this happens, he will not even be able to stand, nor will he appear; he will perish, he will be gone, he will be wiped out root and all, once his deeds are examined. So let no one lament being an orphan, and let no one lament poverty. The more these increase, the more God's help will grow. And let no one be arrogant or puffed up because of power. This is a slippery and precipitous place, and it overturns the unwary with great ease. "The Lord will reign forever, and for ever and ever." Here he answers those who are troubled and disturbed because sinners do not pay the penalty at once. Why are you afraid, he says? Why do you fear? Is the judge temporary? Does his kingdom have an end? Even if he does not exact the penalty now, he certainly will. For the one who exacts it remains, and he reigns forever. "You nations will perish from his land. You have heard the desire of the poor, O Lord; your ear has attended to the readiness of their heart." Another: "Your ear has heard the purpose of their heart." Another: "You will prepare their hearts; your ear will attend." "To judge for the orphan and the humble, so that man on earth may no longer go on boasting." Another: "To judge for the orphan and the crushed." Do you see that the prophet gives the greater part of his words to care for the wicked? For it is they above all who suffer harm. The one who is wronged loses money, but the other is in danger concerning the ultimate things. And what if they do not perceive the sickness they are in? That is the height of insensibility, and for this very reason they deserve the most pity. This is the mark of an immature mind. Children too pay no attention to things that are really frightening; they often even put their hands into fire, yet empty masks terrify them and they tremble at the sight. The greedy are like them. They fear poverty, which is not frightening at all but is rather a ground of security, while they set great store by unjust wealth and greed, which is more frightening than any fire. Greed is an evil everywhere. So the Prophet urges that it be cut out altogether. He threatens, he frightens, and he calls on God to rise up and punish such callousness. That is why he goes on to say: "You nations will perish from his land," [threatening] them with utter destruction…

…do you make [me do], because of the war waged by sinners? Besides what has been said, I have this further reason for not fleeing. When God is the one who helps, and those who make war are sinners, how can the one who advises me to imitate the timidity of birds not earn the utmost shame? Do you not see how the army drawn up against me is flimsier than a spider's web? If the enemy of an earthly king lives in danger wherever he goes, afraid and trembling, much more so does the enemy of the God of all. Wherever he goes, he has everything against him, even creation itself. Just as the elements and the wild beasts fear God's friends, and all creation reveres them, so even senseless things make war on his enemy and foe and spurn him. That is why in those days the beasts tore some apart before they reached the ground, and the fire consumed others. But they have bows and a quiver, and everything is ready for them: "For they have prepared them," he says, "in the quiver." Yet none of this has any strength, and nothing here frightens us. Even if I saw a feeble man holding a bow, I would not be afraid. What use are weapons when there is no strength behind them? Neither are they of any use here, when God's favor is absent. But they stitch together deceits and do not come at us openly. This is the main reason I laugh at them: they shoot in the dark of the moon. Nothing is weaker than a man who plots. He does not need to be caught by anyone else's weapons. He falls by his own hand and is overturned by his own deceit. What could be weaker than a man caught by his own devices? Besides all this, there is something else to say: sinners make war, and with deceit, not only on those whom God helps, but also on the blameless, who have done them no wrong. And this too makes them weak in no ordinary way. Those who kick against the goads do the goads no harm and only bloody their own feet, and so it is with these men. Besides all this, there is yet another cause that dissolves the strength of their war. What is it? "What you established," he says, "they tore down." What he means is this: they war and fight against you, tearing down your law and your commandments. They attempt to tear down your commandments, even though these are firmly established. Either he means this, or that they are transgressors of the law. And this too is no small ground of weakness: to go to war like this without having kept your commandments. For this is why they war against the upright and stitch together deceits: because they do not listen to your commandments.

2. So he has described the weakness of the enemy, and he has shown it not from the things others would point to but from the things that were fitting for him. He did not say that they have no money, or fortresses, or allies, or cities, or that they are inexperienced in war. He passed over all these and spurned them as nothing, and said that they are lawless, that they make war on those who have done no wrong, that they tear down the things of God. Now he goes on to speak of the battle line of the righteous, and from this too he shows how easily the enemy is overcome. Let us also judge the strong and the weak in this way, and not by the standards of the ridiculous among men [?]. Another version: "He who loves injustice hates his own soul." [?]

…those who harm. Do you see how easy this alliance is? There is no need to go anywhere, or run, or spend money, since God is present everywhere and does all things. "He will rain snares upon sinners; fire and sulfur and a stormy wind are the portion of their cup. For the Lord is righteous and has loved righteousness; his face has beheld uprightness." Another version: "He will rain coals upon the lawless." Another: "Their face will see uprightness," that is, the face of the righteous, or of God himself. He has spoken of the punishment that comes from wickedness itself. But since many think little of that, he next shakes the minds of the wicked with the blow that comes from above. He uses vivid language and fearsome words. He says that [snares], sulfur, stormy wind and coals will rain on them from above. By the metaphor in these words he wants to show that the retribution cannot be escaped, that the punishment is abundant, that the blow falls easily, and that it consumes.

3. What does "the portion of their cup" mean? This is their lot, he says, this is their possession; in this they will dwell, and by these they will be consumed. Then comes the reason: the one who oversees all things will not allow these things to pass unpunished. Another prophet [?] says the same: "Your eye is too pure to look on evil, and you cannot look upon toil." This prophet makes the same point when he says: "For the Lord is righteous and has loved righteousness." This above all is God's distinctive trait: to approve what is just and upright. He would not tolerate forever what is done otherwise. That is why at the beginning of the psalm he said: "In the Lord I have put my trust; how will you say to my soul, Flee to the mountains like a sparrow?" Those who trust in worldly things are no better off than the sparrow, which relies on solitude and so becomes easy prey for everyone. Such is the man who hopes in money. The sparrow is caught by children, by birdlime, by snares and by countless other things, and in the same way the rich man is caught by his own household and by his enemies. He lives more dangerously than the bird, for he has many who lay lime for him, and before them his own wicked desires. He is a fugitive, always shifting with the times, fearing the anger of executioners, the king's wrath, the plots of flatterers and the deceits of friends. When enemies attack, he trembles more than anyone, and when there is peace he suspects plotters, for the wealth he has is neither lasting nor secure. So he is always flying and migrating, seeking out deserts and mountains, living in moonless darkness, finding thick darkness at midday, and stitching together deceits. But the righteous man is not like this. For the paths of the righteous shine like light. They do not choose to plot, nor to do wrong; their souls are at ease. But these men, always stitching deceits, are always in darkness and fear, like robbers, housebreakers and adulterers. Even by day they see darkness, because fear strikes their souls. How, then, might this darkness be dispersed? If he removes himself from all these things [and clings] to hope in God, even if ten thousand times… [?] In this reading, "their face" instead of "his face" [?]. "and by those."

…he takes refuge in God's providence, saying: "Save me, O Lord." By this he shows nothing other than this: I need the hand from above, the help from heaven, that alliance. For since I am walking the road opposite to everyone else, I need a great deal of providence. And he did not say, "Save me, because there has been no holy man," but "because the holy man has failed," showing that even those who did exist were lost, since wickedness prevailed and the disease won out. Paul fears the same thing when he says: "Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump?" And again: "Bad company corrupts good morals." What does "Truths have diminished" mean? There are many truths. With colors and other kinds of things, some are true and some false. There is true purple and false purple, and the same goes for saffron, for stones, for spices and for other such things. So it is with the virtues too. For truth is what truly is, and falsehood is what is not. These things had been perverted and obscured. They had not lost their substance of their own accord; men had driven them out. That is why he did not say only, "Truths have diminished," but added "from the sons of men," wishing to show this very point. Consider: there is true adornment and there is false. What, then, is true adornment? The adornment of the soul. And the false? That of the body. There is true wealth and false wealth. Money is false wealth; good deeds are true wealth. There is a false joy and a true one, and the same holds for beauty, power and glory. But most people abandon what is true in these things and pursue what is false. Just as there is a true man and a false one, the true being the one who lives and acts, the false the one who is painted, so with the virtues too there is…

2. "Each one spoke vain things to his neighbor; with deceitful lips, in heart and in heart they spoke evil." Another version says: "He speaks with one heart and another." He names two evils here: that they spoke vain things, and that they spoke them to their neighbor. By "vain things" he means either falsehoods or what is superfluous and useless. Paul says something similar: "Do not lie to one another." What is worse, everyone was corrupted. That is why he did not say "so-and-so and so-and-so" but "each one." The wickedness was not merely on the surface; it was deep-rooted and came from the heart. "In heart and in heart," which another translator rendered "with one heart and another," teaches that their hearts were full of duplicity. This is more bitter than any enemy. Enemies are open and evident, and so they are easy to guard against. But these men put forward one mask while being something else, and so the people they plot against find them hard to detect. They are far worse than men who hide swords. "May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips and the boastful tongue, those who said, We will magnify our tongue." Another version: "We will prevail." "Our lips are our own." Another: "Are with us." "Who is lord over us?" Another: "Who will lord it over us?" Do you see the Prophet's concern, how he prays for them? For the [?] is not against them [?]. [?] and with saffron [?]. being others [?]; and being something else, and so reads [?].

…in salvation; I will act boldly in it." Another version: "I will set manifest salvation." Learn how great the strength of humility is. The power of the poor (by the poor I mean those who are crushed in spirit) lies in the help that their suffering of wrong brings them. Here he does not speak of their way of life or their virtue. It is their suffering of wrong, he says, that rouses God and calls him out to avenge and defend them. Such is the worth of bearing wrong nobly, such is God's providence for the abused, that misfortune and the suffering of wrong serve in place of the greatest advocacy. Great is the strength of a groan, for it summons help from above. Be afraid, all you who wrong the poor. You have power, riches, money and the favor of judges. But they have a weapon stronger than all of these: their groans and laments, and the very fact that they are wronged, and these draw down an alliance from heaven. This weapon has dug up houses, razed foundations, destroyed cities and drowned whole nations. I mean the groans of people who are wronged. God respects their good grace when, though suffering wrong, they utter no evil word but only groan and lament their troubles. What does "I will set in salvation; I will act boldly in it" mean? I will stand up for them boldly, he says, openly and plainly, so that everyone may learn of it. And when does he not save openly? Sometimes he saves not openly but in secret, for he has no need of glory from men. But in this case it was likely that their enemies would trample on them, leap on them and taunt them for having no God to help them. So that the enemies too might be chastened and become better, learning by experience the Master's alliance, he says: "I will make their salvation manifest." "The words of the Lord are pure words, silver refined by fire, tested in the earth." What connection does this have with what was said before? A close and continuous one. Do not think, he says, that these things were said idly, or that the threat is empty. His words are pure and free from falsehood. Silver refined by fire contains nothing foreign or counterfeit, and so it is with the words of God: whatever he says must certainly come to pass. That is why he says: "Silver refined by fire, tested in the earth." Another version: "Refined, flowing into the earth." And the Hebrew, in place of "flowing into the earth," said "Baalil laares" [?], that is, what is smelted, what flows in the earth. "Purified sevenfold."

4. Do you see how he shows by the image of the metal that God's word is free from falsehood and true? Metal that has been smelted and refined by fire, and has gone through this many times, is free from any foreign matter and carefully purified. So is the pronouncement of God. "You, O Lord, will guard us and preserve us from this generation and forever." Another version: "You will guard them." Another: "You will guard these things, and preserve us from this generation and forever." Another: "Together with the eternal generation." "The ungodly walk around in a circle." [?]

[?]… we do not even give away what is surplus to us; living in abundance, we neglect the saints. Again the earth brought forth for another friend of God so many gifts from its own bosom, so great a harvest, as never before. And why do you wonder that they themselves were held in reverence, when even their garments and their shadows were fearsome to demons, to death and to disease? Angels, too, revered human beings and honored them beyond measure. For how [?] would they not honor the friends of their Master? This can be seen in both the Old and the New Testament. That is why he says: "In keeping with your height you have cared greatly for the sons of men." So, considering how great this honor is, let us make a worthy return for it, so that the very greatness of the honor does not become provision for our punishment. May we all be delivered from that punishment, both those who teach these things and those who learn them, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong all glory, honor and worship, to the ages of ages. Amen.

ON PSALM 12. To the end, a psalm of David. Another version: A victory song of David. Another: For victory. "How long, O Lord, will you forget me to the end?" Another: "Will you forget me completely?" "How long will you turn your face away from me?" Another: "hide." "How long shall I take counsel in my soul?" Another: "set plans." "Pains in my heart day and night." Another: "Anxiety in my mind every day." 1. This too is no small good: to become aware that God has forgotten you. But do not suppose that forgetting is a passion in God; take it to mean abandonment. Many people suffer this, yet they do not even know it and do not lament. But this blessed man not only knew it but also counted the time. "How long" is what someone says when he is showing that the time has been long, and so he laments and mourns. Notice how he never grieves over anything of this life, not over money, not over glory, but always over God's goodwill. "And how," someone asks, "did he know that God had forgotten him?" Because he also knew when God remembered him, and he understood clearly what forgetting is and what remembering is. He was not like most people, who think God remembers them when they are rich, when they are well thought of by others, when everything goes their way, when they get the better of their enemies. That is why they do not know when he forgets them either. Those who do not know the sign of remembrance do not understand the sign of forgetting either, and if they do not recognize the tokens of friendship, they do not recognize those of enmity either. In fact God forgets many who have these things, and these especially; but of others [?]. For when he provides and cares and is despised for it, he lets go for a little and abandons them, so that once their laziness has been driven out, the careless may become more earnest. "Look upon me," he says, "see the enemy exalted over me. If not because of my wretchedness, then because of his arrogance and folly, hear

me." And what are you asking for? To overcome your enemies? He does not say that. He asks that the eyes of the heart be enlightened, that the darkness be driven away which has been poured over the discerning power of my soul and has darkened the eye of the mind. "This is what I ask: Enlighten my eyes. Lest my enemy ever say," when he sees me brought down into the death of sin, "'I have prevailed against him.'" I have overpowered him; what I wanted to see has happened to me. What does "I have prevailed against him" mean? That even if he is not strong in himself, he has become strong against me. Our defeat clothes him in strength and makes him appear strong, mighty and invincible. 2. You see that when we sin, we not only shame ourselves, destroy ourselves and throw ourselves into death; we also proclaim our enemies, by whom we are defeated, to be mighty and powerful. And not only that: we also put them in a state of exultation and gladness. Alas, what folly, what madness, to fight on our enemies' side against ourselves, and to give those who grieve and afflict our [?] reason to rejoice and exult! See how many absurdities there are. We ought to conquer the enemy (for "his swords have failed utterly, and the ungodly man has perished"), we ought to conquer, and instead we are defeated. And not only that: we make him appear mighty and strong. Nor does our madness, the symptom of the worst disease, stop even there; we also furnish him with gladness and exultation. Truly sin is the extreme of drunkenness and the ultimate evil. "They will exult if I am shaken." The prophet brings forward three pleas to move the Master to look upon him, turn his face toward him and hear his prayer: the might and strength of the enemies; before that, their exaltation and arrogance; and third, their gladness and exultation. He is all but saying: "Even if you do not turn your face toward me, Lord, for the sake of my prayer and my wretchedness, then at least do it because of the arrogance of my enemies, because they think so highly of their strength, because they gloat over my misfortunes and laugh at my fall. Hear me, enlighten my eyes. Take away the deep sleep that lies over my sins, in which I slept a little and nodded off toward the death of the soul. For if I am merely shaken from my safety, they count it as joy, boasting and strength; they pride themselves on it and become unbearable. But if I am brought down to death, what would they not do?" Do you see how the prophet regards it as the greatest loss, no less than punishment and retribution, to gladden the common enemy, to let him appear strong and seem exalted? For if he had not considered these the greatest and most unbearable evils, he would not have put them forward to entreat God and to win his favor. Let us do the same: let us take care and strive not to exalt the enemy, not to make him appear strong, not to gladden him, but on the contrary to make him humble, [Note:] Bible: "those who afflict me will exult."

I dedicate this to the benefits I have received, not only singing it now and turning over his kindnesses in my thoughts, but also in time to come [?]. "And I will sing praise to the name of the Lord," carrying the greatness of his kindness in my soul, never to be forgotten. Such a soul, then, not only is easily rescued from its troubles when it has fallen into them, but also becomes more secure against falling into similar ones again. For when it always keeps the kindness in memory, it clearly also keeps in memory the hardships from which it was set free when it received that kindness. And keeping the memory of those evils, it reflects carefully on where they came from and for what cause it was brought into such trouble. Having reflected, it then walls itself in on every side so as not to be swept into similar disasters again. Thus it orders and trains its own life well and gives abundant thanks to its deliverer, and as it found him a deliverer, so it asks to have him as its guardian always in the future. Let us imitate this soul too. If we slip into some sin, let us quickly come to our senses and make the fall an occasion of safety and a starting point for sinning no more. How will you do this? You have David as your teacher. Have you sinned? Do not doze over the sin; rise up. Consider at once that God has turned his face away from you, that he has forgotten you. Then weep, groan, "wash your bed every night" with tears, leap away from the workers [?] … good things, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom [?] … glory and might to the ages [?] … they doubted [?] … David. Say with him: "How long, O Lord, will you forget [?]" … it is said at the beginning: "The fast of the Jews has passed [?]"

handling the [lyre] of David itself, and bringing before you the response that we all sang today. What, then, is the response? "As the deer longs for the springs of waters, so my soul longs for you, O God." [?] … not only with words but also with our very deeds to sing this response; and below: "but so that when [?], you may consider the response to be a covenant." Likewise in no. 6: "For his love can be seen not only from this response but also from the words that follow"; and in no. 7: "Let us not, then, come in here carelessly, nor [?] hear the responses"; and below: "Only keep for me the responses of the psalms which here [?], not once, not twice, not three times, but many times," etc. A little later: "it will furnish us wealth, even if you say again, 'Blessed is the man who fears the Lord.'" And at the end: "But so that I do not seem to burden the more studious by drawing out the discourse, leaving [?] to search out the power stored up in it, I will end the discourse here, having urged you [?] not to come in here carelessly, but to take the responses like pearls and keep them, and [?]." [?]: that Thecla, in the middle of the virgins, [?], standing at the right hand of Virtue, sang with decorum, while the others stood around in a circle, as in the form of a chorus,
[?] he quotes, namely, "Blessed is the man who fears the [Lord]"; [?] another began: "As the deer longs [?] … for God, the living God; when shall I come and appear [?]"

ON PSALM 41. "As the deer longs for the springs of waters." And for what reason the psalm was brought into our life [?]; it is sung with melody. And on the long-suffering of God. 1. The other day, when we took up the discourse on Melchizedek, you were amazed at us for the length of what was said. But I was amazed at you for the eagerness and intelligence with which you listened, and because, though the discourse ran on so long, you followed us to the end. And yet the discourse was not only long but also very difficult. Still, neither its length nor its difficulty got the better of your eagerness. Come, then, let us repay you for that labor by making today's address clearer for you. For one must not always keep the minds of the hearers stretched tight (they quickly snap), nor always slacken and relax them, since that too makes them more sluggish. So the form of teaching has to be varied, and we should take up sometimes more festive discourses, sometimes more combative ones. As I said then, shepherds put down the pipe and take up the sling when wolves attack the flock. So now that the Jewish feasts are over (and the Jews are more dangerous than any wolves), let us put down the sling again and return to the pipe. Let us rest from the more combative discourses and take up some clearer ones, handling the lyre of David itself and bringing before you the response that we all sang today. What, then, is the response? "As the deer longs for the springs of waters, so my soul longs for you, O God." [?] … often each by herself, and often

all of them together sing a single melody in harmony. Women do this too, and travelers, farmers and sailors, trying to ease the toil of their work with song, because the soul can bear everything troublesome and laborious more easily if it hears melody and song. Since, then, our soul has a natural affinity for this kind of pleasure, God set up the psalms as a defense against the demons, so that they would not bring in licentious songs and overturn everything, and so that the same thing would be both a pleasure and a benefit. For secular songs bring harm and ruin and many terrible things: the more lewd and lawless of these songs settle into the parts of the soul and make it weaker and softer. But from the spiritual psalms come great gain, great benefit, great sanctification, and the foundation of all true philosophy, since the words cleanse the soul and the Holy Spirit quickly flies down upon the soul that sings such things. To see that those who sing with understanding call down the grace of the Spirit, listen to what Paul says: "Do not get drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit." And he added how this filling takes place: "singing and making melody to the Lord in your hearts." What does "in your hearts" mean? With understanding, he means, so that the mouth does not speak the words while the mind is off elsewhere, wandering everywhere, but so that the soul listens to the tongue. 2. And just as pigs run where there is mud, while bees settle where there are spices and incense, so demons crowd in where there are licentious songs, while where there are spiritual melodies the grace of the Spirit flies down and sanctifies both mouth and soul. I say this not only so that you will praise it, but so that you will teach your children and your wives to sing such songs, not only at the loom or at their other tasks, but above all at table. For since the devil mostly lies in wait at banquets, with drunkenness and gluttony as his allies, along with unruly laughter and a slackened soul, it is then above all, both before the meal and after it, that we must raise the safeguard of the psalms against him, and rising from the banquet together with wife and children, sing the sacred hymns to God. Paul had unbearable lashes laid upon him, was fastened in the stocks and lodged in prison, and yet at midnight, when sweet sleep comes over everyone most heavily, he went on singing hymns to God with Silas. Neither the place, nor the hour, nor his anxiety, nor the tyranny of sleep, nor the pain of those sufferings, nor anything else at all could force him to give up the melody. How much more ought we, who are rejoicing and enjoying God's good things, to send up hymns of thanksgiving to him, so that if drunkenness and gluttony bring anything improper into our soul, then, when the psalmody comes in, all those improper and wicked thoughts may leap away. And just as many rich people fill a sponge with balsam and wipe their tables with it, so that if any [?] from the food … [?] reads by conjecture: "and brings them to completion (namely, the commands of the Spirit), thus performing the best and most wonderful song, so you will accomplish," etc.

3. It is possible to sing even without a voice, while the mind sounds within. For we do not sing to human beings but to God, who can hear even hearts and enter into the hidden places of our mind. Paul shows this when he cries out: "The Spirit himself intercedes for us with groans too deep for words. And he who searches the hearts knows what the mind of the Spirit is, because he intercedes for the saints according to God." He said this not because the Spirit groaned, but because spiritual men, who had the gifts of the Spirit, did this with compunction and groaning when they prayed for their neighbors and offered up supplications. Let us do this too, and every day intercede with God through psalms and prayers. And so that we do not offer only the words, but also understand the power of the sayings themselves, come, let us bring before you the opening of the psalm. What, then, is the opening? "As the deer longs for the springs of waters, so my soul longs for you, O God." This is the way of lovers: they do not keep their love silent but bring it out to those around them and tell them that they love. For love is by nature a hot thing, and the soul cannot bear to contain it in silence. That is why Paul too, out of love for the Corinthians, said: "Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians." That is: I cannot contain my love and keep it silent; I carry you about always and everywhere, both in my mind and on my tongue. So too this blessed man, loving God and burning in his love, cannot bear to be silent. At one time he says: "As the deer longs for the springs of waters, so my soul longs for you, O God"; at another: "O God, my God, I rise early to you. My soul has thirsted for you like a land trackless, waterless and desert." For that is how another of the translators put it. Since he cannot present his love in words, he goes about looking for an image, so that in this way at least he may show us his affection and make us sharers in his love. Let us, then, follow him and learn to love like this. And let no one say to me, "How can I love God, whom I do not see?" We love many people without seeing them, such as friends of ours who are abroad, or children and fathers, or relatives and kin. Not seeing them is no hindrance; on the contrary, this very thing most of all kindles affection and increases longing. That is why Paul, speaking of Moses, says that he left behind treasures, wealth, royal splendor and all the other brilliance of Egypt, and chose to be mistreated along with the Jews. Then, teaching us the reason, that he did all this for God's sake, he added: "For he endured as seeing him who is invisible." You do not see God, but you see what he has created; you see his works, heaven and earth and sea. And someone in love is warmed through whenever he sees something his beloved has made, or a sandal, or a cloak, or anything else at all. You do not see God, but you see his servants, his friends, his saints

[?] "and has not entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him." And again: "O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and how untraceable his ways!" But what words could set forth the love he has shown toward us? John was astonished at this and said: "For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son." And if you want to hear his own words and learn of his longing, listen to what he says through the prophet: "Will a woman forget to have mercy on the offspring of her womb? Even if a woman should forget these, yet I will not forget you." And just as this man said, "As the deer longs for the springs of waters, so my soul longs for you, O God," so Christ too says: "As a bird gathers her own chicks, so I wanted to gather your children, and you would not." And again: "As a father has compassion on his sons, so the Lord has had compassion on those who fear him." And again: "For as high as heaven is above the earth, so the Lord has made his mercy strong over those who fear him." And just as the prophet looks for an image to show his own longing, so God too uses certain images to make known to us the love he has for our salvation. The prophet spoke of a thirsting deer and a parched land; God spoke of birds' affection for their young, of fathers' care, of the height of heaven above the earth, and of mothers' tenderness. This is not because he loves only as much as a mother loves her child, but because among us there are no greater proofs of love than these standards, measures and images. To see that he loves us not merely as much as an affectionate mother loves her children, but far more, listen to what he says: "For even if a woman should forget her offspring," he says, "yet I will not forget you." He said this to show that his longing for us is warmer than any affection. Gather all these things together and reflect on them within yourself, and you will make your love warm and kindle a bright flame. Since even among us human beings nothing usually kindles friendship so much as remembering the kindnesses we have received, let us do the same with God. Let us count up how much he has done for us: heaven itself, the earth, the sea, the air, the plants on the earth and the many-colored flowers, the cattle and the creeping things, the creatures in the sea and those in the middle air, the stars in heaven, the sun, the moon, in short everything that is seen, the lightning, the good order of the seasons, the succession of day and night, the yearly turnings of the year. He breathed a soul into us, granted us reason, and honored us with the greatest authority. He sent angels, dispatched prophets, and at last his only-begotten Son. And after all that he himself still pleads with you, both by himself and through his only-begotten Child, that you may be saved. And Paul never stops serving as his ambassador: "As though God were making his appeal through us, we beg you on Christ's behalf, be reconciled

…our sins. If we cleanse away our wickedness, we will be able to see clearly into spiritual longing. We will call on God with great eagerness and kindle our love more fiercely, and we will sing this response not only with words but with our very deeds. That is why that blessed man sang the psalms for us, or rather the grace of the Spirit did: not so that we should only say the words, but so that we should practise them in our very deeds. So do not think you come in here only to say the words. When you sing the response, consider it a covenant. When you say, "As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God," you have made a compact with God. You have written a bond without paper or ink. With your own voice you have confessed that you love him more than all things, that you prefer nothing to him, and that you burn with love for him. So if you go out and see some beautiful, wanton woman who entices you and calls you to love her, say to her: "I cannot follow you. I made a covenant with God in the presence of the brethren, the priests and the teachers. In the response I confessed and promised to love him like this: As the deer longs for the springs of water. I am afraid to break the covenant. From now on it is his love that I practise." If you see silver lying in the marketplace, or golden garments, or others strutting about with servants and horses with golden bridles, do not be moved by that show. Instead, sing a charm over yourself again and say to your soul: "A little while ago we sang the response, As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God. We took the text to ourselves and made it our own." So let us love none of these worldly things, so that that love may stay pure in us and not grow weaker by being divided. This wealth will be able to give us all wealth, all treasure, all good repute, all glory, all distinction. Let us gain this, and we will need nothing else. Think of those who love with this shameful love, often burning for some beautiful girl. Their fathers threaten, their friends reproach them, many others slander them, yet they do not even turn back. They stay turned towards her. They despise home, their father's inheritance, glory, reputation and the advice of friends, and they think they have ample consolation for all of it if they find favour with the beloved alone, even if she is worthless, even if she is disgraced, whatever she may be. If that is so, then when will those who love God as they ought even notice human things, whether splendid or painful? Intent on that love, they will not even see the illusions of this present life. They will laugh at all prosperity and look past all adversity. They are bound fast to their longing for God and see nothing but him alone. They picture him everywhere, and they think themselves more blessed than anyone. Even in poverty, in dishonour, in chains, in afflictions, in the worst of evils, they will consider themselves better off than kings, for in all they suffer they have a wonderful consolation: they suffer these things for the sake of the one they long for. [?]

[?] suffers. And often [?] vainglory; nothing else of that kind will take hold of us. The beauty of bodies is quenched far more quickly than the things mentioned, and in short all worldly things are passing and short-lived. They leap away before they have even arrived and appeared. The love of spiritual things is the exact opposite. It is always at its height and in bloom. It knows no old age and does not grow old. It is not subject to any change, any reversal or the uncertainty of the future. It benefits those who have it here too and surrounds them on every side. When they depart from here it does not leave them, but goes abroad with them and moves on with them, and on that day it makes them brighter than the heavenly lights themselves. Blessed David knew this, and so he went on loving. He could not bear to keep his love inside, but hurried in every way to show his hearers the fire that gripped him within. For after saying, "My soul thirsted for God, the mighty, the living," he added, "When shall I come and appear before the face of God?" See how the man is burning, see how he is ablaze! He knew that when he left this world he would see God, and he would not even wait for the delay. He could not bear the postponement, and here he shows us the mind of an apostle. For the apostle groaned at the delay of his departure from here, and David felt the very same. That is why he said, "When shall I come and appear before the face of God?" Had he been some private man, poor, lowly and living in poverty, it would still have been a great thing for him to despise the present life. But it would not have been as great as it is now. Here was a king who enjoyed such luxury and shared in such glory. He had won countless victories and many wars, and he was splendid and renowned everywhere. Yet he laughed at all of it, wealth, glory and every luxury, and longed eagerly for the things to come. This belongs to a great-souled mind, to a philosophic soul given wings for heavenly love. Let us imitate him too. Let us not admire the present, so that we may admire the future. Or rather, let us admire the future, so that we may not admire the present. Suppose we dwell continually on thoughts of those things, and reflect within ourselves on the kingdom of heaven, immortality, life without end, the dance with the angels, life with Christ, that undefiled glory, and the life set free from all pain. Suppose we realise that all these things have been driven away: tears, reproaches, insults, death, despondency, toil, old age, disease, sickness, poverty, slander, widowhood, sin, condemnation, punishment, retribution, and anything else in this present life that is painful and unpleasant. And suppose we realise that in their place have come peace, gentleness, kindness, love, joy, glory, honour, splendour, and all the rest that no words can describe. Then nothing in the present will take hold of us, and we too will be able to say with the Prophet, "When shall I come and appear before the face of God?" If we are disposed like this, we will fall neither into arrogance from the splendours of life nor into despondency from its pains. No envy, no [?] [Editorial notes, partly garbled:] [?] Savile, Morel, Montfaucon [?]. "and on that day" [?]. "He cannot bear the postponement": does not endure delay. Not in Savile: "and towards the heavenly" [?] "winged" [?].

[?] Leaving it to the more diligent to pick out each response and search out the power stored in it, I will end my sermon here. I urge you, beloved, not to come in here idly, but to take the responses like pearls and keep them safe. Practise them at home continually, and say all these things to your friends and to your wives. If a passion troubles you, if desire rises up, or anger, or any other utterly irrational passion, sing them over yourself continually like a charm. Then we may enjoy great calm in the present life and obtain the eternal goods in the life to come, by the grace and loving-kindness of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom be glory, might and honour to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always, and to the ages of ages.

ON PSALM 43. To the end [?], for the sons of Korah. "O God, we have heard with our ears, our fathers have told us the work you did in their days, in days of old." Another translator says, "In the days before." Another says, "In those from the beginning." 1. The Prophet speaks this psalm, but not in his own person. He speaks in the person of the Maccabees, narrating and foretelling what would happen at that time. For that is what prophets are like: they range over all times, past, present and future. First we must say who these Maccabees were, what they suffered and what they achieved, so that what is said may become clearer from its subject. When Antiochus, called Epiphanes, invaded and ruined everything, he forced many people of that time to abandon their ancestral way of life. The Maccabees, however, held firm and were not harmed at all by those trials. When the war blew hard and they could do nothing more, they hid themselves. The apostles did this too. They did not always show themselves openly and leap into danger. Sometimes they withdrew, fleeing and hiding. But when the Maccabees had a little respite, they sprang out of the caves and peered out from their hiding places like noble young hounds. They resolved no longer to save only themselves but others as well, as many as they could. They went around the city and the whole countryside and gathered everyone they found still sound. They also won back many who had grown weary and been corrupted, persuading them to return to the ancestral law. For they said that God loves humankind and never takes away the salvation that comes through repentance. With these words they enlisted armies of brave men. For it was not for wives and children and servant girls, nor against the uprooting and enslavement of their homeland, but for the law and the [way of life?]… [Editorial notes, partly garbled:] One Regius manuscript reads: "To the end, for the sons of Korah, for understanding, a psalm." [?] Regius: "to deny the way of life." But all [?] [?] from those who betray the mysteries [?]. The same says, in place of "to dance away from the ancestral way of life", which [is] 1 Maccabees 1 [?]: "to profane the sabbaths and count them as nothing, and to consider Greek opinions the finest." Nazianzen uses the word in the same sense: "rather, through whom [?] did I dance away from a great and divine mystery?" So Savile.

…the loving-kindness of God, which their fathers also enjoyed: this is a sign of their great humility. And in this way they prepare for themselves no small ground for eagerness, for the name of God alone is enough to end countless wars. 2. "Our fathers have told us." Listen, all of you who neglect your children, who let them sing devilish songs while you neglect the divine stories. Those people were not like that. They spent their lives continually telling of God's mighty deeds, and they made a double profit. Those who had received the benefits became better by remembering them. Their descendants gained from these stories no small foundation for knowing God, and they were led to zeal for virtue. For the mouths of their parents were their books. Every conversation was full of these stories, and nothing was more delightful or more profitable. Plain accounts of events, myths and fictions often charm their hearers. These stories did so much more, for they displayed God's great kindness, his power, his wisdom and his care. They delighted the hearer, stirred him up and made him more earnest. Those who were present at the events, and those who received the account from them, passed it on by word of mouth, and for faith hearing was equal to seeing. For they believed no less than those who were present and saw for themselves, as if [?] they too had seen. This too was no small encouragement to faith for them. Let us see what they told, and whether they recall a similar case. For anyone who means to ask for something and obtain it should ask for things like the favours given to others. What I mean is this. Suppose a servant asks us for a gift. If he shows that someone else has received the same gift, he puts forward the strongest claim to receiving it himself, unless a difference spoils the example. By difference I mean a difference of person or of matter. If the one who received the gift is like the one asking, and the thing asked for is similar, the example holds [?]. But if the first deserved to receive it and the second no longer does, more entreaty is needed. I must also make my meaning clear from the Scriptures. When the Canaanite woman heard, "It is not good to take the children's bread and give it to the dogs," she said, "Yes, Lord, for even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters' table." Paul too wrote: "If others share this authority over you, do not we much more?" Here he makes the claim stronger from the difference of person. And again, writing to Philemon, he said: "The hearts of the saints have been refreshed through you, brother. So although I have great boldness in Christ to command you to do what is fitting, for love's sake I appeal to you instead." Here the example is drawn from equals. For when someone has received first, he opens a door, as it were, for the second, if the one about to ask is similar, or asks for the same things. And it is not only what has been given to others that makes an entreaty strong. Often it is also what has already been given to us ourselves. Paul did this too when he wrote to the Philippians: "Even in Thessalonica you sent help for my needs once and again." That is why many people, when they give to many, tell them not to mention it to others, so that [?]…

That is what Paul feared when he said, "If indeed, having put it on, we shall not be found naked." What money will be able to rescue the man in danger? What servants will stand by their master while he is being flogged? What houses? What precious stones? What baths will be able to scrub off the filth of sins? How long will you deceive yourselves? How long will you fail to see the truth of things and gape after dreams, while the judgment is near, at the very doors? But let us return to the matter before us. "Our fathers have told us the work you did in their days, in days of old." We too may say these words in a spiritual sense. Their fathers told them, but the grace of God has also granted us to learn of their deeds through the coming of the Spirit. How might one take these words in a spiritual sense? By applying them to the achievements of the new grace: that we were raised up to heaven, that we were counted worthy of the kingdom, that God became man and broke down the dividing wall of the barrier. But now let us turn to the history. "The work you did in their days, in days of old." He recalls an ancient story and brings forward ancient deeds. And why does he not mention something new and recent? Among human beings we naturally tell of recent things and win people over with them, since their memory grows weak. But to God all things are known, old and new alike. "For behold," it says, "you have known all things, the last and the ancient." It makes no difference whether one tells an old story or a new one, as long as it suits the subject. So what ancient story, he asks, does he mean to tell? Let us listen: "Your hand destroyed nations," he says, "and you planted them. You afflicted peoples and drove them out." Do you recognise what war he means, what victory, what trophy? Or do you still need us to explain? I think many have already grasped what is said, but for the sake of those who do not know, we must add our explanation. What trophies, then, does he recall? What achievements? Those in Egypt, those in the wilderness, and those in the land of promise; or rather, those in the land of promise. For those who came out of Egypt were not the ones who reached Palestine. They all fell in the wilderness. So when their children, those raised in the wilderness, entered Palestine, they needed no weapons, he says. They took the cities with a shout. After crossing the Jordan they brought down Jericho, the first city they came to, as though they were dancing rather than fighting. For they went out adorned with weapons, not as for battle but as for a festival and a dance. They put on their arms as ornament rather than protection. They wore the sacred vestments, and ahead of the army went… [Editorial notes, partly garbled:] [?] The Septuagint reads "have told." "Of recent things": so Savile, rightly. Morel [?]. …[so that you may not think?] the saying is [?], I wish to tell you an ancient story

that confirms what I have said. There was a certain Naaman, a Syrian. He was struck with leprosy and ashamed of his affliction, and as if his very life were at stake, he came to Palestine (for I must cut the story short), hoping to find from the prophet a release from his trouble. So he came, stood at the man's door and called for the physician. The prophet heard him but did not come out. He sent word telling him to wash in the river Jordan. Naaman would not be persuaded, since the command was a light one, heavily physical and not calling for any lofty thought. But what does he say? "I said that he would come out, lay his hand on me, call on his God and take away the leprosy." Do you see how his soul needed some visible gesture? Not to think the physician's command enough, but to need a hand as well, came from the weakness of the one being healed. Many other questions are also resolved for us by this. This is why Christ too does not always heal by a word, but also with his hand. He put his hand to a mouth and to a tongue. In some places he healed those who came to him by a word alone. In others he did everything by his will. Why, then, did he act like this? Because of the weakness of those who came to him. And so that you may learn it was because of their weakness, he praised those who did not need such things. "Truly I tell you," he says, "not even in Israel have I found such faith." For the centurion did not drag him to his house, but said that his command was enough. In Hezekiah's case nothing of this kind happens. There is only a prediction, and nothing human was brought in. For the same reason a coarser procedure was prescribed in the case of the man jealous of his wife. If you want to take this in a spiritual sense ("All these things happened to them as types," he says, "and they were written down to instruct us, on whom the ends of the ages have come"), think of the best teachers of the Church. They use the word instead of a trumpet and cast down the walls of the enemy, and the peoples are armed with the full armour of Jesus. And the number of seven days dissolves the sabbath for us in advance. For such commandments of the law were not given as primary. That is why he says about the sacrifices: "Who required these things from your hands?" And again: "Do vows and holy meat take away your sins?" And again: "Did you offer me slaughtered beasts and sacrifices in the wilderness for forty years?" And again: "Why do you bring me frankincense from Sheba, and cinnamon from a distant land?" And again: "Sacrifice and offering you did not desire." And again: "Does God desire burnt offerings and sacrifices, or that we obey him?" And: "If you had desired sacrifice, I would have given it." And again: "Good obedience is better than sacrifice." And rejecting the feasts he says: "I have hated and rejected your feasts. Take away from me…" [Editorial notes, partly garbled:] [?] reads Neeman. Another manuscript and Savile read Naiman. Colbert manuscript: "burnt offering and doves." [?]

For what has been planted becomes stable and firmly fixed. What then? Tell me, were they not removed? Were they not carried off into foreign lands? Yes, they were carried off, but not because of any weakness in the one who planted them. It was because of the wickedness of those who were planted. If their own conduct had not stood in the way, nothing would have kept them from remaining in their home. "You afflicted peoples and drove them out." Some say this refers to the Egyptians, but I think it was said of the nations as well. For he exacted punishment from them too, and so displayed his power in both ways: by destroying the enemies and by firmly establishing his own people. "For not by their sword did they inherit the land." Another translator says, "For not by their dagger did they inherit the land." "Nor did their arm save them, but your right hand, and your arm, and the light of your countenance." Another says, "The light." "Because you took pleasure in them." And yet they were all armed when they prevailed in their wars. Armed, yes, but the work was not done by the weapons. It was done by God, who led them as their general. Do you see how he puts forward his counsel in the form of a prayer, urging them to cast everything upon God? And how can he call the matter an inheritance, when their fathers, grandfathers and great-grandfathers did not possess the land but had died in another age? Because the promise was made to the fathers: "Come," he says, "into the land that I will show you," and, "To you I will give the land, and to your seed." Having said "right hand" and "arm", rather physical expressions, see how he raises the discourse by adding: "and the light of your countenance", that is, your help, your providence. For it was enough for them that he merely willed it and was present. Then comes the cause as well: "Because you took pleasure in them", that is, because you loved them, because you willed it. So these things came from grace, not from good deeds. They did not succeed by their own virtue but by the lovingkindness of God. "You are yourself my King and my God, who commands deliverances for Jacob." Another says, "Give command concerning the deliverance of Jacob." And what is the connection here? A close one with what has been said. What he means is this: "We are their descendants, and you are the same God who did those things then and does them now. Where, then, does so great a change come from? That God is not one God and you another. No, you are the same." 6. "Nor again are you the same while I enroll myself under another god. No, 'You are my King and my God.' We have not deserted your rule; we have not enrolled ourselves under another protector." "Who commands deliverances for Jacob": that is, the God is the same and the providence is the same. Where, then, does this change in our affairs come from? And what does "who commands" mean? He who orders, who gives the charge that Jacob be saved. Here again he shows how easily God gives his aid and how great his authority is. And he does not simply mention their ancestor. He puts forward the ancestor's virtue as a claim, wishing to move God by appeal. "Through you we will gore our enemies with the horn." "You are the same," he says, "and the providence is the same. We enroll ourselves under you, and we use the same weapons." That is the meaning of "Through you we will gore our enemies." Another says, "We will gore those who afflict us." "And in your name we will treat with contempt…" [Note: One manuscript places τήν before ἀρχῆς, not a bad reading.]

…he has set this down when he says, "And those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh." [?] Another translator has "Always." The Hebrew says this: "Selah." "But now you have rejected us and put us to shame." Another says, "Even though you have rejected us." Another, "And indeed you have rejected us." Another, "But besides this you have cast us off." "And you will not go out, O God, with our forces." Another says, "And you do not go forth with our armies." For shame follows at once upon rejection, and so does being exposed to everyone to be ill-treated. By "forces" he here means their camps, since the king's strength lies in them. God arranged this well, so that there would be a bond between ruler and ruled. The king needs his subjects, and they need their protector, and they stand in great need of one another. To keep anyone from arrogance, God has arranged that great things often need small ones. He did the same with lifeless things. Often a pebble placed under a tottering column has steadied it, and a small rudder steers a ship carrying ten thousand loads and brings it safe out of danger. And what does "Even though you have rejected us" mean? "Even after suffering such things," he says, "we do not turn away from you. We glorify you, we sing your praises, we take pride in you." "You turned us back before our enemies, and those who hate us plundered for themselves." Another says, "You made us the last of every adversary." See how his words heighten the terrors and dramatize the calamity. He shows that even if they were great sinners, they have still paid a sufficient penalty. 7. The young men in the furnace did this too, and in full measure, when they sang, "You handed us over into the hands of lawless enemies, most hateful apostates, and to an unjust king, the most wicked in all the earth." And again: "We have become fewer than all the nations, and we are brought low in all the earth." He shows the same thing here, all but saying: "We have become the most dishonored of all, since we have been stripped of your providence. And our troubles did not stop there: we have become prey for our enemies, who divide us up as they please." That is the meaning of "They plundered for themselves", that is, with no one to stop them. "You gave us up like sheep to be eaten, and scattered us among the nations." Another says, "You winnowed us." What does "like sheep to be eaten" mean? "You made us easy to attack, you showed us to be worthless." For some sheep are kept as stock, those fit for breeding; others, through age or barrenness, are good only for eating. And what was harder still was being divided among the nations. For them this was heavier than everything else: not even being able to keep the law exactly there, and having lost their ancestral way of life. "And not into one nation," he says, "but everywhere. And we are ready for one thing only, to suffer harm. We have no strength to defend ourselves or to raise our hands in return." That is what the image of the sheep shows. "You sold your people for no price." Another says, "For what will not exist" [?]. Another, "For nothing." "And there was no abundance in their exchanges." Another says, "And you did not set a high price on them." What he means is something like this (for the saying seems very obscure, so pay attention, that you may sing with understanding). What then? [?] [Note: "We are the fewest of all the…" In the printed edition "we are brought low" is absent.] [?] …nor did we deal falsely with the…

"We have not dealt unjustly with your covenant." [?] …raising the spirits of their fellow soldiers. "If we forgot the name of our God, and if we spread out our [hands]…" [?] "For if we have suffered the greatest things," he says, "and are the descendants of those who received great benefits, and have not turned aside in our calamities, we will have great hope of salvation." 8. So I say now what I said at the beginning: in the form of a prayer they strengthen the spirits of their people, as if saying to them, "Why have you despaired of salvation? We have God as our protector. Even if we have sinned somewhat, we have paid a sufficient penalty. We have stood firm and nobly in our trials. Our guide is the one who always protects even sinners. So on every side we must expect a good outcome." And what does "We have not dealt unjustly with your covenant" mean? That is: "We have not done wrong in the things entrusted to us, but have kept them carefully." For it is the greatest injustice when someone transgresses the law that defends him, that does not let him be wronged even by his neighbours, and that holds wickedness in check, and when he is ungrateful to the one who provides such great blessings. "And our heart has not turned back." Another says, "Has not withdrawn." "And you have turned our paths aside from your way." Another says, "Nor were our steps turned aside." Another, "And our heart did not turn back, and did not turn aside our steps." Here he says again what he said before: in such a storm of evils they were not shaken even a little. He put it well. Just as the law leads forward, so lawlessness drives backward; and just as the law commands us to walk the straight road, so lawlessness drives a person into the desert and trackless places. Here, then, he calls the law a "way". As for "You have turned aside", where the others say, "Nor were our steps turned aside from your way", the Hebrew says, "Wattet ashurenu minni orchach." But if someone wished to interpret according to the Seventy rather than the others, "You have turned our paths aside from your way" means this: "You have removed us from your temple and made us live in a foreign land," which did not allow the acts of worship to be performed. "For you humbled us in a place of affliction." Another says, "An uninhabited place." Another, "In a place of Sirens." "And the shadow of death covered us." Another says, "You laid us on your shoulders" [?]. This seems to me to answer what was said above, where they recount their troubles: "The shame of my face has covered me, at the voice of the one who reproaches and slanders." "For you humbled us." If, however, one takes it with "You have turned our paths aside from your way", then it fits here with the sense we have given. For it shows that he drove them from their paths, I mean their way of life and their customs, by leading them off into desert places and leaving them among enemies. That is the meaning of "The shadow of death covered us". He means the dangers that give birth to death, dangers that have death close at hand, just as Scripture also speaks of "the pangs of death" and "the gates of Hades". With both the "shadow" and the "covering" he shows here that there was no escaping these terrors, no release to be found, nor… [Note: Another manuscript has "to have been said". Reg. [?]. One manuscript has "awake".]

…these men said this, though they did not yet know anything about Gehenna or the kingdom and had not been taught to reason about such things as philosophers do. [?] And they bore everything easily. "For our soul has been brought down to the dust; our belly has cleaved to the earth." Since he had said, "You forget our poverty", that is, our affliction, he now describes the affliction. What he means is this: "We are ruined, we are buried, we are no better off than the dead." One could rightly say too of those whose souls melt away into the things of this present life that their soul has been brought down to the dust, and of gluttons that their belly has cleaved to the earth. For a man bound by lust, gaping after clay and enslaving the incorporeal power within him to ashes, may fittingly be said to suffer this. What else is bodily beauty but dust and clay, or rather something more loathsome than these? If you do not believe it, look into men's tombs, and you will see the clay and the dust. When the face has laid aside the present life, then it appears for what it is; or rather even before death. When old age comes on, when disease strikes, then you will see what is visible: it is clay. But God, as a wise craftsman, made a beauty beyond words arise even from cheap material, not so that you might commit fornication, but so that he might give you a proof of his own wisdom. So do not insult the craftsman, and do not make the work of his wisdom an occasion for licentiousness and fornication. Admire the bloom of beauty only so far as to glorify the craftsman. Go no further, feeding the passion. The work is beautiful; then you ought to worship its maker, not insult him. Tell me: if someone took a golden statue of a man, a royal image, and defiled it with mud and other such things, would he not pay the ultimate penalty? If one who shows such contempt in human matters is liable to so great a punishment, what will he suffer who heaps such dishonor on the work of God, especially when the man who does this plainly has a wife? Do not tell me about the desire of nature. Marriage was permitted for this very reason, so that you would not go beyond your proper bounds. See what punishment you will deserve. God provided both for your rest and for your honor, so that you might relieve the frenzy of nature through your wife, do so without danger, and be free of all disgrace. But you heap insult upon the one who provides for you so generously. Tell me: if he had not chosen to establish marriage by law, how much violence would you have had to endure? How much torment? You ought therefore to give thanks and glorify him, because he has cut away the greater part of your struggles by devising no ordinary consolation. Instead you insult him ungratefully, act shamelessly, overstep the boundaries laid down, and disgrace your own wife… [Note: Colb. [?] "wife"; Reg. "when the man who does this has a wife". Ididoth, in Hebrew [?].]

"My heart has belched forth a good word." Another translator has "Crept forth." Another, "My heart was stirred with a good word." I wish that all the Jews and Greeks were here now, so that I could take this book from the Jews and read the psalm to them. You surely know that in the law courts and everywhere else, the testimony to the facts is most beyond suspicion when it is brought by one's enemies. So that this may happen today too, we present testimony from the Old Testament, so that both Jews and Greeks may be put to shame: the Jews because they read and do not understand, the Greeks because they see these books handed to us by our enemies. Surely they will not be able to say that we fabricated them. It is not we but those who crucified Christ who supply us with the books that speak of his power. But whether they are present or not, let us do our part and take up the interpretation. This psalm was written about Christ, and that is why it bears the titles "For the beloved" and "For those who will be changed." For he brought about a great change for us, a transformation and an overturning of the order of things. Paul was pointing to this change when he said, "So if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation." That is why, at the very beginning, he does not say, "My heart has said." Since nothing he was speaking of was human, and he was about to tell of heavenly and spiritual things that came not from his own invention but from God's working, he conveys this by the word "belching". For we do not belch when we choose. Ordinary speech we utter when we wish: we speak or hold it back. Belching is not like that. So, to show that what he says comes not from human effort but from the divine inspiration moving him, he called the prophecy a belching. Just as in belching what comes up has the quality of the food, so it is with spiritual teaching too. He belched forth the kind of things he had eaten. See how elsewhere another prophet likens this working to a physical image: he eats the scroll of the book, and eats it with pleasure. "It became in my body," he says, "like sweet honey." Since, then, they received spiritual grace, such were the things they belched forth. To see that the subject is not this physical belching, nor food, listen to what is belched forth and who is belching. It is not the stomach, which receives food, but the heart: "My heart has belched forth," he says. And what does it belch forth? Not grain or drink, but things akin to its table: "a good word", the word about the Only-begotten, for he is supremely good. "For I came," he says, "not to judge the world, but to save the world." Everything is gentle, everything free of punishment. He belches forth such things because he had cleansed his heart. When the stomach is full of foul humors, it belches up things akin to them; when it is healthy, its belching matches its state. In the same way, since the Prophet's heart was free of sins, it received the grace of the Spirit and belches forth a good word.

[?] …rushing along with a great roar, so too the grace of the Spirit goes forth with great swiftness, producing everything smooth, everything easy. Then, to make this very point clear and to show that nothing he said was human, he added: "Beautiful in loveliness beyond the sons of men." Some say this refers to the tongue, that it is a pen beautiful in loveliness. But to me it seems that he is now speaking of Christ. That is why another translator says, "You were adorned with beauty beyond the sons of men." Out of great fervor and his love for him, he turns his words to him, just as Jacob said, "From a shoot, my son, you have come up; lying down you slept like a lion." For he was inspired, and now he speaks with him and addresses his words to him. He does not say this as a comparison. He did not say "more beautiful" but "beautiful in loveliness beyond the sons of men." "This beauty," he means, "is something different from that." And notice how he begins with the account of the Incarnation. That this concerns the Incarnation is clear from what follows. Having said, "Beautiful in loveliness beyond the sons of men," he added, "Grace was poured out on your lips." God does not have lips; the subject is the Incarnation. Another translator, by saying, "Grace welled up on your lips," made this clearer. What does "welled up" mean, if not, as one might put it, that what was within gushed up and sprang forth? How, then, does another prophet say, "We saw him, and he had no form or beauty, but his form was without honor, falling short of the sons of men"? He is not speaking of ugliness, God forbid, but of his being easily despised. For once he had consented to become man, he went through every kind of lowliness. He did not take a queen as his mother. As a baby in swaddling clothes he was not laid on a golden bed, but in a manger. He was not raised in a costly house, but in the humble room of a carpenter. And again, when he took disciples, he did not choose orators, philosophers and kings, but fishermen and tax collectors. He led this simple life, with no house, no costly clothes, no fine table. He was fed by others, insulted, despised, driven out, persecuted. He did these things to trample human pride with abundant force. Since, then, he was clothed in no pomp or show, and had no attendants or bodyguards, but sometimes even went about alone like one of the crowd, that prophet says, "We saw him, and he had no form or beauty." This one, however, says, "Beautiful in loveliness beyond the sons of men," pointing to his grace, his wisdom, his teaching, his miracles. Then, describing this beauty, he says, "Grace was poured out on your lips." Do you see that the subject is the Incarnation? And what is this grace? The grace by which he taught, by which… [Note: Savile [?]; two manuscripts have "there are times when", one "where". [?] One Reg. manuscript has "power of the Spirit".]

[?] … just as the spirit of a man is akin to the man, so too is the Spirit of God akin to God, yet it remains in its own hypostasis. Paul showed this when he said: "For who among men knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man that is in him? So also no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God." He was not confusing the hypostases, God forbid, but showing the nobility of the Spirit. As great as the harmony of the soul with itself, so great is the kinship of the Spirit with the Father. The Son too is called Word, yet not as something without hypostasis; he is called this so that we may learn his kinship with the Father. In the same way the Spirit of God is called Spirit, yet not as something without hypostasis. And because the Son is the true Son of the Father, he grants us adoption as sons. In the same way the Spirit, since by nature he belongs to the essence of God, supplies us with his gifts. So too a man, because he is a man by nature, can paint the image of a man. "Therefore God has blessed you for ever." Another translator says, "Upon [?]"

Do you see how all the way through he addresses him with affection? That is why elsewhere too he does not simply prophesy but speaks in the form of an accusation, as when he says: "Why did the nations rage, and the peoples devise vain things?" He does the same here when he says, "Therefore God has blessed you for ever." He says nothing about his birth or his upbringing or anything else, but launches his account of him from this point. Why? Because telling everything in order is the task of the evangelists. So he kept these things for them, since they belonged to their narrative.
