The work of prophecy is to take up certain parts and speak about those. This is why the prophets everywhere do it: they bring a few things into the story, cast a shadow over them, and withdraw. That is why this prophet too says, "God has blessed you for ever," meaning that his words were so full of grace. Consider, then, the power of that grace. Once he was passing along by the sea, and he found James and John and said to them: "Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men." And they left their father and their nets and followed him. At another time he said to all the disciples: "Do you also wish to go away?" Peter said to him: "Lord, you have the words of eternal life, and we have believed and come to know that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God; and to whom shall we go?" But why speak of the disciples? The Pharisees themselves sent officers and heard them say: "No man ever spoke as this man speaks." Others again said: "Nothing like this was ever seen in Israel." "And they were astonished," it says, "because he taught them as one having authority, and not as their scribes and Pharisees." 4. If you too wish to learn what this grace is, listen to the weight of his commands, and you will see its power. "Unless someone renounces everything …" [?] … and furthermore Christ, having become a curse. For just as he humbled

himself in order to exalt you, and died in order to make you immortal, so too he became a curse in order to fill you with blessing. What could equal this blessing, when he grants blessing through a curse? He himself did not need blessing; he gives it to you. When I say that he was humbled, I do not mean a change but the condescension of the dispensation. In the same way, when I say that he was blessed, I do not mean that he needed blessing; again I am pointing to the condescension of the dispensation. It was human nature, then, that was blessed. For Christ, raised from the dead, no longer dies and is not subject to a curse. Or rather, he was not subject to it even before this, but he took the curse upon himself in order to free you from it. "Gird your sword upon your thigh, O mighty one." Another translator: "Gird your blade on your thigh." Another: "Put on your blade, as it were, upon your thigh." "In your comeliness and your beauty." Another says: "Your praise and your dignity." Another: "In your glory [?] and your splendor." Why this change, this shift in the words? He was speaking about a teacher, for that is what "Grace is poured out on your lips" means. Suddenly he sketches for us an armed king, and not in the mode of prophecy but in the mode of supplication. He did not say, "He will gird his sword"; he makes a request and says, "Gird your sword." Then he mixes beauty with this armor, now showing a soldier, now someone adorned: "In your comeliness," it says, "and your beauty." Then an archer: "Your arrows are sharpened, O mighty one." And again a victor bearing trophies: "Peoples will fall beneath you," it says, "in the heart of the king's enemies." Then he brings in this same soldier, king, archer and victor once more, anointed with perfumes: "Myrrh," it says, "and stacte and cassia from your garments." 5. What do weapons have in common with perfumes, anointing with a sword, teaching with war, bows with adornment? Some of these are symbols of peace, the others of battle and the battle line. Who, then, is at once peaceful and warlike, dripping with myrrh and fenced about with weapons? Who comes forth from ivory palaces, strikes down countless enemies and works such slaughter? How shall we resolve this difficulty? By recognizing clearly that these things are said about his Father as well. For elsewhere the Prophet presents the Father too as arming himself, as when he says: "If you do not turn back, he will polish his sword; he has bent his bow and made it ready, and on it he has prepared instruments of death." And again elsewhere: "He will put on righteousness as a breastplate." Notice too that the sovereign authority is the same. There he says, "He will polish his sword," not at anyone's command but on his own initiative. So too here: "The arrows of the mighty one are sharpened; peoples beneath you [?]" [?] "in grace", less correctly. [?] "of righteousness".

[?] … demons plotting and corrupting the whole world. That is why Isaiah too said: "And he shall divide the spoils of the strong"; and full of wisdom [?]! But that parricide and [?] young man, how he entrusts him to his own [?] … And again: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach good news to the poor, to proclaim release to captives." That is why Paul too, at the head of his letters, everywhere wrote: "Grace to you and peace from God our Father." And again: "For he is our peace, who has made both one." But when you hear "Gird your sword," do not think of a sword that can be seen; listen to what follows. Having said, "Put on your blade," he added, "In your comeliness and your beauty." This is the sword: his comeliness, his beauty, his glory, his dignity, his greatness and his magnificence. That essence needs nothing to accomplish what it sets out to do, for it lacks nothing. The prophet, then, is appealing to him and leading him out to war on behalf of the world. Then he brings the discourse down again from lofty things to more concrete ones. Having spoken of a sword and a thigh, he went up to comeliness, and from there he comes down again to more bodily things and says: "And bend, and prosper, and reign." By saying "Bend" he indicated the bow and the arrow. Then, showing again that he has no need of weapons, he added, "And prosper, and reign." Another translator says, "Advance." By kingdom here he means the one he established when he came in the last times, the kingdom that consists in our being made his own and coming to know him. 6. These words come above all from the prophet's longing, as he already sees the achievements and the world being led by the hand to the truth. That is why he speaks in the manner of an exhortation. It is customary for inferiors, too, to use such expressions when they feel warmly toward their superiors. "For the sake of truth and meekness and righteousness." He uses the word "truth." Do you see how Scripture interprets itself and shows that the victory belongs to the mind and the spirit? He has mentioned weapons, a sword and bows; how can he now mention meekness? What do meekness and war have in common, or gentleness and battle [?]? A great deal, in fact, if one examines the matter carefully. David and Moses were both meek. That is why Scripture says of the one: "Remember, Lord, David and all his meekness," and of Moses: "Moses was the meekest of all men on the earth." Yet these men, the meekest of all, are seen to be the most vigorous of all in fighting back. But if you like, let us speak first of their meekness. Many times this blessed man had Saul in his hands and was in a position to kill him, yet he did not raise his hand against him. Even when others urged him on, he spared him and let his anger go. And when Shimei insulted him so grossly and trampled on him in his misfortune at that time, and the generals [?] … lets go of the spoils.

of truth, in order to plant it on the earth; of meekness, in order to make people meek who were fiercer than wild beasts; and of righteousness, in order to make righteous those who were under the tyranny of lawlessness, first by grace and then also by good deeds. "And your right hand will guide you wondrously." Another translator: "And your right hand will enlighten you toward fearful things." Another: "And your right hand will show you fearful things." 7. Do you see how he has again given us a glimpse of the dignity of the one who accomplishes such things? Above, having spoken of weapons and a sword, he went up to comeliness and led the hearer to incorporeal thoughts. In the same way, having come down again to the more concrete, the bows and arrows, he now leads the hearer gradually back up by telling the causes of the war, truth, meekness and righteousness, and then the manner of the victory. And what is that? "And your right hand," it says, "will guide you wondrously." What he means is this: the nature is sufficient for itself, the power is sufficient for itself, both to see what must be done and to bring it to completion [?]

Another translator rightly said, "Your right hand is fearful," for what has been accomplished is truly fearful and full of awe. Death was undone, Hades burst open, paradise was opened, heaven was thrown wide, the demons were muzzled, the things below were joined with the things above, God became man, and man sits on a royal throne. The hopes of resurrection were opened, and with them immortal expectations, the enjoyment of ineffable goods, and all the other things he accomplished by his coming. That is why he said, "Your right hand will guide you to these fearful things," showing that the nature, he says, and the power are sufficient in themselves both to discover and to accomplish what lies before them. The Seventy say: "Your right hand will guide you wondrously." That is, we should marvel not only at what was accomplished but also at the paradoxical way in which it was accomplished. Through death, death was undone; through a curse, the curse was abolished and blessing was given. Through food we were once cast out; through food we were brought back in. A virgin cast us out of paradise; through a virgin we found eternal life. The very things that brought our condemnation brought our crown. With this in mind the Prophet said: "Your right hand will guide you wondrously." Is there any need of weapons, of a sword, of bows and arrows? Do you see how the nature, the power, is sufficient for itself? But look at him again, like an excellent dancer, coming down once more from lofty things to more concrete ones: "Your arrows are sharpened, O mighty one. Peoples will fall beneath you, in the heart of the king's enemies." Another says: "In the heart, the enemies of the ki- [?]"

Notice again how, when he mentioned arrows, he added the words "O mighty one," so that you may learn that he does not need arrows but is sufficient for himself. The sequence is this: "Your arrows are sharpened, O mighty one, in the heart of the king's enemies." And the phrase "Peoples beneath [you]" [?] [?] manuscripts: "ran up." [?] manuscripts: "That is why he says, Your right hand will guide … you." [?] namely, "Your right hand will show you fearful things." [?] … so great was the harmony he showed toward them. "And how could it make sense," someone says, "for there to be harmony in opposites

?" Do you not know that eating is the opposite of not eating, drinking of not drinking, and giving of not giving? Yet a physician often does many such things, not contradicting himself but in full agreement with himself, because he looks to one end, the health of the patient. This is what happened with the evangelists too. Summer is the opposite of winter, yet both look to one end, the ripening and abundance of the crops. The whole world is made up of opposites, yet it shows a great harmony that serves our life. Christ too came in a way opposite to John: the one ate, the other did not. "For John came," it says, "neither eating nor drinking, and they say, He has a demon. The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, Look, a glutton and a drunkard." Yet although what they did was opposite, both looked to one end, the salvation of those who were to be gathered into the net. So too with the order John followed in treating the divinity and the dispensation: even if it runs opposite to the other evangelists, it is still in full harmony with them. How so? I will tell you. At the beginning, when the word had not yet been sown, it was fitting to dwell on the account of the dispensation and to train people in the teaching about the flesh, starting from the more concrete things that can be perceived by the senses. But once knowledge had taken firm root and people had received the preaching, the time was right to begin from above. That is why the prophets too, whenever they speak of him, make the dispensation their starting point and preface. See how Micah begins from below: "And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall come forth for me a ruler who will shepherd my people Israel." Yet he did not stop there but went up to the divinity, saying: "And his going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity." And Isaiah again: "Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel," which means "God with us." Do you see how he too went up from the flesh to the divinity? Look at the same thing happening elsewhere, where he says: "A child is born to us, a son is given to us, and his name is called Angel of great counsel, Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Potentate, Prince of Peace, Father of the age to come." Do you see how once again, beginning from the child and the dispensation in the flesh, he climbs as if by steps and comes to rest at the divinity? In the same way his Father was first made known from creation. "For his invisible things," says Paul, "have been clearly seen since the creation of the world, being understood through the things he has made." That is why the Father himself often took on a visible form, leading the human race up little by little to incorporeal thoughts. And why are you surprised that he used such a gradual method with doctrines, when he did exactly the same with precepts and commandments? That is why also [?] [?] "his goings forth." One manuscript: "ascending, he flies." [?]

[?] … saying, "A scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom"? And another again: "His judgment will go forth like light." If you do not know precisely everything about your Master, glorify him for that very reason. Worship him above all for this: for the ineffability of his greatness, the incomprehensibility of his providence, the varied wisdom of his care. "You have loved righteousness and hated lawlessness." Above he spoke of the achievements, the victories, the trophies, the salvation of the world, how he filled it with truth, with meekness, with righteousness. Now, to show that there is nothing improbable in these things having happened, he goes on to speak of the dignity of the one who achieved them: that he is God, that he is king, that he has no end, that he is a judge who cannot be bribed, a lover of the righteous and a hater of evil. "Since he is such," he says, "that is why he has accomplished such things." "So let no one disbelieve," he says. "The one who accomplished so much did so because he was both able and willing." Having spoken of the lofty things of his divinity, he brings the discourse back down to the flesh and says: "Therefore God, your God, has anointed you." Another says: "For this he has anointed you." That is, he says, for accomplishing what has been described: driving out lawlessness, planting righteousness, doing what you have done. Do not be troubled to hear that these things are credited to the Father. He does not say this to deprive the Son of his achievements, but to attribute what is the Son's to the Father, just as the Son says that what is his Father's is his own: "For all that is mine is yours, and what is yours is mine." So too concerning the resurrection Paul says, "God raised him from the dead," while John says: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." And what is "the oil of gladness"? Christ was never anointed with oil, but with the Holy Spirit. That is why he added, "beyond your companions," showing this very thing, that no one was anointed as he was. There were many anointed ones, many christs, before him, but not one like this. There are many lambs, but he is unique; there are many sons, but he is the Only-begotten. Everything about him is unique, not only what belongs to his divinity but also what belongs to the dispensation, for no one was ever anointed with such a Spirit. If he calls it oil, do not be surprised; being a prophet, he speaks rather enigmatically. And he rightly said "of gladness," to show that it is the oil of joy. "For the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace." Another translator said, "with the oil of splendor." The Hebrew has "sason," that is, of adornment, of glory, of ornament. If it also means joy, that too is true. When you hear of a sword you do not think of a sword, and when you hear of arrows and bows you do not think of bows and arrows, but of his power, which accomplished the things I described before. In the same way, when you hear of oil, do not simply think of oil but understand the anointing. For oil was a symbol of the Spirit, and the principal and necessary [?]

[?] … he touched, how he overcame his enemies, how his right hand prospered him, how he planted truth and meekness and righteousness. And again he uses metaphorical language, as though sketching the Church in an image. The apostles said these things afterwards. One said: "I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ." Another: "He who has the bride is the bridegroom." Another: "The kingdom of heaven is like a king who gave a wedding feast for his son." The psalmist proclaims these same things in advance, presenting the bride who is also queen. That is why he says: "The queen stood at your right hand." Another translator: "was set up like a pillar," that is, she stood firm, she stood immovable, as Christ says elsewhere: "The gates of Hades shall not prevail against her." Do you see the overwhelming honor? Do you see the weight of the dignity? Do you see to what height he raised her who had been trampled underfoot and dragged down below, so that she stands beside him? Do you realize to what dignity she has risen, she who was a captive, estranged, a harlot, accursed? She stands with the ministering powers. The Son, being of equal honor, sits at the right hand, but she stands; for although she is queen, she is of created essence. How then does Paul say: "He raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus"? Pay attention to the precision of his words. He did not simply say, "He raised us up with him and seated us with him," but "in Christ," that is, through Christ. Since our head is above, he says, and we are the body, when the head is seated above we too share in the honor, even though we stand. "Clothed in a robe woven with gold, adorned in many colors." Another translator: "In a diadem of gold from Sou- [?]"

With the king we do not think of bows and arrows. In the same way, with the bride, do not think of garments, but through the things of sense grasp thoughts worthy of God. To keep anyone from suspecting anything of the kind, he added: "All the glory of the king's daughter is within." Garments, more than anything else, are on the outside and exist for the sake of those who look at them, but that is when they are bodily garments. When the discussion concerns spiritual things, turn the eye of your mind inward. This is the garment the king wove, and he clothed her in it through baptism. "For as many of you," he says, "as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ." Before this she was naked and disgraced, exposed to all who passed by on the road. But from the moment she put on this garment she was raised to that height and counted worthy to stand at the right hand. He rightly calls it many-colored, for the garment is not all of one kind. Salvation does not come from grace alone; there is need of faith too, and after faith, of virtue as well. But the subject now is not garments. The Spirit was not so eager to describe a woman's golden clothes. Isaiah rebukes women who adorn themselves, and luxury is rejected everywhere in Scripture; how then could he praise a woman adorning herself here? "Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father's house. And the king will desire your beau- [?]" [?] Instead of this: "Another: In a diabema (sic) of gold, Souphir [?]" … "of gold" [?] … "in gold" [?]

…"the daughter of Tyre with gifts." What kind of sequence is this? A very excellent one, for this is the greatest form of exhortation. "Draw near," he says, "for great is his strength, and all will obey him." And instead of speaking of the whole world, the Prophet names the neighbouring city, which was then held fast in impiety: the devil's citadel, the city famous for its extravagance. He points to the whole through the part. It seems to me that he uses this name for all impiety and dissoluteness, for he is used to describing ways of life by the names of cities. So he says, "Hear the word of the Lord, you rulers of Sodom; give ear to the law of your God, you people of Gomorrah." Yet he was speaking to Jews. But since they did [?] the deeds of Sodom, he calls them by the names of Sodom. And why are you surprised that he names them after a homeland, when he even gives them fathers of that kind, saying, "Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite"? He does not stop his accusation even there. He carries his language over to wild beasts too. In the New Scripture it says, "You brood of vipers," and in the Old, "They have hatched the eggs of asps, and they weave the spider's web," and elsewhere, "Are you not like the sons of the Ethiopians to me?" In the same way he has here called those who lived in impiety and licentiousness Tyrians. But I will overcome even these, he says, and master them. I will master them so fully that they will worship, and not merely worship but also bring gifts and firstfruits. That is the highest form of service and a sign of exceeding obedience. "The rich among the people will entreat your face." What does "will entreat" mean? Those who are now great and exalted will honour and glorify you. And this is what happens in the Church: everyone honours and serves those who live in virtue, even people who abound in wealth and rank. For virtue is greater than any affluence. 12. You see the Church honoured by all. And he did well to say "your face," that is, your glory, your beauty, your comeliness. Then, since he had mentioned a face, garments and beauty, he added a warning, so that none of the more literal-minded would think of something physical: "All the glory of the king's daughter is within." Enter into the mind, he says, and learn the beauty of the soul. That is what I am speaking to you about. Even if I say clothing, or beauty, or gold, or fringes, or cloth of gold, or anything else of the kind, the discourse is about the mind, the teaching is about the soul, and what is said concerns virtue and the glory within. Having once corrected the literal-minded hearer by these words, he can confidently bring his discourse back to bodily images: "Clothed in golden fringes, adorned in many colours." Another version has: "With golden clasps [?], embroidered in many colours." Again he calls virtue by the name of gold. Paul does the same when he says, "If anyone builds on this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw." He presents virtue and vice to us under the names of these materials. For in order that… [Notes: Morel. reads "thus saying Scripture," wrongly. … but are dissolved; but these, having died, rather [?] … One manuscript: "having escaped the strait."]

…has its force within its own boundaries, but the commands of the fishermen spread through the whole world. The Roman emperor could not make laws for the Persians, nor the Persian king for the Romans. But these Palestinians laid down laws for Persians, Romans, Thracians, Scythians, Indians, Moors and the whole world. They prevailed not only while they lived but also after their death, and those who received their laws would choose ten thousand times over to give up their lives rather than abandon those laws. "I will remember your name in every generation and generation. Therefore peoples will confess you for ever and for ever and ever." Another translator says, "I will commemorate your name in each generation. Therefore peoples will hymn you continually." Another: "For this reason peoples will confess you." He has shown how great the kingdom is from the length of the earth, the breadth of the world and the number of nations made subject. Now he shows its dignity from another side as well: it will extend not only through the whole world but through all time. Your memory will be immortal, he says. It will be written in our books, written in our ways of life, written in our precepts. See how he also prophesies that his own prophecy will endure. When he said, "I will remember your name in every generation and generation," he made this clear. Even if I die, he says, I will sing to you even in death. The body will be dissolved, but the writings remain and the law endures. "Therefore peoples will confess you." He ended where he began: with Christ. "Therefore." Why? Because you accomplished so much. Because you set up such rulers, drove out vice, planted virtue, joined our nature to yourself and brought about these unspeakable blessings, the whole world will offer you a hymn. It will not be for a short time, or for ten, twenty or a hundred years, or in only part of the world. Land and sea, the inhabited world and the uninhabited, will sing through all time, giving thanks for the blessings that have come about. For all these things let us too give thanks to Christ, the lover of mankind, through whom and with whom be glory to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.

For the end, for the sons of Korah, concerning hidden things. Another version: To the victor, of the sons of Korah. Another: For the youths [?], a song. "Our God is our refuge and strength, a help in the afflictions that have come upon us greatly." Another: "readily found." "Therefore we will not fear when the earth is troubled and the mountains are carried into the heart of the seas." [?] 1. The Prophet uses his usual philosophy. He leads the hearer away from the affairs of this life and lifts him up to the hope that comes from above. Do not talk to me, he says, of weapons and walls and trenches, nor of wealth… [Notes: Another reads "having died, are fixed." Savile reads ἀνύσει ("will accomplish"); the others read ἀνοίσει ("will offer"). [?] Another omits τῶν.]

…[as he is used to proclaiming his strength, at one time] from creation and at another from what happens to human beings, so he does here too. What he says is this: He shakes all things, moves them and shifts them whenever he wishes, so easy and simple is everything for him. It seems to me that here he is hinting at the multitudes of the brave, the proud among the enemy and the countless host of adversaries. His power is so great, he says, that he only has to nod and all these things happen. How then can we be afraid when we have such a Master? Diapsalma. Another version: Always. "The streams of the river." Another: The divisions. The Hebrew: Phalagiau [?]. "make glad the city of God; the Most High has sanctified his tabernacle." Another says: "The holy place of the dwelling of the Most High." "God is in her midst, and she will not be shaken. God will help her early in the morning." Another says: "About dawn." Another: "At the turning of the morning." Having spoken of his power and strength, and of how everything is easy for him, he moves the discourse to the theme of God's providence towards the Jews and briefly sets out the blessings given to them. This one, he says, so powerful, so strong and fearsome, who leads and bears all things, who shakes and moves all things, who shifts and removes them, has filled our city with countless blessings. Here "river" shows the abundance of the gifts supplied from above, unhindered and poured out freely. It is as if he said: All blessings flow to us as if from springs. A river divided into countless channels waters the land beneath it, and in the same way God's providence flows in from every side. It comes abundantly, rushes on and fills everything. It gives us not only safety and unbreakable help but also spiritual joy. So he says, "The Most High has sanctified his tabernacle." And this in itself is no small part of his kindness: that he called the place his tabernacle. 2. He did not put "the Most High" there without reason. He who is so exalted, whom no place contains, the ineffable essence, deigned to call our city his tabernacle, and he holds it together on every side. That is what "in her midst" means, as he says elsewhere, "Behold, I am with you." He fortifies her on every side. So not only will she suffer nothing terrible, she will not even be shaken. The reason is that she enjoys the swiftest of alliances, one that is ready and prepared. That is what "morning" means: help that does not delay or come slowly but is always fresh and vigorous, and comes at the right time. "The nations were troubled." Another version: "The nations were gathered." "Kingdoms bowed. The Most High uttered his voice; the earth was shaken." Here he shows the power of his help. It was not ordinary men who attacked, but kings and nations gathering from every side, surrounding and besieging a single city. Yet the city not only suffered nothing terrible from them; it prevailed, conquered and routed its attackers. That is what "Kingdoms bowed, the Most High uttered his voice" means. One might say: with a shout alone [?]. For he… [?]

…spread peace through the whole world, and he also put an end to their visible war. Isaiah made this clear when he said, "They will beat their swords into ploughshares and their spears into sickles, and nation will not take up sword against nation, and they will no longer learn to make war." Before Christ's coming all men bore arms, and no one was exempt from this service. City fought against city, and war was waged without pause. Now most of the world is at peace. Everyone pursues their crafts in safety, works the land and sails the sea. Only a small body of soldiers is stationed in front of all the rest. Even the need for these would have been removed if we did what we ought and did not need afflictions to remind us. Here he calls his wrath "fire," and he is speaking of something that actually happened: they burned up their enemies' weapons and chariots after a decisive victory, as Ezekiel says. All who love learning know the story. [?] "Be still, and know that I am God. I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted on the earth." Another version says, "Be healed, and know." Another: "Let go, so that you may know." The Hebrew says: Arphu udu [?]. It seems to me that these words are spoken here to the nations, as if he said: You have come to know his strength and his power, which reaches through the whole world. But you need leisure; you need a healthy soul. "Let go" means the same: abandon your error, be rid of your former way of life, breathe again out of the fog of the evils that hold you fast. Then, guided by the teaching of the miracles and with your soul at leisure, you may come to know the God of all things. Miracles alone are not enough unless the soul is also well disposed. Miracles happened among the Jews too, and they did nothing more for their salvation. The sun's rays are not enough unless the eye is clear and healthy, and in the same way miracles alone are not enough here. So, having spoken of those events, he urges those who are to reap their benefit to breathe again out of the evils that hold them, so that they may learn of the God who is over all. "Be still, and know that I am God": not the idols, not the carved images. Be still, then, and I will give you many proofs. That is what "I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted on the earth" means. In other words: I will show myself to you as great and exalted through my works. That pure and ineffable nature has its own exaltedness. But since you do not see this, I will show it to you through my works as well, and not only in Palestine or only in Jerusalem, but among you, the nations. This is how he is exalted: by mastering and prevailing over them, working wonders in Babylon, wonders in Egypt, wonders in the desert, wonders throughout the world, so that from every side they are taught to know him. "The Lord of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our helper." This one, then,…

…I will say: some things must be taken just as they are said, and others in a sense contrary to the words as they stand. An example is the verse, "Wolves and lambs will feed together." We will not take this to mean wolves and lambs, or straw, ox and bull. Instead, we take the image of irrational animals as a picture of human characters. Other things must be taken in a double sense, understanding both the visible meaning and the spiritual one. An example is the offering up of Abraham's son. We know that the son was offered up, and through the son we also draw out something else hidden in the meaning: the cross. In the same way, in the lamb in Egypt we again discern the image of the Passion. This is what we must do here too. The discourse is not simply about the Arabs and their neighbours. He is calling all the nations. "For the Lord Most High is fearsome, a great King over all the earth." From the very beginning, then, he rouses the hearer. He calls him to so great a wealth of good news, to the festival of the whole world, to a divine and spiritual feast, to the sacred mystery brought down from heaven. So he says, "Clap," that is, rejoice and leap. The word of the Gospel commands the same when it says, "Leap for joy." It does not at all command people to jump and bound about, which would be unseemly. It shows how intense the joy is. What has happened deserves great delight. The word of the Gospel has spread over all the earth the sun looks upon, and the whole world has been saved. Those who were once held fast by error have shown a greater philosophy than the Jewish worship. "All you nations, clap your hands." Those hands that were once foul, he says, accursed, stained with blood every day through unclean sacrifices, the hands with which you slaughtered children, dared shameful deeds and went against nature itself: with these clap now. "Shout to God with a voice of exultation." With that tongue with which you tasted accursed things and spoke blasphemous words, with this tongue shout the song of victory. It is the custom of armies, when the enemy's army gives way, no longer to fight hand to hand but to shake the enemy's already broken spirits with a united shout and war-cry. This is the greatest proof of a brilliant victory and triumph: when the war is decided not by hands, but the shout takes the place of hands and of weapons…

The whole work, then, was Christ's. He himself ended this hard war, binding the strong man and plundering his goods. But because he loves mankind, he lets those who did no labour at all enjoy the victory and the trophies. He prepares them to raise the shout of victory as though they had won and prevailed themselves. So we all cry out, not with an unclear voice but with a very clear one: "Where, O death, is your sting? Where, O Hades, is your victory?" And again: "God has gone up with a shout," for this is said in this psalm. And again elsewhere: "You ascended on high, you led captivity captive, you received gifts among men" [?]. [Notes: …as when he says, "Wolves." Savile and two manuscripts read τῇ συστάδην ("in close combat"); Morel. reads τῇ ὑστάτῃ ("the last").]

"Have you come here before the time to torment us?" If they said this then, what will they say when he comes, when the powers of heaven are shaken, the sun is turned to darkness and the moon does not give its light? That is why he says, "Most High, fearsome." Or rather, what could anyone say that is worthy of that day? On that day he will send his angels through the whole world. Everything will be shaken, and the earth will quake as it gives back the dead entrusted to it. Countless bodies will be raised. Heaven will be rolled up like a curtain being rolled up. The fearsome judgement seat will be set up and the rivers of fire will flow. The books will be opened, and he will bring into the open what each person did in darkness. There will be those unbearable punishments and penalties, the threatening powers, the drawn swords, the leading away to Gehenna. All ranks will be dissolved, whether of kings, generals, consuls or prefects. So vast a multitude of angels will be present, with the ranks of martyrs, prophets, apostles, priests and monks. There will be those unspeakable prizes, the rewards, the crowns, the blessings that surpass…

3. What words can set this forth? The Prophet, going over creation, grew weary and drew back, saying, "How magnified are your works, O Lord!" Paul, searching out one aspect of providence, cried out, "O the depth of the riches!" What then could anyone say in describing that day? The Prophet foresaw all these things when he said, "The Lord Most High is fearsome, a great King over all the earth," pointing to the salvation of the whole world. He was a great King before this too, but he was not known. "For the world came into being through him, and the world did not know him." But now he has accomplished this as well: he has become a great King also by making us his own. How could he not be great? He sent poor fishermen out into the whole world: unlettered, untrained men, eleven in number, obscure and without a city, more voiceless than fish, with one tunic each, barefoot and naked. And he won everyone over as if by a command. This is truly a great King. He cleansed the world of error, brought back the truth in a brief moment and overthrew the devil's tyranny. He is a great King even before he has subjects. The strength of his rule lies not in servants, nor in outward show and robes, but in his very nature. "For this," he says, "I was born." This is a great King: his honour is not brought in from outside, he needs nothing in order to be King, and he does whatever he wills. "Go," he says, "and make disciples of all nations," and the word became deed. "I will it; be cleansed." "I say to you, dumb demon, come out of him." "Be silent, be muzzled." "Depart into the fire prepared for the devil." "Come, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world." Do you see his authority everywhere? Do you see his power? He so won over those who obeyed him that he persuaded them to give up their lives rather than transgress his command. For a king, from his own subjects,… [Notes: Others read ὑπέμενεν ("endured"). Morel. and others read προσέχεις ("you attend"). Savile reads ἐξουσίᾳ ("by authority"). A little later, some read τὸ ὑποτεταμένον ("what is subjected"), others τὸ ἐπιτεταμένον ("the intensity").]

Paul says: "For see what earnestness this very thing, your being grieved in a godly way, has produced in you: what defense, what indignation, what fear, what longing, what zeal, what vindication!" That is how much they trembled before the apostles and feared them. And again Luke writes: "None of the rest dared to join them, but the people held them in high honor." And again: "What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and a spirit of gentleness?"

4. [195] Do you see their authority and power? All this was the work of the word he spoke when he sent them out: "I am with you." He himself went before them and removed the obstacles. He himself made everything easy and turned hard things into light ones. And yet everything was full of wars, full of cliffs and crags. There was nowhere to plant a foot or to stand. All the harbors were silted up, every house was shut, everyone's ears were stopped. But even so they went in, spoke out, and tore down all the strongholds of the enemy, to the point of giving up their very lives and enduring countless dangers from then on for what they had preached.

"He chose for us his inheritance, the beauty of Jacob, which he loved." Another version has: "The glory of Jacob." See how precise the prophecy is. A little earlier he said: "He subjected peoples to us, and nations." And indeed the Jews came first, first three thousand, then five thousand, and after that the nations. As he himself said: "I have other sheep too, and I must bring them also, and there will be one flock, one shepherd." Someone might hear the words "He chose for us his inheritance for himself" and be perplexed and troubled, and ask: "How is it, then, that the Jews now do not believe?" To prevent this, he resolved the difficulty with a qualification. As far as his own part went, he chose them too, and as far as it depended on him he left no one out. But if you are asking about the outcome, listen to what follows, for he adds: "The beauty of Jacob, which he loved." Here he seems to me to mean the faithful. Paul made the same point when he said: "It is not as though the word of God has failed. For not all who are descended from Israel are Israel, but 'Through Isaac shall your offspring be named.' That is, it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring." The faithful may fittingly be called the beauty of the people, for what is lovelier than those who believed? He calls the nation his inheritance, not because he ever neglected the others, but to show how intense his love for them was, how close his bond with them, and how much more providence he gave them. And so that you may see how precise the prophet is, notice how he uses the language most people use about goods for sale. When people buy something, they often call the items that surpass the rest "the beauty" of the lot. So to show that not all will be saved, he says: "The beauty of Jacob." The Gospels show the same thing in countless parables.

"God has gone up with a shout." He did not say "was taken up" but "went up," to show that he did not go up led by someone else's hand, but himself [?]

[Note:] [?] all the ears. A little further on Morel reads κατελύοντο; others read κατέλυον, which is better.

[... with the sound of the] trumpet. This shows their unanimity, as Paul also says: [195] "Whether, then, it was I or they, this is what we preach." And again: "The multitude of those who believed were of one heart and one soul." They sounded the trumpet, not calling to war but announcing the victory. In an army, when the troops go into battle, the trumpets lead the way along with the standards and rouse those present, not through sight but through hearing. So it was then too: when the apostles entered each city, the trumpets rang out, and everyone ran to listen.

"Sing praises to our God, sing praises; sing praises to our King, sing praises. For God is king of all the earth; sing praises with understanding. God reigned over the nations." Having described how great the achievement was, he calls the whole world to acclaim it with great eagerness. That is why he repeats himself, and why he does not simply call them to sing but to sing with great understanding. What does "Sing praises with understanding" mean? He means: learn what has happened, and consider how great the achievements are. But I think he is also hinting at something else with the words "with understanding": that we should sing not with the voice only but also with deeds, not with the tongue only but also with our lives. "For God reigned," he says, "over the nations." Another version has: "Above the nations." And what kind of kingship does he mean here? Not the kingship that comes from creation, but the kingship of belonging. Even before this he reigned over all, since he is their Creator and Maker. But now he also reigns over people who are willing and grateful. This deserves the highest acclaim and great wonder. He who was once insulted by the Jews brought about so great a change that he is hymned throughout the world. People who had never read the prophets or been brought up under the Law, but were savage in their ways, were suddenly transformed. They threw away everything that belonged to error and submitted to him: not two or three or four or ten nations, but the people who live in every part of the world.

"God sits on his holy throne." What does "sits on a throne" mean? He reigns, he rules. And he rightly said "holy." For God does not merely reign; he reigns in holiness. What does "reigns in holiness" mean? Purely. When human beings come to power, they use that very power for injustice. But his rule is untouched by anything of the kind. It is pure and holy. No deceit or anything of that sort corrupts or misleads that tribunal. It is pure and sincere, flashing with a purity beyond all purity, shining with unspeakable glory.

"The rulers of the peoples were gathered with the God of Abraham, for the mighty ones of the earth belong to God; they were greatly exalted."

6. [196] Here he shows how far the Gospel reached: it touched not only private persons but also those who wear the diadem and sit on the royal throne. Then, to show that he is the one God of the New and the Old Testament, he says "with the God of Abraham." In other words, this is the very God of the forefathers, the one who gave them the Law. That is why Jeremiah also said: "I will make a new covenant with you, not like the covenant I made with your fathers on the day I took them by the [...]"

[Note:] Some read ἅπαντες ἔτρεχον ("everyone ran"); others, including Savile, read ἅπαντες ἐξεχέοντο ("everyone poured out").

[...] one must, and only praise him, and do it with every kind of extravagance. And we must praise him both for the greatness of his being, which is infinite and incomprehensible, and for the overflowing benefits he has given us. For he willed, and he had the power to do what he willed.

"In the city of our God, on his holy mountain." What are you saying? Are you shutting up the praise of the great and praiseworthy one there, in a city and on a mountain? "That is not what I mean," he says, "but that we came to know this before the others." Either he said "In the city of our God" for that reason, or he wanted to show that his greatness and glory were displayed through the wonders done in that city. The captives, the outcasts, the despised, those held in the enemy's land as if in a tomb: these he suddenly made to shine, so that they overcame their conquerors, returned home, restored the city to its former prosperity, and gave the homeland back its ancient form. "He shows himself," he says, "through the greatness of the visible creation as well." But since most people in those days were rather senseless, he added the knowledge that comes from enemies and from victory. He kept setting up these astonishing trophies, changing things for the better, and working such wonders beyond all hope and expectation. He calls this city his own, not because he denies his providence to the other cities, but to show that these people had something more than the others where knowledge was concerned. The other cities might be called his only because he created them. This one was his also because it belonged to him, and because all the wonders took place there. In those days [198] it was the city that was called God's; now all of us are called God's. "For those who belong to Christ," he says, "have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires." Do you see how virtue has been raised to a higher pitch? For the same reason it was also called the mountain of God, because God was worshiped there.

"Rooting well the joy of the whole earth." This saying is very obscure, so we must pay attention. To someone who just reads it through it causes great perplexity, but whoever goes over it carefully will see the sequence and the precise chain of thought. What he means is this: "Great is the Lord in the city of our God, on his holy mountain, rooting it well"; that is, planting it well, fixing it well, establishing it well, for the joy and gladness of the whole world. Another translator, hinting at this, said: "As a set-apart ornament of the whole earth." For he made it the ornament and the gladness of the whole world. From there came the spring of true religion, the roots and the beginnings of the knowledge of God. Since the city was such, he rooted it and fixed it firmly as the adornment of the world, for the exultation and the joy of the whole earth. In those days Jerusalem was the school of the earth, and those who wished to enjoy joy, to be beautified and adorned, learned there what they needed. That is why, to make this clear, he did not say "rooting" but "rooting well." And if you want to take it in the higher, spiritual sense as well, you will see the truth of the matter. For it was from there that exultation came to every part of the world; from there the [...]
[Note:] Two [manuscripts read] ἐμάνθανον. "And he did not say 'rooting.' That is why also [...]" § [?]

[...] was happening. Countless nations came against the city (this is what he indicates by the great number of kings), and they did not simply come, but were massed and drawn up in battle order. Yet such things happened that they went away astonished at the extraordinary events. The war turned in such a way that they withdrew filled with numbness and shuddering. The many leapt back in great anguish, fearing the few; the ranked army feared the scattered; and they were in no better state than a woman in labor. From this it is clear that the war was not won by any human course of events. God was the general in command of the battle. He not only threw down their pride but also shook their minds, put birth pangs into them, and filled them with an unspeakable fear. It was just as if a great naval fleet had gathered and a fierce wind fell on it, shattered all the ships, sank the triremes, and suddenly threw everything into great confusion. Here [200] he seems to me to use this comparison to show both how easy the victory was and how great the confusion. For these enemies too used a naval fleet and came from a distant, foreign land, and they all perished by the wrath of God as if by a violent wind. That is why, to indicate the place they came from, he added: "Tarshish." The Hebrew also made this clear by its wording, which we have set beside the text for your benefit when it is read. So we may take it either this way, or the way I said before: that just as a fierce wind falling on the ships of Tarshish has often shattered them, so God threw those multitudes into confusion.

"As we have heard, so have we also seen, in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God." Do you see how he explains the earlier word, "rooting well"? He did not say "having rooted well" but "rooting well," that is, continually providing, continually caring, continually putting a wall around it. Having told what happened then, he brings the discussion back to the ancient stories, showing that these events are akin to those. "What we heard in words," he says, "we have seen in deeds: the victories, God's trophies, his care, his extraordinary wonders." For God has never stopped doing these things. So it is his work both to rescue from dangers and to lead people by the hand to the knowledge of God. And the prophet rightly recalled things that happened long ago. For they had to be taught both from the ancient stories and from recent deeds, so that the duller among them might, from what was happening before their eyes, believe also what had happened in the past, reap a double gain, and have hearing serve them in place of sight.

"God has founded it forever. We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your people." Another version has: "We have pictured your mercy, O God, in the midst of your people." And the Hebrew has: "Echalach demmenu." "As your name is, O God, so is your praise to the ends of the earth."

3. Since he said, "What we heard, we have also seen," he tells both what he heard and what he saw. What, then, did he hear, and [?] and the place seems to me to indicate, for the Hebrew also uses this word. That is why we have also set the Hebrew wording itself beside it. So he means either this or that.

[Note:] [?] εὐρίζῳ. See above. One [manuscript reads] διηνεκῶς προνοῶν ("continually providing for").

"Encircle Zion and embrace her." Another version has: "and go around her." "Tell of it in her towers." Another version has: "Count her towers." Another: "Praise." "Set your hearts on her strength." Another version has: "on her circuit wall." Another: "her wealth." "And go through her palaces." Another version has: "Measure her royal palaces." "So that you may tell it [202] to another generation." Another version has: "to a later generation." "For this is our God forever and ever. He will shepherd us forever."

Why does he command all this: to go around the city, to count the towers, to look closely at the buildings, to consider its beauty, to reckon up its circuit and its walls, to measure the houses and the palaces? There is no need for us to explain it; the text explains itself. Having said these things, he immediately added the reason. And what is it? "So that you may tell it," he says, "to another generation." What he means is this: "Be filled with delight, rejoice, leap for joy. But do not do it casually or carelessly; study her strength with care. For she had become a ruin. She had been torn up by the roots, her very ground had almost perished, and people had given up hope that she would ever change for the better. They said: 'Our bones have dried up, we are lost, we are cut off,' and they did not expect to get her back. Yet they did get her back, and not as she was when they lost her, but far better, more brilliant, more splendid, greater, richer, more powerful, and more spacious in her buildings, her markets, her power, and the abundance of her resources." For, he says, "The latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former." He is exhorting the people and all but saying: "Look at this city, given up for lost, without hope, a ruin: see how she has returned to an even more brilliant state! Study these very things, then: her buildings, her brilliance, her splendor. Then, having learned from this how strong God is, how he made the city that had been given up for lost greater than before, you may tell your descendants of God's power and of his unfailing providence: that he has never stopped caring for us, protecting and shepherding us." These stories will give those who come later a subject for much wisdom, an occasion for the most exact knowledge of God, and a concern for virtue. That is why he tells them to go around the city: so that they may become careful teachers of their descendants.

4. So let us too keep looking toward it always and continually, and keep in mind our city, Jerusalem, picturing its beauties at all times. It is the metropolis of the King of the ages, where the spirits of the righteous dwell, the choirs of patriarchs, of apostles, and of all the saints. There everything is free from strife and nothing passes away; there [?]

[...] is properly used when someone speaks into another's ear, straining himself and bidding the other pay attention to what is said. "Give ear, all who inhabit the world." "And if some are not counted among the nations, but are mixed peoples or scattered nomads, I call them too to listen." And see the orator's skill. First he roused their minds and made them alert to listen by calling everyone at once. Then, having called them, he checks their conceit, so that their numbers may not lift them up into arrogance. Such hearers are especially needed when someone is about to speak words of wisdom: hearers who are contrite and subdued, free of arrogance and of being puffed up. How, then, did he subdue their minds? By reminding them of their nature. Having said "nations," he added: "Both earthborn and sons of men." He named the substance from which our birth began; he reminded them of the common mother of us all. And why did he say "sons of men"? Because he had said "earthborn," and he did not want anyone to think, like the mythmakers outside the faith, that human beings first sprang up out of the earth, as some have fabled when they bring in certain "Sown Men." That is why he added: "the sons of men." Your fathers are human beings, and the source of your birth and of theirs is the earth. Why, then, is earth and ashes proud? Think of your mother and check your conceit. Trample down your pride. Remember "that you are earth, and to earth you will return," and cast out all arrogance. That is the kind of hearer I need. That is why I am restraining you: so that I may find you ready to receive what is said.

"Rich and poor together." Do you see the nobility of the Church? How is it not nobility, when it does not divide its hearers by rank, but pours out the whole of its teaching equally, and sets a common table for rich and poor alike? He had spoken of what unites everyone, being earthborn and sons of men, and had shown what their nature has in common. Then he brought in the difference and inequality that seems to come from the affairs of this life, and he casts that out too with his words, calling everyone in common (for our nature is common): "I call everyone in common, for the world is our common city. But you have invented a distinction based on wealth and poverty and brought in inequality. This too I cast out. I do not admit the rich while dishonoring the poor, nor do I call the poor while casting out the rich. I call both these and those, and not merely both, with some first and others last, or the latter last and the former first, but together. [205] Let the gathering be common, the word common, the hearing common." Even if you are rich, you were made from the same clay; you entered the world the same way as the poor man, and were born the same way. You too are a son of man,

[?] for instead of a teacher I now see a hearer. You called us as people about to hear something useful. But after arriving, gathering everyone together and promising to say something wise, you have not yet uttered a word. You have left the teacher's rank and passed over to the hearer's place. "I will incline my ear to a parable," he says. Why does he do this? Very wisely, and in keeping with what he has said. He said, "I will speak wisdom," so that no one would think his words merely human, and "the meditation of my heart," so that no one would suspect them of being his own invention. With these words he shows that what is said is divine, and that he utters nothing of his own but speaks what he has heard. "For I inclined my ear to God," he says. "I heard it from him, and I speak the things brought down from above into my mind." That is why Isaiah also said, "The Lord gives me a tongue of instruction, to know when I must speak a word; he has given me an ear to hear." And Paul again: "Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God." Do you see that he too first became a hearer and only then a teacher? That is why another translator said, "And my heart will murmur." What does "will murmur" mean? It will sing; it will utter some spiritual psalm. And if he speaks of "meditation," do not be troubled. What he received from the Spirit he meditated on continually and turned over within himself, and then, having turned it over, brought it out to others. What does "to a parable" mean? The word has many meanings. A parable can be a byword, an example, or a reproach, as when it says, "You have made us a byword among the nations, a shaking of the head among the peoples." A parable is also an enigmatic saying, what many call a riddle. It points to something, but its meaning is not plain from the words themselves; it holds a hidden sense within. Samson's saying was like this: "Out of the eater came food, and out of the strong came something sweet." So too Solomon: "He will understand a parable and a dark saying." A likeness is also called a parable: "He put another parable before them, saying: The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed." Figurative speech is also called a parable: "Son of man, tell them this parable: The great eagle with great wings," where the eagle means the king. A type and an image are also called a parable, as Paul shows when he says, "By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac; he who had received the promises was offering up his only son ... and from there he received him back in a parable," that is, in a type and an image. 3. What, then, does "parable" mean for him here? It seems to me to mean the narrative. And if he makes the saying enigmatic and very difficult, do not be troubled by that either. He does it to rouse the hearer. Besides, ease leads many people into laziness, and that is why he speaks in a parable. Christ too spoke much in parables, but explained them privately to the disciples. For a parable separates the worthy from the unworthy. The worthy person searches to find out what is meant, while the unworthy one passes it by. That is just what happened then too. For the Jews, not roused even by the difficulty to ask questions [?] ... [Editorial note, damaged: [?] the editions read [?]; "for enough." Shortly after, [?] "then." The words "this ... provoking" are missing in [?]; but one manuscript reads "of fear, and what of compunction."]

[?] men pay attention to none of these things. Since many people are more foolish than children, he makes this distinction and tells us what we ought to fear. It is not the things most people think fearful, I mean poverty, disgrace and illness. These are not only fearful to most people but also burdensome and oppressive, yet he lists none of them. It is sin alone. That is the meaning of "The iniquity of my heel will surround me." This, then, is the enigmatic saying; this is the new and paradoxical manner of speech. For to most people it seems very new and paradoxical to say that we need not fear any of the painful things in life. "Why then should I fear in the evil day?" he says. For one thing only: that the iniquity of my way and of my life may surround me. Scripture is also accustomed to call deceit a "heel." "He who eats bread with me," it says, "has lifted up his heel against me." And again Esau said of Jacob, "This is the second time he has supplanted me." Such is sin: deceptive, and able to seize us suddenly. "This is what I fear," he says, "the sin that deceives me and surrounds me." 4. That is why Paul calls it "easily besetting," meaning that it surrounds us continually, easily and readily. In these courts of ours people fear many things: great wealth, power, insult and deceit. There, nothing of the kind. Sin alone is fearful there, surrounding those it captures on every side, more terrible than armies. We must do everything we can not to be surrounded by it. When we see it trying to close around us, we must escape its grip, as brave soldiers do. And if we are caught, we must quickly cut our way through it, as David did when he cut through its strength by repentance. He was surrounded by it, but he quickly escaped it. Whoever fears this will never fear anything else. He will laugh at the good things of the present life and look down on its painful ones, with this one fear alone shaking his mind. Nothing, nothing else is fearful to the one who has this fear, not even death, the chief of all fearful things; only sin is. Why? Because it hands us over to Gehenna and sends us on to undying punishments. And once this fear is achieved, it brings in every virtue. Think how great a thing it is not to be puffed up by good fortune or brought low by hardship, to take no account of anything present, to look to the things to come, to await that day, and to live with such a fear. Such a person will be an angel, fearing this alone and nothing else. For he will fear nothing else if he fears this alone, as one ought to fear it. In the same way, whoever does not fear this will be subject to many terrors. "Those who trust in their power and boast in the abundance of their riches." Another translator has: "who vaunt themselves." "A brother does not redeem; will a man redeem?" [Editorial notes: [?] the manuscripts and Savile read "in the fearful day"; "in the evil day" is more correct. Others read "he has supplanted me" (another form). [?] should read "will set before."]

"Brothers, my heart's desire and my prayer to God for them is for their salvation." What, then, did his prayer accomplish? Nothing. And why do I speak of prayer, when he even prayed to be accursed for their sake? What then? Are the prayers of the saints useless? Not at all. They have very great power when you also help them along. That is how Peter raised Tabitha: not by prayer alone, but also through her almsgiving. That is how the saints protected others by their prayers. That holds here, where the arenas and the wrestling matches are. There, none of this applies; salvation comes only through works. He also seems to me to mock the rich here very sharply, and those who are puffed up. He did not say, "Those who have money," or "Those who possess power," but "Those who trust in the abundance of their riches and boast in their power." He laughs at them and rebukes them because they trust in shadows and pride themselves on smoke. And he rightly said, "He will not give the price for the redemption of his soul." For not even the whole world is the price of a soul. That is why it says, "What does a man gain if he wins the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?" And so that you may learn that not even the whole world is the price of a soul, hear what Paul says about other saints: "They went about in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, afflicted, ill-treated, of whom the world was not worthy." Indeed, the world exists for the sake of the soul. A father would not choose his house over his child, and in the same way God would not choose the world over the soul. What is needed is works and good deeds. Do you want to learn how great the price of our souls is? When the Only-begotten was about to redeem the soul, he did not give a world, or a man, or land, or sea, but his own precious blood. That is why Paul said, "You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of men." Do you see how great the price is? So when you lose what was bought at such a price, how will you ever be able to buy it back yourself? "For Christ, raised from the dead, dies no more." Do you see how costly the price is? Do you see the dignity of the soul? Do not, then, despise it, or make it a captive. "And he toiled forever, and he will live to the end." Another translator says, "And he ceased forever." Another: "Having rested in this age, he will go on living forever." He has spoken about the rich and about the powerful, and shown that nothing is gained from wealth and power. Now he speaks about those who have lived in virtue, in toil and hardship, anointing the athletes of the true philosophy for the contest. "Do not tell me," he says, "that he had toil and labour. Think of the fruit: the man becomes immortal, and an immortal life will follow, a life that has no end." How much better it is, then, to labour a little here and reap eternal rest than to indulge oneself a little and be in pain forever! Then, to show that the prizes and crowns are not there only, but that the first fruits of the rewards begin here, he adds: "Not [?]" [Editorial notes: One manuscript reads "for Israel." Morel reads "of the mighty."]

[?] enjoyment, and not even to relatives and acquaintances, but often to enemies and foes? That is why he did not say "to others," but "They will leave their wealth to strangers." What does "The fool and the senseless will perish together" mean? "Together with those mentioned before," he says. Here, it seems to me, he takes up the subject of the ungodly, who are infatuated with the present and give no thought to the future, and he calls them senseless on this account too. For if you think there is nothing after this life, why do you wear yourself out and toil, gathering countless riches from everywhere, enduring the labour but having no share in the enjoyment? "And their tombs are their houses forever." He says this as they suppose it to be. "Their dwellings are from generation to generation; they called their names upon their lands." What could be worse than this folly: to think of tombs as a lasting house, and to compete in ambition over them? Indeed, many have often made their tombs more splendid than their houses. They labour and toil either for enemies or for the worm and the dust, spending their wealth on things that serve no purpose. Such is the wisdom of those who hope for nothing in the future. But here I am moved to groan, because many even of those who hope for the life to come imitate in this respect the people who have no hope of the future. They build tombs, put up splendid monuments, bury gold, and hand their possessions on to others, and in this they are worse than the others. The man who expects nothing after this life acts irrationally, but because he expects nothing, he at least labours over the present. But you, O man, who know of the life to come and of those ineffable good things, according to the Gospel saying, "Then the righteous will shine like the sun," what pardon could you have? What defence? What punishment would you not justly suffer, spending everything here on dust, on ashes, on monuments, on foes and enemies? "They called their names upon their lands." See yet another kind of folly: putting their names on buildings, estates and baths, thinking they gain the greatest consolation from this, and chasing the shadow instead of the reality. If you long for a lasting memory, O man, do not put [?] names on buildings. Raise trophies of good deeds instead. These both preserve your name in the present life and prepare an immortal rest for you in the life to come. If you long for and desire remembrance, I will teach you the true and plainest way: cultivate virtue. For nothing makes a name so immortal as the very nature of virtue. The martyrs show this; the relics of the apostles show it; the memory of those who have lived in virtue shows it. How many kings founded cities and built harbours, put their names on them and then departed? Yet they gained nothing from it. They have been silenced and handed over to oblivion. But Peter the fisherman did none of these things, and since [he pursued] virtue [?] ... not a statue, not a city, not children [?].

[?] the beasts of the field, the birds of the sky and the fish of the sea, that pass along the paths of the seas. And indeed this is the greatest honour: to entrust him with the sceptre over all visible things, and that when he had as yet achieved nothing. Before he had even fashioned him, God said, "Let us make man according to our image and likeness." Then, explaining "according to the image," he added, "And let them rule over the fish of the sea, the beasts of the earth and the birds of the sky." This small creature, three cubits tall, so much weaker in bodily strength than the irrational animals, he made higher than them all through his kinship with reason, granting him a rational soul, which is the chief proof of his honour. Through this, man built cities, cut a path across the sea, adorned the earth, invented countless arts and overcame the wilder animals. Greatest and first of all, he came to know God who made him, was led by the hand toward virtue, and learned what is good and what is not. He alone of all visible things prays to God. He has enjoyed revelations, and again he alone. He has come to know many ineffable things and been instructed in the things of heaven. For his sake there is earth, for his sake heaven, for his sake the sun and the stars. For his sake there are the courses of the moon and the changes of the seasons and solstices. For his sake fruits are produced, and plants, and so many kinds of animals. For his sake there is day and night. For his sake apostles and prophets were sent, and for his sake angels were often dispatched. Why say more? It is not possible to go through everything. For his sake the only-begotten Son of God became man, was crucified and was buried, and for his sake those awesome wonders took place after the resurrection. For his sake there is the law, for his sake paradise, for his sake the flood. For this too is a very great form of honour: to correct him through both benefits and punishments. For his sake there were all the countless dispensations of former times, and the coming judgment itself will take place on account of the honour shown to him. That is why Job says, "What is man, that you have brought him into judgment?" just as this same psalmist says elsewhere, "What is man, that you are mindful of him?" For his sake, again, the Only-begotten will come, bestowing countless good things. Some he has already given: the good things provided through baptism, the mysteries and the rest of our initiation; and he has filled the earth with other wonders. Others he has promised to give: the kingdom of heaven and eternal life, to make us his heirs and to prepare us to reign with him. That is why Paul said, "If we endure, we shall also reign with him." Taking all this into account, the Prophet rightly compares to irrational animals those who have handed over such nobility to wickedness and deserted to the animals' passions. Other prophets do this too, wanting to shame the shameless hearer by the comparison. One says, "They became stallions mad for mares." Another says, "The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master's manger," and he speaks more severely than David. For David says, "He was compared to the cattle [?]" [Editorial notes, damaged: [?] "changes, and the chorus of solstices." "Psalmist" in [?] edition.]

[?] way. They bind themselves; they shackle their own feet. "And afterwards they will take delight in their own mouth." What he has said here is the most grievous thing of all, and the cause of the other evils. Those who sin and offend in this way and are so foolish congratulate themselves and admire themselves. They say they are to be envied, and they are pleased with what they do. Think how much evil desire grows when wickedness is praised, even by the very people who commit it! Wickedness is censured, insulted and refuted. It is scourged and torn by the conscience of anyone with any sobriety at all, and it is hated, yet even so it blooms shamelessly and grows every day. What happens, then, when the things that restrain it are absent: accusation, the reproof of conscience, criticism of what is done, repentance over one's deeds, shrinking back, hiding one's face, groaning and lamenting? What if everything is the opposite? Those who commit it praise themselves and weave encomia for themselves. They think themselves better than others for this very reason, and after acting they praise what they have done. That is the meaning of "And afterwards they will take delight in their own mouth." Where would wickedness not run off to then? They are so deranged and so out of their minds that even after fulfilling their desire, when they ought most of all to see their lawlessness and be ashamed, they exult, hold their heads high and are pleased with what they have done. For such is sin. Before it is committed, it veils its ugliness and wraps its foulness in the drunkenness of pleasure. But once it is committed, the pleasure of the desire gradually recedes and the accusation of conscience arrives, scourging the thoughts it has laid bare, and then above all its harmfulness appears. These people, however, are not like that even after fulfilling their desire. They see their wealth swollen, their tombs raised, their vain buildings completed. They ought then at least to be pierced with compunction and groan. Instead, even after this, after the deed, after the fulfilment, their sickness grows still worse. Since, then, their part is over, God's part now follows. 9. Those who condemn themselves for their sins anticipate God's sentence and ward it off, as Paul says: "For if we judged ourselves, we would not be judged." In the same way, those who are sick without repenting, who sin but do not condemn their offences, draw God's punishment down upon themselves with great severity. These people either seize what belongs to others or spend their own goods vainly and at random. They spend on tombs, worms and moths what they ought to spend on the poor. They do not repent of what they have done but remain incurably sick. So hear what happens next. What happens, then? They are handed over to God's punishment. That is why he added, "Like sheep they are laid in Hades; death will shepherd them." He is not pointing to their gentleness here by calling them sheep. For what could be more savage than those who overlook the naked bodies of the poor and bellies wasting away with hunger, while adorn[ing] [?] ... [Editorial note: Savile and one manuscript read "over what was done" (another construction).]

…is good. Or rather, if you like, let us take the argument up to another, greater example. Suppose a king is wicked and a private citizen is good. Let us see who is master of whom, and where lordship shines out: who is the ruler and who is the ruled. How then shall we find this out? Let the king order the private citizen to do something wicked and full of wrongdoing. What then will the good citizen and subject do? Not only will he refuse to yield or obey, he will even try to turn the one giving the order away from his purpose, even if he must die for it. Who then is free: the one who does what he wishes and does not fear even the king, or the one who is despised by his own subject? And so that we do not carry the argument forward on a vague example: was not the Egyptian woman, Potiphar's wife, a queen? Did she not rule all Egypt? Did she not have a king for a husband? Was she not clothed with great power? And what of Joseph? Was he not a slave? Not a captive? Not a servant bought with silver? Did she not arm herself with her whole battle array against the young man, not entrusting the war to another but coming out to the battle line herself? Who then was in slavery at that time, and who was in freedom? She who begged, pleaded and implored, and had become a captive not even of a man but of a most wicked passion? Or he who despised the diadem, the scepter, the purple and all that pomp, and cut short her schemes? Did she not go away thwarted, and become the slave once more of another passion, irrational rage and bloodthirstiness? And did he not come out with countless crowns on his head, showing freedom shining all the more brightly in slavery itself? 10. For nothing is so free as virtue, and nothing so slavish as vice. That is why someone says elsewhere: "A wise servant will rule over foolish masters." Just as a captive, even if he has boundless wealth, is for that very reason the easiest prey for everyone, so too the one taken captive by the passions is feebler than a spider. And what of war? Do we not see the virtuous prevailing? And what of affairs and counsels? Do their counsels not stand, even if no one obeys them? And what of the life after this? Did not the rich man beg for a drop like a beggar, and not get it? And was not the poor man, because he was earnest and virtuous, in the greatest good fortune, sharing the same lot as Abraham? [220] And what of the apostles? Though they were bound, scourged and suffered countless terrible things, did they not get the better of those who did these things to them? Think how deep a perplexity they threw those men into, so that they said: "What shall we do with these men?" And yet they held them bound and under arrest in the middle of the courts.
