The one group stood in the rank of judges and rulers, the other in the rank of defendants, and yet the defendants prevailed over the judges. And everywhere, if one follows the argument carefully, he will see the virtuous man prevailing over the wicked. This is prevailing in the proper sense: not the false prevailing of the many, which is deceptive and easily refuted, but the kind that is firmly fixed and immovable. "And their help shall grow old in…"

…when the glory of his house is increased." Since this is how things are, he says, why do you fear the things of the present? Why does poverty grieve you? Why do you fear the wealthy? You have heard about the resurrection, the lot of the good and the punishment of the wicked. Why then do you still fear shadows? Those things are lasting and fixed, while these are like withering flowers. That is why he left everything else aside and leapt upon the citadel of evils, the desire for wealth: once it is cast down, the rest are destroyed along with it. 11. "But how can I not fear people who have so much power?" someone says. Power is temporary, strength lasts an hour, prosperity passes by. Money, wealth and all that great honor are like shadows and dreams. That is why he added: "For when he dies he will not take everything with him, nor will his glory go down with him." Here he gives the reason for not fearing temporary things. Death came, he says, and cut the root, and the whole crown of the tree came down with its leaves, and the house became easy prey for everyone. Sheep and goats set upon a tree lying on the ground after it has been felled. In the same way, with those who are rich like this, many enemies, many friends and many of those they once benefited are found ravaging their possessions. And the man who was surrounded by so much, who had so many cupbearers and cooks, silver and gold mixing bowls, acre upon acre of land, houses, slaves, horses, mules, camels and whole armies of servants, departs alone. No one goes away with him; he does not even take his clothes with him when he goes. Indeed, the more splendid the things laid about him, the more lavish the table he lays for the worm as he departs, the greater the craving he stirs in grave robbers, and the greater the plot against his wretched body. By the very things with which he adorns himself the more, he ensures that he will be the more violently outraged, arming and summoning against himself the hands of those who dig up tombs. [222] "So what?" someone says. "Here at least he boasts greatly and puffs himself up until his death." In fact many do not even manage that until death. When plotters fastened on them, they suffered things harsher than countless condemned criminals: stripped of their money, covered with dishonor, living in prison. The man who yesterday rode in a carriage is in chains today. The one who yesterday was courted by flatterers is now surrounded by executioners. The one who smelled of perfumes is drenched in blood. The one who reclined on a soft couch is thrown on the hard ground. The one courted by all is despised by all. "But even at his death his funeral is splendid and magnificent." And what is that to him, when he perceives nothing? The stench is greater, the loathing greater, the envy fiercer. Even after his death, that extravagance brings his children unending war. And notice the precision of the expression and the intensity of the philosophy. He not only strikes at the rich man with the fact that his wealth does not go away with him. Even here he strips him of all his pomp, and shows that it is not even wealth, even while its owner enjoys it. For he did not say, "When his glory is increased," but "the glory of his house." These things…

…in the congregation of gods." And again: "I said, You are gods." And Paul: "For although there are so-called gods, and many lords." And Moses: "You shall not revile gods." And elsewhere: "The sons of God, seeing the daughters of men." [? misplaced lines: "…and the foundations of the earth. For hear, he says, you ravines and foundations of the earth, for the judgment belongs to God."] And again he himself says: "Whoever curses God shall bear sin; and whoever names the name of the Lord shall be stoned." And again: "Let the gods who did not make heaven and earth perish from beneath heaven." Whom then does he mean by this name in those testimonies, and whom does he call gods here? The rulers. That is why he adds: "You shall not revile gods, and you shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people." He also uses the word for those born from some virtuous ancestor. Enosh showed great virtue and was called by the name of God. All those descended from him then intermarried with the descendants of his brother. So he calls the descendants of the virtuous man sons of God. "For they began," it says, "to call upon the name of God." He also uses it for the Jewish people, who were honored with this title when he said: "I said, You are gods, and sons of Israel." For he called their people this out of his own love for humanity. This also explains the saying: "Whoever curses God shall bear sin." That is, whoever speaks evil of a ruler sins. "And whoever names the name of the Lord shall be stoned." That is, whoever gives the name of the God who truly exists to things that do not exist. Since the sin is unpardonable, its punishment is also most severe. The gods of the Greeks are also called gods. This is not as a mark of honor or a gracious title, but because of the delusion of those who were led astray and called them so. That is why Paul too says, "For although there are so-called gods," showing that they do not exist and do not even have the title as a mark of honor. Here then, whom does he mean when he says "God of gods"? It seems to me he means the Greek gods, not as though they existed, but as they are imagined by those who have been led astray. The Jews were still rather dull and not entirely freed from idolatry. They were still gaping after idols and kept many remnants of their lawlessness. So he pulls down their notions from this side too, showing that he is the Master of those gods as well. For he is also Master of the demons, I mean of their very beings. Their dispositions, and all their wickedness, came from themselves. This psalm also seems to me to be connected to the previous psalm. Here too a rebuke and an accusation of those who have sinned are written. But there he called the whole world to listen, while here he calls the very elements that stretch over the whole world. Here there is another theater and another audience. There it was the nations, the earthborn, the rich and the poor. Here it is heaven and earth, and he brings in God himself pleading his case, and sets out the words God speaks as he argues his case against the people of the Jews. Therefore… [Notes: "beneath heaven" is missing in Savile and in one [?] manuscript. Genesis 4:26: "He hoped to call upon the name of the Lord God." [?] … another has "they were more dully disposed" … "they were freed" [?].]

…of God, and he did this once, twice and a third time. Therefore "Fire shall burn before him, and around him…" [?] And when John began to reveal him, he said to him: "Let it be so now." That is: Be silent now, for it is not yet time for the secret of the dispensation to be revealed. I still wish to escape the devil's notice, so be silent, he says, "for this is fitting for us." And when he came down from the mountain, he ordered them to tell no one that he was the Christ. For at that time he came as a shepherd, seeking the lost sheep and wanting to hunt down the runaway prey. That is why he kept himself in the shadows. A physician does not immediately show a frightening face to the patient. In the same way, he did not wish to make himself known from the outset, but quietly and little by little. That is why this same prophet, pointing to this noiseless coming of his, says further on: "He will come down like rain upon a fleece, and like drops falling on the earth." For he did not come with a crash. He did not throw things into turmoil, shake the earth, hurl lightning or convulse heaven. He did not bring companies of angels with him, or split the firmament down the middle and so come down on the clouds. Instead he came noiselessly, through a virgin's womb, carried for the term of nine months. He is born in a manger as a carpenter's son. In humble swaddling clothes he is plotted against. He flees with his mother to Egypt. Then, after the death of the man who had committed such lawless deeds, he returns. He went about looking like one of the many. His clothing was humble and his table humbler still, and he walked constantly, so constantly that he grew weary from walking. But that is not how he will come then. He will come so openly that no one will be needed to announce his coming beforehand. That is why he himself, showing how plain to see it would be, said: "If they tell you, Look, he is in the inner rooms, do not go in; or, He is in the desert, do not go out. For as the lightning comes from the east and shines as far as the west, so will the coming of the Son of Man be," showing and proclaiming itself. This is what happens with lightning. We need no one to announce it: in the same moment it appears, it becomes known to everyone, and to everyone at once. So too Paul says: "For the Lord himself will come down from heaven with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel, at the last trumpet." The prophet too saw him like this, borne on the clouds, with a river drawn along before him, and the fearful judgment seat and the reckoning no one can escape. For then, then it is the time of the court and of judgment. That is why he no longer appears as a physician but as a judge. Daniel, at any rate, sees his throne as well, and the river drawn before the judgment seat, and everything is shown to him as made of fire: the chariot and the wheels. But when he came at the beginning, at his first coming, he showed nothing of the kind: no fire, no river, nothing else of that sort. Instead there was a manger, a lodging, a hut and a poor mother. In another way, this also shows that he does not change and cannot be altered. Daniel said that the one seated on the throne had hair white as wool and clothing like snow. So that you would not think of literal hair or clothing, but understand that everything is pure, transparent fire, he says… [Note: … "that he is in the desert" [?]. [?]]

…to them from this, and he mocks them, saying: "Those who make his covenant with sacrifices." That is, those who think that slaughtering the bodies of dumb animals is enough for their salvation. "And the heavens shall declare his righteousness." Here again he wants to show the brilliance of his righteousness: its radiance, its clarity, how it cannot be disputed and is acknowledged by all. So he brings in the senseless elements proclaiming it, in the same way as he spoke before. "For God is judge." That is, he says, he determines what is just for each. He did not put "judging" here in a general sense. He put it to show that God is just and also grants justice to others. In God's case "judge" is taken to mean "just," as Paul also used it when he said: "For then how will God judge the world?" [228] For this above all is judgment, and this above all is a judge: not simply to give a verdict, but to give a just verdict. And the Jews will be judged, both those of that time and those who later transgressed under the New Covenant. The former have nature and the law as their accusers; the latter have these, and also what Christ did for them. What could they say, or what reason could they offer for not believing? But pay attention to what is being said, I beg you, so that you can silence those who argue against us. It is better for them to be defeated by us now and set right than to go there thinking they have won and be condemned by the Judge of the whole world. What then could the Jews say? Why did they kill Christ? What charge, small or great, did they have against him? "That he made himself God," they say. And yet those were not the words at the time of the cross; there were others. They did not say, "Whoever makes himself God," but "Whoever makes himself a king is no friend of Caesar." And yet they often wanted to make him king, and he fled. "But before this," they say, "they accused him of making himself God." So what? If he did this falsely and unjustly, without being God, the charge had some basis. But if he did it justly, he ought to have been worshiped, not crucified. Let us see, then, whether it was not because he truly was God that he made himself God, that is, showed and revealed himself as God. Where then do you want to learn this from? From the events of that time? From those of today? From those surrounding his birth? Who was ever born of a virgin? Who showed such a star? Who led Magi on so long a journey, not by compulsion and force, but by persuasion and revelation? Do you see the whole of creation recognizing its Master? Nature is the first to give way. It does not object or resist, saying: "I do not loosen the pangs of birth. I have never learned to bring forth a child from a virgin's womb. I do not know how to make a mother without marriage." Rather, it stood aside and gave up its own boundaries, for it recognized its Master. Again, when he was born, angels came, announcing [on] earth [?] the one who is in heaven, and earth became heaven, since the King was there. And Magi worshiped him, having come from so far away. The child lay in a manger in Palestine, while men from a barbarian country brought him as much honor and homage as it is fitting to bring to God. But perhaps they will not accept these things, and will look for other signs, those of the present generation. We will not be at a loss for these either. For such is the truth… [Notes: These words, "Israel, and I will testify against you," were missing in the editions. [?] "they were repelling" [?].]

…I will rebuke you; your whole burnt offerings are before me continually." For this is how the other prophets accuse them too. They neglected the greater part of virtue and placed their hopes of salvation in these things. They were going to offer this as their defense: "We pour out sacrifices," "We offer whole burnt offerings." But I have not come to plead my case over these things, he says, nor to accuse you as though they had been neglected. And Isaiah strikes at them even more forcefully, saying: "What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me? I am full. I do not want burnt offerings of rams, the fat of lambs, or the blood of bulls and goats. For who asked these things from your hands?" [250] And yet much is said about sacrifices. But God does not lay down these laws because he primarily wants them; he does it in condescension to their weakness. And Jeremiah too says: "Why do you bring me frankincense from Sheba, and cinnamon from a distant land?" Practically all the prophets say that this is nothing great. That is why he himself said at the beginning, "I am God, your God," showing by this that such a manner of worship is unworthy of him. God must be worshiped not with smoke and the savor of burning fat, but with a most excellent way of life, incorporeal and spiritual. The demons of the pagans are not like this; on the contrary, they demand these things. A certain Greek poet clearly shows this too, saying: "… For this is the honor that falls to our lot." But our God is not like that. The demons thirsted for human blood and wanted to lead people little by little into such murders, and so they constantly demanded these things. But he wanted to draw people away little by little even from the slaughter of animals. So he made use of this condescension and permitted sacrifices in order to abolish sacrifices. "I will not accept calves from your house, or goats from your flocks. For all the wild beasts of the forest are mine, the cattle on the mountains and the oxen. I know all the birds of the sky, and the beauty of the field is with me." See how little by little he lifts the minds of these earthbound people. He opens their hardened understanding and shows that he did not command these things because he needed them, or make laws about them because he welcomed them. If I wanted to be worshiped in this way, he says, since the whole world under the sun is mine and I myself am the creator of all things, I would have provided myself with abundant sacrifices. Then, mocking and ridiculing them to make the accusation sting all the more, he added: "If I am hungry, I will not tell you, for the world and all that fills it is mine." He had permitted these things in order to lead them away from them little by little, but they stayed fixed in this paltriness and reaped no great benefit from his condescension. That is why he speaks somewhat more coarsely and in more human terms, saying: "If I am hungry, I will not tell you." That is: I am not hungry, for God does not hunger or grow weary. And if I wanted to be worshiped with these things, I would not lack countless sacrifices and burnt offerings. And… [Notes: Morel: "and God"… Others read "after a little." [?] "the flesh of [?]"… Morel had "thanksgiving and praise," unlike [?]…]

"…and I will deliver you, and you will glorify me." Do you see how lavishly the reward is given? What, then, could equal such lovingkindness, when he gives us rewards even for virtue itself, rewards far greater than our labours, and given exactly when they are needed? "And why," someone asks, "did he say, 'Call upon me'? Why does he wait to be called upon by us?" Because he wants to make our closeness to him greater and our friendship toward him warmer, by giving, by being called upon, and by receiving. Virtue brings us close to God, and the reward does the same, and prayer in turn strengthens this closeness. That is why he says: Give to me, and I give to you. And in giving, it is you who receive, for he himself has no need of these things. So even if you become gentle, moderate and self-controlled, you have added nothing to God; you have made yourself splendid and better. Yet he still appoints the greatest rewards and crowns for you for these things, as though you were doing him a service. And even before those crowns you enjoy no small pleasure, nourished by a good conscience and given wings by good hopes. By "the day of affliction" here he does not mean days of misfortune or of calamity. He means that even if sin wages war on you, even if the devil besieges you and brings in evil desires, you will have plenty of help. "And I will deliver you, and you will glorify me." Here again he says this not because he needs glory from us (how could God need glory?), but so that the hymn of thanksgiving may keep the benefit in memory, so that our disposition toward him may grow warmer, and so that we may first of all [?] receive the greatest well-being. 6. But anyone who said that here he also calls the coming day a "day of affliction" would not be wrong, for that affliction never ends. Here, death comes and puts an end to misfortunes; friends console us; an end is expected; often a change of circumstances is hoped for. Length of time softens the soul's grief, and the … [?] … of the wicked, and seeing many such examples has seemed to many a great consolation. But there, nothing of the kind exists. No one is present to comfort; all are in a wilderness without friends. No length of time softens the pain (how could it, when the flame presses on without a break?). There is no hope of release, for the punishment is eternal; no expectation of death, for the penalty is deathless, and the bodies being punished are deathless too. There is not even what many think brings consolation, the sight of others being punished. In the first place, it is not even possible to see those being punished, because the darkness overshadows the eyes, more effectively than any partition. Then the excess of pain does not allow one to feel even this consolation. The rich man, at any rate, drew no word of consolation from this, nor did those who gnash their teeth. "But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my statutes?" Do you see the perfectly tuned lyre, the harmonious cithara, sounding a single harmony through different notes? For this thought can be seen in the apostles too, and it is set down in other prophets as well. Paul says something like this, showing also … [?] when you accuse wickedness, you will accuse yourself rather than others. And you take up the … [?] "will make a covenant": Savile.

… [?] and the lips move in vain, and only to the condemnation of the speaker. But if anyone examines the mind, he will find a great war going on there. "But you hated instruction, and cast my words behind you." By "instruction" here he means the teaching of the law, which brings order to the soul, drives out wickedness and plants virtue. How then can you handle it and sow it in others, when you yourself do not possess it in your deeds? "For you cast my words behind you," he says. 7. You not only added nothing from the teaching of the law; you even maimed what you have from nature. For the principles of what must not be done, and of what is not such [?], are implanted in us by nature. But you thrust them away and did not keep them in memory. "If you saw a thief, you ran along with him, and you cast your lot with adulterers." It is impossible to find a human being entirely without sin. That is why someone said, "Who will boast of having a pure heart? Or who will be bold enough to say he is clean from sin?" And Paul, having said, "I am conscious of nothing against myself," added, "But I am not justified by this." And: "The righteous man is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech," evidently of his own sins. So that no one may say, "If all are in sin, and he has commanded the sinner not to recount the statutes, who will there be to recount them?", so that no one may say this, he sets out the kinds of sins one by one. For there is a sin unto death, as Eli said: "If a man sins against a man, the priest will pray for him; but if he sins against the Lord, who will pray for him?" In the law, too, some sins were incurable, so that they were punished even with death, while others had a very quick remedy. So too Christ in the New Testament: "If your brother sins," he says, "reprove him between you and him alone. If he does not listen, take two more with you," he says. "If he does not listen even to them, let him be to you as the Gentile and the tax collector." And yet elsewhere, when Peter said, "How often, if my brother sins against me, shall I forgive him?", he was told, "Up to seventy times seven." Here, though, after two admonitions, he shows that the offence is great and does not oblige you to remain with the man any longer. What then? Do these sayings contradict those? Far from it. He says "seventy times seven" if the man repents. For how could anyone forgive someone who does not even admit that he has sinned, and does not repent? When we ask a physician for remedies, we also show him the wound. Who then is the sinner of whom Scripture speaks here? Let us listen carefully. For he sketches him in what follows, saying: "If you saw a thief, you ran along with him, and you cast your lot with adulterers. Your mouth abounded in wickedness, and your tongue wove deceits. You sat and spoke against your brother, and against your mother's son you laid a stumbling block." Do you see the colours of wickedness, as in a portrait? Do you see how the wicked man has become a beast through wickedness, betraying the nobility of his nature? Let us not pass over the portrait casually, then, but examine it carefully, detail by detail. [?] … "to speak of the passion": Colbert and Savile. "For by speaking of necessity, to blame poverty" … [?] "groans, mourns" [?] … taken from the manuscripts; it was missing in [?]

…does he need? Does he require helpers? No, but he wants you to become his servant in this, so that you may not fall into the same sins, since you become more self-controlled through your indignation against another, and so that by this too you may show your love for God. When you pass over another's sin without prosecuting it or grieving over it, you make your own soul more careless and more prone to fall, and very often you prepare it to fall into the same sins. You also do the other man no small harm by this untimely kindness, making his reckoning in the future more severe and making him more careless in the present. This is said not only about thieves but about every sin. He has put the least of the offences first so that you may know that someone who finds no pardon in such a case will be still less able to enjoy this consolation in another. Hear, then, what he says next: "And you cast your lot with adulterers." He has moved on to the greater sin, for theft is much less than this. Someone who compared these sins put it this way: "It is no wonder if someone is caught stealing, for he steals to fill his hungry soul." If, then, this is unpardonable, adultery is much more so. Here he calls fornication adultery. So if you see one of those who flock with you committing fornication and approaching the mysteries, say to the one who ministers at their distribution: "So-and-so is unworthy of the mysteries; hold back his profane hands." If he is not even worthy to recount the statutes, consider how far his punishment will go when he touches the holy table as well. And not only his, but also that of the one who covers for him. He did not say, "And you committed adultery," but, "You cast your lot with adulterers." Ah, how great an evil it is to cover up the rottenness of others, when he says that such a person shares in the punishment for the offence, and no less than the offender! The offender at least can plead his passion, even if the excuse is unpardonable, just as the thief pleads hunger; but you cannot plead even this. Why then do you share and take part in the punishment, when you do not enjoy the pleasure? This is why secular judges punish not only those who dared the deed but also any servants they find to have been privy to it. And the masters who are betrayed [?] would gladly drink their blood and taste their flesh, and they hold them responsible for the license that made the deed possible no less than the woman who committed adultery. For those who drew back the curtains have themselves given greater license to those in hiding; they have insulted the adulteress, the wronged husband and the adulterer himself. If they had warned beforehand, if they had made it known, they would have scared off all the prey. Those most responsible for driving game into the snares are the ones who conceal the snares, sit around those about to be caught, hide the trick on every side, and allow no noise or anything else that could frighten them off; such a person deserves punishment [?]. In the same way, the guilty one is the one who speaks evil, not the one who hears it, provided that the latter gives no reasonable grounds for the slander. So let us not strive to avoid being ill spoken of (for that is impossible, and there is a sentence of Christ that says,

"Woe to you when all people speak well of you"), but rather to give no handle ourselves. For someone who wants to be well spoken of by everyone often destroys his own soul out of love for human glory, serving where he should not and pleasing where he ought not, so as to buy their favour. On the other hand, someone who does not care if everyone speaks ill of him destroys himself as well. Just as it is impossible for a virtuous man to be well spoken of by all, so it is impossible for someone who has given many handles from many sides not to be ill spoken of by all. But if there are accusers even though you give no offence, then your reward is greater too, as happened with the apostles and those noble men. One must also know this: even if someone speaks ill of us about a matter for which our conscience does not condemn us, we should not for that reason disregard the accuser, because of the harm to him. We should do everything with fitting care, so as to remove even an unreasonable pretext. That is why Paul, in the matter of money, sent many people to carry the provisions for the poor, and he gives the reason: "So that no one may blame us in this generous gift which we are administering." He did not see that they were going to take offence wrongly and then overlook and disregard it. Since it was in his power to remove the stumbling block, he took thought even for those who took offence. And again elsewhere he says: "If food makes my brother stumble, I will never eat meat, so that I may not make my brother stumble." And yet these things were indifferent. Nevertheless, he says, if it causes offence, then even if it does me no harm, I do not disregard the salvation of those who take offence. If the harm would outweigh the salvation, disregard the one who takes offence; if not, then do not. This would be a general rule and canon, teaching when one must disregard those who take offence and when not. For example: the Jews took offence because Paul did not keep the law, and for this reason many tens of thousands were turning away and limping in the faith. What then does he do? He wished to heal the offence (for the salvation of so many tens of thousands was the greater thing) and to set the lameness right, so for the time being [?] he refrained from showing that he did not keep the law, which was the greater matter. Again, they took offence because he preached one who had been crucified. Here he disregarded those who took offence, for the gain of the preaching was greater. Christ does the same. When he was talking to them about foods and they took offence at his saying, "It is not what goes in that defiles a person, but what comes out," he says: "Let them be. Every plant which my Father has not planted will be uprooted." But when they demanded taxes from him, though he knew that he need not pay, he still said, since the time did not yet demand that his dignity be revealed: "But so that we do not offend them, go, cast a hook into the sea, and the…" Savile and others read: "let this be a general [rule]." Savile and others read: "though having said that."

…the Pharisee, the tax collector; rather, he became more righteous than the Pharisee, because he called himself wretched. "These things you did, and I kept silent. You imagined, wickedly, that I would be like you. I will reprove you, and set your sins before your face." 11. Do you see his unspeakable lovingkindness? Do you see the excess of his goodness? Do you see the boundless wealth of his long-suffering? For by "silence" here he means long-suffering. "You dared so much," he says, "and I did not prosecute you. I endured and bore it, giving you room for repentance. But you not only gained nothing from this; you even ran aground on greater wickedness. You did not change, you were not ashamed, you did not condemn yourself for what you had done. You even supposed that I, who was long-suffering toward you, who forbore, who kept silent, who bore so much, bore it not out of long-suffering and lovingkindness but because I did not wish to correct these things and was not indignant at what was being done." "Understand these things, you who forget God." What things? The things that have been said, he says. What does "understand" mean? Perceive. For what has been said obscurely? What needs much investigation? Above all, the very manner of the teaching introduces a changed way of life. Making little account of sacrifices, he introduces the legislation of the gospel. Besides, they had been buried under a great heap of sins. Wishing to pull them out of the swamps of wickedness, as it were, and to clean away the evil habit that had taken hold of them like rheum from the eyes [?], he rouses them to remember what had been done, so that they would not consign it to oblivion and go away without profit. For habitual sin produces great callousness of soul; it makes people senseless and blinds the keen eye of the mind. "Lest he seize you, and there be none to deliver." O unspeakable lovingkindness! These are the words of a loving mother, or rather of a goodness that infinitely surpasses that tenderness. He who set out such an accusation, who displayed such wrath, secures them in advance. He who said, "I will reprove you, and set your sins before your face," and pronounced a sentence of condemnation, revokes the sentence again. He does not hand them over to punishment as condemned men; he entrusts them to admonition and counsel as people who ought to be corrected, bringing them to their senses by fear and saying, "Lest he seize you like a lion, and there be none to deliver." "A sacrifice of praise will glorify me, and there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God." He has shown his lovingkindness; he has admonished, counselled, threatened and frightened; he has set unmixed punishment before them and brought in counsel. Now he also tells them the way by which they can set right what has been done, saying: "A sacrifice of praise will glorify me." What he means is this: "It will not only stop my wrath or cancel the condemnation; it will also glorify me." See the greatness of the achievement, when God is glorified through a human being! "And there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God." Do you see the unspeakable reward? Do you see the excess of lovingkindness? For the way of God … [?] … "accusation, he who such" is missing in [?] … not to be satisfied even with a second punishment, but to ask that so many be brought upon him. What follows is still much harsher than this. For he also prays for orphanhood and widowhood upon those

he leaves behind. And yet these things necessarily happen once a man has departed. Nevertheless he puts these too among his curses, seething with anger. He does not stop even at orphanhood; after such misfortunes he goes still further, heightening the horror and asking that the man's family become wanderers and exiles. "Let his sons be tossed about and wander," he says, "and let them beg." That is: may they find no rest in their wandering, may they not have enough of the food they need, may they never stop moving from place to place, driven out and pursued over the whole earth, finding nowhere a place to stand. Along with this he also prays that they may be poor, with an utter and unbearable poverty, so that they get no help even from their relatives but go around begging it from strangers and people they do not know. Listen to how he sets this out to make it plain. After saying, "Let his sons wander and beg," he adds: "Let them be cast out of their homesteads; let the creditor search out all that he has, and let strangers plunder his labours." This is another kind of misfortune: to have their goods given over to plunder, to endure the schemes of creditors, to be mistreated in every way, and, harsher still, to be without a protector amid such evils. This too he prays for, saying: "Let there be no one to help him." For the evils are unbearable in themselves, but when someone has no one to stand by him they are much harsher. "Nor let there be anyone to pity his orphans." Ah, what a depth of anger, when not even orphanhood before its time finds mercy, and is not only denied mercy but overwhelmed with utter destruction! "Let his children be given over to destruction," he says. "In a single generation may his name be blotted out." Do you see speech full of anger that never stops? He prays that they may live amid misfortunes of every sort and kind, be handed over to total ruin and perish without a name. And as though the misfortune of the children were not enough, he adds again: "May the iniquity of his fathers be remembered, and may the sin of his mother not be blotted out. Let them be before the Lord continually, and may their memory be destroyed from the earth." For this is especially typical of anger: breaking into pieces the misfortunes one has stated in general, and turning the same things over and over. Having said, "May the iniquity of his fathers be remembered," he added, "and not be blotted out." And yet it is the same thing. Nevertheless anger made him say both. What he means is this: "Kill him, slaughter him, destroy him!" Do you see the multitude of curses? If you like, I will gather them up again from the beginning. May he fall among wicked men, he says; may he be accused; may they seize him; may he be condemned; may he suffer an untimely death; may he be cast out of his office and see it pass not to his descendants but to others. May his wife perish; may his children endure poverty, orphanhood and [?] the life of beggars; may they be condemned and driven out on every side; may they have no one to help them; may they also fall from God's favour; may they have no harbour and no refuge. May his name be blotted out from the earth and may he perish without a name. May his father and mother pay the penalty for their sins, and after that may they perish utterly and before their time. 12 [?]. Does what has been said not astound the hearer? [?] … reads: "may he perish utterly and before his time."

…do wrong. Christ, too, used a manner of this kind, calling out in the form of prophecy rather than curse, imitating one who laments, and saying: "Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida!" And again, as when he says: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets!" About whom, then, is the psalm spoken? Some of it is about Judas, the Spirit prophesying through David, and the rest is about others. This too is a manner of prophecy. In many places we shall find it composed this way, with the opening addressed to one person and the rest spoken about another. And so that you may see this very thing from elsewhere too: when the Jews were entering the land of promise, Joshua the son of Nun was commanded by God to divide the twelve tribes into twelve parts, and to have some bless and others curse. Both the blessing and the curse were prophecies of what was to come. For he said: "Cursed are you in the city, cursed in the field"; and by putting together countless curses of this kind the tribes completed a long discourse. The same may be said here: a prophecy has been composed in the form of a curse. It announces and foretells what would befall Judas, and then after him takes up another subject, and stands against certain people who rose up against the priesthood, so that we may learn how great an evil it is to rise up against the priests of God and to use deceit and injustice against them. For what is said here is nothing other than a teaching about what will befall those who wrong their neighbours, who rise up with deceit and a corrupt mind against those who have done no wrong. And if he asks that the children be punished, do not be troubled, beloved. By "children" he here means those who have shared in the wickedness of such people. Scripture is accustomed to call "children" not only those related by kinship but also those who have lived in wickedness together, even if they are not children by nature, as when it says: "You are sons of the devil." Yet the Jews were not by nature sons of the devil. How could those clothed in flesh be sons of the incorporeal one? But by sharing in his wickedness they took on the kinship. In the same way he also casts them out from Abraham, saying: "If you were Abraham's children, you would do the works of Abraham." For it is surely plain to everyone that a son is not punished on account of his father, nor a father on behalf of his son. This is shown to be stated in the law too, unless the father has brought the son up badly; and even then he is punished not on behalf of the son but for his own negligence, as Eli was.

3. If you like, let us also go through the psalm from the beginning. "O God, do not pass over my praise in silence." Another translator says: "God, do not be deaf to my hymn." Another: "Do not be silent." That is: do not pass over the punishment, but proceed against what has been done. For you are the glorious one, the great one, able to set such things right. "For the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of the deceitful has been opened against me. They spoke against me with a deceitful tongue, they surrounded me with words of hatred, and they fought against me without cause. In return for loving me, they slandered me; but I prayed." Do you see wickedness stretched out? Do you see a partnership… [Savile: "those who have shared in wickedness with some."] …of Christ a little [?]

…of the man who by his deeds pushed away the favour that comes from God and drew upon himself the blow sent by God. "And he put on cursing like a garment, and it entered like water into his inward parts, and like oil into his bones." Here he shows both the severity of the blow and the permanence of the punishment. He makes clear that for all people evils come from within, from their own will, since by their works and deeds they push good things away and throw themselves into punishments. "Let it be to him like a garment that he wraps around himself, and like a belt with which he is always girded." He says this to show the unspeakable wrath of God that will pursue such people. What he means is this: evils will hold them so fast that they will not even undergo any change, but will be firmly fixed in them and remain secure. Then, to show that God punishes wickedness and corrects vice, and that such a sentence will lie not against Judas alone but against all who are liable to what has been said, he added: "This is the work of those who slander me before the Lord." That is: this is the punishment, this is the penalty, of those who oppose me, who plot against me, who make war on me, "and who speak evil against my soul." So there is an accounting for words too, and a most bitter one.

4. Having then completed what he had to say about that man, he flees again to God for help for himself. He does not stop at the punishment of those who plot against him. He shows that those who suffer wrong have both an avenger for the wrongs done to them and themselves receive much help, and so he goes on to say: "And you, O Lord, deal with me for your name's sake." See his right-mindedness, see his humility. Yet his suffering gave him ground enough for pleading his case. (This too can be seen in many places in the Scriptures: those who suffer unjustly at the hands of men have greater ground of confidence for obtaining help [?] from God.) But he leaves this unsaid, flees to God's loving-kindness alone, and says: "Deal with me for your name's sake," as if to say: "Not because I am worthy, but for your own sake, because you are loving and merciful." That is why he adds: "For your mercy is good." And he put it well: "For your mercy is good." Human mercy is often not like that; there are times when people use it to do harm and to corrupt. But God everywhere uses it for what is beneficial. "Deliver me, for I am poor and needy, and my heart is troubled within me." You see him again asking to be saved, not as someone worthy, nor as righteous, but as one utterly overthrown, worn out, having suffered countless evils. "And my heart is troubled within me." Such is the power of misfortunes: they not only harm the body but also disturb the soul. "Like a shadow when it declines, I was taken away; I was shaken off like locusts." He speaks of the severity of the plots of those who wronged him, of the unspeakable ill-treatment, and in turn of what came from himself in the… [Savile: "for it will be firmly fixed."] …against the Jews, and against Paul of Samosata,

and against those who hold the views of Arius, and against those who hold the views of Marcion, and against the Manichaeans, and against all who disbelieve in the resurrection, he draws up his battle line. Since the battle is against so many, we too need many eyes, so as to watch the wrestling bouts closely. In the contests outside the church, if one of the bouts is overlooked, the spectator comes to no harm, because that theatre is gathered for enjoyment, not instruction. But here, if you do not know precisely where he draws up his line and where we strike at him, you will suffer no ordinary loss. So that this does not happen to you, rouse your mind and make your hearing alert. We strike the Jews first and draw up against them, taking the Prophet as our ally against them from his own words. For when we say that these things are clearly said about Christ, they do not accept it but invent other explanations. So let us first refute their account, and then demonstrate our own. For now let us ask them: who is the lord of this righteous man? "The Lord said," it says, "to my Lord." Here he mentions not one person, but one person speaking with another. Whom, then, do they say is the speaker? God. And the hearer? Abraham. Others say Zerubbabel, and others someone else, like drunkards who say nothing consistent, or rather like people walking in darkness and bumping into one another. Tell me, then: is Zerubbabel lord of David? How could that make sense, when he himself was called David by way of great honour? What follows also shows that nothing here is said about Zerubbabel, nor about David, for neither of them was honoured with the priesthood; but here something is said about someone who holds a strange and extraordinary priesthood. "For you," it says, "are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek." But for now let us unfold the matter in hand. They also offer other explanations even staler than these, saying that these things were said about the people. But the people never became a priest, nor could the other things said ever fit it. So let us pass over this too as stale, since it needs no argument to refute it, and bring forward another thing they say. What do others say, then? That Abraham's servant says these things about his own lord. And what could be staler than this? What business has Abraham's servant here? Where did his lord become a priest, when he himself had Melchizedek as his priest and sought blessings from him? How would it make sense that it was said of Abraham: "From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you"? How would these words fit David, or Zerubbabel, or the people? What is said here is beyond human nature. And "Sit at my right hand": what interpretation could it have if those persons were meant? Not a single one [?]. How did he say to Abraham, "Sit at my right hand," when Abraham thought even standing beside angels worthy of the greatest honour? But what is their wise argument? "How," they say, "can you introduce another Lord, when Scripture says expressly: 'The Lord your God is one Lord; him alone shall you serve, and besides him there is no God'?" [Regius: "What again could be more senseless than this?"] …to them [?]. So much more, then, do ours; for

we too have believed. You are one nation, but we are the whole world. Moses did not persuade you as Christ has persuaded us. Your institutions have ceased, but ours stand. Do you argue from the prophecies? Ours are more numerous. So if you do away with ours, you overshadow your own as well. From the signs? You have no sign of Moses to show, for it happened and passed away. We, however, can show many and various signs of Christ still happening even now, and prophecies shining brighter than the sun. From the laws? Ours are more philosophical. From the fact that you went out while the Egyptians tried to stop you? It is not the same thing to prevail while the whole world wars against you as to overcome the Egyptians alone. I say this not to set the Old Testament in conflict with the New (far from it!), but because I wish to stop the mouths of the ungrateful Jews. Both the one and the other were given and came about from the same God. What I want to establish is this: the Jew who does away with the prophecies about Christ ruins the greater part of the prophecies, and could not clearly demonstrate the nobility of the Old Testament unless he accepted the New. That what is said is not about a man is evident to anyone with sense, from the words "Sit at my right hand," from his being called Lord just as the Lord who speaks is, from his having been begotten from the womb before the morning star, from his being a priest according to the order of Melchizedek, and from the words "With you is your rule." And if another Jew pops up before us again wearing the mask of a Christian (Paul of Samosata, I mean), it is possible to answer him from the New Testament too. Still, so that we do not seem to leave the matter in hand and go off to another part of the battle line, let us strike him too from this passage. What, then, does he say? That he was a mere man, and has existed only from the time he was born of Mary. Tell me, then: what will you say to the saying, "From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you"? The other things that were said to the Jews must also be said to his followers. We are not to blame for this; they are, since their doctrines are closely related to those of the Jews. So we will use the same weapons against them, for those who wage the same war must be struck with the same arrows. What, then, does the sharing of the throne mean? Here equality of honour is shown, which is enough to stop the mouths of those who hold the views of Arius as well. That is why Christ too, when the Jews said that he was the son of David, went on to say: "How then does David, in the Spirit, call him Lord, saying: 'The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand'?" Paul, going further, also takes up the account of the economy, interpreting it more clearly, and deals a fatal blow to Marcion, to Mani, and to all who are sick with such ideas, when he explains (for he interprets with the understanding fitting to him) how he became a priest according to the order of Melchizedek. But let us return to the matter before us. "The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand." Do you see the equality of honour? For where there is a throne, [?] … does not overshadow.

…he worked the miracles; beginning from there, the preaching spread everywhere in the world. And if you want to take what is said in a higher, spiritual sense, hear Paul saying: "But you have come to Mount Zion, and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to the church of the firstborn." "The Lord will send forth the rod of your power from Zion." The rod is sometimes used for punishment and for doing good, and sometimes for comfort, and it is a symbol of kingship. To see that it is both, hear the Prophet saying: "Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me." And again: "You shall shepherd them with a rod of iron; you shall shatter them like a potter's vessels." And Paul: "What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and a spirit of gentleness?" You have seen how it belongs to discipline; now see how it belongs to kingship. Isaiah says: "A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall come up from his root." And David: "Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; a rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom." Here he called power a rod. With this power the disciples travelled through the world, correcting people's ways and leading human nature from irrational vice to reason. "Go," he says, "and make disciples of all nations." Moses too had a rod, but it had received the working of God, and through it he acted in all things. That rod divided rivers; this one broke the impiety of the world. One would not be wrong to call the cross, too, a rod of power. This rod turned land and sea around and filled them with great power. With this rod the apostles went out everywhere in the world and accomplished all those things. Carrying it, they achieved everything, starting from Jerusalem. "And rule in the midst of your enemies." See a prophecy shining brighter than the sun! What does "Rule in the midst of your enemies" mean? In the midst of Greeks, in the midst of Jews. For this is how the churches were planted in the midst of cities; this is how they prevailed and won through. This is proof of a brilliant victory: to set up altars in the midst of enemies, to be like sheep among wild beasts and lambs among wolves. This is what he said when he sent them out: "Behold, I send you out as sheep in the midst of wolves." That is no lesser wonder than the first. To overcome wolves while being in the position of sheep is no less than prevailing while hemmed in by enemies; indeed it is much greater, and greater still that, being only twelve in number, they drew the whole world to themselves. "And rule in the midst of your enemies." He did not say, "Conquer in the midst of your enemies," but "Rule," to show that the trophy is not won in battle but that the lordship comes by command. This is how the apostles prevailed: having Christ within them, they did everything as if by command. That is why every house was opened to them, and believers obeyed them more readily than any slave, selling what they had and laying the proceeds at the apostles' feet, not even daring to take anything for their own needs. Thus [variant readings, partly illegible: [?] … Morel: "stripping off what they had" … "to put into need" [?]]

thus they leapt for joy, held fast under Christ's lordship, sparing neither money, nor bodies, nor the present life. Those who did these things had once been foes and enemies; but the invincible power of Christ not only freed them from their enmity but brought them into service and into such close friendship. So even if the Father is said to put the enemies under his feet, this is not said, as I have said, as though the Son did nothing, for the whole achievement belonged to the Only-begotten. It is said so that, as I said before, you may understand the Father and the Son as one God, while the distinctive property of each is preserved, and so that you may not think of two unbegotten beings. That the whole achievement is his, consider from what has already been achieved; and do not take what is said simply in a human way, or great absurdity will follow. So that you too may learn this, hear what I am about to say. Some who were formerly enemies became friends, while others still remain enemies. That he himself made the enemies friends, Paul shows when he says, "When he hands over the kingdom to God the Father." The Saviour shows it too, when he says to the Father himself: "I glorified you in the world; I completed the work that you gave me to do." But subjecting the enemies was the Father's work. And yet the one is greater than the other, for it is not the same thing to punish enemies who remain enemies and to make friends of those who are enemies. Yet the Son is not less than the Father on this account, nor is the Father less than the Son. So that you may learn that the first kind of work also belongs to the Son, just as the second belongs to the Father, hear: "Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels." It is the Only-begotten who sends the angels to gather the weeds, and everywhere we see him punishing the devil. The demons themselves admit this when they say: "Have you come here to torment us before the time?" So it is he who will torment them. Do you see that even if what happens is said to be done by the Father, these are the Son's achievements? And to see that the Son's works are also the Father's, hear him saying again: "No one comes to me unless the Father draws him." And again: "No one can come to the Father except through me." So such things must not be taken in a human way. Thus "your enemies" must also be understood in this way, not as his enemies alone. "For whoever does not honour the Son," he says, "does not honour the Father."

5. So the Jews are enemies not of him alone, but of the Father too. That is why he brought utter destruction upon them, threw their city to the ground and made it a ruin. Yet he did not do this immediately after the cross. He gave them a long time to repent, if they had been willing, and he left them the apostles, so that by learning his strength through them they might turn back, even if late. But when they proved incurably sick, he brought the crowning evil upon them. Even by this he was again calling them to repentance, so that, having lost their old way of life, they might be led by the hand to the truth, if only by the sheer compulsion of events, when they saw the one they had insulted worshipped everywhere, and their own… [Savile: "not even while they live, after [?]" … [?]]

the veil was torn, the rays of the sun turned away, and darkness seized the whole world; the bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised; a thief went back to his ancient homeland; the vaults of heaven [258] were thrown open; the nature that had been trampled underfoot was led up to the heights, above the heaven of heaven, and, greater still, it was seated on a royal throne, with angels and powers standing beside it. All wickedness was driven out, virtue was brought back, the grace of the Spirit was given; fishermen and tax collectors and tentmakers sewed shut the mouths of philosophers, turned back the tongues of orators, and overthrew the tyranny of demons. The altars and temples, the pagan feasts and festivals, were dissolved; the reek of burnt fat and smoke and all the accursed sacrifices were driven out by force. Soothsayers, begging priests of the Mother and augurs, and the devil's whole workshop ran away. Churches sprang up all over the world, choirs of virgins were formed, and orders of monks; the desert as well as the cities was filled with piety. Choirs of just and holy men took their stand and answered the angelic powers above in song. Peoples of martyrs and multitudes of confessors were planted all over the world. Virtue was achieved with great ease. Barbarian nations were taught to live the life of wisdom, and men wilder than beasts showed themselves rivals of the angels' way of life. As much land as the sun looks upon, so much did the word run over after the cross and the resurrection. Considering all this, the Prophet said: "With you is the rule in the day of your power."

6. If you want to see the day to come as well, and to learn how that too is a day of his power, think how great a thing it is to see heaven rolled up, and the whole of nature that had been corrupted rising again, and everyone standing before him at his nod; the devil put to shame, the demons bowing down, the righteous crowned; each person giving account for his offenses and receiving prizes for his good deeds; and another state of life coming into being. For there will be no more death, no more disease and old age; no more poverty, abuse and plotting; no more houses and cities and crafts and voyages; no more putting on of clothes, no food and drink, no roofs and beds and tables and lampstands; no more plots and battles and law courts; no more marriages, labor pains and births. All these things are shaken off like dust and dissolved, and another, better state of life is given, a life of incorruption and immortality, with great power bestowed on the body. Paul made this clear when he said: "For the form of this world is passing away." But if you disbelieve what has been said because you do not see these things before you, take your proof of what is to come from what is present. Go over the whole world in your mind: the land, the sea, Greece, the barbarian lands, the inhabited world and the uninhabited, the cities on land, the [259] islands in the sea, the mountains and the glens; and when you see the power of Christ shining out everywhere, ... ⁸ Reg.: "of the sun were darkened."

and he will then put on unspeakable glory. "In the splendors of the saints." So as not to show him only as fearsome, he shows his gentleness and kindness too, saying: "In the splendors of the saints." And this too belongs to his power: to make them so splendid. Paul made this clear when he said: "Who will transform the body of our lowliness so that it may be conformed to the body of his glory"

7. Then, since he had said something great and beyond words, he added: "according to the working by which he is able to subject all things to himself." Do not ask how, he says, or in what way, for everything he wills is possible for him. But why did he not say "in the splendor of the saints," but "in the splendors"? Because the prizes are many and various. "For there is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory. So it will be," he says, "with the resurrection of the dead." And Christ says: "In my Father's house there are many dwelling places." That is why that splendor has no end. It does not yield to night or give way to darkness; it is unspeakable and great, and far surpasses the light we see, and it has this as well, the greatest thing of all: it admits no limit. This belongs to the unspeakable power of the King, to bring bodies that are corruptible and perishable to such strength and power. Then, since he had said great things and given the hearer wings with these hopes, he shows that it is fitting for these things to happen, since the one who accomplishes them is so great. And who is it that accomplishes them? The one who is consubstantial with the Father. To show this he added: "From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you." But those who twist these words to suit their own opinion say that they were spoken about his birth according to the flesh. Then how, tell me, "before the morning star"? "He meant the night in which he was born," they say, "since he was born before dawn." But that was not the point in question, nor was he speaking for the sake of history. Besides, they cannot show that the prophets, who uttered most things in veiled form, would have said what the evangelists taught. Here, then, "before the morning star" does not mean before the rising of the morning star, but before its nature, before the morning star came into being. For Scripture knows how to distinguish when it means "before the nature" and when "before the activity." For example, when it says: "One must anticipate the dawn to give you thanks, and meet you before the rising of the light," it is speaking of the dawn. It did not say "before the sun" but "before the rising"; not "before the nature," since nothing came into being before the nature of the sun, but "before the rising of the sun," to indicate the dawn. Elsewhere, [261] when it means before the sun's nature, it does not say "before the rising" but "before the sun," as when it says: "Before the sun his name endures, and before the moon, for generations of generations." So just as "before the sun" is one thing and "before the rising of the sun" another, the latter indicating the sun's activity and the dawn, the former its nature, so here too, if he had wanted to indicate the night, he would not have said "before the morning star" but "before the rising of the morning star." Besides, Christ too referred this psalm not to the economy in the flesh but to the ... ⁸ Reg.: "for your thanksgiving" [dative]. The Greek Bibles have this passage thus, Wisdom 16:2[?]8: "One must anticipate the sun to give you thanks." [?] Patrologia Graeca LV.

he says, and without beginning. For what that man had in shadows came about in truth in Jesus. And just as the names ran on ahead, such as "Jesus" and "Christ," so did this. Melchizedek, then, appears to have neither beginning of days nor end of life, not because he did not have them, but because no genealogy is given for him. Jesus, however, had neither beginning of days nor end of life, not in that way, but because in him there is no temporal beginning or end at all. The one was a shadow, the other the truth. So just as when you hear the name "Jesus" used of Joshua you do not suppose it means the true Jesus, but take only the type contained in the name and look for nothing more, so too when you hear that Melchizedek was without beginning and without end, do not look for this in him as a matter of fact; be content with the mere designation, and learn the truth in Christ. And when you hear of an oath, do not think it is an oath. For just as anger in God is not anger but his power to punish, and not a passion, so neither is the oath an oath. God does not swear; he states what will certainly come to pass. Having spoken, then, of the splendor of the saints, of the enemies being placed under his feet, and of the day of power, he goes on to speak of present things. And see what order he gives his discourse, softening the hard-hearted hearer. First he frightens him with the account of the judgment and softens his stubbornness, and only then does he introduce the account of present things. That is why he makes this kind of mixture. Look: "Until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet." This concerns the future. Then the present: "The Lord will send out the rod of your power from Zion; rule in the midst of your enemies." Then the future: "With you is the rule in the day of your power, in the splendors of the saints." Then the present again, no longer involving punishment but kindness: "You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek." For this is the removal of sin and reconciliation with God. Then, having dwelt on these things as long as he wished, he takes up the economy again, reshaping his words toward what is lowlier, and says: "The Lord at your right hand." Yet above he said that he himself sits at the right hand of the Father. Do you see that one must not [265] cling simply to the words? What does "The Lord at your right hand" mean? Since he had taken up the economy, he turns his words to the flesh, which receives help. For he is seen in agony, and sweating, sweating so much that drops ran down, and being strengthened. Such is the nature of the flesh. "He will crush kings in the day of his wrath." One would not be wrong to take this both of the present, of those who rise up against the Church, and of the future, of their giving account for their sins and impieties. "He will judge among the nations, he will heap up corpses." What does "He will judge among the nations" mean? He will pass judgment, he says, and condemn the demons. And to see that he did judge, hear Christ saying: "Now is the judgment of this world; now the ruler of this world will be cast out." And elsewhere: "And I, when I am lifted up, will draw all to myself." If he has used rather physical language, do not stumble; this is Scripture's custom. "He will crush heads upon ... ³³ Savile: "adding."

one could see in irrational animals. What good is it to a donkey to be weighed down by a great bulk of loads, even if it enjoys them ten thousand times over? And what harm is it to another donkey to be free of all these, provided it enjoys the food it needs? That is why Christ, making his disciples lofty, since they were going to speak to the whole world, freed them from all cares, giving them wings and making them tougher than adamant. For nothing puts strength into the soul so much as being free of these things, and nothing makes it so weak as being entangled in them. Just as it is not easy to find grief in the one condition, so it is not easy to find pleasure in the other. The one man has many masters and mistresses, savage and inhuman; the other is a slave to no one but rules over everything with great freedom, enjoying the sunlight, delighting in the air, and having no one to trouble him. Anger does not tear him apart, nor envy, nor malice; cares do not waste him away, nor jealousy, nor vainglory, nor pride, nor anything else of the kind. His soul is like a calm harbor free from waves, and he makes his way easily toward heaven, held back by nothing in this present life. So that we too may enjoy this freedom from fear, and cheerfulness in the present life, and ease at our departure, let us pursue this way of life, so that we may also enjoy the eternal good things that surpass all speech and mind and understanding, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and power forever and ever.

"I will confess you, O Lord, with my whole heart." 1. What does "with my whole" mean? With all eagerness, intently, freed from the cares of this life, lifted on high, and with the soul released from the bonds of the body. "With heart": not merely in words, not only with tongue and mouth, but with the mind as well. So too Moses, giving the law, said: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your mind." Here "confession" seems to me to mean thanksgiving: "I will sing your praise," he says, "I will give thanks." For he spent his whole life on this; he begins with it and ends with it. This was his constant work: to offer thanksgiving both for the benefits done to him and for those done to others. For God looks for nothing so much as this. This is sacrifice, this is offering, this is the sign of a grateful soul, this is a blow against the devil. This is why blessed Job was crowned and proclaimed victor: when countless trials were brought upon him and his wife tried to trip him up, he was not overturned, but went on giving thanks to the Master for everything; not only when he was rich, but also when he became poor; not only when he was healthy, but also when he was struck in his flesh; not only when his affairs went with the current, but also when that terrible storm swooped down upon his whole house and upon the very nature of his body. For this above all [?] ... those who [?] ..., and the whole gloomy

appearance of the house, how they shrink, how they are humbled, how they are crushed! For though they have enjoyed countless teachings and gained nothing, from that sight they suddenly become wise, learning the cheapness and frailty of human nature and the rottenness and instability of their own power, and foreseeing their own misfortunes in the misfortunes of others.

2. For if, even with death existing, there is so much robbery, so much greed, and the stronger swallow the weaker as fish do, then if there were no death, when would they ever have stopped their greed? If, knowing that they will not enjoy what they seize, but willingly or unwillingly will have to give it up to others, they still rage and go mad like this, then if they held it securely, when would the flames of their wicked desire ever have been quenched? And what of this: are not the crowns of martyrdom woven through death? [267] And what of Paul? Did he not set up countless trophies, saying: "I die every day, I swear by my boasting in you"? For death is not evil; an evil death is evil. That is why it says: "Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his holy ones." And elsewhere it says: "The death of sinners is evil," calling it evil to depart with an evil conscience, weighed down and oppressed by many anxieties over one's offenses. The one who has a clean conscience, by contrast, runs to the prizes and goes off to his crown. And to learn that it is not the nature of things but human disposition that causes the turmoil, hear how Paul longs for death, saying at one point: "For we who are in this tent groan, awaiting adoption, the redemption of our body"; and showing the same thing elsewhere: "But even if I am poured out as a libation upon the sacrifice and service of your faith, I rejoice and rejoice with you all. In the same way you too should rejoice and rejoice with me." And if death is not burdensome but even desirable to those who live rightly, much more so are poverty and all the rest. "Sought out in all his wishes." Another version: "Made exact." Here he seems to me to be speaking of created things, proclaiming the wisdom of God. Above, by "works" he meant the prodigies and wonders that he often performed in governing the human race (even though we, for the sake of the faint-hearted and with another meaning, applied it to these things). What does "Sought out in all his wishes" mean? Made exact, he says, as another interpreter also put it: prepared, perfected, brought into being, completed, sufficient to carry out his wishes, able to bear witness to his power, not lame or deficient in fulfilling his commands. As he says elsewhere: "Fire, hail, snow, ice, stormy winds that do his word," that is, his commands. So too the Prophet said: "He made the moon for seasons; the sun knew its setting; you made darkness, and it was night." And they not only accomplish what they were made for; even if he commands the opposite, there too their obedience is great. He gave the sea a command, for instance, and not only did it not drown the Jewish people, which was its nature, but it smoothed out its waves and carried them across more safely than solid rock. The furnace not only did not burn, but also

he says: "Go to the ant, you sluggard, and imitate its ways, and become wiser than it. For though it has no farm, and no one to compel it, and is under no master, it prepares its food in summer and lays up a great store at harvest. Or go to the bee and learn how hard it works; kings and commoners use its labors for their health." ⁸ [269] Though weak in strength, it was advanced because it honored wisdom. And the bee will speak to you again, so that you do not simply admire the beauty of bodies when there is no virtue of soul, nor despise plainness when the soul happens to be adorned. The writer of proverbs made this very point when he said: "The bee is small among winged creatures, but its fruit is the chief of sweet things." Think of the birds, I beg you, and take wisdom from them. That is why Christ said: "Look at the birds of the air: they neither sow nor reap, and your heavenly Father feeds them." For if irrational creatures do not worry about food, what defense will you have if you do not show even as much disdain for present things as the birds do? And if you want to despise finery too, the flowers of the field will teach you not to love adornment. Christ made this clear as well when he said: "Look at the lilies of the field: they neither spin nor toil. Truly I tell you, not even Solomon was clothed like one of these." So whenever you want to fuss over beautiful clothes, remember that however hard you strive, the victory goes to the grass, and you will never be able to compete with it; and put an end to this senseless madness. There is much else from which one can learn wisdom: from animals, from flowers, from seeds. "Confession and magnificence is his work." That is, each of his works, for he is not saying this about a single work. Another interpreter said: "Praise and dignity is his working"; but this one says "confession," that is, thanksgiving and glory. For each of the things we see is enough to lead the observer to thanksgiving, to hymns, to praise, to doxology. One cannot say, "Why this? What is this for?" Darkness and day, famine and plenty, desert and uninhabited land, rich land and deep soil, life and death, all the things we see are sufficient and able to stir to thanksgiving those who study them carefully. God made this clear through one of the prophets, when he set punishments in place of benefits: "I overthrew them, as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah; I struck them with blight and with mildew." And again through another: "I brought them up out of the land of Egypt, and redeemed them from the house of slavery"; thus counting punishments among his benefits. So it is with these things too. For they too bring benefit: they correct, instruct, discipline, train, and cut away wickedness. Human beings do some things out of kindness and others out of hatred and aversion, but God does everything out of love. In his kindness he placed man in paradise, and in his kindness he cast him out of paradise; in his kindness he brought the flood, and in his kindness ⁸ Other manuscripts: "offer."

you will give account after your departure from here, and you will pay the penalty for your wickedness. For God abides forever, and he has a justice that abides forever and is in no way cut short by death, [?] for repaying the labors undertaken for virtue, [?] for paying back the punishments due for wickedness. "He has made a memorial of his wonders." What does "He has made a memorial of his wonders" mean? He has never stopped working wonders, he says; he does it continually. That is what "He has made a memorial" means: he has not ceased, he has not left off working wonders in every generation and rousing the duller sort by his portents. The lofty, philosophic person needs no signs at all, for "Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed." But since God cares not only for such people but also for the duller sort, he does not stop working wonders in almost every generation. The whole visible creation is wonder enough. Yet to shake the many out of their sloth he displayed many portents in the middle of this theater, both privately and publicly. Think of what happened at the flood, at the confusion of tongues, at Sodom; what happened to Abraham, to Isaac, to Jacob; what happened in Egypt, at the exodus of the Jews, in the wilderness, in the land of Palestine, in Babylon, after the return, in the time of the Maccabees; what happened after Christ's coming and at the coming itself; what still happens to this day. Think of the fall of Jerusalem, the building up of the Church, the word that runs everywhere, that was lifted up by the waves and grew through wars, the throngs of martyrs, and all the rest. One could also see many private wonders, done in households and in cities. But for now let us look at the general ones, which are plain and known to all and happen in every generation. How many wonders took place under Julian, who surpassed everyone in impiety, when the Church was under attack? How many under Maximinus? How many before those emperors? And if you want the things that have happened in our own generation, there were the crosses suddenly imprinted on people's garments; the temple of Apollo brought down by a thunderbolt; the translation of the holy martyr Babylas at Daphne and the manifest victory over the demon; the strange death of the treasurer of the imperial funds; the slaying of the emperor himself, Julian himself, who surpassed everyone in impiety; the destruction of his uncle and the springs of worms; countless other things; the famine, the drought, the scarcity of water that fell on the cities after him; and countless other things besides.

5. You also know what happened in Palestine at that time. When the Jews wanted to rebuild that temple which had been pulled down by God's decree, fire leapt out of the foundations and drove them all away, and the work, which remains unfinished, bears witness to it. "Merciful and [?]" [?]. When he says, "He has declared the power of his works to his people," he means nothing other than that he displayed his

power. He did not simply drive out the nations. He did it in a way that let them know most clearly that, even if what came before was enough [?], the blow falling on those nations was sent by God, and that the enemy's fate was decided with God himself as general. For he taught them not only by words but also by deeds: by sandals, by garments, by food, by light at night and by day, by the cloud, by wars, by peace, by victories, by farming, by rains. Everything gave out a voice proclaiming the Master and pricking their hardened minds, and there was no time when he did not show continual signs. "The works of his hands are truth and judgment." Having spoken of his power, he now speaks of his just judgment: in what he did then God showed not only power but also great justice.
