He did not drive out the nations simply because he wanted to bring in the Jews. He did it with justice. That is why Moses also said elsewhere, "For the sins of the Amorites are not yet complete." These words do not apply only to the Jews and what happened to them. Again, the statement is general: all the things he does are truth and judgment, and "judgment" means justice. Scripture often uses "truth" to mean loving-kindness as well. What he is saying, then, is this: God has blended everything with justice and loving-kindness. For if he had applied only the rule of justice, everything would have

6. That is why this same prophet says elsewhere, "Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no one living will be justified in your sight." And again, "If you mark iniquities, Lord, Lord, who will stand?" Everything he does, then, is full of both. If he demanded only justice, everything would have perished. If he used only loving-kindness, most people would grow more careless. So he works out human salvation in varied ways and uses both for our correction. "Faithful are all his commandments." He does here what he does in many places: he passes from the wisdom and care shown in the varied work of creation to the giving of the law, and so takes up this other part of providence too. For God set the human race right not only by making so great and so vast a creation, but also by laying down the law. That is why in the eighteenth psalm too he divides the two parts. At the beginning he says, "The heavens declare the glory of God." Then, coming to the middle and having finished speaking of creation, he adds, "The law of the Lord is blameless, converting souls; the commandment of the Lord is radiant, enlightening the eyes." So here too, having spoken of his portents, his wonders and his works, he turns the discussion to the commandments: "Faithful are all his commandments, established forever and ever, made in truth and uprightness." He did not say "all" casually. He used this word to bring in a great range of commandments. For there are also commandments of crea[tion]… [?]

[?] redemption. "The Lord has sent redemption to his people." In the historical sense he means the liberation of the Jews; in the higher sense, the liberation of the whole world, as what follows also shows: "He has commanded his covenant forever." Here he means the New Covenant. He had mentioned commandment and law, and the law was transgressed and brought about wrath. So he says, "He has sent redemption to his people," just as Christ himself said, "I did not come to judge the world, but to save the world." For when the law was transgressed it punished. "For the law brings about wrath," Paul says, "and where there is no law, there is no transgression either." And again, "All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace." That is why he says, "The Lord has sent redemption to his people." 8. Yet there is not only redemption: after the redemption there is also law, so that we may show a way of life worthy of the grace. "Holy and awesome is his name." He has reflected on everything that proclaims God's care and providence: in the Old Covenant and in the New, in his works, through his commandments, through his wonders and his portents. Inspired and struck with amazement at his majesty, he ends his discourse in praise and offers a hymn to the one who did all this. "Holy and awesome is his name"; that is, full of astonishment and great wonder. And if his name is so, how much more his being! How is his name holy and awesome? Demons tremble at it and diseases fear it. Using this name, the apostles set the whole world right. Using it as a weapon, David brought down that barbarian. By it countless things have been accomplished, and by it we are initiated into the sacred mysteries. So he thinks of all the wonders his name works and all its benefits: how it breaks up his enemies and keeps his own people safe. He considers deeds that go beyond the course of nature and defeat human reasoning, and says, "Holy and awesome is his name." And if it is holy, it needs holy mouths to sing its praise, mouths holy and pure. "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, and good understanding belongs to all who practice it." What does "beginning" mean? Source, root, foundation. He has said so many great things about the Master of the world and been filled with such amazement. So he fittingly adds this, showing that whoever fears him is filled with all wisdom and becomes wise. Then, so that no one thinks wisdom stops at knowledge, he adds, "and good understanding belongs to all who practice it." Faith is not enough unless a way of life in keeping with that faith goes with it. How is the fear of the Lord the beginning of wisdom? It frees us from all wickedness and achieves every virtue. He means wisdom not in words but in deeds. Even the outside philosophers defined wisdom as the knowledge of things divine and human. The fear of God teaches this art: it removes wickedness and plants virtue.

not for the reward stored up for them, but for the sake of the one who laid them down. It means pursuing virtue with pleasure, not out of fear of hell, threat of punishment or promise of the kingdom, but for the sake of the lawgiver. He does the same elsewhere, it says, showing the pleasure he takes in God's commands: "How sweet your words are to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth." Paul asks for this too when he says, somewhat obscurely, "Just as you presented your members as slaves to uncleanness and lawlessness, leading to lawlessness, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness, leading to sanctification." That is: pursue virtue with the same zeal and desire with which you pursued vice, though vice had no prize to offer, only punishment and retribution. Yet he also said that he was asking only a moderate measure. Before saying this, he put it this way: "I am speaking in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh." He was showing that we should show for virtue a desire not much less than we showed for vice. What he means is this: if people do not show the same virtue [?], what defense or pardon could they have, when they do not even approach it with the same desire? That is why this prophet says, "He will delight greatly in his commandments." Whoever fears him as he should receives his injunctions with great desire. Love for the lawgiver makes the law gentle, even if it seems to have some difficulty. And let no one find fault with my words for using this kind of example, since Paul also used it when he said, "Just as you presented your members as slaves to uncleanness, so now present them as slaves to righteousness." A man in love with a harlot may be insulted, reviled, beaten and disgraced. He may be driven from his homeland, lose his inheritance and his father's goodwill, and suffer things harsher still. Yet he bears it all with pleasure because of his licentious love. If such people accept those things with pleasure, how much more should we accept with great pleasure the ordinances of God? They bring salvation and are full of glory; they give us much wisdom and make the soul better. How much more should we think nothing in them difficult? It is usually not the nature of the commands that makes them difficult, but the carelessness of the many. Anyone who accepts them eagerly will find them light and very easy. That is why Christ said, "My yoke is easy, and my burden is light." And here is how you can learn that this is so: the carelessness of the many makes even easy things hard, while zeal makes even hard things very easy. When the Jews were enjoying the manna, they complained and prayed for death; but Paul, wrestling with hunger, rejoiced and leapt for joy. They said, "Our soul [?] at this manna. You led us out of [?]" [?]

[?], even if he has great power outwardly. If such strength exists on earth, think how much power such people will enjoy in heaven. "The generation of the upright will be blessed." Do you see it shining out and having countless heralds, praisers and admirers? Not just anyone, though, but the wise. None of those who cling to the ground could even perceive it. It is these above all who will praise it, admire it and proclaim it: those whose minds are not perverted. Think, then, how great a possession it is, falling short not even of the angels, the apostles, or the great and wonderful. For if those who praise it must be such people, consider and reckon how great it must be. "Glory and wealth are in his house." Again he passes from the things of sense to the things of the mind. Scripture also uses "wealth" for wealth in good works, as when it says, "to do good, to be rich in good works." This is true wealth, since the other kind is a bare name for wealth with no reality behind it. Even if someone takes it to mean that kind, we will still not be at a loss for an answer. Who was richer, even in money, than the apostles, to whom everything flowed as if from springs? "As many as were owners of lands or houses sold them, and brought the proceeds and laid them at the apostles' feet." Do you see the generosity of that wealth? They held everyone's goods yet were free of worry about them, being stewards rather than masters. The owners gave up ownership and brought their goods to the apostles this way: they turned them into silver and cash themselves, but left the distribution in the apostles' hands. That is why Paul said, "as having nothing, and yet possessing everything." The wonderful thing is that, though they lived amid so much wealth, they stood above that abundance, for the mass of money had no hold on them. This is wealth above all: not needing wealth. "Glory and wealth are in his house." Here it needs no explanation. They had the glory that comes from God, and wealth followed too, in keeping with the divine word that says, "Seek the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you." What was more venerable than they were? People received them as angels of God; those who brought money laid it at their feet. They were more splendid even than those who wore the diadem. What king ever made an entrance with such splendor as Paul had, admired everywhere when he spoke? He undid deaths, drove out diseases and put demons to flight, and did such things even through his garments. He made earth into heaven and led everyone by the hand toward virtue. 3. If such things happen on earth, think how great a glory they will enjoy in heaven. What does "in his house" mean? [?] enjoyed. So too with Daniel and the other prophets. If anyone wants to take these words in another higher sense, he will see it fulfilled in the world. For when darkness held land and sea

and error was spread everywhere, the sun of righteousness rose from below. People in those days had abandoned heaven and were looking for God on earth. So he appeared to them from there, coming down to the weak in order to lead them up to infinite heights. "The Lord God is merciful and compassionate and just." He had said, "His righteousness endures," and gave comfort that way. But many merciful people, and many who live upright lives, meet with the opposite here. So he brings in another consolation, saying, "The Lord is merciful and compassionate and just," and so builds a twofold argument. If he is merciful and often grants pardon even to sinners, much more will he not allow those who do right to depart uncrowned. Even if he does not repay them here, he will certainly repay them there. Then he adds "just." If he is just, as indeed he is, he will give each person what he deserves, even if he does not do it here. This is the greatest proof of the resurrection. Many virtuous people clearly suffer countless terrible things, while the wicked enjoy great license. Where, then, will each receive what he deserves, unless there is to be a resurrection and another life, a judgment and a recompense? Then, having mentioned justice, he has frightened the listener with the thought of giving account for his sins. So he quickly adds the remedy: "Good is the man who shows pity and lends; he will manage his words in judgment." 4. See how many prizes he sets before the humane man: his fruit remains forever; he will be freed from trials; he will imitate God, for God is compassionate; he will receive pardon for his own sins. That is the meaning of "he will manage his words in judgment": he will find an advocate and a defense, and there will be no condemnation for him then, because his almsgiving will have arranged his defense well. Another translator renders it, "managing his affairs with judgment." That is, he will enjoy great prosperity and suffer nothing untoward, because he has been an excellent manager. The cruel, inhuman and unmerciful man, by contrast, manages very badly. What could be worse than a man who, when his soul is about to be in danger, spares his money and neglects his soul? That is why Christ praised the steward who, when he was about to be in danger, tore up the bonds and cancelled the debts. Isn't it absurd? When we are in danger in this present life, we give up everything we own to buy our way out of the danger. Yet when we are about to be handed over to a perilous punishment, we do not use the same kind of management. That is why he calls the merciful man a prudent steward. He buys much for little: he purchases heaven with money, the kingdom with a garment, the good things to come with bread and a cup of cold water. What could equal this management, when the perishable [?]... [Editorial note:] Reg. reads "so as to be rescued from the dangers" in place of "on danger," which is to be rejected [?]. Shortly after, the same manuscript reads "therefore an excellent steward." Others read "for the salvation of the many." But "of the wicked" [?]

…to become more earnest, and at last to be rid of wickedness. Where, then, are those who build costly tombs and put up splendid houses? Let them hear what makes an everlasting memorial: not a building of stone, not a circuit of walls and towers, but the display of good works. He sets this down for the sake of those who are utterly faithless and pay no heed to what is to come, so that by drawing them through things present and visible he may lead them by the hand to the things to come as well. Besides, he shows that virtue, as I have often said, has its reward in itself even before those prizes. He shall not be afraid of an evil hearing. Another version has: He shall not fear evil tidings. Just as above he did not say that he would not be plotted against, but that when plotted against he would not be shaken, so here too he did not say that he would not hear evil tidings, but that when he hears them he will not be afraid. 5. And how will he not be afraid? Even if he sees war approaching, or an earthquake overthrowing cities, or robbers and burglars carrying everything off, or barbarians overrunning the land, or disease threatening death, or a judge's anger, or anything else whatever, he does not fear. For he has already stored his wealth in an inviolable place. Not only does he not tremble when death comes, he is even eager to go quickly to the place where his trading lies. For where a man's treasure is, there his heart is also. If merchants, having sent many cargoes home ahead of them, are eager every day to see their wealth, much more will this man, who has stored all his substance in heaven beforehand, want to tear himself away from present things and hasten toward those to come. Nothing, then, could throw him into fear. His heart is ready to hope in the Lord. Another says: His heart is firm, meaning the same thing and explaining the word “ready.” What he means is this: there is nothing that draws him aside [?] and nails him to present things; he is wholly and entirely stretched out toward God, awaits that hope, and stands fixed in that expectation, continually supported by it, neither weakened nor distracted by anything present. For such are the cares of affairs: they split the mind and cut the will in two. So it is necessary to repeat that saying of the Gospel: Where a man's treasure is, there his heart is also. His heart is established; he shall not be shaken. Do you see the man who builds his house on the rock? For what can a man fear who is stripped and travels light, and gives nobody any hold on him? What can he fear who has God gracious and kindly toward him? So his security comes from both sides, from the help that comes from above and from his own readiness below, and nothing can shake him: not loss of money, not abuse, not slander. For there is nowhere he can be harmed, since he has moved his anchorage from here to heaven, to a place that no wickedness or plotting can reach. You know well that all plots are about money and for the sake of money, and that all men's zeal is spent on it. Until he looks down upon his enemies. And who is the enemy of such a man, if not the wicked? For he has stored his wealth beforehand. [Note, garbled: [?] Savile; but Morel reads “the cares of present things,” [?] which is good.] [?] …of the sycophants and plotters you will quench the desire.

…and inhuman, will not praise and admire him. For such is virtue: it is praised even by those who do not practise it, just as wickedness is loathsome and full of reproach even to those who practise it. That is why even those who receive from such men, harlots, charioteers and dancers, do not praise them, but even speak ill of them. But this man will be admired and loved by everyone, not only by the poor who received from him, but also by those who had no share in his generosity. The sinner shall see and be angry; he shall gnash his teeth and melt away. Such is virtue: heavy and burdensome to wickedness. For just as fire burns up thorns, so kindness provokes the inhuman and cruel, because it refutes them and accuses their wickedness. But see how even as he melts away he does not dare to accuse it or to meet the bright eye of virtue; he wastes away in his mind and shows his pain through his teeth, yet dares not utter a word, but only melts and strains. For such is wickedness: even if it mounts to the very sceptres and stands beside those who wear diadems, it is meaner and more cowardly than anything, like some uproar and confusion, like a raging sea, though it be clothed with boundless power. Virtue is the very opposite. Even in the depths of poverty, even in prison itself, it is more splendid than kings. It enjoys great security and sits in calm, in a harbour without waves. Not only does it suffer nothing from the wicked; even by keeping silent it can avenge itself on them and exact from wickedness the utmost penalty. For what could be more wretched than a man who lives in wickedness, when on top of being a slave to money he is stung by the successes of others, counts their good name as his own punishment, and exacts the penalty from himself, lacerating his own conscience, racking his own mind, becoming his own executioner? Do you see the surpassing power of virtue? Do you see the weakness and wretchedness of wickedness? Yet his misfortune does not stop here; it extends to much else besides. He showed this himself when he added: The desire of sinners shall perish. What does “The desire of sinners shall perish” mean? It stands firm nowhere, he says. Since the things he desires are fluid and fleeting, his desire too imitates those things: it is quenched and perishes, and has no root. If the sinner's lot is like this here, think how terrible it will be in the age to come. So that we may not suffer this, let us flee this road and choose the other, and walk continually on that safe and unconquerable road, full of pleasure, filled with glory, which procures heaven for us, wins us God's favour in all things, and trains us in true wisdom, which holds more good things than any word can describe. May we all obtain them by the grace and lovingkindness…

[?] For he adds: Blessed be the name of the Lord, he says, from this time forth and for evermore. What are you saying? Is it not blessed unless you pray for it? You see that he is not speaking of the blessedness that belongs to him and is bound up with his nature, but of the blessing that comes about through men. Paul too speaks of this when he writes: Glorify God in your body and in your spirit. He himself, then, is high and great and worthy of praise in himself; but he also becomes so among men when those who serve him show such a life that all who see them bless their Master. This is what Christ commanded us always to say when we pray: Hallowed be your name; that is, let it be glorified through our life as well. For just as it is blasphemed when we live badly, so it is glorified, blessed and hallowed when we cultivate virtue. What he is saying, then, is this: Make us worthy always to live a virtuous life, so that your name may be blessed through us too. From the rising of the sun to its setting the name of the Lord is to be praised. Do you see him already sounding the prelude to the new way of life and giving a glimpse of the nobility of the Church? For it is no longer in Palestine, nor in Judea, but everywhere in the world. And when did this come about, if not when our faith flourished? For in the old days his name was not only not blessed in Palestine, it was even blasphemed because of the Jews who lived there. For because of you, he says, my name is blasphemed among the Gentiles. But now it is hymned everywhere in the world. Another prophet showed this too when he said: The Lord will appear and will utterly destroy all the gods of the nations, and they will worship him, each from his own place. And another again: For the doors shall be shut among you [?], and my altar shall not be kindled for nothing; for from the rising of the sun to its setting my name has been glorified among the Gentiles, and in every place incense is offered to my name, and a pure sacrifice. 2. Do you see how he put down the Jewish observances and brought them to an end, and extended the Church's way of life everywhere in the world, and proclaimed its worship in advance? For the prophet who says this lived after the return from Babylon, and that is why he prophesied it then: so that the Jews could not say that he meant the shutting of the doors and the desolation in Babylon. For after those things had ended and they had returned to their former way of life, the messenger says this, pointing to the desolation that took place under Vespasian and Titus, after which there would be no further change in that desolation. For the affairs of the Church took its place. That is why he says: Great is my name among the Gentiles, that is, blessed, praised through their life, just as here too he said: Blessed be the name of the Lord. The Lord is high above all nations. Do you see again the nations receiving his worship, and not simply… [Note: Reg. and Sam. read “hymned.”]

…he who fills heaven and earth, who is present everywhere, who says: I am a God near at hand, and not a God far off; who measured heaven with a span and the earth with a handful; who holds the circle of the earth? But since his words were addressed to Jews, he uses this kind of language for the time being, raising their minds little by little, giving wings to their thoughts and leading them upward gently. That is why he did not simply say, Who dwells on high and looks upon lowly things, but first said, Who is like the Lord our God? and only then added, Who dwells on high and looks upon lowly things; and he said the first to show why he said the second. It was because of the weakness of the Jews, who were infatuated with idols and worshipped gods shut up in places and temples. That is why he makes the comparison little by little, although God surpasses all things beyond any comparison. But, as I said before (and I will not stop saying the same thing again and again), he adjusts his words to the weakness of his hearers. For at that point he was not seeking to say something worthy of God's glory, but something they could take in. That is why he leads them upward little by little; and yet even so he does not remain at that low level, but opens up other, loftier thoughts once more. Having said, Who dwells on high and looks upon lowly things, he again carries the discourse higher and says: In heaven and on earth, showing that he is everywhere, both there and here. For he does not look at the things on earth from afar like someone shut up in heaven; he is present everywhere and stands beside all. 3. Do you see how little by little he gives wings to the minds of his hearers? Then, having lifted the hearer up from the earth and fixed him to heaven, and having prepared him to imagine something greater still, he comes to another proof of God's power, saying: Who raises the poor from the earth, and lifts up the needy from the dunghill. For it belongs to great and quite unspeakable power to exalt even what is small. Elsewhere, however, he sets down the opposite as well, that he also humbles what is great, saying: Who deals out ruin against strength, and brings misery upon the fortress. Here, though, it is said that he can lift up the small. This, then, is a general statement. But if anyone wishes to take it in the higher, spiritual sense, he will see it fulfilled in the Gentiles; he will see it fulfilled in us human beings at the coming of Christ. For what is poorer than our nature? Yet he raised it up, brought it to heaven together with our firstfruits, and seated it on the Father's throne. And lifts up the needy from the dunghill, to seat him with princes, with the princes of his people. By “dunghill” he means lowliness here, and the sudden change from it, showing that all things are easy and simple for him. Then he comes to something else, greater still. What is it? That he can not only change circumstances, and not only turn lowliness into dignity, but even alter the boundaries of nature itself and make a barren woman a mother. That is why he added: Who settles the barren woman in a house, a mother rejoicing over children. This happened in the case of Hannah [?] … other benefits [?], where indeed he even endured the cross itself, and then took possession of the world, through the… [Note: Reg. reads “shows.”]

…works, displaying his care. This is what the psalm here shows when it says: When Israel went out of Egypt, the house of Jacob from a barbarous people, Judea became his sanctuary. That is, at the going out, at the deliverance, at the liberation from Egypt. And he did not simply say “Egypt,” but added “a barbarous people,” showing God's care by the very name he gives the enemy. For they could never have been freed from those harsh, savage Egyptians, so barbarous in disposition, had they not had the help of the mighty hand and the invincible right hand. For the Egyptians were fiercer than wild beasts and harder than rock; struck with countless plagues, they would not give way. So by calling that people barbarous he shows the surpassing greatness of God's power: that this people, so barbarous and so cruel, he at one time persuaded, at another compelled even against its will, to let the slaves go; and when they later strove against him he gave them over to the sea, and so set his people free.

What does “Judea became his sanctuary” mean? It stands for: a people that serves him, a people dedicated to him, a people made his own. “Sanctuary” properly meant the temple, the inner shrine, the Holy of Holies, as Zechariah too introduces some who ask: Has the sanctuary come in here? Or shall we fast? He is referring to the return of the ark and of everything else. Judea became his sanctuary. For before this the land was unclean, as it were, and polluted; but when the people returned, the city became his sanctuary; that is, it was held to be a sanctuary because of his watchful care, the sacrifices, the worship, and the other holy rites. Israel his dominion. What does “Israel his dominion” mean? Under his rule, he says. And yet the whole world was under his rule; but these belonged to him in another, closer way, since they received prophecies, and he spoke with them, and ordered their affairs more fully. Then in another way too they were called his people. For often they went out to war at his nod, and did many other things the same way. Having freed them from the hands of barbarians, from tyranny, from slavery, from the utmost danger and from a lawless will, he became their king. This is what he said elsewhere, too, when pleading his case and showing that he had first done his own part before demanding theirs: Have I become a wilderness to the house of Israel, or a land laid waste? What he means is this: Have I been unfruitful to you? Did I not show you countless good things? Did I not change nature itself? Did I not set the elements in order to serve you? Did I not grant you a way of life free of human toil? That is why he says: Have I become a wilderness to the house of Israel? That is: Did I not bear countless fruits for you: freedom from Egypt, deliverance from barbarians, the display of wonders, the sojourn in the desert, the inheritance of Palestine, the mastery over the nations, the continual trophies, the victories one after another, the extraordinary wonders, the constant portents, the plenty of the land, the increase of your race, the … everywhere in the world [?] [Note: “and to rank them” [?]]

…snatching and consuming. The Jordan turned back. Do you see the miracles happening both at different times and in different places? So that they might learn that God's power extends everywhere and is not confined to any place, he was present working wonders in the desert, in the land of the barbarians, and everywhere: now at the sea, now at rivers; at one time under Moses, later under Joshua. Everywhere they were escorted by signs, so that their unfeeling will and hard mind, softened by the miracles, might be made docile and more fit to receive the knowledge of God. The mountains skipped like rams, and the hills like lambs of the flock. Here no small question arises for us. Some raise this difficulty: “We know that the earlier events happened, for history has recorded that the Red Sea was divided at the exodus and that the Jordan turned back when the ark passed over; but that mountains and hills skipped we find written nowhere.” What, then, should we say? That the Prophet, wishing to convey the joy and the greatness of the miracles by hyperbole, introduces even inanimate things all but dancing and leaping, as people do when they rejoice. That is why the image is added: Like rams, and like lambs of the flock. For when those irrational creatures are glad, they show their pleasure by leaping. In the same way, in times of calamity another prophet says that the vine mourned, and the wine, not because the vine mourns (for how could a vine mourn?), but because he wishes to show how extreme the gloom was, and speaks hyperbolically as though it reached even inanimate things. So here too he introduces creation sharing in the joy, to show how great the gladness was. We too have a habit of saying, when there is great rejoicing here, whenever we see some honoured person arrive: “You have filled the house with joy”; we are not talking about the walls, but expressing the excess of our gladness. What ails you, O sea, that you fled, and you, Jordan, that you turned back? You mountains, that you skipped like rams, and you hills, like lambs of the flock? He carries the discourse forward by questions and converses with the elements, in the same spirit in which he said they skipped. For just as he said that not because he attributed feeling to them, but, as I said before, to show the excess of joy and the greatness of the mighty deeds, so too he puts questions to them, not as if they could answer and had feeling, but to make his meaning clearer and to show the…

3. For he brings in the question as though something new had happened, something outside the ordinary course of things, and adds the answer. What was it? At the presence of the Lord the earth was shaken, at the presence of the God of Jacob. Here again by “shaking” he means amazement, wonder, astonishment, so as to show the greatness of what had happened. Then, showing how great a man's virtue is, from the… [Note: It seems we should read “and adds the answer,” unless perhaps you take “and adds to the answer” [?] … in the answer [?] … in the question not [?] …] Patrologia Graeca 55.

…may glorify your Father who is in heaven.” So just as he is glorified when we live in virtue, he is blasphemed in turn when we spend our lives in wickedness. He showed this through the prophet as well, when he said: “Because of you my name [297] is blasphemed among the nations.” But since the Prophet has no other ground on which to plead for them, he takes refuge in this one, as Moses also did. God, however, does not always act on this ground, because he cares about the salvation of human beings. If he were always going to do so, many of the careless would have grown worse. They would hold, as the strongest guarantee that they would never suffer harm, the fact that they were constantly being saved for the sake of his glory. But this does not happen, for he does not care as much about his own glory as about the salvation of human beings. If even human beings think little of glory, much more does God, who needs nothing from us. But, as I said, the Prophet holds the position of an advocate, so he makes his plea from what is at hand. He doubles the words and says, “Not to us, Lord, not to us,” showing how utterly unworthy are those who are being saved; “but to your name give glory.” We deserve countless evils, but act so that your name may not be profaned. “For the sake of your mercy and your truth.” Another translator says, “Because of your mercy.” Do you see how he too knows clearly that God often disregards his glory and looks to one thing alone, the correction of sinners? That is why he added, “For the sake of your mercy and your truth.” In other words: help us because of your mercy. Even if you do not care about the glory that comes from human beings, help us for the sake of your mercy and your truth. For it is possible, quite possible, to gain glory by punishing too, and not only by showing mercy. “But not in that way,” he says, “but because of your mercy. Glory ought to have been given to your name by us, through our life and conduct. But since we have betrayed that, bring it about through your help, through your mercy and your love for humankind.” “Lest the nations should say, Where is their God?”

4. I hear many people saying these words even now when they pray. But the fear is rather that [?] may say on other grounds, “Where is their God?”, when many are plundering, doing wrong, and committing countless terrible deeds. “But our God is in heaven and on earth; he has done all that he willed.” Here he corrects the error of the foolish. Since many do not know that there is a God, he corrects that kind of belief and says, “But our God in heaven has done all that he willed.” And if in heaven, much more on earth. What does “In heaven he has done all that he willed” mean? He means either the powers above and the countless hosts there, or else the commands, which are carried out with ease. And if the earth is full of confusion and disorder, do not be surprised. This comes from human wickedness and the evil of those who practise it, not from any weakness in God. For that he is strong and [?] is theirs… [?] “Those who fear the Lord have hoped in the Lord; he is their helper and protector.” Through these words he also pro-

-claims [299] the power of God and his incomparable supremacy over all things. He brings forward what was done for the Jewish people and shows that his kindness to them was twofold, or rather threefold. First, he freed them from demons; next, he made himself known to them; and third, he gave them help from himself. He divides his words between Israel, the priestly race, and those from the nations who come to him. A priest is not on a level with a layman; the priest has something more, so it is reasonable for him to make this division, since greater honour was given to the priests. 5. Then, to show that God's providence was not shut up within Jewish affairs, he also mentioned the proselytes who come from the nations, saying that the help and the blessing reached everyone: “The Lord has remembered us and blessed us. He blessed the house of Israel; he blessed the house of Aaron; he blessed those who fear the Lord.” What does “he blessed” mean? He filled them, he says, with countless good things. A human being blesses God too, as when one says, “Bless the Lord, O my soul.” But the one who blesses God is himself the gainer: he makes himself more glorious and bestows nothing on God. When God blesses, on the other hand, he makes us more glorious and receives nothing himself, for the Divine has no needs. So on both sides the gain is ours. How did he bless them? He gave them bread from heaven and rained water from a rock. He guarded their goings out and their comings in, and multiplied their herds and their flocks. He called them a special people and a royal priesthood, gave them a law, and sent them prophets. Proclaiming these things elsewhere too, the Psalmist says: “He has not done so for any other nation, and he has not made his judgments known to them.” And another says: “What nation is so wise [?] that the Lord God draws near to it?” “The small together with the great.” Not a single class, he says, was left without a blessing; these things reached everyone. “May the Lord add to you, to you and to your children.” Do you see another kind of blessing, the increase of the race? That is why another writer, setting out the opposite as a punishment, says: “We have been made small, and we are fewer than all who dwell on the earth.” They enjoyed this blessing even when they were in Egypt, although countless things stood in the way: the forced labour, the misery, the cruelty of their overseers. Yet nothing cut short God's word. The blessing advanced so far that in two hundred years they became six hundred thousand. Back then, however, the blessing lay in these things; now, under the New Covenant, it lies in far better ones. That is why Paul says: “Blessed be God, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places.” And again: “Now to him who is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask…” [?] Reg.: “the earth.” Elsewhere he says, “And he made [families] like sheep” [?] “sheep in affliction”; “this blessing.” [?] “do not hold back over their place.” [?]

6. Do you see how great the power of the blessing is? His words become deeds. It was his word that made the heavens: “By the word of the Lord,” it says, “the heavens were established.” That is the word with which he blesses you, a word that can do so much. “The heaven of heaven is the Lord's, but the earth he has given to the children of men.” What are you saying? Did he choose heaven as a dwelling for himself, take the upper storey, and set aside for us the things down here? Far from it. That is not the meaning; the language is accommodated to us. If that were the meaning, how could the other saying of God stand: “Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord.” The one would contradict the other, if we take the words at their surface meaning and do not examine the deeper sense stored up in them. What, then, does he mean by “The heaven of heaven is the Lord's, but the earth he has given to the children of men”? He is using accommodating language, not shutting God up in heaven. Neither “Heaven is his throne and the earth his footstool” nor “I fill heaven and earth” is said in a manner worthy of him; that too is accommodation. For he himself contains all things and bears all things. He needs no place, but holds all things together himself. Heaven is called his house because it is a place free of wickedness. So just as heaven here is not an exclusive choice, neither is it when he says, “He fixed the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God,” or that “He chose the house of Jacob.” Here too he is not saying that the Jews are his and the rest of humanity no longer are, as though they were bereft of his providence and cut off from his creation. God is the God of all alike. He uses this language to show his love for them, since in some way they seemed better than the others. That he did not choose them alone but cared for everyone is shown by what happened before Moses, no less by what happened in his time, and by the particular events after him. He gave the sun, the earth, the sea and everything else to all in common, and he sowed the natural law in everyone. He loved Abraham, who was a Persian, and moved him to a new land; and through him he [?] the Egyptians, the people in Canaan, and those who had come from Persia. Again, through Abraham's son and grandson he made many of their neighbours there better, as far as it lay with him. And after Moses was born, he used what was done for the Jews to lead the Egyptians by the hand to the knowledge of God, then the people in Palestine, and after that those in Babylon. So when he says, “The heaven of heaven is the Lord's,” he means that God takes his rest among those who dwell there, because they are free of all wickedness. And you too, if you are not nailed to the earth but become an angel, will quickly ascend to heaven and to your Father's house, and… [Note:] Reg.: “If you do not remain a human being and [attached] to the earth.”

…experience alone [303] shows how blessed it is. May we all attain it, by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and power, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.

ON PSALM 114. “I have loved, because the Lord will hear the voice of my supplication.” 1. “And who does not love being heard?” someone asks. Many worldly people. They do not want what is good for them to be granted. Instead they ask for things that are not good for them, and then, when something comes about, they fret and are upset. What is good for us is what God knows and understands to be good for us, whether you mean poverty, famine, sickness, or anything else of the kind. Whatever God judges to be good for us and gives us, that is what profits us. Indeed, listen to what he says to Paul: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” What was good for Paul was this: persecutions, afflictions and hardships. And when he heard that this was good for him, he said: “Therefore I am content with weaknesses, insults, persecutions.” So it is no ordinary person who rejoices when God hears him by granting what is good for him. Many people want what is harmful and take delight in it. Not so the Prophet. What then? He loved, because God heard him and gave him what was good for him. “Because he inclined his ear to me.” Again he presents God's assent in human language. And he hints at something further by this expression, as if to say: “I was not worthy to be heard; he himself came down to me.” “And I will call upon him in my days.” What does “in my days” mean? “I will not leap away,” he says, “and grow more careless just because I have been heard. I will make this my work all my days.” “The pangs of death encompassed me; the perils of Hades found me. I found affliction and sorrow, and I called upon the name of the Lord.” Do you see what a strong weapon this is? Do you see a comfort that dissolves every terror? Do you see a soul warmed through with longing for its Master? What he means is this: “Calling on God was enough to deliver me from the evils that surrounded me.” Why, then, do we often call on him and not find deliverance from our troubles? Because we do not call as we ought. For he is always ready to give; listen to what he says in the Gospels: “Which of you, if his son asks for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a snake? If you, then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give good things to those who ask him?” Do you see how great his goodness is, when ours, [304] set beside it, looks like wickedness? Since our Master is like this, let us always flee to him and call on him alone as our helper, and we shall find him ready to save. If people who have been shipwrecked and are being carried along on a plank can, by calling out, persuade those far away to take pity on them, even though they have nothing in common… [Note:] “And to Paul”: Reg. and Savile; other manuscripts read “And Paul.”

…destroys [?], working for our salvation on both sides. 2. Then, to show that he leans more towards love for humankind, he goes on to say: “And our God shows mercy.” He was right to say “Our God,” in contrast to the gods he mentioned earlier. Their business is to slaughter and kill and to wage war without truce. His is to show love, to pardon, and to snatch people from danger time after time. This above all, together with everything else, shows that they are demons and accursed, and that he is guardian, protector and true God. “The Lord guards the little ones; I was brought low, and he saved me.” Here he brings up a very great form of his providence. Having said, “He is merciful and just, and he shows mercy,” he points to a work of his very great love. What is it? His care for infants. We have reason, which teaches us to guard against some things and to choose others, to ward off evils that are coming and to undo those that are present; we also have strength and know various skills. Children are without all of these and have no one to defend them, yet in every way they have God's providence. If they did not enjoy it continually, they would all have perished. A snake could have destroyed the child while it was still in swaddling clothes, or a domestic fowl could, or many other creeping things found in houses. Neither nurse nor mother nor anyone else is able to show them perfect care unless they have the help that comes from above. Some say this saying was also spoken about unborn children who have not yet come out of the womb. “I was brought low, and he saved me.” He did not say, “He did not let me fall into dangers,” but, “After I fell, he saved me.” Having spoken of God's providence in general, he goes on to apply the words to his own person, since it is his custom to establish these things both from the general and from the particular. So do not seek a life full of security, for it does not profit you. If it was not good for the prophets, much less is it good for you. That it was not good for them, listen to what he says: “It is good for me that you brought me low, so that I might learn your statutes.” The thanksgiving here is twofold: that God let him fall into dangers, and that when he had fallen God did not abandon him. Both are in some way forms of kindness, and the first is not less than the second, but, if I may say something surprising, even greater. The one put an end to the dangers; the other made the soul [306] wiser. “Return, my soul, to your rest, for the Lord has dealt kindly with you. For he has delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, and my feet from slipping. I will be pleasing before the Lord in the land of the living.” In its historical sense the passage speaks of deliverance from terrible straits, and of a kind of relief and freedom. But if one takes it in the higher sense, one will be able to… [Note:] Savile: “and truly God.”

…having departed from here. “I will be pleasing before the Lord in the land of the living.” Another translator has “In the presence of the Lord”; another, “I will walk about.” Paul shows this too when he says: “And we shall be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord.” And he was right to say “In the land of the living.” That is truly life: freed from death, its good things unmixed. “When he has destroyed,” it says, “every rule and every authority and power, the last enemy to be destroyed is death.” Once these are destroyed, nothing painful remains, no anxiety, no toil. All is joy, all peace, all love, all good cheer, all gladness; everything is true, pure and firm. None of the slips we know here exists there: no anger, no grief, no love of money, no bodily lust, no poverty, no wealth, no disgrace, nothing else of the kind. So let us too long for this life and do everything with it in view. That is why we are told to say in the prayer, “Your kingdom come,” so that we may always look towards that day. Whoever is gripped by that love and fed on the hope of those good things is not overwhelmed by any present trouble or dragged down by any of the pains of this world. People travelling to a royal city are not held back by anything along the road, whether meadows or gardens, ravines or deserts. They pay no heed to any of it and look to one thing only, the homeland that awaits them. In the same way, whoever pictures that city to himself every day and feeds his longing for it will think none of the terrible things terrible, nor any of the bright and splendid things bright and splendid. Why do I say “think”? He will not even see them, for he will acquire other eyes, the kind Paul urged us to have when he said: “While we look not at the things that are seen but at the things that are unseen; for the things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are unseen are eternal.” Do you see how he described the way in different words? Let us hold fast to those things, then, so that we may attain them and enjoy the life that knows no corruption. May we all attain it, by the grace and love for humankind [308] of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and power, now and always, and to the ages of ages.

1. Blessed Paul also recalled this saying and spoke roughly as follows: “Since we have the same Spirit of faith, in accordance with what is written, ‘I believed, therefore I spoke,’ we too believe, and therefore we also speak.” So we must first explain how the Apostle used it and what he was talking about. In that way the prophet's meaning will also become clear to us. Besides, this is the best way of teaching: not to cut off the thread of the argument, nor to take a part… [?] …that prophet who said, “The hidden and secret things of your wisdom you have made known to me,” he who was filled with such great wisdom, being about to… [Note:] Reg.: “the splendour of wealth.”

…[?] received this [?]. And just as a rock never bore fruit, neither was Abraham able to; but I hewed you out from there, and from that one man I filled so many lands. That is also why he leads Ezekiel out into the plain and shows him a heap of bones, and raises them up through his prophesying. He shows them the bones and says: “If I can raise the dead, how much more can I restore you, who are alive.” So much for them. But how does this prophet put it? “I believed, therefore I spoke.” That is: “Faith is needed for what has been promised. I too pondered these things and reckoned them up, and when I brought in faith, I drove out all turmoil.” What Paul is saying, then, is that faith is needed even for our good things that are perceived by the senses and can be seen. And if it is needed for the things of sense, much more for the things of the mind. If they needed faith to accept that they would get their own city back, much more do we, who are waiting for heaven. When something is great, beyond understanding and higher than our reasonings, we must take up faith and not examine the matter by human logic, for God's wonder-working is higher than all of that. So for this reason too we must muzzle our reasonings, run back to faith, and glorify God. Whoever stubbornly tries to work out God's ways by reasoning does not glorify him, since he wants to subject God's ineffable dispensations to the lowliness of his own reasonings. 2. That is why Paul, in discussing Abraham, says that this above all glorified God, since Abraham did not do this but rebuked his reasonings and looked to the power of the one who had made the promise: [310] “He did not waver in unbelief concerning the promise of God, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God, and fully convinced that he was able to do what he had promised.” What does “Since we have the same Spirit of faith, in accordance with what is written, ‘I believed, therefore I spoke,’ we too believe, and therefore we also speak” mean? Here he reveals a great mystery to us. What is it? That the New Testament and the Old belong to the same Spirit; that the same Spirit who spoke in the one has spoken here too; and that faith is the teacher of all things, and without it we cannot say anything at all. “For we too believe,” he says, “and therefore we speak.” Take faith away, and it is impossible even to open one's mouth. And why did he not say, “Since we have the same faith,” but rather, “Since we have the same Spirit of faith”? To make clear what has been said, and to show that we need the Spirit's supply to rise to the height of faith and to think little of the weakness of our reasonings. That is why the same Apostle says elsewhere: “To each is given the manifestation of the…” [?] …to come to the prophet's words and to say what the blessed… says. [Note:] Savile, in the margin: “but the prizes are in the future.”

[?] …this one. What, then, does he say? "I believed, therefore I spoke." And yet he had not yet spoken anything. He means what had already been spoken in his mind. And what had already been spoken? "When I considered," he says, "the calamity, the tragedy of the Jews, that utter ruin and final desolation, I did not despair of a change for the better. I even hoped for it, and I announced it and spoke of it. In the earlier psalms too I said much about it, and I spoke and announced it because faith had taught me." Now see how another man, who was not well schooled in faith, limps and is thrown into confusion. David speaks that psalm too, but not in his own person. He is describing the experience of those who limp when he says: "How good God is to Israel, to the upright in heart! But as for me, my feet were almost shaken, my steps had nearly slipped." He is not speaking of feet and steps but of limping thoughts. And he adds the cause: "Because I envied the lawless." That is, he saw the barbarians prospering and the affairs of the Jews brought low. And what does he say this limping looked like? "And I said, Surely in vain have I kept my heart righteous and washed my hands among the innocent." And he says what led him to say such things: "For behold, these are sinners, and prospering forever they have laid hold of wealth." Then see how he recovers himself: "If I said, I will speak thus…" "This is toil before me," he says, "until I enter the sanctuary of God and understand their final end." What he means is this: I toiled, I was worn out by my reasonings. That is what reasoning is like. Then I reflected that I was taking on a laborious task. If I search into these things, I will be able to know nothing clearly until I reach my homeland. Do you see how great an evil it is to entrust the things of faith to reasonings rather than to faith? If he had been firmly fixed in faith, he would not have said these things. He would not have been confused or disturbed, his feet would not have been shaken, his steps would not have nearly slipped. But the prophet was not like this. He stood on the rock and was neither confused nor disturbed. He saw the affairs of the Jews in this state and those of the barbarians in the opposite one, and still he proclaimed the return continually, in many psalms, with a clear voice and a fully assured mind. He was full of confidence. He paid no attention to the power of the barbarians or to the lowliness of the Jews, but only to the power of God, who had promised these things. That is why he says: "I believed, therefore I spoke; but I was brought very low." Another version says, "But I was sorely afflicted." "But I said in my ecstasy, Every man is a liar." Another version: "And I said in my distress, Every man proves false." Here again the splendor of faith is shown, that not even the… [Notes:] So the LXX; others read "of Israel." Savile [?]. [?] writes in the margin [?] "power." The words "says, But I was sorely afflicted" were missing in Morel. But [?] [?]

…brought in nothing worthy of what was hoped for; and "the year has proved false," meaning this same thing again. Man is a worthless and paltry thing, and it is especially in times of calamity that we usually reflect on such things and consider the weakness of our nature. So this man too, having fallen into despondency, saw nature put to the test and its paltriness and nothingness shown on every side, and he says, "Every man is a liar," that is, man is nothing. That is why he said elsewhere: "Surely man walks about as a shadow." "What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?" See how he shows the greatness of the benefit not only from what was done but also from the kind of person it was done for. He is describing in different words, but with the same thoughts, what is in the other psalm. There he said, "What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you visit him?" and so it is here too. A benefit is shown to be twice as great when it is great in itself and is also given to someone worthless, and this heightens both the benefit and the grace. Wishing to bring this out, he says, "What shall I render to the Lord?" He shows that God judged man worthy of so great a gift, man who is a falsehood, worthless and paltry. "For all that he has rendered to me." It is the mark of a grateful mind to go about seeking to give something back to one's benefactor in return for the good received, and after paying everything to think one has given nothing worthy. He hinted at this at the start of his repayment, and as he goes on he promises to make it. He displays a double gratitude: he gives what he was able to give, and while giving it he thinks he has given nothing worthy. What, then, is he going to give? Listen to him, for he goes on: "I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord." Those who take the passage in the spiritual sense say it refers to communion in the mysteries. But for now we hold to the historical sense, and we say that here he means libations, sacrifices and hymns of thanksgiving. In ancient times there were various sacrifices: the sacrifice of praise, offerings for sins, whole burnt offerings, offerings for deliverance, peace offerings, and many others. What he means, then, is this: I have nothing worthy to offer, but what I have, I offer. I will bring God a sacrifice of thanksgiving, and I will remember him for my deliverance. "I will pay my vows to the Lord before all his people." By "vows" he means here his promises and pledges. In these terrible straits he took refuge in God and made himself a debtor, promising that if he escaped the dangers he would offer these sacrifices. "Since the calamity is over," he says, "I will pay my vows to the Lord before all his people." "Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his holy ones." Another version has "Honored." How does this follow? How does it fit with what came before? Anyone who examines it carefully will find the connection to be strong. He had said, "What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?" Now, to show God's benefits, he says that not only the life but also the death of the holy ones is very precious to God. [Notes:] [?] "opposite to this." A little later the same has "this also Christ."

…says: "In the bond of love"; and, "which is the bond of perfection." There is also a bond of the opposite kind, as when it says: "Each one is bound fast by the cords of his own sins." Christ was hinting at this when he said: "This woman, a daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has bound like this, ought she not to be set free?" And Isaiah says of Christ: "I have given you as a covenant to the nations, saying to those in bonds, Come out." These are the bonds he burst, then, and he did not merely loosen them, since bursting is more than loosening. If anyone wants to take it in the spiritual sense as well, saying that these are the bonds of sins, he will not miss what is fitting. And the whole old man… There is also another bond, a most beautiful one, which Paul always carried about with him, saying: "Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ." And again: "For whom I am bound with a chain." "To you I will offer a sacrifice of praise." See how above, below and everywhere he sets down this repayment to God. Above he says, "I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord." Here he says, "To you I will offer a sacrifice of praise," that is, I will give thanks, I will sing hymns. "And I will call upon the name of the Lord." Have you seen what a sacrifice of praise is? "I will pay my vows to the Lord before all his people, in the courts of the house of the Lord, in your midst, O Jerusalem." He did this not to make a display or out of ambition. He wanted to lead everyone to share his own zeal and to have them as partners in his thanksgiving. All the saints do this: whenever something good happens to them, they call not only people but the whole of creation to join in the praise. Nothing is so earnestly desired by God as that we be grateful, not only in prosperity but also when things go against us. This above all is a sacrifice; this is the greatest offering. This is how Job won renown, and Paul, and Jacob. This is how each of the righteous showed his good heart and his gratitude to God, above all in hard times. Let us do this too and remain grateful always, so that we may also attain the eternal goods. May we all attain them, by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and might, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.

ON PSALM 116 [?]. "Praise the Lord, all nations; praise him, all peoples. For his mercy has prevailed over us, and the truth of the Lord endures forever." 1. It is clear to everyone that these words are a prophecy of the Church of believers, a proclamation in advance of the preaching that has spread over the whole inhabited world. The psalm calls not just one or two or three nations, but the whole earth and sea. This happened when the coming of Christ shone forth. Then he also gives the cause of their salvation. They were saved not by their own good deeds, nor by their way of life or their boldness before God, but by God's love for humankind alone. "For his mercy," he says, "has prevailed over us." [Notes:] Savile has "transfers"; but "sets" seems to be the reading [?]. In the edition [?] verses [?]: "and the," "name," [?], "virtues" [?]. b Savile: "but also in the contrary circumstances of affairs" [?] Reg. [?] "Jacob" (Iakobos). c Savile: "to enjoy." d In Savile "only" is missing. Next, the same has "which indeed happened then." A little after, the same has "he states the cause."

…"the lost sheep of the house of Israel"; and to the Canaanite woman: "It is not good to take the children's bread and give it to the dogs." He did and arranged everything for their salvation. If they proved unworthy of his kindness, let them blame their own lawlessness and the depth of their ingratitude. "Let the house of Aaron now say that he is good, that his mercy endures forever." Here he calls on the priests separately to sing praise, showing how far the priesthood surpasses the rest. The greater these men were than the others, the greater the honor they received from God, not only in the matter of the priesthood but in everything else as well. When fire came down, it came down on their account; the earth opened, the rod blossomed, and countless other wonders took place through them, or rather for them. "Let all who fear God now say that he is good, that his mercy endures forever." For these above all are able to see his love for humankind and to learn his goodness in all things. What does "for his mercy endures forever" mean? It is continual, he says, never interrupted, but shining out and displayed in everything. If many do not see it, they fail to see it because their own reasoning is weak. People with diseased eyes cannot see the sun, mainly for this reason, and even those who are healthy cannot always gaze at it because of its overwhelming brightness. In the same way it is impossible to understand all of God's providence precisely, because the greatness of his understanding and wisdom far surpasses human reasoning. There are also many passions that darken the minds of the foolish, so that they cannot see it at all. The first is love of pleasure, which is why they pass over even what is plain to everyone. Second, along with this, comes folly and a perverse judgment. Is it not absurd that when they see a father beating his child they approve and praise him, and think him a true father precisely for this, but when God chooses to exact punishment for what has been done, they are vexed and distraught? What could be worse than this perversity? They are vexed at opposite things: at one moment they are distraught that he does not punish, at another that he does. When they see people robbing and grasping, they want them punished; but when they sin themselves, not at all, and this is the mark of a corrupt judgment. Third, besides these, they do not even know what is good and what is evil. They go wrong in judging things, because they love wickedness and are inclined to vice. Fourth, they do not take their own sins into account. Fifth, the distance between God and human beings is unspeakably great. Sixth, God does not wish to display everything everywhere, since what is done in part is enough. 2. In all things, then, we must not insist on learning… [Notes:] [?] Morel.: "how then [?]" [?] a reading given by Savile in the margin: "to consider; but God, if he should wish." a Morel.: "for what."

…of what comes from God, but he wished to impress them with human resources, because he feared their attack. That is why he showed them his treasures: his hopes were in his treasures. And so God was provoked and said, "They shall take all these things," that is, the very things you hoped in and trusted. Israel too is accused of this, of trusting in money and horses. That is why the prophet urged them to appease God by doing the opposite and to say, "We will not ride on horses." God honors you, and do you dishonor yourself? God honors you by promising you his alliance, and do you run to human hopes and entrust the hope of your salvation to lifeless matter, to money? For he seeks not only to save you, but to do it with honor. He loves you greatly. That is why he draws you away from everything and fastens you to himself, cuts away everything and leads you to himself. Through what he does he all but says: Put your hopes in me, and keep your attention on me always. "The Lord is my helper, and I shall look upon my enemies." Do you see that he does not avenge himself or pursue them, but leaves it to God to take vengeance on his enemies? "It is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in man. It is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in rulers." He does not put this forward as a comparison. Scripture is in the habit of speaking this way even about things that cannot be compared, because of the weakness of its hearers at that time. So he says this not to make a comparison but to come down to their level. For this reason another prophet said: "Cursed is everyone who hopes in man." Nothing is more paltry than this hope. It is flimsier than a spider's web; indeed it is not only weak but treacherous. Those who have often trusted in people, and been brought down along with them, know this. But hope in God is not only strong but secure, and it never changes. That is why Paul said, "Hope does not put us to shame." And another wise man says, "Look at the generations of old and see: who hoped in the Lord and was put to shame?" "But I," someone says, "hoped and was put to shame." Hush, man, do not contradict the divine Scripture! If you were put to shame, it was because you did not hope as you should, because you gave up, because you did not wait for the end, because you lost heart. Do not do this. When you see troubles pressing on you, do not collapse. For this above all is what it means to hope: to stand upright in the midst of difficulties. 3. What was more wretched than those barbarians, I mean the Ninevites? Yet even standing in the very [?] and expecting the city to fall, they did not despair, but showed a thorough repentance. That is why God's sentence too into the [?]… [Note:] Savile: "then do not collapse."

…a power working wonders allowed both to remain. Some such wonder took place then too. They rushed at him like fire, they attacked eagerly like bees, they had him shut in, and yet they could do nothing. For the unconquerable weapon, the invincible alliance, the name of God, drove them all away. "I was pushed and overturned so that I might fall, and the Lord helped me." He has described how great the dangers were from the number of the attackers, their array, their eagerness and their anger. Now he describes it from what he himself suffered. "The dangers overpowered me so completely," he says, "that I came very close to falling and being brought down. I was pushed and overturned so far that I was about to fall. But when I was on the point of going down on my knee and being laid low, and all human hope had been abandoned, then he showed his alliance." God does this so that no one may claim the glory for himself. He did this in the history of the Judges with Gideon. For this reason too, in the time of Hezekiah, he set up the trophy while it was night. Hezekiah contributed nothing to the victory and the war, and even so he grew proud. If he had only stood in the battle line, if he had seen the slain falling, would he not have suffered this still more? So when human hope for a situation is gone, that is when God brings in his own alliance. He did this with Goliath; he did it with the apostles. That is why Paul said: "But we had the sentence of death within ourselves, so that we would not trust in ourselves but in God who raises the dead." "The Lord is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation." It is as if he said: He became my power and my help. And what does he mean by "my song"? My glory, my praise, my adornment, my renown. For he not only rescues people from dangers but also makes them illustrious and renowned. One can see this everywhere: salvation is given together with glory. He also hints at something else here. What is it? "This," he says, "is my continual song, this my continual voice: the hymn to him. This is my work, to praise him continually." 4. Let those who rot in satanic songs hear this, and see what harm they suffer and what pardon they could hope for. This man praises the Savior continually, while they wallow continually in the songs of demons. "The voice of rejoicing and salvation is in the tents of the righteous." When God has accomplished everything, those who share in the victory rejoice and leap for joy. Their delight is double: they have been saved, and they have been saved by God. He who set up the trophy makes this a festival. Then, to show what occasioned such an alliance, he added: "in the tents of the righteous." He did not say "in houses" but "in tents," wishing to show how makeshift their dwelling was. Such was Abraham's tent when he came back after overcoming the barbarians, made illustrious by his achievements. Such was Paul's tent when he came back after overcoming the demons, overthrowing error, and recounting his achievements. "The right hand of the Lord has done mighty things; the right hand of the Lord has exalted me." [Notes:] a Savile: "and be bent"; but in the margin, "be laid low." b Savile: "praising the Savior," and below, the same has [?]. In the margin, another reading [?]: "both of being saved and of being saved through God," etc. Ibid.: Savile has "he makes this a festival"; Morel., "this makes the festival."

[?] …that everything lay in his power. So he gained a twofold salvation: release from his dangers and release from wickedness. That is why Paul too, writing to the Hebrews, said: "If you are without discipline, then you are illegitimate children and not sons." "Open to me the gates of righteousness; I will enter through them and give thanks to the Lord." The gates are opened to those who are disciplined, to those who put away their sins. 5. The one who has been disciplined can say with confidence, "Open to me the gates of righteousness." For the saying must also be taken in the anagogical sense, and the gates understood as the gates of heaven. These are shut to the wicked, and we must knock at them through virtue, through almsgiving, through righteousness. "This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it." There are gates of death, there are gates of destruction, there are gates of life, there are gates that are narrow and hard. Because there are many, he gives the mark that distinguishes the Lord's gate, adding, "This is the gate of the Lord." For those others are not the Lord's. And what is its distinguishing mark? That those who are disciplined, those who are afflicted, enter through it. For it is narrow and hard, and if it is hard, the afflicted will walk through it, just as the road to destruction is broad and spacious. "I will give thanks to you, for you heard me and became my salvation." He does not simply say, "You heard me." He means that you first disciplined me and made me better. That is why he gives thanks, not for being heard, but for being disciplined, for that is the reason he was heard. Everywhere in him this kind of thanksgiving is prominent. As I have said, and will never stop saying, this above all is a sacrifice and an offering. "The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner." That this was said of Christ is plain to everyone. He himself cites this prophecy in the Gospels, saying: "Have you never read, 'The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner'?" The saying does not seem to hang on the historical narrative itself. The prophecy breaks into the middle of the sequence. If so, there is nothing surprising or new in that. Most of the prophecies in the Old Testament were uttered in this way, because for the time being they had to be veiled, so that the books themselves would not be destroyed. The prophecy about his birth also seems to hang on the historical narrative, yet it has nothing in common with it. For example: "Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel," which translated means "God with us." "The stone which the builders rejected." By the builders he means the Jews, the teachers of the law, the scribes, the Pharisees, because they rejected him, saying, "You are a Samaritan and have a demon," and again, "This man is not from God, but leads the crowd astray." Yet the one who was rejected in this way proved so approved that he became the head of the corner. Not every stone is fit for a corner, only the most approved, which binds together the walls from either side [?] Savile: "but the middle of the sequence." Below, "in the Old" is missing. Savile: "and you shall call."

6. What, then, could equal this day? On it God was reconciled with humankind and a long war was ended. Earth was shown to be heaven, and human beings who were unworthy of earth were shown worthy of the kingdom. The firstfruits of our nature was carried up above the heavens, paradise was opened, and we recovered our ancient homeland. The curse vanished and sin was undone. Those who had been punished through the law obtained salvation apart from the law, and all the earth and sea recognized their own Master. Countless other things happened too, which cannot be gone through in speech now. For this reason the Prophet considered all these things and ascribed the whole to God, showing that what has happened is God's work. "Let us rejoice and be glad in it." Here he means a spiritual gladness, a gladness of the intellect and the mind. "Let us rejoice and be glad in it," because we have obtained such great goods. For this too is no small achievement: to rejoice in good things, to leap for joy, to be glad, to receive God's benefits with delight. "O Lord, save now; O Lord, prosper now." He saw the world's prosperity, the change in affairs, the turn for the better. So, rejoicing with those who enjoyed them, he said, "O Lord, save now; O Lord, prosper now." That is: preserve those who enjoy these things, so that they may be filled and may show fruits worthy of the grace. Make their road easy for them, so that once they have obtained such goods they may not fall away from them. "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord." Our affairs do not stop at what has already happened. They go on to other, greater things: the resurrection, the kingdom, our portion with Christ. Wishing to set all these before us, he added, "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord." Christ too said this to the Jews: "Truly, truly I tell you, you will not see me until you say, 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.'" They kept putting forward this charge over and over: that he was not from God, that he was God's adversary. So he says to them: You yourselves will testify for me that I am not God's adversary, when you see me coming on the clouds and raise this cry, saying, "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord." With these words of praise you will cut yourselves off from any defense. The glory of what happens then will move them to raise this cry, at once praising him and making the charge against themselves more bitter. "We have blessed you from the house of the Lord; the Lord is God, and he has appeared to us." He means the whole faithful people, who enjoy blessing in the house of God. Everywhere, indeed, the prophets are seen calling blessed those who would believe. Why did you bless them, and where does this beatitude come from? Because God has appeared to us. "For the saving grace of God has appeared," it says, "training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly desires, and to live soberly, righteously and godly, awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ." Here, then, the Prophet marvels at the incarnation: that he who is God and Lord, and of that divine essence, deigned to appear [?] "Showing": one manuscript has "saying." [?] Savile: "let us rejoice." [?] "we have blessed." [?] "he himself offers this sacrifice; but also partners" [?].

…the reason they are called this. According to the historical sense, it is because they speak of the return from Babylon and recall the captivity there. According to the anagogical sense, it is because they lead us by the hand onto the road of virtue, for some have understood them this way. The road that leads there is like a flight of steps. Little by little it raises the virtuous and philosophic man and sets him in heaven itself. Others say that these psalms allude to Jacob's ladder, which was shown to him fixed on the earth and reaching to heaven. For in this way places that are inaccessible and lofty become accessible, when steps and ladders are set beneath us. But those who have climbed are bound to grow dizzy once they are carried up to a height. So we must secure ourselves not only while we climb, but also when we reach the summit itself.
