There is one security: that we do not look at how far we have climbed and grow proud, but look at how much is left to climb, and strain toward it. Paul showed this when he said, "Forgetting what lies behind and straining toward what lies ahead." That is the anagogical account. Now, if you please, let us come to the historical sense and look at those who were freed from the captivity. How, then, were they freed from it? By their longing for Jerusalem. Those who did not achieve this gained nothing from God's grace, but stayed in slavery and died there. If we copy them, we will suffer the same. Unless we are seized by love of heavenly things and longing for the Jerusalem above, we will not be able to recover our homeland. We will not, if we stay nailed to the present life forever, wallowing in the mud of worldly cares. "In my affliction I cried to the Lord, and he heard me." Do you see the gain of affliction? Do you see how ready his love for humankind is? Affliction was a gain because it led them to pure prayer. His love was ready because he granted their request as soon as they called. He had done this before for those in Egypt too. That is why he says: "I have surely seen the affliction of my people, and I have heard their groaning, and I have come down to deliver them." So you too, beloved, when you are in affliction, do not despair or lose heart, but rouse yourself then above all. For then prayers are purer and God's goodwill is greater. Live your whole life in such a way that it is a life of toil for you. Know that "all who want to live godly in Christ Jesus will be persecuted," and that "through many afflictions we must enter the kingdom of God." So do not love the soft and dissolute life, and do not wish to walk the broad road, for that road does not lead to heaven. Walk the narrow and hard one. If you want to reach the dwellings above, flee pleasures and trample on the showy life of this world. Hold wealth, glory and power in contempt. Acquire poverty, a contrite mind, confession and springs of tears, and pursue everything that can win salvation. These things make their possessor more secure and lift prayers higher. If you prepare yourself in this way, [?] Savile: "steps." Shortly after, the same: "but since those who go up." [?] "Jerusalem": others add "the mother city." One manuscript, according to Savile: "as also in Egypt, seeing." Another: "springs, and pursue all these things, which also make you more secure."

…a punishment worthy of this wickedness? Isaiah said to the Jews, "Why should you be struck any more, adding lawlessness?" The psalmist says the same here: "What shall be given to you, and what shall be added to you, against a deceitful tongue?" Either he means this, or else that this very thing is a punishment. Even before the judgment you exact the penalty from yourself, because you give birth to wickedness from within. For wickedness is the soul's greatest punishment, even before the judgment. What penalty, then, could be worthy of such a person? Here, none. Only the blow that comes from God. A human being could not repay him as he deserves, for wickedness goes beyond every punishment. But God will bring the blow. To show this, he quickly added: "The arrows of the mighty one, sharpened, with desolating coals." Here again he calls the punishments arrows. Another translator says, "The arrows of the mighty one are sharpened, with coals heaped up." Another says, "With coals of juniper." Each heightens the dread of the punishment by the metaphor in the words. "Heaped up" and "juniper" have the same sense: the first conveys the quantity of the punishment, the second its quality and intensity. The Seventy showed this when they rendered it, "With desolating coals," that is, coals that lay waste, consume and devour. The Scriptures take the things we fear and use them to depict God's punishments too, calling them arrows and fire. Here it seems to me that he alludes to the barbarians. That is why another translator, to show this, said, "Rescue my soul from a lying lip" [?]. Such are their words, such their tricks and plots: everything full of deceit and great wickedness. "Woe is me, that my sojourning is prolonged; I have dwelt among the tents of Kedar." Another translator says, "Woe is me, that I have lingered as a sojourner." Another says, "Ah me, I have been an alien in a long exile." These men lament the captivity in Babylon. Paul laments our stay here, saying: "For while we are in this tent we groan, being burdened." And: "Not only that, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan within ourselves." For the present life is a sojourn. And why do I call it a sojourn, when it is something even more fleeting than a sojourn? That is why Christ also called it a road, saying, "Narrow is the gate and hard the road that leads to life." This is the best teaching of all, and the first: to know that in the present life we are sojourners. That is why the ancients confessed it, and they were admired above all for this. Paul showed this when he wrote: "For this reason God is not ashamed to be called their God." What reason, tell me? That they confessed they were strangers and exiles. This is the root and foundation of all virtue. The one who is a stranger to the things here will be a citizen of the things above. The one who is a stranger to the things here will not grow fond of the present. He will not care for a house, [?] "So either he means this": one manuscript, according to Savile, adds "what punishment will be found worthy of wickedness?" [?] Savile: "they consume"; others: "they devour." [?] Savile: "that leads away." "accusing the present life."

…gape after shadows, and want to cross the narrow strait of the present life while being tossed about by endless waves, storms and shipwrecks? Paul was not like that. He hurried and pressed on, and one thing alone held him: the salvation of human beings. "With those who hate peace I was peaceable; when I spoke to them, they made war on me without cause." Do you see how he shows how burdensome the stay there was? He did not say, "With those who do not have peace," but "With those who hate peace I was peaceable." Do you see the gain of affliction? Do you see the fruit of captivity? But now, which of us will be able to say this? We are content if we are peaceable with the peaceable. But he was peaceable even with those who hate peace.

How, then, shall we too achieve this? By living as sojourners. I am bringing the discussion back to the same theme again: by living as strangers, and by not being held fast by any of the things of this present life. Nothing breeds strife and war so much as love of present things: desire for glory, or money, or luxury. But when you cut all these ropes and do not let your soul be held by any of them, then you will see where war has its origin, and where virtue will find its foundation. That is why he commands us to be sheep among wolves, so that you may not say, "I suffered this and that, and so I turned savage." Even if you suffer countless things, he says, stay a sheep, and in this way you will overcome the wolves. So-and-so is wicked and corrupt? But you have power enough to overcome even the wicked. What is gentler than a sheep? What is fiercer than a wolf? Yet the sheep will overcome the wolf, and this was shown in the apostles. For nothing is mightier than meekness, nothing stronger than patience. For this reason Christ commands us to be sheep among wolves. Having said this, he adds something more, as though this gentleness, the sheep's, I mean, were not enough for the disciple he wishes to produce: "Be innocent as doves." He combines the meekness of two tame and guileless creatures. So great is the gentleness he demands of us when we are among the savage. And do not tell me, "He is wicked, and I cannot bear him." That is the very time to display meekness above all: when we deal with the savage and the untamed. Then its strength is shown, then its work, its achievement and its fruit shine out. "When I spoke to them, they made war on me without cause." Another translator says, "And when I spoke to them, they made war." He is either alluding to "With those who hate peace I was peaceable," or meaning "Because I spoke to them, they made war." What he says is this: At the very moment of our conversation, he says, when I was showing love most of all, when I was speaking the friendliest words, that was when they turned savage, when they stitched together plots, and nothing held them back. Yet even while they were so disposed, I displayed my own virtue. We too must be disposed in this way. Even if they strike us, even if they beat us who love them, even if they plot against us, we must display what is ours to give. We must remember that parable which commands us to be disposed toward enemies as we are toward friends [?]. [?] "more obedient" [?]. [?] "this than those." Savile: "I put forth." One manuscript has "philosophy."

[?] …you have become [?]; now they acknowledge the Creator of the world. "My help is from the Lord." It is not from human beings, or from horses, or from money, or from allies, or from walls. "Our help is from the Lord." This alliance cannot be conquered, this help cannot be overcome. It is not only invincible, but also easy and ready to hand. One need not walk a long road, or flatter doorkeepers, or spend money, or send an embassy. Without leaving the spot, one can draw down this support from above, if only one withdraws from human things, clings to that hope, keeps a keen eye, and looks to the heights. For this reason God made this creature alone upright in form and set its eyes high up on the body. Through the senses too he teaches that we must look upward. This creature alone is formed like this. All the others look down and are bent toward the earth. But this one is stretched toward heaven, so that he may survey the things there, reflect on them, picture them, and keep the soul's eye keen. That is why a wise man said, "The wise man's eyes are in his head." That is, he is free of all things below, lives as a citizen of heaven, and pictures things on high. "Do not let your foot be moved, and let him who keeps you not slumber." Do you see how much effort the word demands of us? They had spoken of help and were calling on the support from above. So he exhorts and advises them, all but saying: If you want to enjoy this help, contribute your own part. And what does he advise? Listen: "Do not let your foot be moved." That is: do not be overturned, do not stumble, and then you will have God stretching out his hand to you, not abandoning you, not letting you go. So the beginning lies with us, and in this we are masters. Since we are masters, whenever we want to obtain something, we too must contribute our own part, for that is how God wills it. Our part is small and paltry, yet we must still contribute it. We must not be idle, or sleeping and snoring, or lying back, but working and striving to be saved. That is why he hired workers even at the eleventh hour. And yet what great work were they going to do at the eleventh hour? He did it so that he might have their work as an occasion, a pretext for the crowns. So he says, "Do not let your foot be moved, and he who keeps you does not slumber." If you supply your part, his will follow. Something more is also shown by this: even if we contribute our part, we still need his support, so that we may be safe and stay unshaken. 2. Who lets his foot be moved? The one who steps onto slippery things that give no firm footing, such as the love of money, or the longing for worldly things. That is why such people keep being overturned and falling, and [?] the account of the last things… Savile and two manuscripts: "runs past more quickly." Savile: "saying again." Savile: "and where did this happen?"

…he will be able to set you free from everything and make you free [?]. “The Lord will guard your coming in and your going out.” Another translator says, “your approach.” Do you see the unfailing alliance present everywhere, as you come in and as you go out? [?] What could equal this love, this kindness? Here, though, he hints at the whole of life, for the whole of life consists of these things, of comings in and goings out. And to make this clearer he added: “From now and for ever.” Not for one day, he says, nor for two, or three, or ten, or twenty, or a hundred, but continually. This is not so among human beings. With them the changes are many, the reversals constant, the shifts sudden. Today’s friend is tomorrow’s enemy; today’s helper abandons you tomorrow. Often he does not merely abandon you, but wars against you and plots against you more harshly than any enemy. But the things of God are immovable, unfailing, deathless, abiding, and without end. So, that we may obtain them, let us also contribute our own part, so as to enjoy great security and to obtain the good things to come in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

ON PSALM 121. “I rejoiced at those who said to me, Let us go into the house of the Lord.” 1. But nowadays many are even irritated by this saying. If someone calls them to go up to the horse races or to the theatres of lawlessness, many come running together; but if he calls them to the house of prayer, few are those who do not hesitate. But the Jews were not like this. And what could be worse than this, when Christians show themselves more slothful even than they? How did the Jews come to be like this? Again I say: they became better through the captivity. So it was that those who had earlier been nauseated, who abandoned the temple and the hearing of the divine oracles and gave themselves over to mountains and glens and hills and to great impiety, now fixed their desire on that worship. They are warmed toward the very promise; they are roused up, they stand, they exult in mind. For since they had come into famine and thirst, not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but for hearing the word of the Lord, they were punished by this penalty, and now with greater desire they seek the things from which they had earlier fallen away. So they even embraced the very ground, saying, “Your servants have taken pleasure in her stones, and will have pity on her dust”; and again, “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?”; and again, “I will remember you from the land of the Jordan and of Hermon, from the little mountain”; and again, “These things I remembered, and I poured out my soul within me.” What did you remember, tell me? “That I shall pass through to the place of the wonderful tabernacle, as far as the house of God.” That is, that I used to pass through the dances, the festivals, that worship. “Our feet were standing in your courts, O Jerusalem.” Another translator: “I rejoiced when they said to me: We have come into the house of the Lord; our feet stood in your courts, O Jerusalem.” Do you see the overflowing pleasure? As though they were enjoying the things themselves, even at the words… [Note:] [?] “house, many are those who hesitate,” which is perhaps the true reading.

…so that by wandering everywhere they might find pretexts and outlets for the worship of idols. For this reason he commanded that sacrifice be offered there, that prayer be made there, that the festival be held there. By the narrowness of the place he walled in their wandering mind, checking it and reining it in as it rushed toward impiety. He himself showed this when he said: “The tribes of the Lord, a testimony for Israel.” What does “a testimony for Israel” mean? It was the greatest testimony, refutation and proof of God’s providence: no defence was left to them when they kicked free, leapt away and deserted to the idols. For this was the greatest evidence of his providence, his power and his wisdom. There the law was read, containing the narratives and histories of the ancient achievements. There too they were bound together in love as they mingled with one another. For the occasions of the feasts gave them an opportunity and a reason to mix with one another. Fear of God grew greater, piety flourished, and countless good things came about from their being together in the city. “To give thanks to the name of the Lord.” That is, to give thanks, to worship, to pray, to make offerings, to sacrifice. These things led them to piety and made the strictness of their way of life more secure. “For there thrones were set for judgment, thrones over the house of David.” See, he names another advantage of the city. What is it? That the palace was there. This is what “For there thrones were set for judgment, thrones over the house of David” means. Another translator: “of the house of David.” For the twofold rule, that of the priests and that of the kings, was yoked together there, and through all these things the city was adorned as with a double crown and diadem. The judges were there too, and to them were referred the matters that were beyond the many. If a verdict in the other cities was in doubt, as happens with appeals, they referred it to the judgment of the judges in Jerusalem, and the matter was settled there. Such were things in former times, but things now are far more grievous. For there is utter desolation, razing and burning; a few remains of the buildings [?] … holding only a reminder of its former [?] and a riddle. For this reason he does not end his discourse on gloomy things, but leads it back to the hope of brighter ones, saying: “Ask now for the things that make for the peace of Jerusalem.” What does “Ask for the peace of Jerusalem” mean? It means “Entreat, beseech.” Another translator says, “Greet Jerusalem.” That is, pray that she may return to her former prosperity, be freed from her frequent wars, and enjoy security from now on. So either he is saying this, or he is prophesying: “Ask for the peace of Jerusalem.” That is, peace will overtake her. “And abundance for those who love you.” Another translator: “They will be at rest.” Another: “May those who love you prosper.” [?] [Notes:] [?] was omitted in the Hexapla [?]. Two manuscripts have “of these” [?]. Morel has “does not dissolve”; [?] Savile has “does not close” [?]. Our Hexapla has “may they prosper” [?] … only benefit them. One [manuscript has] … benefit them.

…her, in security, and that those freed from their sins may persevere in this best of changes, so that all together may obtain the heavenly goods. May we all enjoy them, by the grace and kindness of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and power for ever and ever.

ON PSALM 122. “To you I have lifted up my eyes, you who dwell in heaven.” You see the gain of the captivity shining out everywhere. Those who were always nailed to worldly things, who trusted in Assyrians and Egyptians, in encircling walls and great wealth, now tear themselves away from all of these and flee to the invincible hand. They hang on that hope and acquire a lofty mind, freed from the earth and from being busy about the temple, since their enemies had overthrown their temple. From now on they call upon God from heaven. He is said to dwell in heaven not as though enclosed by a place (far from it, for he fills all things), but rather as resting among the powers there. After all, he is also said to dwell in human beings: “For I will dwell in them and walk among them.” So when they came into the land of the barbarians, they were taught no small doctrines: to be separated from all worldly things, and to know clearly that God, when called upon anywhere, readily grants the request. For since the ray of the new way of life was soon to rise, the Prophet begins to sound a prelude to what was to come, gently loosening, somehow, and through riddles, the observance of places. “Behold, as the eyes of servants look to the hands of their masters, as the eyes of a maidservant to the hands of her mistress, so our eyes look to the Lord our God, until he has pity on us.” See the intensity of piety here again. They do not hope only for a short while, but continually, fixed on him and waiting open-mouthed. For this reason they brought forward the example, hinting at this as well: that they had no hope of help or alliance from anywhere else, and looked to no one else. The maidservant and the household slave have this single resource for food, clothing and the rest of their living: to look to their masters. The slave does not go away, but stays until he receives, and when he receives he is grateful; and this is their continual work. Wishing to show this, then (that they look to him, that they do this continually, that they have no other hope, that they are fixed on the expectation of help from that alliance, and that all their affairs are in his hands), he mentioned the maidservant and the slaves. See how those who earlier, when urged to run to God, were nauseated and fell back have now become so much better through their calamity that they do not wish to leave him, but to stay and serve and seek what comes from him. “Until he has pity on us.” He did not say, “until he pays the wage,” nor “until he gives the recompense,” but “until he shows mercy.” You too, then, O man, stay continually, whether you receive or not. Even if you do not receive, do not go away, and you will certainly receive. For if a widow’s persistence bent that cruel ruler, what [?] could you have… [Notes:] [?] “overthrew.” [?] “this example.” [?] “to no one,” [?] the same has “for he does not go away.” Savile has “all,” [?] a little after, “persistence.” [?] of the contempt [?] of the proud.

…beloved; but remember the Prophet who says, “It is good for me that you humbled me, so that I might learn your statutes.” Receive the calamity as medicine, use the trial as you ought, and you will be able to obtain greater relief. May we all be found worthy of it, by the grace and kindness of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and power for ever and ever. Amen. [ON PSALM 123.] “If it had not been that the Lord was among us.” 1. What I have often said I say now too, and I will not stop saying it: great is the fruit of the captivity, and able to lead those who pay attention to philosophy. For see: those who used to run to idols, who despised God, who had run aground on impiety, what do they say now, after the captivity, and how they ascribe their own salvation to God! And the Prophet, like an excellent choir-leader, keeps bidding them say the same things. After saying it first himself, he charges them too, as a teacher charges his disciples, to say: “Let Israel now say, If it had not been that the Lord was among us, when men rose up against us, then they would have swallowed us alive.” For they were unarmed and naked, captives and slaves, only just freed from their evils, with an unwalled city, or rather not even a city, and after the return they lay before everyone as ready prey. But God became their wall and tower. Let us too say this now: “If it had not been that the Lord was among us, then they would have swallowed us alive.” For what would our enemy the devil not have done, if the Lord had not been among us? Hear what Christ says to Simon: “Simon, Simon, how often Satan has demanded to sift you like wheat, and I prayed for you that your faith may not fail.” For the beast is wicked and insatiable, and if it were not continually bridled, it would have overturned and confounded everything. In the case of blessed Job, having received only a small permission, he tore up his house by the roots, ravaged his body and staged so great a tragedy: he destroyed his property, buried his children, made worms boil up in his flesh, set his wife against him, and got his friends, his enemies and his servants to say such things. If he were not held back by countless bridles, how would he not have ruined everyone? That is why this man too says, “If it had not been that the Lord was among us.” For they were very few and of no account, and many attacked them when they returned. In this too God’s wisdom was shown: he did not give them security all at once, but gently and little by little. He did this to keep them in the knowledge of God, and not to let the correction they had gained from the captivity drain away. For since release from evils usually makes people more slack, even in the very giving of good things he lets them be tried continually, so that they might have their trials as a constant training in philosophy. For this reason he neither leaves people always in calamities, lest they grow weary, nor always in ease, lest they grow more slack, but varies their salvation with alternations… [Notes:] Savile has “attacked together.” “Let us drag aside, but [?].” So another.

…for the torrent is fearsome for a time, and then it sinks away beyond measure. “Then the water would have drowned us.” Another translator says, “Then the waters would have swept us aside, like a ravine-stream passing over our soul.” “Then our soul would have passed through the irresistible water.” Another says, “Then the overweening waters would have passed over our soul.” Do you see how great God’s alliance is? How in such great evils he did not let them be submerged? For this is why he lets terrors grow: not to sink us, but to make us more proven and to give a greater proof of his own power. Here he calls the enemies “proud”: they attacked more violently than any torrent and any unbearable water, yet did them no harm at all. The cause was God’s alliance, his influence from above, his invincible help. So, having spoken of the release from evils, he also names the one who provided the release, and does so with praise: “Blessed be the Lord, who did not give us as prey to their teeth. Our soul was rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters.” Do you see how he sets out both their own weakness and the strength of the others? The enemies came on like beasts and lions, ready to taste their flesh, armed with both power and rage; the others were weaker than any sparrow. For God’s wonders are shown most of all when the weak overcome the strong. Nor was the plot unbearable only in this, that the enemies were strong and fearsome, full of great rage and ready to taste their flesh, while these were weak, few and easy to attack. It was unbearable also because they were caught in the midst of terrors, had entered into the very difficulties, and had wars surrounding them on every side. But God, who is resourceful and able to save from every side, even after we fell into terrors, released us, he says, with great ease. Wishing to show this, he said: “Our soul was rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters. The snare was broken, and we were rescued.” Then, showing how, he added: “Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth.” Do you see the power of the Creator [?]? Do you see his strength? He removed the very occasions of the plot. One could also take this by anagogy as referring to the devil and the human race. For it shows how he snatched us away, how he undid the devil’s plots. This happened from the time when he said to the disciples, “Tread upon snakes and scorpions, and upon all the power of the enemy.” For the battle is no longer face to face [?], nor the battle line; but he lies prone, fallen down, while you stand upright and strike from above. He has been hamstrung, while you are strong. How then does he often win? Through our sluggishness, through the slackness of those who sleep. So if you choose to stand against him, he does not dare to draw up his line. If he overcomes someone asleep, this comes not from his power but from your negligence. For who would not overcome a sleeper, even if he were the weakest of all? “The strong man was bound…” [Notes:] Savile has “the change,” Morel “the release” [?]. A little after, Savile has: “Blessed be the Lord, adding, who did not.” [?]

…[do not] seek a life [?] free from affairs and from toil, but one that is not swept away by dangers. For it is not the same thing to display your skill sitting in harbour and tossing on the open sea. The one becomes sluggish, slack and limp. The other endures many hidden rocks, many reefs, many violent winds and the other terrors of the sea, comes through them all, and makes his soul stronger. This is why you were brought out into the present life: not to be idle, nor to lounge about, nor to suffer nothing terrible, but so that by suffering you might become more glorious. Let us not, then, seek ease, nor a life full of luxury. That desire belongs not to a noble man but to a worm, to an irrational creature rather than a rational one. Pray above all not to fall into temptation; but if you ever do enter it, do not be vexed, do not be alarmed or troubled, but do everything you can to become more glorious. Do you not see how the bravest soldiers, when the trumpet calls, look to the trophies, the victories, the crowns, the ancestors who succeeded? You too, then, when the spiritual trumpet sounds, stand firm, becoming fiercer than a lion. Step in, even if it is fire, even if it is iron. Even the elements know how to respect the truly brave. Even the beasts know how to fear such noble men. Though a beast is savage from hunger or by its very nature, it forgets everything when it sees a righteous man, and masters its passion. Fortify yourself with these weapons, then, and you will not fear even fire, though you see the flame rising to heaven. You have a noble general, able to do all things, who undoes terrors with a single nod. All things are his: heaven and earth, sea, beasts and fire. For him it is easy to transpose and shift them all with ease. Why, then, are you afraid, tell me? For no other reason than sluggishness and your own slackness. Is death not the culmination of evils? But this too is the debt owed by nature. Why do you not trade with the debt? If you must travel this road whether you will or not, why not travel it with profit? With tortures, you say? Yes, but not [?] lasting ones; ones that give a pleasure greater than the pain. If these things seem harsh to you, think of those who are handed over to long wasting without any reward, those who wrestle with constant hunger, those who have incurable and long illnesses, because of which they have often prayed to end their lives, and many have even rushed to the noose and the sword. But heaven lies before you, and the good things in heaven, and you do not shudder, you are not afraid as you grow soft, and that when you have such an ally? Do you not hear the Prophet saying, “Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion”? He said “mountain” to show how unshakable hope in God is, how firmly fixed, how impregnable, how invincible. For just as someone who brings up countless siege engines will be able neither to uproot a mountain nor to shake it, so whoever attacks one who has his hope in God will go home empty-handed. For hope in God is far more secure than a mountain. “He who dwells in Jerusalem shall not be shaken for ever.” Another translator… [Notes:] Savile has “but if you ever also fall, do not.” [?] another has “those so brave.” Savile has “only.” Soon after, the same has “transpose and set.” [?] “tortures that are harsh, but temporary, and greater.” [?] “trade, but.” [?] “temporary … pleasure … pain.” A little after, Savile has “without reward to long wasting.” Morel [?] “and often.” Savile has “thus attacking.” [?] “terrible [?] of it,” not badly.

"Do good, O Lord, to the good." Another translator has "Make good." "And to the upright in heart. But those who turn aside into crooked ways the Lord will lead away with the workers of iniquity." Do you see that everywhere the beginnings come from us, both of enjoying good things and of undergoing punishment? But even if the beginnings come from us, God's loving-kindness still shows itself great [?] even so. For he far outdoes us in his repayments: for sins he brings a punishment in proportion, but for good deeds he grants a recompense that goes beyond them. By "upright" here he means the guileless, the unaffected, those who have nothing shadowy or underhanded. For such is uprightness, which God seeks above all everywhere. Such is virtue: something smooth and easy, just as wickedness is twisted, intricate, a road with no way through. And you can see this from the facts themselves. Think of the man who wants to lie and stitch together deceits: how much he has to undertake, how much intricacy he needs, what fabricated words, how much cleverness! But the one who tells the truth needs no toil, no [?], no pretense, no contrivances, nothing of the kind, for the truth shines out by itself. Just as ugly bodies need many artifices and coverings from outside to shade over their natural ugliness, while bodies that are beautiful by nature shine of themselves, competing on their own merits, so too you can find it with falsehood and truth, with vice and virtue. From this it is clear that even before punishment vice brings its own punishment, and even before recompense virtue gives its reward. For just as virtue has its prizes within itself even before the crowns, so vice has its penalty within itself even before the punishment. For what could be harsher than sin, by way of penalty? That is why Paul, speaking of those who had prostituted themselves, who sold their own youthful bloom and overturned the laws of nature, said that this was the greatest penalty, even before punishment. "For men with men," he says, "committing shameless acts, and receiving in themselves the due penalty of their error" — calling their licentiousness and the act itself the penalty of their sin. "Peace be upon Israel." He closed the discourse with a prayer. For such are the souls of the saints: to their exhortation and counsel they add prayer, bringing the greatest of allies to their hearers. By "peace" here he means not only this peace that the senses perceive, but also the peace higher than it, from which this one too is born. He prays that the soul may not be at strife with itself by bringing in the war of the passions. Let us too seek this peace, so that we may be able to obtain the promised good things, by the grace and loving-kindness of the Lord. [Variant: "his care is shown." (?) Others read: "the souls of the saints."]

[?] but because from this all will come to know God's providence toward us. "For then," he says, "they will say among the nations, 'The Lord has done great things for them.' 'The Lord has done great things for us.'" The repetition is not set down idly; it is there to show the great joy they had. The first is the saying of the nations, the second is their own in reply. And notice: they did not say "He saved us," or "He delivered us," but "He has done great things," wishing by the term "magnify" to present how unexpected and full of wonder it was. Do you see that, as I kept saying, the world was being taught through this nation, both when they were led away and when they were brought back? For their return served as a herald. Their fame went round everywhere, making God's loving-kindness plain to all, since the wonders done for them were truly great and unexpected. For Cyrus himself, who held them captive, let them go, though no one asked him; God softened his mind. And he did not simply let them go, but sent them off with gifts and presents. "We became glad. Turn back our captivity, O Lord, like torrents in the south." How is it that at the beginning of the psalm he said, "When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion," but here, "Turn back"? He is speaking as of something still to come. Another translator leads us to this reading above all, saying not "When the Lord turned back" but "When he turns back." For the matter was then only beginning, and the whole was not accomplished at the outset; there were many returns of theirs: a first, a second and a third. This, then, is what it means. Or else he is praying that the deliverance may become complete. For many of the Jews wished to stay on in the land of the barbarians. Therefore, longing for it to happen in full force, he says, "Turn back our captivity like torrents in the south": that is, with a great rush, with great vehemence, driving and pressing them on. That is why another translator, showing this very thing, said "Like rushing streams [?]." Another: "Like channels." Another: "Like outflowings." "Those who sow in tears will reap in joy." This was said about the Jews, but it could have its place in many other settings too. For such is virtue: it has splendid rewards for its labors. We must first toil and endure hardship, and only then seek rest. One can see this happening everywhere, even in the affairs of everyday life. That is why he brought his discourse round to these things, I mean sowing and harvest. For just as the sower needs toil, hardship, sweat and winter, so does the one who pursues virtue. For nothing is so ill-suited to ease as a human being. That is why God made the way narrow and hard. Or rather, not only the things of virtue but the affairs of this life too he made [?] laborious. [Notes: (?) "is added," placed before the words "has done great things..." Others read "no one entreating" instead of "no one asking." In these words Savile has: "'Turn back, O Lord,' he says, as of something to come." Savile: "in the barbarian land" (?). Savile: "in the barbarian land." Savile: "he called the way leading to virtue narrow and hard" (?).]

[?] speaking not of the earlier building, that of Solomon, but of this later one, after the deliverance from the Persians. A long time was spent while the temple, the city and the walls were being built (the building of the city took far more), and so the Prophet goes through these things to teach them again to take refuge in God. He shows that everything is done at random and in vain unless they draw down the help that comes from God. For not only being freed from captivity, but also raising the wall once they were freed, was impossible without God's help. And why do I speak of raising walls and building a city? Even once it was built and completed, no one could guard it if deprived of that alliance. He said this to persuade them in every way to take refuge again in his help, so that they would not grow slacker in their ease. That is why he did not give them the good things all at once, but gently and little by little, so that a very swift release from their troubles would not make them run back to their former wickedness. Even while giving them good things he kept reminding them, constantly rousing them from their slackness through the attacks of their enemies. The saying is spoken in general terms, but it took its starting point from this occasion. It must apply to everyone, not so that we may grow slack or lie on our backs, but so that, once we have contributed our own part, we may cast the whole on God, hanging always and in all things on hope in him. For just as without God's help it is impossible to bring matters to completion, so, even if God helps, those who are idle and lying back cannot reach the goal. "It is in vain for you to rise early; you rise up after sitting." Another translator says, "They are slow to sit." Another, "They delay sitting." What he means is this: even if you stay awake, even if you rouse yourselves at dawn, even if you are slow to take your rest and spend all your time in toil and hardship, unless you enjoy the help that comes from above, all human efforts will come to nothing and this zeal will gain you nothing more. "You who eat the bread of pain." He says this to show that they lived a laborious life, being soldiers and builders at once. With one hand, it says, they carried a basket or a stone, and with the other a sword, dividing themselves between building and fighting, and they carried the gravel along with their shields. For since the city was unwalled and bare, they feared every hour the sudden and unexpected attacks of their enemies. So they wove the walls together under arms; swords, shields and daggers lay ready beside them, and lookouts far off reported any unforeseen approach and sounded the trumpet whenever they saw the enemy coming from a distance. "But even if you do these things," he says, "and [eat] the bread of pain [?]" [Notes: It was read, "of the later deliverance with the Persians." These words, "for the building of the city took far more," [?]. "... reminded them, by the attack of enemies," less correctly. Who translated "They delay sitting" is unknown. Savile: "For with one hand they carried a basket or a stone, and with the other a sword." Savile: "his things, God." Savile: "provides what is from him."]

[?] children, through their weapons, through their strength, they will not hide their faces when they see their enemies, but will meet them with great courage, priding themselves, high-minded, adorned, while through all these things God displays his help on their behalf. For the sum of all good things and the crown of blessedness is to be able, from then on, to be adorned with God's alliance. That is why he ended the discourse here, teaching everyone to seek that adornment before all else and to be radiant in it. Let us too strive after this, so that we may obtain the eternal good things, by the grace and loving-kindness of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom be glory to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.

On Psalm 127. "Blessed are all who fear the Lord." 1. See how he begins from the point where he ended before. Just as there he called them blessed because they are not put to shame, since they have God as their helper and with them, so here too he begins from the same point, saying, "Blessed are all who fear the Lord." Again he makes the saying general, after taking his starting point from them. And he did well to say "all." Whether someone is a slave or a master, poor or maimed in body, whoever he may be, none of these things prevents him from having the blessedness he speaks of. The other kind, false and counterfeit, which many covet, is barely produced even when many things come together, and unless they all coincide no one would be counted blessed among men. Let me give an example. If someone is rich, that is not enough for blessedness; health must be there too. For if he is rich but maimed in body, his blessedness limps, and he is more wretched than the poor. Indeed, many who are wealthy but wrestling with illness call blessed the poor who pass through the alleys, and think themselves wretched for all their countless talents. Again, if he is healthy in body and rich but enjoys no esteem, that is another obstacle. For there are some who possess great wealth and a sound body, yet suffer intolerable things from those enrolled in the army and invested with power. Because they share in no honor, they think themselves the most wretched of all, bowing down to men whose own slaves are often richer than they. Again, if he has esteem, wealth and bodily health, but safety is lacking, with countless people plotting against him, envying, begrudging, hating, accusing and slandering him, such a man will be the most wretched of all. He lives the life of a hare, suspicious even of shadows, trembling at everyone and afraid. And if he is rid of these too, and loved by all, and everything flows his way, esteem, wealth, safety and honor (an impossible combination, but let it be granted for the sake of argument), even if all these flow in and nothing breaks the stream, but there is the goodwill of the people, great esteem and abundance of wealth, [?] [Notes: Savile: "the radiance," and shortly after, "showing." Savile: "be deemed worthy to obtain." Savile: "in that God..." Savile: "'all,' showing that even if a slave." "invested with power, and dragging them into the army." [?] "safety" [?] of the body; but "and afraid" is better [?]. Morel: "is rid"; Savile: "has been rid." "removes the twistedness," in the same sense.]

[?] makes it beautiful and bright, scouring it and completely straightening what was bent. In the same way the fear of God will accomplish everything, and in a short time, and it lets no human misfortune trip up those who are steeped in it. Was not Timothy sickly? Was he not constantly in illnesses and hardships? Yet who was more blessed than he? And what of Job, tell me? Was he not in poverty? In childlessness? In a most grievous affliction of the body? In reproaches? In insults? In abuse? In hunger? In every human misfortune? Yet he too became the most blessed of all. Not only did none of these things trip him up; they made him firmer. And besides all those, his wife pressed on him with reproaches, and still he shone through it all. With all this in mind, the Prophet said, "Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways." So that you would not think fear is enough for you, he added, "who walk in his ways," showing both: that they fear and that they walk. For many who have an exact faith but a corrupt life have become the most wretched of all. So that the saying would not seem to be refuted on this score, he added, "who walk in his ways." And what are the ways of God but a life lived according to virtue? Through this one can ascend to heaven, take hold of the mother city, and see God himself, as far as a human being can see him. They are called his ways because through them one can go to God. And he did not say "way" but "ways," showing that they are many and varied. That is why he cut many of them, making the entrance easy for us by the abundance of ways. Some people shine in virginity, others excel in marriage, others are adorned by widowhood. Some have stripped themselves of everything, others of half. Some go by an upright life, others by repentance. That is why he cut many ways, so that you might travel easily. Were you unable to keep your body pure after baptism? You can make yourself pure through repentance; you can do it through money, through almsgiving. But you have no money? You can still visit the sick, go to the prisoner, give a cup of cold water, take the stranger under your roof, give two small coins like the widow, and groan with those in pain. For this too is almsgiving. But you are utterly destitute and poor, weak in body, and cannot even walk? Bear all this with thanksgiving, and you have reaped a great reward. This was Lazarus's achievement. He helped no one with money; how could he, when he did not even have the food he needed? He did not go into a prison; how could he, when he could not even stand upright? He did not visit the sick; how could he, lying exposed to the dogs' tongues? Yet even without these things he carried off the prize of virtue by bearing everything nobly, by [?] [Notes: Others read "knowledge [is enough] for you"; Savile has, better, "fear [is enough] for you," as in the text. Savile in the margin: "knowledge; therefore he added." Morel: "of the city." Savile: "possible to behold." Shortly after, the same: "one can come to."]

[Notes: Savile: "keep the body pure." Shortly after, the same: "through repentance make [yourself] pure." Savile: "so as not even to be able to walk." In the same place: "and you will reap [?] a great reward." Savile: "carried off the prize."]

[?] to receive, and after receiving to be deprived. So bear all that befalls you nobly, for this counts as a martyrdom for you. It is not only refusing to sacrifice when ordered to, choosing instead to have one's flesh torn rather than do it, that makes a martyrdom. When pain drives a man toward blasphemy, choosing to hold out under the suffering and say nothing out of tune also makes a martyr. For Job too was crowned, not because he refused to sacrifice when ordered, but because he bore his pains nobly. And Paul won his renown from this: from the scourgings, from the afflictions, from everything else he endured with thanksgiving. "You shall eat the labors of your fruits; blessed are you, and it shall be well with you." Why does he double the blessing? Because he knows how great it is, he lingers delightedly over the picture of it. And what does "well" mean, tell me? "Your wife shall be like a flourishing vine on the sides of your house." Another translator says, "in the innermost parts." Another, "at the thighs" [?]. "Your sons like new olive shoots around your table. Behold, thus shall the man be blessed who fears the Lord." What are you saying, tell me? Is this the blessedness? Is this the gain: a prosperous household, enjoying the fruit of one's own labors, many children, and a wife? Not this; this comes as something extra. "Seek first the kingdom of heaven, and all these things will be added to you." Since he was still speaking to the less perfect, he leads them on like little children by means of things the senses perceive. And do not be surprised. If Paul does this, in a time of so lofty a philosophy, when speaking to those who still walk on the ground, much more would the Prophet. And where does Paul do this? In many places. When he speaks about virginity, he says nothing to them about the things to come, but sets out only the release from the troubles that come with marriage. And when he speaks about honoring parents, he uses the same method, saying: "This is the first commandment with promises. And what is the commandment? Honor your father and your mother, and you will live long on the earth." And when he writes about the philosophy of conduct toward enemies, again he sets out a prize the senses can grasp, saying: "For by doing this you will heap coals of fire on his head." But Christ does not do so, for he is not speaking to the weak. For virginity he sets out the kingdom, and for loving one's enemies, becoming like God, as far as it is possible for human beings to become like him. So too in the Old Testament, where people were led on through things of the senses, we shall see that those who knew how to live the philosophic life were led on by greater things. Paul showed this when he said, "These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them from afar and greeted them." So the reward of those who fear God is not only this, the enjoyment of their own goods, a wife, children and a prosperous house. These come as extras, by way of addition. The chief and great things are, first, the very fearing of God, which holds its reward within itself, and then also those ineffable [?] [Notes: Savile: "your sons." [?] wrongly. Below, Morel [?] has "weaker"; others read "less perfect." Savile: "looking at the ground." Shortly after, the same: "does Paul do this? Elsewhere too. For..." [?] "of him." "But Christ." Savile: "chief great things." Savile: "first, then."]

…against some, and they turn aside his wrath by repentance, the punishment is halted. In the same way, if he promises good things but those who are to enjoy the promise prove unworthy, the promise is held back. As far as it depended on him, then, he promised them all their days; but by their own wickedness they cut off the gift. I say this so that we neither despair when he threatens, but turn aside his wrath by repentance, nor grow slack when he promises good things, but by zeal and care in how we live call his promises into effect. For unless we do this, the promise alone is not enough to save us. After all, he also promised Judas that he would sit on a throne with the eleven disciples, and he did not sit there; and the fault lay not with the one who promised, but with the one who proved unworthy of the promise. So we too, who have the promise of a kingdom, must not be lazy, but must contribute our own part, so that we may be able to obtain the eternal goods, by the grace and lovingkindness of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and power forever and ever. Amen.

Many times have they fought against me from my youth, let Israel now say. Many times have they fought against me from my youth, and they could not prevail against me. Another translator says, "But they could not prevail against me." This psalm too is connected with the one before it. Since the building was being interrupted and the work was not moving toward completion, he leads them to good hopes so that they will not [?] despair, prepares them to take courage about the future from the past, and teaches them to say these words. What words? That their enemies often attacked them but could not overcome them, nor win a complete victory. "And yet," someone says, "they led them away captive, transported them to a foreign land, and won many wars." Even then, above all, they prevailed not by their own strength but because of the sin of the Jews. Besides, they did not remain victors to the end. They could not wipe out the race entirely, nor blot out the city, nor destroy the nation for good; they prevailed for a little while, God permitting it, and then were defeated again. How were they defeated? When the Jews returned to their former prosperity. Another translator shows this when he says, "But they did not overpower me." On my back the sinners wrought; they prolonged their iniquity. What does this mean? They did not plot against me casually, he says, but contrived and labored at much, stitching [?] together deceits and attacking in secret. For "on my back" signifies either what is treacherous and underhand, or what is done by force and with great violence. That is, they tried to crush my very strength. Another, instead of "wrought"… [Notes:] Savile: "against some; but for those who turn aside the wrath by repentance, [the punishment] is halted." Savile: "these things indeed." Three manuscripts begin thus: "This psalm is connected again with the former one [?] … words. For often." Savile: "the words. What words? That often," and so on. Savile: "the race, or blot out the city." Below, the same reads [?]. Morel: "having prevailed," which is better. [?] but soon after "he said" is read [?].

On Psalm 129. Out of the depths I have cried to you, O Lord; Lord, hear my voice. 1. What does "out of the depths" mean? Not merely from the mouth, nor merely from the tongue—for then the words pour out while the mind wanders—but from the very bottom of the heart, with great zeal and eagerness, from the very foundations of the mind. Such are the souls of those who pray in affliction: they stir up the whole heart and call on God with deep compunction, and that is why they are heard. Such prayers have great power; they are not overturned or shaken, even if the devil attacks with great force. A strong tree that sends its root deep into the earth and grips its hidden recesses withstands every blast of the winds, while one lying near the surface is shaken when even a slight breeze falls on it, and is torn up by the roots and left lying on the ground. So too with prayers: those that rise from below and are rooted in the depths remain intent and unyielding, and are not overturned, even if countless thoughts assail them, even if the devil's whole battle line comes on; but those that come forth from the mouth and lips and do not rise from below cannot even ascend to God, because of the carelessness of the one who approaches. For such a mind is overturned by any noise, and dragged away from its supplication by any commotion; and the mouth [?] … but the heart is empty and the mind deserted. The saints did not pray like this, but with such intensity that they even bent their whole body. Blessed Elijah, when he prayed, first sought solitude; then he put his head between his knees and, kindling himself with great fervor, poured out his prayers in that way. If you want to see him standing upright in prayer, look at him again stretched out toward heaven, and so stretched out that he brought fire down from above. So too when he wished to raise the widow's child, he stretched his whole self out and so brought about that resurrection—not lolling about or yawning as we do, but glowing with the eagerness of his prayer. But why do I speak of Elijah and those saints? I have often seen women praying in this way out of the depths for a husband abroad or a sick child, and shedding such fountains of tears that they obtained the very thing they prayed for. If women are so fervent in prayer for a child or a husband abroad, what pardon will a man have who is slack when his own soul lies dead? That is why we often pray and then go away empty again. Hear about Hannah, how she prayed out of the depths, what fountains of tears she shed, how she was lifted up by her prayer. Whoever prays like this reaps great goods from his prayer even before he receives what he asks: he calms all the passions, softens anger, drives out envy, melts desire, withers the love of worldly things, and settles the soul in deep calm [?] … [Notes:] [?] … Below: "lest anyone say that he sinned," Savile. Other manuscripts: "dragging down" and "casting in."

…God passed over it and called him, and counted him worthy of much grace. And what of Peter, that chief of the apostles? After countless wonders and signs, and after so much exhortation and counsel, did he not convict him when he fell into that grievous fall? Yet he passed over that too, and appointed him first of the apostles. That is why he said: Simon, Simon, behold, Satan has demanded to sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail. And after this, if he does not come to judge with mercy and lovingkindness, but to make a strict examination, he will certainly find everyone guilty. That is why Paul said: I am not aware of anything against myself, but I am not justified by this. If you should mark iniquities, Lord, Lord… The repetition is not idle: it belongs to one who marvels and is astounded at the vast abundance of his lovingkindness, his boundless greatness, the yawning sea of his goodness. Who will endure? He did not say, "Who will escape?" but, "Who will endure?" No one, he means, will even be able to stand. For with you is propitiation. What does "with you is propitiation" mean? Escaping punishment lies not in our own good deeds but in your goodness. Escaping the penalty rests on your lovingkindness. If we do not enjoy this, what is ours is not enough to snatch us from the coming…

3. He showed this also through the prophet when he said: I am he who blots out your iniquities. That is, this is my doing, the work of my goodness, of my lovingkindness. Your own deeds are never enough to set you free from punishment unless what belongs to my lovingkindness is added. And again: I bear with you. For your name's sake I have waited for you, Lord. My soul has waited for your word. My soul has hoped in the Lord. Another has: "For the sake of your law." Another again: "So that your word may be known." What he is saying is this: Because of your lovingkindness, because of your law, I have looked for salvation; for if I had looked to my own deeds, I would long ago have despaired, long ago have given up hope; but now, attending to your law and your word, I have good hopes. Which word? The word of lovingkindness. For it is he who says: As far as heaven is from the earth, so far are my counsels from your counsel, and my ways from your ways. And again: As high as heaven is above the earth, the Lord has made his mercy strong toward those who fear him. And again: As far as the east is from the west, he has removed our iniquities from us. That is: I have saved not only those who did right, but I have also spared those who sinned, and in the midst of your offenses I have shown my help and my care. Another says: "That you may be feared, I have waited for the Lord." Feared by whom? By my enemies, by those who plot against me, by those hostile to me. And what, again, does "for your name's sake" mean? That "even if I am a sinner," he says, "and full of countless evils, still I knew that, so that your name might not be profaned, you would not overlook us as we perished." Which he himself also in the… [Notes:] [?] … is lacking in Savile. Soon after, the same reads: "but who will endure? showing that he will not even be able to stand. For with you is propitiation. Not in our…" So in some manuscripts. One manuscript: "his sea."

…and he himself knows the right time exactly. Let us persevere, then, in supplication and entreaty, trusting in his mercy and lovingkindness, and let us never despair of our own salvation, but contribute our own part; and what comes from him will certainly follow, since his mercy is unspeakable and his lovingkindness boundless. May we all obtain it, by the grace and lovingkindness of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom be glory to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

On Psalm 130. Lord, my heart was not lifted up, nor were my eyes raised high. Another has: "Nor were they lifted up." Nor have I walked among great things, nor among things too wonderful for me. Another has: "Among greatnesses." Another: "Among magnificences, nor among things surpassing [?]." What is this? Paul, even when there was necessity, calls praising oneself folly; that is why he added: I have become a fool in boasting; you compelled me. How then did the Prophet not know this, and now boast, not before two or three or ten people, but before the whole world, saying, "I am lowly and modest, lowly beyond measure, and simple"? For that is what "like a weaned child upon its mother" means. Why then do you do this? Because the thing is not forbidden everywhere; there are times when it is even necessary, or rather times when we become fools not by boasting but by not boasting. That is why Paul says: Let him who boasts boast in the Lord. Whoever does not boast in the cross is the most foolish and lawless of all; whoever does not boast in the faith is the most wretched of all; whoever does not boast and speak boldly about these things will certainly perish. That is why the Apostle said with confidence: But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ. And again: Let not the rich man boast in his riches, nor the wise man in his wisdom, but let him boast in this, in understanding and knowing the Lord. When, then, is boasting evil? When we do it like the Pharisee. "And why," someone says, "did Paul say, 'I have become a fool in boasting; you compelled me'?" Because he was recounting his achievements in his life and conduct, which he ought not to bring forward when there was no necessity. Elsewhere he says: Even if I wish to boast, I shall not be a fool, for I shall be speaking the truth. So whoever speaks the truth when the occasion calls for it is not a fool. Neither, then, is the Prophet a fool when he boasts, for he was speaking the truth. But what is the reason he brought his discourse to this? To teach his hearers not to return to arrogance after their deliverance from evils, nor, once freed from their bonds, to kick up their heels again and fall under the compulsion of another captivity. That is why, in recounting his own conduct, he sets the hearer right. And he does not say, "I was lifted up, but I restrained the passion," but what? "My heart was not lifted up"; that is, it did not even touch [?] … [Notes:] [?] … Savile: "in understanding," with the other form in the margin. Better: "wishing to show."

…in misfortunes, I clung to God. "And if I was not like this," he says, "let it be repaid upon my soul"—that is, may I pay the ultimate penalty. Let Israel hope in the Lord, from now and forever. Do you see what I said at the beginning, that in matters of faith and doctrine we must boast continually, even when there is no cause, and whoever does not boast is lost; but that in the achievements of our life we must never refuse to boast when the occasion calls for it? What occasion? There are many different ones, and one of them is to instruct the hearer. The Prophet knew this too, and to show that he tells of his achievements for this reason—to draw the hearer to the same zeal—he added: Let Israel hope in the Lord, from now and forever. "Even if misfortunes," he says, "even if despondency, wars, captivities, or any unexpected terrors surround you, hold fast to your hope in God and to that expectation, and you will certainly reach a good end, God repaying you for this fine hope by releasing you from your terrors," in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and power forever and ever. Amen. On Psalm 131. Remember, Lord, David and all his meekness. 1. Elsewhere they ask to be saved only on account of the memory of their ancestors; here they also tell of his achievements, and of the cause of all good things—gentleness, humility, meekness—for which Moses too was especially admired. For he was, it says, the meekest of all men on the earth. But some of the heretics attack his conduct and this saying, and they say: "What are you saying? Was he the meekest, that man who kicked the Egyptian and killed him; who filled the Jews with civil bloodshed and wars; who ordered the killing of kinsmen; who split the earth by his prayer and brought thunderbolts down from above, drowning some and burning up others? If he was meek, who is irascible and harsh?" Stop; do not talk idly. That he was meek, the meekest of all men, I say and will not stop saying; and if you wish, I shall try to show his meekness not from elsewhere but from these very things that have been mentioned. I could, of course, cite what he said to God about his sister, the supplication he offered for the nation, all those apostolic words worthy of heaven, the gentleness with which he spoke to the people. I could cite these and list many more besides. But if you wish, let us leave these aside and show, from the very things put forward by his enemies, that he was the meekest of men—from the very things that make some think him harsh, hard and irascible. How then… [Notes:] Savile: "them." Savile: "terror" [singular]. Morel's "any … terrors surround" is better. Savile: "who kicked [?] the Egyptian and killed him." Savile: "and" instead of "not."

…and by the slaughter of a few bodies to remove the sin, check the wrath, and make God propitious to those who had committed such offenses? If you examine the just man's deeds in this way, you will see that he was the meekest of men precisely on these grounds. 2. But let us leave these points for the studious to gather from what has been said, so that we do not make the digression larger than the task in hand, and let us go on to our subject. What was our subject? Remember, Lord, David and all his meekness: how he swore to the Lord, how he vowed to the God of Jacob. Having set out to speak of meekness, he leaves aside the story of Saul, of his brothers, of Jonathan, his long-suffering toward the soldier who heaped countless insults on him, and much else besides, and brings his discourse to another heading, one that showed especially great zeal. Why does he do this? For two reasons. First, because God delights in this above all: For on whom shall I look, he says, but on the meek and quiet, who trembles at my words? Second, because the most pressing matter was the raising of the temple, the building of the city, and the restoration of the old way of life, he presses his discourse toward this especially. The one point—meekness, which was plain to all—he passes over as clear and agreed, and the thing he most needed for his present purpose he brings into the open. For what did they long to see? The temple raised up and the ancient worship restored. Since David shone especially in this, he asks God for the building of the temple as a kind of reward for David's zeal, and says: Remember, Lord, David and all his meekness: how he swore to the Lord, vowed to the God of Jacob: I will not enter the dwelling of my house, I will not go up onto the bed I lie on, I will not give sleep to my eyes, or slumber to my eyelids, or rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob. "And what is that to you?" "I am his descendant," he says, "and since you accepted his zeal and said you would establish his line and his kingdom, that is why we now claim the fulfilment of these covenants." And he did not say, "until I build" (for that was not permitted to him), but, "until I find a place for the Lord and a dwelling." Then he passes over the one who built and puts forward the one who promised, so that you may learn how great a good a right intention is, and how God always measures the reward by our choice. This is why he mentions David rather than his son: because David is more truly the builder than his son was. The one promised; the other was commanded. And see his eagerness. He says not only that he will not enter a house or go up onto a bed, but that he will not even enjoy freely what came from natural necessity, until he finds a place and a dwelling for the God of Jacob. They themselves were charged with the very opposite by God, who says: [?] … [Notes:] Savile: "propitious" [variant form]. [?] "who washed [?] him with countless insults." Shortly after, the same: "for two reasons" [variant form]. [?] "was especially; for indeed the raising…" [?] Savile: "but not even what was from natural necessity, nor…" [?]

…to establish, but because you also made covenants with him. "For the sake of David your servant, do not turn away the face of your anointed." Whose anointed, he means? The one who had been anointed at that time, who led the people and stood at their head. "The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not set it aside: Of the fruit of your body I will set upon your throne." Since he had remembered David, the man's virtue and his zeal for the temple, he recounted the old stories as well, and asked that they might be restored to their former way of life. So he puts forward the weightiest point of all, reading out the covenants of God. And what are they? "Of the fruit of your body I will set upon your throne." Yet the covenants were not made unconditionally, but with a certain stipulation. And what was the stipulation? Listen, for he goes on: "If your sons keep my covenant, and these my testimonies which I will teach them, their sons also shall sit upon your throne for ever." When God had laid down these covenants, he put the written bond into their hands, and they in turn said, "All that the Lord has said we will do and obey." Then, since he sees that the one party has broken the covenants, he turns his discourse to the place, stirring up words of appeal from every side and saying: "For the Lord has chosen Zion; he has desired it for his dwelling. This is my resting place for ever and ever; here I will dwell, for I have desired it." That is, it was not a man who chose the place; God himself decreed it, condescending to their weakness. What he means is this: the place you took, the place you chose, the place you decreed, the place you judged fit, do not let it fall into ruin or perish. For you yourself said these things: "I will dwell here." But these words were spoken together with those covenants. Which ones? "If your sons keep my covenant." "I will abundantly bless her provision." Another translator has "her store of food." By "provision" he means plenty of goods for sale and abundance, and he prays that everything may flow to them as from springs. For in ancient times the Jews did enjoy such a life, untouched by the necessities of nature, whenever they had God favorable to them. There was no shortage of grain among them, no famine or plague, no untimely death, nothing else of the kind that usually befalls human beings; everything flowed to them as from springs, since the hand of God corrected the weakness of human affairs. [579] So this is what he says here: you promised to bless her provision, that is, to supply an abundance of necessities in great security. "Her poor I will satisfy with bread. Her priests I will clothe with salvation, and her saints shall rejoice with great joy. There I will make a horn spring up for David; I have prepared a lamp for my anointed. His enemies I will clothe with shame, but upon him my holiness shall flourish." See prosperity on every side [?]. [Textual notes, largely illegible:] [?] "he will not set aside." [?] "his" [?] "their" [?]. Another reads: "and he prays that all things." Morel: "of grace."

…for he, being high priest, was anointed with this ointment, and it dripped down over him on every side. From this anointing he was full of grace, sweet and lovely to those who saw him. Just as that man, he says, anointed with this ointment, is splendid in bearing, radiant in face, filled with fragrance, and a delight to the eyes of those who look at him, so this too is good. That sight is not only beautiful to behold but gladdens the eyes, and in the same way this fills the soul with pleasure. "Like the dew of Hermon, which comes down upon the mountains of Zion." He has brought in another image too, one full of delight that gives joy to whoever looks on it. He did not set these down without purpose. Before the captivity the ten tribes and the two had been divided, and this caused much lawlessness and threw them into factions, quarrels and wars. So that this might not happen again, he exhorts them and counsels the people never again to be torn apart, but to live together, to be joined as one, to be ranged under one leader and king, and to let love flow from beginning to end, just as dew passes over everything. He compares love to ointment and to dew, wishing to show its fragrance by the one, and by the other its refreshment and its pleasantness to the eye. "For there the Lord commanded the blessing." Where is "there"? In such a dwelling together, in such concord, in such unity of voice, in such sharing of one tent. For this is a blessing, just as its opposite is a curse. That is why someone praises it, saying, "Harmony among brothers, friendship among neighbors, and a husband and wife who live in agreement." And another, hinting at its strength in a riddle, says, "If two lie down together, they have warmth; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken." Here he shows both its pleasure and its strength, and makes clear that when they are at rest there will be great pleasure, and when they are at work great strength. And again, "A brother helped by a brother is like a fortified city." Christ too says, "Where two or [581] three are gathered in my name, there I am in their midst." Nature itself demands this. That is why God, when he first formed man, said, "It is not good for the man to be alone"; and when he made this creature, I mean the woman, he bound her to the man by the necessity of need, drawing us together to one another in countless ways. "And life for evermore." He rightly added this. For where there is love there is great security and great help from God. Love is the mother of good things, their root and spring; it does away with wars and wipes out quarrels. To make this plain he went on, "And life for evermore." For just as faction and quarrelling bring about deaths, and untimely deaths, so love and concord bring about peace and harmony; and where there is peace and harmony, life is lived without fear and in complete security. And why speak of present things? Love grants us heaven itself, and the ineffable [?]… [Textual notes:] Savile: "from the judgment." [Variant:] "and friendship of the neighbor." [?] "and another": this passage [?]. In Morel the words "He rightly added this" were missing.

…a perfect blessing, when your life speaks in harmony with your words, and you glorify by your deeds the God who made you, as the Gospel says: "Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven." "May the Lord bless you from Zion, he who made heaven and earth." That is, if you do these things you will obtain the blessing that comes from God: if you keep vigil through the night, if you pray in holiness, if you are worthy to stand in the house of the Lord, if you make yourself a fitting temple. Having exhorted them as he should, he then closes his discourse with a prayer. For this is the mark of an excellent teacher: to correct the hearer by counsel and to strengthen him by prayers. What does he want to show by saying "Zion"? The name was dear to them, and there the whole matter of their sanctification was carried out. So he prays that they may recover their former way of life, return to that sanctification, and enjoy this blessing. Then, leading them up to loftier doctrines, and teaching that God is everywhere, that he ordained the temple to be built because of their weakness, and that he must be called upon from every place, he added: "He who made heaven and

But they called upon him there in those days, whereas we call upon him in every place, in every spot: at home, in the marketplace, in the desert, on a ship, at an inn, and wherever we may be. For prayer is in no way hindered by the place, [585] so long as the way of life accords with the prayer. Let us then achieve this and call upon God everywhere, and he will stand by us and help us, make every hardship easy and light for us, and count us worthy of the good things to come. May we all obtain them, by the grace and loving-kindness of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and might, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.

ON PSALM 134. "Praise the name of the Lord; praise the Lord, you servants [?]. You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God. Praise the Lord, for the Lord is good." 1. Again he himself calls them to this sacrifice offered through praises. For this is a sacrifice and an offering to God. That is why he says elsewhere, "I will praise the name of my God with a song; I will magnify him with praise; and it will please God more than a young calf that puts forth horns and hoofs." He constantly mentions the house and the courts, fastening them to the place and not letting them break away. For that is why he ordained at the beginning that it should be built: so that gathering everyone into one place might do away with all their impiety and idolatry, and not allow them, in their self-will and license, to wander about everywhere and take groves, springs, hills and mountains as occasions for impiety, sacrificing there and pouring libations on the high places. For this reason he judges anyone who sacrifices anywhere outside the temple guilty of murder, saying, "Whoever does not bring it to the tabernacle and sacrifice it, blood shall be imputed to him." For this reason, from every side… [Textual notes:] Savile: "you glorify." Savile [?]: "will bless." "Good things" is missing in Savile. Patrologia Graeca LV.

…has he displayed his loving-kindness? That is why he said at the beginning, "Praise him, for the Lord is good." "For I know that the Lord is great." See, he gives another reason for singing hymns. But tell me: do you know, and the others do not? They do know, but not as I do. For it belongs above all to the saints and to those who have ascended high to know his greatness more precisely: not all of it as it really is (that is impossible), but more clearly than others. "And our Lord is above all gods." Look, someone says: he who said, "The Lord is great" and "I know," now goes on to diminish his statement, comparing him with the others [585] and granting him superiority only by comparison. Not at all, he says. He was speaking to the weakness of his hearers at that time, leading them up to this little by little. To call God greater and say he is great above those others is not a very telling proof of his greatness; but, as I said before, he fits his words to the meanness of his hearers, raising them up little by little. For it was welcome enough for them, for the time being, to hear this and be persuaded. 2. That he surpasses all things beyond comparison he shows in what follows, setting down the greatest proof of his power and making clear that the earlier words were spoken because of the hearers' weakness.
