That is why, when he simply makes a statement, he says small things, but when he builds his case, demonstrates, and offers proof of God's greatness, he sets down great things. What, then, does he set down after this that is worthy of him and belongs to God alone? See, he goes on: "Whatever the Lord willed, he has done, in heaven and on earth, in the seas and in all the deeps." Do you see an all-sufficient power? Do you see a fountain of life? Do you see invincible strength? Do you see incomparable supremacy? Do you see an authority hindered nowhere? Do you see that all things are easy and simple for him? For "whatever he willed," he says, "he has done." Tell me where. "In heaven and on earth." That is, not only here but also in heaven; not only in heaven but also on earth; not only on earth but also "in the seas and in all the deeps." By "the deep" he means what lies beneath the earth, just as by saying "in heaven" he means what lies above the heavens. Though these realms are so many and so vast, his will is nowhere obstructed but reaches everything. And what is truly wonderful, the maker did not make them by toil or labor, nor even by a command, but by his will; he simply willed it, and the work followed. Do you see how he has shown the ease of it, the abundance of the things created, and the unhindered authority? Then, passing over heaven and sea themselves, he sets down the things in them; and not even all the things in them. Passing by the things in heaven, wonderful as they are, he speaks of the things around heaven. Why? Because the former, though great, were hidden from most people, while these, though lesser, are visible and have everyone as their spectators. For his discourse was addressed to people who were not so much trained by faith to have a notion of invisible things as led by the hand through visible ones. [Textual note:] Perhaps [?]: "unphilosophical."
[Textual notes:] [?] One reads: "all-powerful." [?] "and the work immediately followed." Elsewhere: "and having a notion of invisible things."

…and the water in the fire: neither did this dry up that, nor did that quench this. And yet [587] lightning is sharper, brighter and more piercing than the sun's fire. Our eyes bear witness: they gaze constantly at the sun's rays, but cannot bear the rush of lightning even for a moment. The sun runs across the sky over a whole day, but lightning crosses the whole world in a single instant, as Christ also testifies, saying, "As the lightning comes from the east and shines as far as the west." "He brings the winds out of his treasuries." Here again is another kind of thing in nature, of no small use to us, but so great that it contributes much to our life: it restores weary bodies, cools them, and makes the air lighter. For this is the work of the winds: to fan the air so that it does not go stale by standing still, to ripen the fruits, and to nourish our bodies. What could one say of their uses in sailing, of the seasons in which they arrive in due order and give way to one another, dancing over the sea and carrying sailors across? One sees a ship off and another takes it over; they travel opposite ways and serve, and even their conflict proves useful to life. One could name countless other works of the winds. Yet the Prophet passed over all these and left the hearer to gather them up, and himself showed only the ease of creation. For saying "out of his treasuries" does not mean that there are certain treasuries of winds, but shows the ease of the one who presides, the readiness of creation, its being prepared. Just as someone who keeps things in a treasury brings them all out freely, whenever he wishes, so the maker of the universe made all things easily and handed them over to nature. Do you see how much variety there is in the air, just as there are many changes in water and in fire? Of water, some is from springs, some from the sea, some in the air, some in the clouds, some in heaven, some above the heavens, some beneath the earth. Of fire, some is in the sun, some in the moon, some in the stars, some in lightning, some in the air, some from wood [?], the fire around us, and that of lamps, and some from the earth; for in many places fire of this kind rises up from the earth, as springs of water do. Some is in stones rubbed together, some in the foliage of trees when these too rub together, some in thunderbolts. So too in the air: some is denser, the air around us; some is finer; and the higher air again is more fiery. And the winds differ in many ways: one is finer, another denser; one colder, another drier; one moister, another warmer. Air and cloud move, some slowly, [588] some more swiftly, as if on horseback. So too with clouds and winds: some clouds are like water jars, at times full of water, at times carried along empty; others are like fans. When you see these things, their variety and their diversity, marvel at the Creator. "He struck the firstborn of Egypt." Having spoken of things in general, and having shown God's provi[dence]… [Textual note:] [?] "constantly illuminated."

…[through] famine [?] and through plenty, and after that through blow upon blow of plagues. Since they condemned God for weakness, and themselves killed the firstborn and reddened the river with blood, he showed them his strength even at that very time, though by fainter signs. For the Egyptian midwives despised those cruel orders, outwitted the king's harsh decree, and enjoyed great prosperity. Both of these came from God's providence: making women braver than those who wore crowns, and rewarding them by spreading their families out into a great number. For "He did good to the midwives" means this: their kindred were multiplied. By the very means with which they did good to the Jews, they received their rewards from God. Since they did not kill the Jews' children, God granted them, too, many children. But since the Egyptians persisted in their insensibility, he brought a sharper blow upon them. The whole world learned of it, and the Egyptians learned of it too: the world by hearsay, they in their own sufferings, seeing God's power with their eyes and knowing it by experience. That is why he foretold it to them, so that the blow might not be thought a mere accident or a death that came by chance. What is said elsewhere of the Savior can be said here too. What is that? "Rule in the midst of your enemies." For he did not lead them out into the desert, or anywhere else, but brought the blow upon them in the city itself. And see his loving-kindness even in the blow: he began first with the cattle, and only then went on to the people. Who, then, would not marvel at his power, how he brought everything down in a single instant, and at his sparing, his unspeakable wisdom? He did not bring this plague first, since he wanted to correct them by other means; and when he did bring it, he did not bring it without warning. [590] Why? So that he might bring them to their senses by words, and they might not come to experience the deeds. Nor again, when they were not corrected, did he let the blow be open to doubt. So that no one might think it came by chance, or was a disease or plague that had broken out, see how many things happen. First, they all died in one night. Second, it was all the firstborn. For if it had been a plague, it would not have touched only the firstborn and spared the second-born; it would have fallen on everyone without distinction. Third, if it had been a plague, it would not have kept entirely away from the Jews and touched only the Egyptians. It would far rather have destroyed those bodies worn down by toil and misery and so many evils, wasted away by poverty and famine [?] to such a degree, and not the royal bodies or those of men in high office, who enjoyed great ease and received great care. If it had been a plague, it would not have come all at once, but would first have shown all the signs of its approach. But as it was, these things together… [Textual notes:] Next, Savile: "and they themselves killed the…" [?] Another: "he showed them." Ibid., Morel: "and the… at that [?]." "[they made] houses for themselves, that is": in the margin he gives our reading [?]. Savile [?]: "the children, and to them many children." Savile: "from the cattle." Next, another: "the blow went on."

…benefiting everyone by both. And why does he not do good to these as well? Because most people usually come to know God when they are struck, rather than when they are treated kindly. For to see that he himself did not wish to punish, look at how he kept holding back the blows, and through both showed both his power and his love for humankind. Indeed, after one plague, and a second, and a third, it would have been enough to destroy them utterly as people sick beyond cure. But he did not wish to. Although he foresaw the future, and knew that not even at the fifth, nor the sixth, nor the tenth would they become better, he did not stop doing his own part. This is why we should especially marvel at his power, his care, his wisdom and his goodness: his power, because he struck; his care, because he held back; his wisdom, because, knowing the future, he still did his part. And this is itself especially a mark of his love for humankind: to begin from the lesser things, from the more irrational creatures. Then, as he went on, he struck even the king, and this above all caused what happened to be proclaimed abroad. For what happens to private persons may well go unnoticed, but when the one who receives the blow is prominent, nothing prevents the events from being noised abroad everywhere. Having stated, then, the reason why he struck, he also speaks of the plagues. Yet he does not list them repeatedly, nor one by one, but hints at them all in a single phrase and passes on, saying: "He sent signs and wonders into your midst, O Egypt." Then again he leads the people out of Egypt into the wilderness, showing everywhere that God is not a local god, nor one who rules over a single country, but over the whole world. That is why he added: "Who struck many nations, and killed mighty kings." Throughout the whole journey he gave pledges of his power in various ways, and led them as their general while teaching them through events. For through the wars he also taught the earlier lessons: that it was not the nature of the air, not the power of the elements, nor anything else of that kind, but the hand that commanded them that waged the war. And each was shown by the other: the events in the wilderness by those in Egypt, and those in Egypt by those in the wilderness. For when they themselves, without weapons, battle line or fighting, struck down their enemies, he made it clear to them that in Egypt too he had not set these things in motion against the Egyptians because he needed the elements. Rather, he wished to display his own power in various and diverse ways, and so he used the things that exist for this purpose. "Sihon king of the Amorites, and Og king of Bashan." He does not go through the cities, nor describe the battle in detail, but again magnanimously passes over countless showers of wonders. For though he could have lingered and amplified that tragic tale, he does not do so. Though he stands amid a wealth and abundance of God's works, he goes through them all in passing. And yet the one side were armed, lived in walled cities, and were practiced in tactics, while the others were fugitives, inexperienced in war, just freed from long slavery and prolonged tyranny, worn out by hunger and punishment, exposed to everyone to suffer harm… [Note: Savile reads "does not cease."]

…especially in the openings of his Epistles, as when he says to the churches of Galatia: "Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, who gave himself for our sins according to the will of our God and Father, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen." And in the Epistle to the Romans: "Theirs is the adoption, and the glory, and the worship, and the promise; theirs are the fathers, and from them, according to the flesh, is Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen." And again elsewhere: "To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only wise God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen." In the same way the prophet here, reflecting on God's providence over all things, the blow struck in Egypt, the benefits given in the wilderness, so various and diverse, those done for the Jews and those done against their enemies on their behalf, was set on fire by God's unspeakable love for humankind and offered up a doxology, saying: "O Lord, your name endures forever, and your remembrance from generation to generation." That is, your glory is everlasting. For nothing mars it, nothing interrupts it; it exists always and remains unchanging, unalterable, blooming, at its peak. And what does "your remembrance from generation to generation" mean? The memory of you, he says, is unending and has no limit. "For the Lord will judge his people, and will be appeased concerning his servants." Either both of these can be said of the people, meaning that he will exact a penalty, and after that will stop and restore them; or, dividing them, "will be appeased" refers to the people, and "will judge" to the enemies. That is, he will restore the one, for this is what "will be appeased" means, and he will judge the enemies, that is, he will exact a penalty from them on his people's behalf. 7. Then, since he could not cite any achievements of their way of life, he uses these claims instead: the name of "people" and the name of "servants." And by saying "will be appeased," he shows that the reconciliation comes from God's love for humankind, not from their merit. For where there is appeasing, there is need of pardon; and where there is need of pardon, it is not a matter of merit for good deeds but an occasion for love toward humankind. Since, then, he said above, "your remembrance from generation to generation," and at that time they alone of all the nations claimed God as their own, he hints at something like this here and says: "The salvation of your people displays the glory that you have among the many." For the glory that belongs to him by nature remains undiminished, indestructible and unalterable even if there is no one to worship him; but the praise he receives from the many will be shown by our salvation as well, when we recover the city, the sanctuary and the temple, and once more live under our former polity. "The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the works of human hands." Since at the beginning he said, "Our Lord is above all gods," and seemed to introduce a superiority by comparison because of the weakness of his hearers, see how he intensifies this in his argument. For beginning from God's power… [Notes: [?] … "to the wise God honor"; Morel, however, reads "invisible, the only wise God" [?]. Morel reads "in the wilderness" with the dative; [?] "in the wilderness" with the genitive. [?] Shortly after, Savile reads "the things from us"; Morel "the things among us."]

…the Lord. House of Levi, bless the Lord. You who fear the Lord, bless the Lord. Blessed be the Lord from Zion, he who dwells in Jerusalem." Why does he not call everyone together, instead of dividing them into ranks? So that you may learn that there is a great difference in blessing. For the priest blesses in one way, the Levite in another, the layman in another, the general populace in another. And saying "Bless" is the mark of one pointing to that blessed and pure nature. "Bless," he says, "because you have been freed from the opposite, because you have been counted worthy to worship such a God, because you have come to know the truth." For he himself is blessed, having blessing in his very nature, and needs no praise from others. Still, you too should bless him, not as adding anything to him, but as reaping something great yourselves. For even if he is blessed by nature, as indeed he is, he still wishes to be blessed by us too. And again he mentions Zion and Jerusalem. Their polity had been organized there, their worship had its foundation there, and from there they were instructed and set in order, so he wants to make these places venerable by the name of God. He wants them, being revered, to be more cherished by the people; being cherished, to draw them more strongly; drawing them, to bind them fast to worship; and binding them, to lead them to greater virtue, for the sake of which everything was done. But then it was Jerusalem and Zion; today it is heaven and the things in heaven. Let us too, I beg you, be bound fast to this, so that we may also obtain the good things to come, by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

ON PSALM 135. Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever. 1. Having spoken above about the kindness God has shown to humankind, he now also discusses the extent of his mercy. He does not measure it, for that is impossible, but wishes to present its greatness by its infinity. And he summons everyone to give glory, calling out and saying, "Give thanks to the Lord," that is, thank him, praise him. "For his mercy endures forever." What does "forever" mean? It means, he says, that God does not do good at one time and withdraw at another, nor show mercy at one time and stop at another. That is what happens with human beings, who are hindered by passion, cut short by poverty, obstructed by the demands of others, and prevented by the pressure of circumstances. God is not like that. He shows mercy continually and never stops doing so, even if he does it in various and diverse ways. So he is always merciful and never ceases doing good to humankind. Then, having said that he shows mercy always, he also gives the proofs of his mercy, and of its enduring always, drawing his demonstration from visible things. And since he was leading them by the hand toward piety, see how he again takes aim at the gods of the Greeks, once more making use of the same condescension. For what does he say? "Give thanks…" [Notes: Savile reads "as reaping something great themselves." Savile reads "were being done." [?] "having come about." Savile reads "it" (feminine).]

…he allowed them to live there even after the sin, and did not forbid them its use after that sin. And he did not make one heaven only, but another as well, showing from the very beginning that he will not leave us on earth but will transfer us there. For if he were not going to move us there, why was heaven brought into being at all? This element is of no use to him, since he needs nothing; but because he wished to transfer those from the earth to that place, he prepared the dwellings. 2. That is why the prophet, knowing this, adds to each verse, "For his mercy endures forever," amazed at his love for humankind. "To him who made the earth firm upon the waters." See his love for humankind here too. Since we became mortal and found ourselves in many needs, not even then did he abandon us. Here too he gave us a suitable lodging for the time in between, and filled the earth with so many proofs of his love for humankind that they cannot even be set forth in words. So the prophet, falling into the abyss of these benefits and seeing their vast open sea, sprang back, crying aloud and saying: "How great are your works, O Lord! In wisdom you have made them all." And if anyone looks at the sun and the moon and the ordering of the seasons, he will again see the whole of his love for humankind. For these elements contribute no small amount to the good order of life and to life itself: they nourish, they ripen the fruits without which life would be impossible, they show us the seasons, mark the hours, separate the courses of day and night, guide travelers on land and sea, and provide countless other services. Do you see how his mercy endures forever, and how the prophet adds this at each of the verses? For "to rule the day," another translator said, "to prevail over the day." Another said, "to rule in the night." "To him who struck Egypt together with their firstborn, and brought Israel out from their midst, with a strong hand and an uplifted arm." He keeps returning to the wonder in Egypt because of their great ingratitude, and because they always forget these things even though they hear them. This mercy, too, is no small sign: it freed them from captivity and slavery, and for those who came after it became a basis for the knowledge of God. And he hints at something else here. What is it? That even after that blow, freeing them from slavery was the work of his power, since he shook the Egyptians with fear and drowned them in the sea. He says this so that none of the more foolish would think that when God ordered them to take the gold and the silver vessels, he gave that order out of weakness. He did this too because he wished to be fearsome to his enemies on every side, and to show that he can do everything both by power and with authority, and can also deceive and outwit them. For what he did openly he did not do because he was unable to deceive; and what he did by deception he did not do because he was unable to take it openly. In each case he was showing his own strength. For that this too instilled great fear… [Notes: Savile reads "for not to him." [?] "Of these" is in Savile. Three manuscripts read "likening the night, travelers" [?]. Below, Morel reads "at each of the elements"; Savile, better, "at each of the verses."]

…he added, "To him who led Israel through its midst," since this too was a work of God's power. For it was not enough that the sea drew back and made the passage easy for them. In fact, that very thing would most of all have astounded and frightened them and kept them from daring to cross, since its strangeness would have produced great fear. It was the work of God's power, even after the sea had withdrawn, to put courage into them and persuade them to cross that new and strange road. For with the waters heaped up on each side, they needed a lofty and noble soul so as not to fear the crossing, nor to suspect that the seas heaped up on either side would come down on them and drown the whole host. "And shook off Pharaoh and his army into the Red Sea." He used this word because he wished to show how easily they were drowned. But consider how, along with his power and his indignation, he also showed his patience. He did not destroy them earlier, although they were so shamelessly and contentiously disposed, but waited until they willingly rushed headlong to their own destruction. Nor was the army punished without reason: since they shared in the sins and took part in the pursuit, they also share in the punishment and the retribution. "To him who led his people through the wilderness, for his mercy endures forever." This is no less than leading them through the sea. For even if there was dry ground beneath them, able to bear the host, there were still many other things to distress them. Hunger, drought and thirst, sunshine beating down hotter than it should, a multitude of wild beasts, and the lack of all necessities were enough to consume everyone and hand them over to a most grievous death. You know how many things a human being needs. Yet stripped of all of them, without shelter, food, sufficient clothing, shoes or anything of the kind, they walked through all that wilderness as if they were dancing in the middle of cities. But consider how many wonders done in the wilderness he passed over, and how many years of leadership; and he mentions only two wonders, those concerning those kings. He omits that new table, the marvelous shelter, the torch such as had never appeared before, the garments that lasted, the sandals that never wore out, the springs from the rocks, and the other new and marvelous things by which he made the journey easy for them. He mentions only two: how he killed the kings of the barbarians, and how he set up the trophy and granted them the victory. The rest he leaves to the listener to gather up carefully. That is why he says: "To him who struck great kings, and killed mighty kings: Sihon king of the Amorites, and Og king of Bashan." And at each of these he adds, "For his mercy endures forever," showing that even if enemies succeeded enemies, none overcame them. Why? Because continually of his love for humankind… [Notes: Others read "that untrodden and strange." Others read "upon them and bury and drown." [?] "distressing, and enough to consume… For enough…" [?]. Savile reads "never yet seen," not correctly. Three manuscripts read "sending the rest on to the." [?]]

By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered Zion. 1. Great was these men's longing for the city, great their desire to return. As long as they had the good things in their hands, they went on being fastidious and insolent; but once they were cast out of them, then at last they came to desire them. In fact, this is why he cast them out: to lead them to a greater longing. And God often does this. When we revel in his good things without appreciating them, he places us where we are deprived of them, so that, brought to our senses by the loss, we may seek to enjoy them again. And why were they sitting by the rivers? Because, as captives taken in an enemy land, they were camping outside walls and cities. "On the willows in its midst we hung up our instruments." Another translator says, "our citharas"; another, "lyres." And why did they take their instruments with them when they went into captivity, if they were not going to use them? This too was arranged by God, so that even in a foreign land they would have reminders of their former way of life, and would be stung all the more when they saw the symbols of that worship. "For there those who took us captive asked us for the words of songs, and those who led us away said: Sing us one of the songs of Zion." From this too they gained no small benefit, in that the barbarians pressed them and wanted to hear their songs. See here too how much correction they received from the captivity. For these people, who had danced away from their own worship, kicked against it and trampled on the laws in every way, showed such exactness in a foreign land that, even when the barbarians pressed them, threatened them, surrounded them on all sides and wanted to hear, not even then would they gratify their desire. Instead they preferred the law and kept it exactly. For "those who led us away," another translator said, "those who [?] us," practically indicating this: those who previously trampled on us and rose up against us have over time become so gentle, reasonable and tame as even to want to hear our songs. Yet even so these men did not give in. Do you see how affliction makes people strong? How it makes them contrite? How it crushes the mind? For they wept and kept the law. And those who had laughed at the prophets when they wept, who had mocked and jeered at them, now, with no one reminding them, turned to tears and lamented. From this even their enemies gained a great deal. For they saw them weighed down not by captivity, nor lamenting their slavery or their stay in a foreign land, but lamenting that they had lost their own worship. That is why he adds: "when we remembered Zion." For they do not simply lament; they make it their business. That is also why at the beginning he said, "We sat and wept," clearly meaning that we sat together for this very purpose, [?]

[?] …not only in the release, but also in the plotting of those who made war on them, the prophet foretells the evils that will befall Babylon, and he calls her wretched because of the evils that will overtake her. In this way he instructs the Jews and shows that God's strength reaches everywhere on earth. "Blessed is he who will repay you the recompense with which you repaid us." Another translator has: "what you did to us first." "Blessed is he who will seize your infants and dash them against the rock." These words are full of great wrath and of heavy punishment and vengeance. Even so, they are the words of the captives' suffering, as they demand great vengeance and some strange and unheard-of punishment. For the prophets say many things not on their own account but as an account of other people's sufferings, which they bring forward for all to see. If you look for his own mind, you will hear him saying, "If I have repaid those who repaid me with evil," and so going beyond the measure that the laws allowed him. But when he describes other people's sufferings, he portrays their wrath and their pain. That is what he has done here: he brings forward the desire of the Jews, who stretched their anger even to those of tender age. But the teachings of the New Testament are not like this. We are commanded to give our enemies drink and to feed them, and to pray for those who mistreat us. We do this because of the law that has been laid down. What law is this? "Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees," he says, "you will not enter the kingdom of heaven." So let us show great zeal and keep the whole of it in abundance, living from now on as citizens of heaven while on earth, and dancing with the angels. In this way we shall also attain the good things to come. May we all attain them, by the grace and lovingkindness of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and power for ever and ever. Amen.

ON PSALM 137. "I will confess to you, Lord, with my whole heart." 1. I have often spoken to you about this verse, so I will pass over it and come to what follows. What does this mean: "And before the angels I will sing psalms to you"? Another translator put it, "Boldly, O God, I will sing of you." Another: "Before the gods I will sing melodies to you." If he means the angels in heaven, the sense is something like this: "I will strive to sing with the angels. I will be eager to compete with them and to join the dance of the powers above. For even if I differ from them in nature, I will still vie in eagerness to stand with them." But if we take the saying according to the version of the other translators, I think he is speaking of the priests. For Scripture is accustomed to call the priest both an angel and a god. At one point it says, "You shall not revile the gods, and you shall not speak evil of the ruler of your people"; at another, "The lips of the priest shall guard judgment, and they shall seek righteousness from his mouth, for he is the angel of the Lord Almighty." If we are to take it this way, then we must understand it like this: "With the priests, in their presence, with the fitting [?]…" [?] we discussed. [?] "Before the gods I will sing melodies to you." [?] "Before the gods I will sing to you." [?] "I will speak boldly to you." [?] "Before the priests." [?] "Boldly, O God, I will sing of you." [?] I will strive; and if he means angels, as those in heaven, he says this, that with [?] them, and I will be eager. We follow Savile.

[?] …"you strengthened my soul with power." For in the earlier phrase too, in place of "Hear me," another translator said, "You heard me." So what does the saying mean? Lofty things are called "meteora," from being raised up, and the waves and swells of the sea are called its "meteorismoi," from being raised. So "You will greatly regard me" means "You will lift me up, you will exalt me." He used this word elsewhere too, saying, "According to your height you have greatly regarded the sons of men," that is, "you lifted them up, you exalted them." In the same way he said "You will greatly regard me" to show this: "You will fill me with great gladness and make my soul lofty. And greatest of all, you will not let this elation and gladness become rotten. You will make it strong and mighty, firm and immovable." That is the meaning of "You will greatly regard me in my soul with your power." 2. What he is saying is this: "With power you will greatly regard me, with strength you will exalt me, and you will help me." That is why another translator, conveying the same sense, said, "You strengthened my soul with power." He was right to say "my soul." For it is above all God's own work to restore souls even in afflictions, as happened with the apostles: when they were flogged, they went away rejoicing. So greatly was their soul regarded. This above all is the work of God's power, and this above all shows his strength: that he does not let the soul be dragged down in the midst of dangers. "Let all the kings of the earth confess to you, Lord, for they have heard all the words of your mouth." See his gratitude. He is not content to give thanks by himself. He takes all who rule into partnership in his thanksgiving, even those who wear diadems. "For even if their authority and power are great," he says, "they all owe you thanks, including for what has been done for others." To show this he added, "They have heard all the words of your mouth." So if they give thanks, they will reap and gain great things from it. For your gifts are of such a kind that they are set out openly for all, so that whoever wishes may share in them and enjoy them. Nothing, then, not even kingship, can benefit them as much as hearing your words. This is their safety, this their strength, this their adornment, this their comeliness, this their kingship, this the splendor and power of their rule. "And let them sing in the ways of the Lord." Another: "Let them sing the ways of the Lord." If it is "in your ways," the saying means "in your laws, in your commandments." If it is "your ways," he means, "Let them tell of these achievements of yours, let them hymn them, let them proclaim them"; for that is what "let them sing" means. "For great is the glory of the Lord"; that is, evident to all, clear to all, plain to all, ready to bestow benefits on all, holding all in debt for his grace. "For the Lord is high, and he looks upon the lowly." "High in nature," he says, "high in essence." But here, for the time being, it is said in a more condescending way, with a view to the care of the [Jews?]… [?] This is the interpretation "You strengthened my soul with power." [?] Another: "You strengthened my soul with power" [?]. From "being raised aloft." Three manuscripts: "not always to be oppressed." Savile: "is not content." "Let them sing in the songs of the Lord." "If then in the songs of the Lord."

ON PSALM 138. For the end, for the giver of victory. "Lord, you have tested me and known me." 1. What are you saying? That God knows after testing, but does not know before testing? No, God forbid! How could that be, when he knows all things before they come to be? Rather, "You have tested me" means "You know me exactly." When the Apostle says that he searches the hearts, he speaks not to indicate ignorance but exact knowledge. In the same way, when this writer says "You have tested me," he points to the clearest knowledge, that is, "You know me exactly." "You knew my sitting down and my rising up." By sitting down and rising up he means the whole of life, for our life consists in these: our actions, our activities, our comings in and goings out. At the start he had said "You have tested me." Some foolish person might then think, because he said "You knew my sitting down and my rising up," that God knows from testing or from the experience of events. See how he corrects this by what he adds: "You understood my thoughts from afar." By this he shows that God does not know by testing and has no need to test, but knows all things by his power of foreknowledge. For one who knows the thoughts lying in the mind has no need of testing through deeds. Besides, he knows them not only when they stir in the mind but even before they stir; and not merely before they stir, but long beforehand. Wishing to show this, he added, "You understood my thoughts from afar." If God knows even our thoughts, then why does he bring testing through deeds? Not so that he himself may learn, but so that he may make those who endure it approved. He knew Job before the trial, and that is why he bore witness to him, saying, "A man righteous, true, God-fearing." Yet he brought the trial to make Job more steadfast, to expose the devil's wickedness, and to make others more zealous through his example. And why are you surprised that he did this with Job, when he does the same even with sinners? He knew clearly that the Ninevites were not worthy to be destroyed but would become better through repentance. Nevertheless he also brings the trial through events. Everywhere he provides many proofs of his care and his lovingkindness, not content with his own knowledge. That is why the Only-begotten also said, "If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me; but if I do them, even if you do not believe me, believe the works." Many people who are coarser in mind and insensible say many such things: that he chose so-and-so, and loved so-and-so, and hated so-and-so, and that this is why one became wicked and another worthless. So he persuades them from events, correcting the opinion of each of them and bringing forward… Savile: "our." Savile: "from afar. And if he knows, he says." Two manuscripts: "to stop up the wickedness, and [?]." Savile: "this same thing." Shortly after, Savile: "not being worthy to perish… and nevertheless he brings." Perhaps it is better to delete the particle "not." Another: "with his own knowledge."

[?] …was created, he is before all things." This concerns his work of creation. Then, to show his providence, he adds, "And all things hold together in him." Again John, pointing to both, said, "All things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being." He said this to point to the creation. Then the providence: "In him was life, and the life was the light of men." The prophet hints at this here too when he says, "You formed me." This concerns creation. He also spoke of providence: "And you laid your hand upon me." What does "you laid" mean? You hold me together, you sustain me, you bear me up. Paul shows this too when he says, "For in him we live and move and have our being." We need his power not only to come into being, but also to exist and to endure. "Your knowledge has become too wonderful for me; it is too strong; I cannot attain to it." Another: "It surpasses me." In place of "it is too strong," another: "It is lifted high above." What he means is this: "I enjoy your providence, and I know that you foreknow all things and that you made me out of nothing. Yet I cannot have an exact, clear and complete knowledge of you. It has become too wonderful; that is, it has surpassed me, it is lifted above me, it is too strong to be grasped by my reasonings. So wonderful is it, so great." What then? Even if it is wonderful and great, can it still be grasped? Not at all. That is why he added, "I cannot attain to it," so that you would not say this. When he says "knowledge," he does not mean "I do not know God," but "I do not have a complete and clear knowledge of him." As Paul says: we know that he is, but what he is in essence we do not know. "For whoever approaches God must believe that he is." And he did not say what he is in essence, for that is known to no one. We know that he loves mankind, that he is kind, that he is good; but how much, we do not know. But the psalmist passes over all these things and puts forward something else that seems easier, and says he does not know even that. "I am not speaking of what he is in essence," he says, "nor of how good he is, for it is agreed that these things are incomprehensible. But I cannot even say how he is everywhere. This too is beyond our comprehension." So, having said "Your knowledge has become too wonderful for me," he added: "Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend to heaven, you are there; if I go down to Hades, you are present. If I take up my wings at dawn and dwell at the farthest ends of the sea" (another: "remain"), "even there" (another: "still there") "your hand will guide me, and your right hand will hold me." By Spirit and face he means God himself. That is, "Where shall I go from you? You fill all things, you are present to all, not part by part, but whole, to all at once." By naming the things above and the things below, breadth, length, depth and height, he shows that God is present everywhere. And he did not say, "Wherever I go, [he] follows…" [?] "through" … has it thus: "that he is, but not what he is in essence; for this is not known," with the same meaning. [?] After "for even there" one manuscript adds "another: still there." [?] Another: "being in temptations."

…did you see a furnace blazing and dew whistling through it, and neither the one quenched nor the other dried up, and hail and flame together? Tell me, how did this happen? I want to learn how it came about. Or rather, I do not even want to learn the manner, for that is not possible. But I believe what happened, and I worship the one who did it. "For most of his works are hidden." Did you not see that in broad daylight the Egyptians groped as if in darkness, while the Israelites could see when darkness held everything? And again, at the beginning, when there was darkness, light shone out in the midst of it. For everywhere the Lord who made it is master of the nature of things. He does not bring forth what does not exist; rather, he makes things appear otherwise while they remain in their nature. "For darkness will not be darkened by you." Another: "with you." "And night will be lit up like day." Another: "But night will shine like day." "As its darkness, so also its light." Another: "Its darkness and its light are alike." He was right to say "by you," that is, "with you." He shows that if you wish, darkness will not be darkness but will display the properties of light. That is why he added, "And night will be lit up like day," making the first phrase clearer. He shows that the night will display the properties of day as if they were its own. For when God wills, the operation of the elements changes to its opposite, and as exactly to its opposite as to what was allotted to it as its own at the beginning. "If you wish, the night will be such, and will have light allotted to it just as it had darkness." To show this he added, "As its darkness, so also its light." These things are said literally of the elements, but metaphorically of events. They show that God can give those who fall into afflictions as much relief in them as he gives those who live at ease, taking care of the affliction. This is what is wonderful and beyond expectation, and it is what happened with Joseph. He did not enjoy as much ease and honor while living in his father's house as he did after being sold and brought up in a barbarian household. Through the very men who plotted against him, the diadem was woven for him and the purple robe prepared, and the very occasion of his disgrace became the starting point of honor and kingship for him. Do you see how we have interpreted "Night will be lit up like day"? As for "As its darkness, so also its light," we must again say the same: just as the one, so the other will be its own, not in mere appearance, but because you, the Lord of natures, change things. "For you possessed my kidneys, Lord; you took hold of me from my mother's womb." And how does this follow from what was said? It follows very closely indeed. Since he had spoken of God's great power, he now shows that God uses this power for what benefits human beings and for doing them good. For some foolish person might say, "And what are these things to me, if he is great and powerful and foreknowing?" The reading "Its darkness and its light are alike" [?] not [?]. Savile: "but will display light." Savile: "to the opposites, as to its own, as at… allotted"; and shortly after, "such will be the night." Savile: "he interpreted." Another: "is interpreted."

…he spoke thus: "My bones were not hidden from you, with which I was made in secret." Another: "My strength did not escape you, which I was made in the hidden place; I was embroidered as in the lowest parts of the earth." Another: "My power did not escape you, nor my bones from you, for I was made in secret, I was fashioned in the lowest parts of the earth." They all say the same thing: "You know me exactly, even while I am being formed part by part. You know each of my limbs, and my growth." As Christ also says, "Even the hairs of your head are all numbered." The saying points at once to providence and to knowledge. "Your eyes saw my unfinished state." Either he is saying the same thing again, "You knew me even when I was unformed" (for another translator put it this way: "Your eyes saw me unformed"), or he is speaking of his actions: "Your eyes saw even what has not yet been done." "And in your book all will be written. Days will be formed, and no one among them." The saying is obscure, but we must hunt out its meaning from what follows and from the other translator. What he is saying agrees with the earlier phrase. And what was the earlier phrase? "Your eyes saw me unformed"; that is, not yet given a shape, still being formed, still being woven. "Even so they saw me as clearly as one already shaped, already molded, already complete and needing no further day to be finished." To learn that this is the meaning, listen to the other translator's version: "Your eyes foresaw me unformed, together with all those written in your book, formed in days, with none lacking." "You saw me with them," he says, "you saw me just like them, those formed in their days, days in which not one day was lacking." He says this not as though there were a book up above, or as though certain things were written in it. He uses the book to signify exact knowledge, just as when it says, "The Lord heard and wrote it in a book," and again, "Books were opened." "But to me your friends, O God, are greatly honored." Another: "Your companions became precious." This too is no small virtue, to hold God's friends in great honor. "You took thought for me," he says. "You brought me forth when I did not exist, you sustain me, and I give you this return: I honor your friends." "Their principalities became very strong." That is, they themselves became strong. Another says, "How numerous are their heads!" This is even clearer, for he adds, "I will count them, and they will outnumber the sand." "I honor them, and you make them many, more than the sand; and not only many, but strong." For that is what "they became strong" means. He speaks of a twofold prosperity: in numbers, and in growth of strength. "I awoke, and I am still with you." Another: "I will awake, and I will be with you for ever." 5. This is no small sign of virtue: to keep one's virtue while living in prosperity. Many, at any rate, have enjoyed good fortune and forgotten. "But not I," he says. [?] …to form me, or to do anything in life, etc. In another [?]: "days will be formed." One manuscript: "with none lacking to them."

…learning. For the words "Test me" [?] mean this here. And: "See if there is a way of lawlessness in me, and lead me." What is the everlasting way, if not the spiritual one, which leads up to heaven and has no end? All other things have proved perishable and are dissolved along with the present life. That is why he passes all of them by and seeks that way: the immortal, the boundless way, which never comes to an end. How might someone be led to it? By enjoying the help that comes from God while contributing his own part: pursuing virtue, holding fast to the philosophic life, rising above the things of this world. What comes from that way is not short-lived or temporary. That is the nature of virtue. Its fruits bloom forever and never wither, and its goods are immortal, incorruptible and endless. May we all attain them, by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and might, now and always, and to the ages of ages.

ON PSALM 139. "Rescue me, Lord, from an evil man; deliver me from an unjust man." 1. Where now are those who say, "Why are there wild beasts? Why scorpions? Why vipers?" Look, a creature has been found that shows more wickedness than these, not by nature but by choice: man. That is why the prophet passes over all those others and asks to be delivered from this one. What then, tell me? Since man is like this, should human beings not have been made at all? It is the height of folly to say so. Nothing harms a human being except sin alone. Once sin is removed, everything is easy, smooth and calm; while it is present, everything is reefs and storms and shipwrecks. Let none of you condemn us for saying that a man living in wickedness is worse than a beast. A beast, even if it is not gentle by nature, can easily be outwitted, and it shows itself for what it is. But the man who practises wickedness and wears many masks is harder to guard against than any beast. He often puts on a sheep's skin and hides the wolf inside, and so many people fall in with such men off their guard. Since beasts of this kind are hard to detect, the prophet turns to prayer and calls on God's help, so as to be rid of such a plot. For the devil, too, often slips into such people and strikes through them. Many, then, are the enemies plotting against us on every side: an evil man does it, a savage demon makes war, and unbearable temptation harasses us. That is why we are taught to say in prayer, "Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one." The battles are of many kinds and the battle lines are drawn many ways, and we must be prepared for everything. For just as… [Notes: Savile: "and…" [?]; both readings are good. Shortly after, "has become" follows "perishable". In Savile, "savage" [?]. Ibid., Savile: "and unbelievable [?] temptation harasses". [?] "to be prepared". "And sea" is missing in Savile [?] … order [?]. Savile: "the fall did harm."]

…but now no longer, since the heavens have at last been opened to us and human beings have become angels. A beast that charges with great force onto the point of a spear seems to be attacking the man who holds it, but it impales itself and takes the worse wound. Likewise, whoever kicks against the goads bloodies his own feet. 2. Virtue is like this: goads and a sharpened sword. The wicked are all worse than beasts and more irrational. So when they attack the good, they impale themselves all the more grievously. They often cause the good to lose money or suffer in body, but they themselves are harmed in the soul, and that is the real loss. If losing money harmed us in our virtue, Paul would not have told us to suffer wrong rather than do wrong. If suffering wrong were an evil, the lawgiver of good things would not have commanded evils. Still, even though this is so, we should not leap upon the wicked or come to close quarters with them. We should flee them and avoid their company, but when they attack, we should meet them with courage. This is why we are told to pray that we may not enter into temptation. So the psalmist too, having said, "Rescue me, Lord, from an evil man," adds, "Deliver me from an unjust man," once again using a general name for wickedness. He does not mean only a man who is unjust in money matters, but one who is unjust in everything. He asks to be delivered so that he will neither fall into that man's hands nor become like him. And he does not simply ask; he has contributed his own part as well. That is why, having fled from them and their company at the end of the previous psalm, he now asks for God's help. There he contributed his own part, saying, "Men of blood, turn away from me, for you are contentious in your reasonings"; here he calls on God to deliver him from their wickedness. To be rescued from such gatherings and to live as far as possible from the company of the wicked is no small thing. It makes for safety, freedom from fear, liberty and every pleasure; indeed, it is the greatest happiness. Then he describes their wickedness and goes on: "Who devised injustice in their heart; all day long they drew up wars." Do you see how hard these beasts are to guard against? They brew their evils in the mind and hide their plots in secret. "They devised in their heart," he says. That is, they had not yet brought it out but kept turning it over inside, in labour with their wickedness. What is worse, they were not swept along or overcome by it; they made a practice of it. That is the meaning of "They devised": with zeal, with all eagerness. "All day long they drew up wars." By this he means their whole life. And by "wars" he does not mean those fought in battle lines with weapons, but those fought through plots, which people wage in marketplaces and in homes, without putting on breastplates or holding up shields… [Notes: Savile: "to ward off". Another: "and more savage". Savile: "if then it harmed us". Three manuscripts: "he calls on the help there" [?]. "Brewing": Morel has "hunting", less correctly. Ibid., Savile: "and hiding". [garbled] [?] … "swept along, nor carried off, but making a practice…" Others as in the text. In Morel the words "nor overcome" [?]. Savile in the same place: "not seized, nor overcome, but making a practice of the thing."]

…not only in kinsmen or friends or a wife, but set the snare in the body itself? "I said to the Lord: You are my God. Give ear, Lord, to the voice of my supplication. Lord, Lord, the power of my salvation." Another translator has "the strength of my salvation." Having spoken of the war and the plots, and shown the dangers to be unbearable, he at last takes refuge in the alliance that cannot be overcome, calling down from heaven the helper who is able to put an end to all this. This is the mark of a noble soul and a philosophic mind: when such things press in on every side, not to take refuge in human alliances or mortal calculations, but to look to heaven and call on God, who is present everywhere, and not to give way to despondency, turmoil and agitation. And see how worthily he frames his words. He did not say, "I accomplished this and that, and performed such and such righteous deeds." What did he say? "You are my God." He puts forward as his strongest claim to help the very fact that he takes refuge with his Master, Creator and King. "Give ear, Lord, to the voice of my supplication. Lord, Lord, the power of my salvation." He said "power of salvation" to show that there is also a power of chastisement and punishment. "But to me," he says, "you have shown the power of salvation. You can harm and destroy, but you have always used your power for my salvation." And see the longing of the speaker. By repeating the word and adding "of my salvation," he shows great affection. "You overshadowed my head in the day of war." Do you see the grateful soul? He reminds himself of past events, how God set him in safety; that is what "You overshadowed" means. And see how he shows God's readiness to help. He did not say, "before this," but, "on that very day, when the dangers rose up, when the battle was joined, when my life was at stake, then you set me in safety." God needs no preparation or summoning, for he knows all things, present, future and past. He can do all things, and he always stands ready to help. Then, to show how complete the victory and the safety were, he did not say, "You saved me." What did he say? "You overshadowed me." That is: "You did not let me suffer even the slightest distress, not even as much as one suffers from the heat. You set me in such safety, and with safety in such pleasure and ease, that I did not even feel any troublesome heat but delighted in the shade," meaning release and freedom from dangers. That is why he added "You overshadowed." He shows this very point, and through the word "shade" he also shows how easily God helps, as if to say, "It is enough for you merely to be present, and everything is resolved." "Do not hand me over, Lord, from my desire to a sinner." Another translator: "Do not grant, Lord, the desires of the lawless." What he means is this: "Do not grant from the desire against me," that is, "Do not let him accomplish what he desires against me." And he did not say, "what he desires," but "from my desire"… [Notes: Savile: "calling God". Another: "delay".]

…having taken counsel by their own will, they were puffed up and perished." Show me, and tell me where this very thing happened. It happened with Joseph's brothers. They wanted to make him a slave and destroy him, and it was their own lives that came into danger. Indeed, for their part, they themselves fell into both slavery and death. And Absalom, who wanted to destroy his father by seizing power, was himself caught by that very attempt. "Coals of fire will fall upon them; you will cast them down into fire." What he means is this: wickedness by itself is enough to destroy those who surround themselves with it, and on top of that they will also suffer wrath sent by God. By "coals of fire" and "fire" he means the punishment that comes down from above. Often it has also happened with actual fire, as with Dathan, Korah and Abiram, and with those who stood around the furnace in Babylon. "In miseries, and they shall not withstand them." Another translator: "They will fall into pits, never to rise again." Another: "Swiftly, and may they not rise." According to the first translator, the meaning is something like: "Destroy them so that they never rise again." According to the other, it means "with great speed," for that is what "swiftly" means. "A talkative man will not prosper on the earth." Having spoken of God's wrath, he shows once more that wickedness by itself is enough to destroy those who have it. And this is no small kind of wickedness: being rash and not controlling one's tongue. By "talkative" he means the insolent man, the babbler, the slanderer, the man who barks without ceasing and is no better than a dog. Tell me, what is the fruit of this? "He will not prosper," he says, "on the earth." Another translator: "He will not be established"; that is, he will be overturned, brought down, destroyed. This is the slanderer's fruit: such a man is hostile to everyone, unpleasant to everyone, burdensome and offensive to everyone. The patient, gentle man who knows how to keep silent is secure and steady and pleasing to all. In the same way, but in reverse, the talkative man leads an unstable life. He draws countless enemies on himself from every side and, before anyone else, troubles his own soul. He does not let it rest in peace; even when no one is bothering him, he stirs up countless wars and tumults inside it. "Evils will hunt down the unjust man to destruction." Another wise man says the same: "Transgressions hunt a man down." See again how wickedness is enough to destroy the one who has it. But why did he use the word "hunt"? So that you may see that there is no escape, and so that you will not be confident even if you are not caught at once while doing wrong. That is how hunting is: it does not always succeed, or not right away. Yet even when wild animals are not caught, the hunted are still not safe, even if they have not yet been driven into the nets. So let no soul take confidence when it does wrong and has not yet been caught, for sooner or later it will be caught. If you want to be safe, stop doing these things, and you will enjoy great freedom from fear. Why did he say "to destruction"? Because many have been hunted for salvation, such as those caught by the apostles and by holy men. But not the wicked… [Notes: Savile: "has come to be. Accordingly, therefore". Three manuscripts: "the meaning of some of the things said".]

This is no small ground for accusation: that people who sing psalms every day and speak the words with their mouths do not look for the force of the thoughts stored up in those words. Anyone who sees clear, pure water cannot resist going up to it, touching it and drinking. Anyone who often walks into a meadow cannot bear to leave without picking some of the flowers. Yet you, from your earliest youth to extreme old age, go on reciting this psalm knowing only the words. You sit beside a hidden treasure and carry around a sealed purse. Not one of you has been stirred even by curiosity to learn what on earth is being said; no one has asked, no one has searched. Nor can anyone claim that the psalm is so clear that it lulled everyone to sleep and left them nothing to look for in what lies plainly before them. It is obscure, and able to rouse anyone who is not sound asleep, or rather even one who is. For what does "Do not incline my heart to words of wickedness" mean? What does "The righteous man will chasten me in mercy and reprove me" mean? And tell me, is what follows not darker than any gloom? "For still my prayer also is in their good pleasures. Their judges were swallowed up beside the rock." Yet though there are so many obscure passages, most people run past them as though it were just some song. But so that we do not make our sermon tiresome by stretching out the accusation further, come, let us go on to examine what has been said. Pay close attention, though. I do not think the fathers appointed this psalm to be said every evening without good reason, or merely because of the one phrase that says, "The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice." Other psalms contain this word too, such as the one that says, "Evening and morning and noon I will tell and declare"; and again, "Yours is the day, and yours is the night"; and again, "Weeping will lodge for the evening, and rejoicing comes in the morning." One could find many psalms suited to the evening hour. So that is not why the fathers prescribed this psalm. They ordained that it be said as a saving remedy and a cleansing from sins. Whatever stains we pick up through the whole length of the day, in the marketplace, at home or wherever we spend our time, we may strip off when evening comes through this spiritual incantation. For it is a remedy that does away with all these things. The morning psalm is of the same kind, and nothing prevents us from mentioning it briefly as well. It kindles longing for God and rouses the soul. It sets the soul on fire and fills it with great goodness and love, and so lets it come before God. Let us see where it begins and what it teaches us: "O God, my God, I rise early to you; my soul has thirsted for you." Do you see how these words reveal a soul on fire? Where there is love of God, everything evil departs. Where there is remembrance of God, sins are forgotten and evils destroyed. "So I appeared before you in the sanctuary…" [Notes: Another: "would not endure… without gaining". Savile: "nor yet for this did they prescribe the psalm". So Savile. Others: "having set on fire and filled with much goodness and love, thus lets it approach; for…" [garbled] [?] "…for to say that 'O God … my soul'" [garbled] [?]. Manuscripts: "release of sins and". But "forgetting" is read in all [?].]

"When I cry to you." See another virtue of prayer. He asks to be heard not only because he prays earnestly, but also because he offers the kind of prayer that is worthy of those sleepless eyes. What kind is that? When a person does not pray against enemies, or for wealth and gain, or for power and glory, or for any of these perishable things, but for the incorruptible and immortal things above. "Seek the kingdom of God," he says, "and all these things will be added to you." "When I cry to you." Do you see how he wants us too to call on God with earnestness and eagerness? It is at that moment above all that the devil lies in wait. He knows that prayer is the greatest weapon. He knows that even if we are sinners and covered with shame, we still accomplish great things when we pray carefully and in keeping with God's laws. So at that moment he works hard to throw us into sloth and to stir up stray thoughts, so that we come away from prayer with nothing gained. Knowing this, we must build our earnestness up like a wall against him. We must never pray against enemies but imitate the apostles. They suffered countless hardships, were thrown into prisons, and faced the danger of death; yet they took refuge in prayer and said, "Look upon their threats." And what came next? Did they say, "Strike them down," or "Kill them," as many people often say when they curse? Not at all. What did they say? "And grant to your servants to speak your word with all boldness." How, and by what means? By killing the plotters? By wiping them out and handing them over to utter destruction? Not at all. How then? "By working signs and wonders through the name of your holy Child Jesus." Do you see a prayer full of philosophy, which after so many hardships asks for no punishment on its enemies? That is how the apostles prayed while still alive and breathing. Stephen, as he was about to be torn away from this present life, not only asked for nothing bad to befall his killers. He even worked through his prayer to snatch the men who were stoning and killing him away from the wrath that this sin deserved, and he said, "Do not hold this sin against them." What pardon, then, could those who pray against their enemies deserve? What defence could they offer? How could such a prayer be heard, when it is offered against God's laws? Let us say nothing of the kind. We must not only refrain from praying against our enemies; we must also get rid of our anger against them. That is why he says, "I want the men to pray in every place, lifting up holy hands without anger or argument." That is: even if you have an enemy, quench your anger, and approach the Master that way. Do not merely avoid saying anything against him with your mouth; rid your mind of the venom as well. If your prayer is like this, and you call on God with earnestness, you will be heard even before you finish praying. This is what he himself asks for when he says, "Attend to the voice of my supplication when I cry to you." [Notes: …praying. The same; one has "to throw", and a little later "stirs up thoughts". Savile: "prison". Savile: "but what [defence]". [?] As Savile attests, "appears". Shortly after, one has "the anger" [?]. "Even if you have enemies". Others: "the incense".]

…and fragrant, yet it shows its fragrance most of all when it meets the fire. So too prayer is good even in itself, but it becomes better and more fragrant when it is offered up from a warm and fervent [451] soul, when the soul becomes a censer and kindles a strong fire. For the incense was never put on unless the brazier had been lit first, or while the coals were not yet burning through. Do the same with your mind: first kindle it with eagerness, and then lay your prayer upon it. He prays, then, that his prayer may become like incense, and the lifting up of his hands like an evening sacrifice. Both are acceptable. And how could this come about? If both are pure, if both are blameless: the tongue and the hands. The hands must be cleansed of greed and robbery, the tongue freed from wicked words. For just as a censer must hold nothing unclean but only fire and incense, so the tongue must bring out no stained word but only holiness and praise, and so the hands too must become a censer. Let your mouth, then, be a censer, and take care that you do not fill it with dung. That is what people are like who utter shameful and unclean words. And why did he not say "morning" but "evening"? To me this too seems to have been said with no particular difference. For if he had said "morning", the curious would have asked why he did not say "evening". But if someone wants to hear an explanation without prying too far, it is this: the morning sacrifice waits for the evening one, while the evening sacrifice, once offered, completed the sacred service. After that the day's worship is in no way unfinished; it has been brought to completion and reached its end. But what does the stretching out of the hands in prayer mean? These hands serve many evils: blows, murders, robberies, acts of greed. For this very reason we are commanded to raise them, so that serving in prayer may become a bond that holds them back from vice and frees them from wickedness. Then, when you are about to rob or defraud or strike someone, you will remember that you are going to send these hands to God as your advocates and through them send up that spiritual sacrifice, and you will not shame them and strip them of confidence by making them serve wicked deeds. Cleanse them, then, with almsgiving, with kindness, with protection of the needy, and bring them to prayer in that state. For if you do not allow them to be raised in prayer unwashed, much less could you rightly defile them with sins. If you fear the lesser thing, shudder much more at the greater. To pray with unwashed hands is not so very wrong; but to bring them forward befouled with countless sins brings down great wrath. 4. [452] Let us reason the same way about the mouth and tongue, and, keeping it closed to wickedness, thus… [Notes:] One [manuscript reads] "not burnt". [?] "was placed… but of the coals [?]". "The tongue must have nothing stained": so certain manuscripts. Below, Savile: "[?] fill the censer with dung." "But if someone should wish to examine it more curiously": the same manuscripts. Savile: "and lead away from the". [?] "and lead away from the". [?] "to send up". Savile: "them unwashed". Savile: "befouled" [a variant form].

…[?] to speak. For if it had to be open all the time, there would be no doors; and if it had to be shut all the time, there would be no need of a guard. What would anyone guard in something that is shut? No, that is why there is a door and a guard, so that we may do each thing at the proper time. Another says, "Make a yoke and a scale for your tongue." He demands greater precision: we must not only bring out the words we ought to, but also weigh them, so to speak, with proper precision and examine them. For if we do this with gold, a perishable material, much more must we do it with words, so that nothing falls short or runs over. That is why someone says, "Do not hold back a word in a time of salvation." Do you see the time for going out? Another speaks of a time for silence and says: "If you have something to say, answer; if not, put your hand over your mouth." And again, "Whoever talks too much will be hated." And, "Better a man who hides his folly than a man who hides his wisdom." Have you heard something? Let it die with you. Take courage, it will not burst you. And again, "A fool goes into labor over a word, like a woman giving birth to a child." Then he also speaks of measure: "Speak, young man, if you must, barely twice, and only if you are asked; sum up much in few words." For our thoughts need close supervision, so that we use the power of the tongue with great caution. That is why he also said, "There is a reproof that is not timely, and there is one who keeps silent and is found wise." For we must not only keep silent and speak at the right time, but also speak with great grace. That is why Paul said, "Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you know how you ought to answer each person." Consider that this is the member through which we speak with God, through which we offer up praise. This is the member through which we receive the awesome sacrifice. The faithful know what I mean. That is why it must be pure of all accusation, reviling, foul talk and slander. If some lewd thought forces its way in, you must choke it inside and not let it come out in words. If some faintheartedness leads you to complain, you must dry up this root too, keep the door secure and the guard strict, and not let wicked plans be born; and if they are born, you must choke them inside and wither the root. 5. Job kept such a guard; that is why he uttered no discordant word, but kept silent for the most part… [Notes:] [?] "answer me". In Sirach one reads "answer your neighbor". [?] "need of testing" [?] Savile, a reading that fits: "there is one who is silent, and he is prudent." One [manuscript]: "we accept".

…opposites. Have you seen the Pharisee perishing because of it [?]? Look at the tax collector saved because of it. Have you seen the boastful barbarian punished? Look at the righteous man being modest and saying, "I am dust and ashes." Have you seen the man who gloats accused and punished? Look at the one who shares another's grief being saved. "Put the mark," it says, "on the foreheads of those who sigh and grieve." That is why Paul said, "Rejoice with those who rejoice, and weep with those who weep." Even if you can do nothing else, he says, by grieving with the sufferer you will bring him no small gift. Have you seen the one who laughs handed over to lamentation? Look at the one who mourns enjoying comfort. "For blessed," it says, "are those who mourn, for they will be comforted." Have you seen those who complain punished? Look at those who give thanks saved. "Blessed are you, Lord, and praiseworthy is your name, for you are just in all that you have done to us." And a little later, "All that you have brought upon us, you have done in true judgment." The first said, "Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord"; the others said the opposite: "Your eye is too pure to look on evil." The first called strangers blessed, because they prosper while doing lawless deeds; he calls blessed those whom God helps. "Blessed," he says, "is the people whose God is the Lord." And again, "Do not be envious [?] of evildoers, nor envy those who do lawlessness." Have you seen the saints exhorting others and themselves standing unshaken in temptations? Listen to Jacob saying, "If the Lord gives me bread to eat and clothing to wear." And to Abraham: "I will not take anything of yours, not a thread or a sandal strap." And when his wife was about to be defiled and famine was pressing hard, he uttered no discordant word. And when the boy said, "Father, here are the wood and the fire, but where is the sheep?" see how gently and with what a philosophic mind he answers, saying: "God will provide the sheep for himself, my child." Neither nature nor compassion turned him aside at the boy's words. He did what he did alone with the boy alone, just when his longing was likely to be kindled most fiercely. For so that no one could say he did not mourn because he was ashamed before others, he separated himself from them, and when he was alone he showed the strength of his philosophy. 6. Have you seen people punished for laughter? Look at those saved through lamentation and fasting: think of the Ninevites. Have you seen people punished for reviling? Look at those who receive a reward for speaking well. "Whoever blesses you is blessed, and whoever curses you is cursed." "Bless those who persecute you, pray for those who mistreat you, so that you may become like your Father in heaven." Do you see that the mouth must neither be shut altogether nor opened to everything, but that we must know the right time for each? Because the prophet knew this, he said… [Notes:] [?] "give me". [?] "and I will praise". [?] "good", as above. [?] "becoming". "See him answering with gentleness and a philosophic mind, and that after three days and nights, in which he lay down alone with the child alone, so that his longing was especially warm": so certain manuscripts. [?] so certain manuscripts. Savile: "nor be opened". [?] Gen. [?].

…[?] reversed the order, and spoke first about the mouth and only then came to the heart? He does not do this idly or at random. Think of prisoners who want to escape. Those in charge of them make it their first task to secure the prison doors, and everyone is eager about this; once it is done, the rest is easy to put right. He does the same here, and by his exhortation all but says: Let the doors be shut, and wicked thoughts will quickly be overpowered. That is why he does not even let them come in from outside in the first place, and pulls up the evil root, saying: "Do not incline my heart to words of wickedness." Not that God inclines it, God forbid! What he means is this: Do not let it be bent, do not let it be turned toward wicked thoughts. For the heart is the source of virtue and of vice. And what are the words of wickedness? There are many kinds. There are words that stitch together plots, words that slander God, that turn away from virtue, that chase after vice. There are words about corrupt doctrines and a careless life that people enjoy hearing, and other such things, all uttered out of great wickedness. But just as there are thoughts and words of wickedness, so there are thoughts and words of life. That is why the disciples said to Christ, "You have the words of eternal life; to whom shall we go?" Words of life are those that give life, and words of salvation are those that bring about salvation. That is why a wise man says, "Do not hold back a word in a time of salvation." Words of wickedness are also those that make the people who speak them wicked. 7. For just as there are pestilential, disease-bearing airs, so there are such words. What those do in the body, these do in the soul that takes them in. So he prays in the words he added, saying: Do not let my heart take in such words, do not let it be bent that way. Do you see how he shows free will, and shows that our nature does not have wickedness in itself but takes it in when it is bent through slackness? "To make excuses for sins." This above all is the road to ruin: either the sinning soul itself loosens its [458] fear and invents excuses for slackness, or, when someone has committed adultery, another person who wants to dissolve his remorse says, "It isn't your fault, is it? Desire is to blame." It is bad to sin, but denying it after sinning makes it worse. This above all is the devil's weapon. This is what happened with the first-created too. Adam ought to have confessed his offenses, but he shifts the blame onto another, and she in turn onto the devil. They ought to have said, "We have sinned, we have done wrong," but they did not… [Notes:] [?] Morel continues thus: "that is, do not let it be bent, do not let it be turned [?] toward thoughts; that is, do not let it be bent, do not let it be turned toward wicked [?]. For the heart is the source of virtue and of vice. Showing this, then, he spoke thus, not that God [?]." [?] "corrupted". [?] "listening with pleasure". [?] "he prays, then" [?] "do not let". In the same place [?]. In Savile "we have done wrong" is missing after "we have sinned".

…with such people, saying, "I did not sit in the council of those who make sport." That is also why Paul does not allow us to eat with the wicked, or even to associate with them at all. He says: "If anyone does not obey our word in this letter, take note of him and do not associate with him." "And I will not join with their chosen ones." Another version: "Nor may I eat their delicacies." Another: "May I not lodge among their delights." Here he states the apostolic precept: we must flee even their luxuries and banquets, where sin grows most and where license is greatest. 8. It is no small sign of virtue, no small road to amendment, to flee such banquets and gatherings: not to be swayed by friendship, and not to become a slave to the belly, slackening the vigor of the soul and undoing the firmness of philosophy. This is how many people, out of regard for friendship, have been rolled into the surf of drunkenness. This is how they have been caught by fornication and have kindled the fire of pleasure, chasing after banquets and theaters full of lawlessness.
