He shows that he himself acted this way, so as not even to share such a table: "Let the righteous discipline me in mercy and reprove me, but let not the oil of a sinner anoint my head." Another version: "Let the righteous show me mercy and reprove me." Along with the former, this too is no small form of virtue: not to flee [?] or the rebukes that come from the righteous. What he means is this: May I never take part in the gatherings of those who flatter me to my harm. But those who are bitter medicine and correct me, those I would choose: people who reprove, who cover [?] offenses, who rebuke. For setting wounds right belongs above all to mercy and kindness. "But let not the oil of a sinner," he says, "anoint my head." Do you see a soul knit firm by virtue? It bears even the rebukes of the righteous gladly, but beats back even the flattering words of the lawless. Why? Because the lawless, by showing pity, have often destroyed people, while the righteous, by rebuking and being bitter medicine, [?] have corrected them. Mercy is the lot that goes with the reproof of the righteous, and death the lot that goes with the mercy of the lawless. That is why someone said, "The wounds of friends are more trustworthy than the eager kisses of enemies." And see how he points here to the apostolic saying: "Reprove, rebuke, exhort." For such is the reproof of the saints too. Physicians do the same: they do not only cut, they also bandage. That is also why Christ, to make reproof easy to accept, does not let the rebuke be made public from the start. He says: "Go and reprove him between you and him alone." Paul did the same, showing reproof combined with mercy. At one time he says, "O foolish Galatians," and at another, "My little children, for whom I am again in labor." For whoever reproves must think of many ways to make the reproof acceptable, and whoever applies this remedy needs great understanding. Indeed, the one who reproves needs more understanding than the one who cuts the body. How… [Notes:] Savile: "with the council". Three manuscripts: "were drowned". [?] "who expose", a reading not [?]…

…to Hades. Another version: "As a farmer, when he [?] the earth, so our bones were scattered at the mouth of Hades." Another: "Like one who breaks up and splits the earth, our bones were scattered into Hades." Another: "As one who tills and digs the earth, our bones were scattered beside Hades." Having said that his words are full of pleasure, he also speaks of the old calamities. Although we suffered the worst, he says, and like earth torn open and ploughed or dug up we were all scattered and perished and came to the very gates of death, yet even in this condition we would rather choose discipline and correction from the righteous than pity from sinners. For whatever may happen, we cling to our hope in you, and would never fall away from looking to you. That is why he added: "For my eyes are on you, O Lord, Lord; in you I have hoped; do not take away my soul." Though countless terrors come, he says, though wars and battles, deaths and the gates of Hades, we do not let go of the sacred anchor. We hold on to our hope in your help as our ally, and, laying aside weapons and battle lines, we look for deliverance from that source, from your favor. "In you I have hoped; do not take away my soul." Another version: "Do not pour it out." That is, do not let me go away empty-handed. "Keep me from the snare they have set for me, and from the stumbling blocks of those who do lawlessness." Here he is not speaking simply of plots, but of secret, hidden ones, which are hard to guard against and hard to detect, and that is why they especially need help [?] from above. That is why he closes his words with a prayer. He began from there and ends here, showing that some things are his part: hope in God, always looking to God, fleeing their gatherings, hating their wicked desires. Other things are God's part: help, alliance, lifting him above the most unbearable trials. This is how virtue is woven, when our effort is brought in and God's help fights alongside it. "Sinners will fall into his net; I am alone until I pass by." Into whose net will they fall? Into God's own. That is, they will be caught and overpowered. For what happens to the righteous goes only as far as correction and the rousing of their philosophy; but what happens to sinners, since they are incurably sick, goes as far as punishment and retribution. "I am alone until I pass by." Another version: "I am together until I pass by." Another: "In the same place." That is, joined together, knit firm, not scattered; or, according to the Seventy, freed from the wicked, pure of their company, living as if alone, which is the greatest form of virtue. And he does not say to do this for one, two or three days, but for one's whole life. This is safety, this is a wall, this is progress in virtue: to flee the wicked, to be knit firm and gathered into oneself for one's whole life, and to live apart from those who corrupt. For it is not solitude… [Notes:] [?] "alliance" [?], which is the same. A little later Morel has "his own in the net", but in the others it is "his". Thus [?]: "for all, neither by voice". Savile: "and by his own". One [manuscript]: "and the inner [?], which he had".

[?] ...to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved. And writing to the Corinthians he said: "That is why many among you are weak and sick, and a good number have fallen asleep. For if we judged ourselves, we would not be judged. But when we are judged, we are disciplined by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned along with the world." And Abraham said to the rich man: "You received your good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus his bad things; and now he is comforted here, and you are in anguish." And David too, when Shimei cursed him, said: "Let him curse me, for the Lord has commanded him, so that he may see my humiliation." And everywhere in the Scriptures we will find that those who bear afflictions with thanksgiving not only wash away many of their sins, but also gain from this no small boldness before God. "When my spirit was failing within me, you also knew my paths." Just when the faint-hearted among people lose heart most of all, and many even utter blasphemous words, that is when this man most of all lives as a philosopher, having as the teacher of his earnestness the

So when you see someone falling into despair because of affliction, or uttering some bitter word, do not consider the affliction the cause, but the faint-heartedness of the one who says such things. For the nature of affliction usually produces the opposite: attentiveness, contrition of mind, a resolute will, heightened reverence. That is why Paul too said: "Affliction produces endurance, and endurance proven character." And if the Jews grumbled when afflicted, the words of grumbling came not from the affliction but from their own folly; for the saints, when afflicted, became more radiant and more wise. That is why this same man said: "It is good for me, Lord, that you humbled me, so that I might learn your statutes." And Paul: "And because of the surpassing greatness of the revelations, so that I would not be too elated, a thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to buffet me. Three times I begged the Lord about this, and he said to me, 'My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.' Therefore I am content in afflictions, in weaknesses, in persecutions. For when I am weak, then I am strong." Do you see how this man too is roused all the more in affliction, and takes refuge in God, and clings to him the more with great intensity, even at the very bottom of his troubles (for that is what "When my spirit was failing within me" means), and becomes more earnest precisely then? As for "You knew my paths," another translator said, "For you know." "In this way on which I was walking they hid a snare for me. I looked to the right and watched, and there was no one who recognized me." Here he shows the intensity of the calamity and the mounting dangers, and the plots of his enemies, how they approached and drew ever closer, wishing to trip him up; and, what was harder still, that not only did he have no helpers or allies, but no one even recognized him. 2. This is the height of desolation, the extreme of [?] hardship. (Notes: one manuscript reads "doing." One reads "but there was no one, he says, who recognized me." Shortly after, Savile reads "this is the height of desolation." [?] a few.)

...let us not grow slack. "You are my portion in the land of the living." That is: my lot, my treasure, my wealth, you are all things to me. "In the land of the living." Here he calls his own homeland the land of the living. For he is accustomed often to call the captivity in Babylon Hades and death. Then, since while in a foreign land he could perform none of the customary worship, whereas there all the rites of holiness were fulfilled, for this reason, he says, "You are my portion in the land of the living." "You always protected me," he says, "and made me your own in the land of the living, and I have had great fellowship with you." "Attend to my supplication, for I have been brought very low." Do you see how what he said above he sets down here too as a plea in his defense—being brought low, I mean, paying the penalty for his sins in full measure? The word "very" is not an accusation against what happened, but expresses the grief and weakness of the sufferer. For if you look at what the sins deserved, the humiliation is not severe; but if you look at the weakness of the one bearing it, it is exceedingly severe. For nowhere does God exact the punishment that our offenses deserve. And if it seems unbearable to those who suffer, this is not because of the nature of what happens, but because of the weakness of those who endure it. "Rescue me from those who persecute me, for they have grown stronger than I." See, here again is another reason: the unjust plotting of those who abuse him, and the fact that he himself is in great weakness. "Bring my soul out of prison, that I may give thanks to your name." "Confess" here stands for "give thanks." What he means is this: Free me from my troubles. For by "prison" he hints at the overwhelming weight of his misfortunes. 3. "So that I may give thanks to your name." This too is no small thing: when we have come into prosperity, not to fall into forgetfulness of the benefit. For many people are more earnest in afflictions but more careless in times of ease; others again are careless in ease, and in afflictions despair of themselves and grow more listless still. But this man, through every change of circumstance, keeps the same reverence: affliction did not make him lose heart, but rather drew him to supplication and prayer; nor did ease make him listless, but even then he prepares himself for thanksgiving. "The righteous will wait for me, until you repay me." Another version: "The righteous will be crowned when you do me good." What does this mean? This, he says, will benefit the righteous too. For they too will be glad, they will rejoice, they will leap for joy when they see my deliverance from troubles. For such are the souls of the saints: they grieve with those who suffer, and they do not envy those who prosper, but rejoice and are glad and take delight with those who receive benefits. Paul too commanded this, saying, "Rejoice with those who rejoice, and weep with those who weep." This is no small virtue. For many gloat over those who have fallen and envy those who rise, giving birth to both passions out of cruelty and great inhumanity. But the righteous are not so; rather... (Notes: [?] reads "that is, my whole treasure, my wealth." [?] "he calls prison the encirclement of misfortunes." [?] ...is healthier and [?], and sweeter to drink; often. So Savile, citing B. One reads "Prayer is also the promise.")

...advises, saying: "Do not repeat a word in your prayer." He does not give this advice and counsel so that we should not say the same things a second time when we entreat and beseech God—away with that! For we are commanded to persevere in prayer. Rather, it is so that we should not put things off when we have promised something to God, but should hasten. That is why he says elsewhere: "Do not delay to fulfill your vow." For the future is uncertain. Sickness, or unexpected business that comes upon you, may prevent you. And if death comes and cuts you off, you have no excuse. Here, however, he calls supplication and entreaty a prayer. That is why he added, making this very point clear: "Give ear to my supplication in your truth." Another version: "in your faithfulness"; another: "in your steadfastness." That is: Grant the request and carry it into effect, confirming it by your truth; use your power to fulfill what I ask. But let us see what kind of supplication it is. Among human beings, when someone presents a petition, those who receive it consider this: if it is just and lawful, it is heard. But among people petitions are made for honors and money, and often to prevent injustice; and some even ask for things beyond the power of the judges. We, however, ask forgiveness for sins, and we come to supplication when the judge does not acquit us—the judge within, I mean, the conscience seated in us. For it has no authority to acquit. And just as no one dares approach a king about a torn cloak, or about ten obols taken from him, so you too—indeed with far greater reverence—do not approach God about cheap and worthless matters, such as someone having wronged you over money or insulted you; but about the ways the devil wrongs you, where above all there is need of help from above. But you have no patron to present your petition? Call out as the king comes forth, and seek a suitable moment. When then does the king come forth? Always and continually. And when is the suitable moment? Whenever you wish, whenever you make yourself worthy. The Jews were commanded to stand at the foot of the mountain when they appeared before God, to have white garments, and not to approach a woman. But you, instead of your garments, scrub your soul clean, and come with self-control and gentleness, and with great leisure, and journey to the King, if you wish to succeed as you ought. The journey does not need great expense: take virtue as your provisions. And where does this King dwell? Near to the broken in heart. Take that road. "The Lord," it says, "is near to all who call on him in truth." There you will find him, there you will meet him. He is near to those who break their bread for the hungry and do works of mercy. If you go this way, you will find him ready, granting your request. "For while you are still speaking I will say, 'Here I am'"; and you will not need... (Notes: Savile reads "advises—away with that—and counsels." [?]. Shortly after, Savile reads "cuts you off" [?]. Another reads "power to fulfill." Savile reads "but let us see also what the supplication is." Two manuscripts read "those who present." Savile reads "deem worthy. But we ask forgiveness for sins, and when the judge does not acquit us, the one within, the..." The same reads "for these pitiful and bare things." [?] reads "going about.")

...applied a painless cure. So do not let this trouble you, that they were all drowned together at once. For how does this differ from dying little by little? How does dying on his own benefit the one who has departed, or dying with everyone harm him? "Hear me in your righteousness," that is, in your loving-kindness. That this is what it means is shown by what he added: "And do not enter into judgment with your servant." Job too asks this, though he was righteous, true, God-fearing, and kept himself from every evil deed: "Would that there were one to arbitrate and decide between us both"—and yet, when God appeared, he said, "I will lay my hand on my mouth," even though God was challenging him and saying, "No; but gird up your loins like a man." And he reproaches the Jews with this, saying: "What fault did your fathers find in me, that your rulers transgressed against me?" He does this not wishing to make the sentence harsher, but to bring them to awareness and confession of their own sins, and then to grant forgiveness, so that in this way they might see the greatness of the benefit. That is why he says: "State your iniquities first"—not "so that you may be condemned," but "so that you may be justified." For this reason he does not state them himself, but prepares the sinner to do so. For if he wished to punish, he would have made the accusation himself; but now, since he wishes to show mercy, he leaves it to the one who has sinned, so that he may receive the crown of gratitude and through confession draw down mercy. What could equal this loving-kindness? Nothing. "Speak," he says, "and I ask nothing more; confess, and it is enough for me; speak, and I have received everything." "Do not enter into judgment with your servant." This awareness has been achieved in many from the fact that God is going to judge. The right-minded know it even before this; but the senseless learned it from the prophets' constantly saying, "The Lord has a case against his people, and he will argue with Israel"; and again, "Hear, you valleys and foundations of the earth"; and, "Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth." So from his being constantly said to judge, this was achieved even among the insensible. For some of the Jews said: "Why have we fasted, and you did not see?" and, "Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord"; and, "Those who do lawless deeds are built up, and we call strangers blessed"; and, "The way of the Lord is not right." And the blessed Job, when he fell into that trial, did not speak from such a mind as the Jews, nor say such things—God forbid! Yet he did say: "Would that there were a mediator, to decide and to reprove between us both. Let him take his rod away from me, and let not the fear of him torment me." For this very reason God says to him: "I will question you, and you answer me." Then, since he was struck with dismay and said, "Why am I still judged, being admonished, and reproving the Lord?" and... (Notes: [?] reads "he says this." Three manuscripts read "[?] puts forward, saying." One reads "into reproof." [?] reads "will be argued." Shortly after, one reads "so from his constantly wishing to judge." [Another reads:] "Would that there were our mediator, both reproving and hearing between us." "An accusation, though being a man." So one manuscript.)

...having become, he thinks tables and harlots and luxury to be great things. What could be lower than that? Yet many call such people great-souled; but these are far more lowly than the others in turn. Let us learn, then, what true loftiness is, and what produces baseness. For nothing makes a person so lofty as despising these things. Now, then, the prophet speaks of the humiliation that comes from misfortunes: "He has made me sit in dark places like those long dead." He describes a double misfortune: both that it is in dark places, and that it is like those long dead, hinting by both at the captivity of that time. For since it is possible even in the dark to do something by lighting a lamp, wishing to show with greater intensity the extremity of the evils, he heightened the tragedy with the word "dead." Such too are those who live in sins. For they are like the dead in darkness; even if they carry about countless lights, even if they look at the sun, even if they appear splendid in their clothing and the rest of their grooming, they are in no better condition than those who have died once and for all and lie in darkness—indeed far worse, inasmuch as the one is a matter of nature, the other an indictment of the will. There is also the darkness of the future, about which he says, "Take him and throw him into the outer darkness." There is also the darkness of wickedness: "Those sitting in darkness," it says, "and the shadow of death." And Paul: "We are not children of darkness." And again: "They became futile in their reasonings, and their senseless heart was darkened." For this reason, just as those in darkness do not know the nature of things, so those who live in sins are blinded and do not discern what appears before them, but run after shadows as if after reality, pursuing wealth and luxuries and power; they do not recognize enemies, and they do not recognize friends, trusting enemies as friends and clashing with friends as with foes. Do you not see poor people every day crying out, in anguish, and no one listening? Why then do they not listen? Because the devil has made them sit in dark places like those long dead. For what darkness and death are to others, inhumanity is to these. It belongs to those who sit in darkness not to see the evils coming upon them. These people suffer the same: they do not see the calamities lying almost right beside them, and they are swept down into pits and over cliffs. It belongs to those who sit in darkness to dare shameful things with complete impunity. Those who live in wickedness do this too: as though sitting in darkness, and as though there were no one to see what they do, they dare everything with impunity, breaking the law in the middle of cities as if in a wilderness. 4. Those who sit in darkness are in constant fear; so are these. For no greedy person or robber is free from dread, even if he boasts endlessly and appears cheerful outwardly. Such is the nature of conscience. And while these people were deprived of all excuse before, much more so now, because even though the Sun of righteousness has shone, they still sit in darkness. And how, when the sun has shone, do they still sit in darkness? Because of the weakness of their own eyes. For into hiding places or dens or holes... (Notes: Savile reads "in darkness." "Just as" is missing in Savile. One reads "hiding places of wild beasts." [?] Savile reads [?]. Shortly after, in the same Savile the phrase "because of the weakness of the eyes" is missing. Patrologia Graeca 55.)

...ate the same spiritual food; but with most of them God was not pleased." Sometimes he speaks from the things to come: "They will pay the penalty of eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of his might." And again: "But wrath has come upon them to the uttermost." "For the Day will disclose it, because it is revealed by fire." And again: "For because of these things the wrath of God is coming upon the sons of disobedience." But he speaks this way when he must chasten; when he must comfort, he comforts from both: from the past, speaking thus: "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the God of mercies and Father of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction, through the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God"; and from the future: "The sufferings of the present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us." That is why this man too says: "I remembered the days of old; I meditated on all your works." He did not simply say, "I remembered," but, "I meditated"—that is, I made it my task and my constant study to unfold within myself the things that happened to those of old. For great comfort and wisdom come to us from the history in the Scriptures. That is why Paul said: "Through endurance and through the comfort of the Scriptures we have hope." And again: "All Scripture is inspired by God and useful for teaching, for reproof, for correction." 5. And so this man too was already comforted by this, though in such great affliction and turmoil, by unfolding the ancient events within himself and recalling the dispensations of God that had come about in various ways. Another version, at any rate, says, "And I meditated on all your deeds." "I meditated on the works of your hands." Another: "I meditated on the works of your hands." By this he shows that in doing this he reaped great comfort and became more intimate with God. That is why he added, making this plain: "I spread out my hands to you." He did not say, "I stretched out," but, "I spread wide," showing the great disposition of his heart, all but leaping out of the body in its eagerness and running up to him. "Inspired, then, by the memory of your mighty deeds, and reckoning up all your loving-kindness, and the discipline that came from misfortunes, and the freedom that came from deliverance, I fled to you again." "My soul is like a waterless land to you." Another version: "Like a land thirsting for you always"—for this is what "Diapsalma" means. "In misfortunes and in prosperity, and in every change of circumstance, I showed the same earnestness," he says. And what does "Like a waterless land to you" mean? Just as thirsting land longs for rain, so I long to be with you continually. And the weight of his afflictions especially intensified this longing; that is why God allowed them to increase, displaying his great providence. For he did not only make his creatures, but also cares for them once made, both human beings and all the rest. Paul, knowing this, said: "For in him we live and move and... (Notes: Savile reads "from the face of the Lord, and from the glory of his strength." "Must" is missing in Savile [?], but "unfold" [?]. For "I meditated" others have "I spoke of.")

…his face, so that we may not fall into the pits of wickedness while so much darkness holds sway. Even those who have fallen can rise again, so those who fall must not stay lying on the ground. The pit full of fierce beasts and teeming with darkness is the nature of sin. So let us let down the ropes of the Scriptures and offer our own free choice, and we will quickly rise, even if we fall. How does the road begin? It begins if, having fallen, we neither grow careless nor despair, but chant to ourselves these prophetic words: "Does the one who falls not rise again?" And again: "Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion." Let us bind ourselves with these thoughts and draw ourselves up. "Let me hear your mercy in the morning, for in you I have hoped." Another version has "Let me hear your mercy from daybreak," that is, quickly. 6. Do you see a soul afflicted and troubled? Before it experiences anything, it wants to hear, so that it may be lifted up by hope and expectation. What he means is this: "Raise me up by your promise." Then he adds his claim to receive it: "For in you I have hoped." For God seeks nothing so much as that we should gaze eagerly toward him without ceasing. "Make known to me, Lord, the way in which I shall walk, for to you I have lifted up my soul." What are you saying? Our nature holds the law that God planted in it from the beginning, and the writings of Moses renew it. How then can you ask again, "Make known to me, Lord, the way in which I shall walk"? It means one of two things. Either: "Since my conscience has been buried by wickedness, I ask that it be renewed." Or else by "way" he means here the many things unknown to human beings, as Paul also shows when he says: "For we do not know what we ought to pray for." If Paul was ignorant after so much knowledge, why are you surprised that this man says these things? See how he seeks nothing material here, but the way that leads to God, and supplies the starting point from his own side. He did not simply say, "Make known to me, Lord, the way that leads to you." What did he say? "Since to you I have lifted up my soul"; that is, "I gaze eagerly toward you, I look to you." It is above all to such people that God makes things known. That is why, when he was asked why he spoke to the Jews in parables, he said: "Because seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear." "I lifted up" means "I have moved, or transferred, my soul over to you." "Rescue me from my enemies, Lord; to you I have fled for refuge." See how everywhere the one praying also brings forward reasons. "Do not turn your face away from me," he says, "for I have hoped in you. Make known to me the way, for to you I have lifted up my soul. Rescue me from my enemies, for to you I have fled for refuge. Teach me to do your will, for you are my God." He did not simply say, "Teach me your will," but "to do your will" [?] … for I have fled for refuge. [?] "will be heard" [?]; but he himself reads "will not hear."

On Psalm 143. [?] my Lord, who trains my hands for battle, my fingers [?] for war. 1. What are you saying? Is God a teacher of wars, of fighting and of battle lines? Certainly no one would go wrong in crediting the victory in these things to him as well. For this is what "who trains my hands" means: he is the one who makes me prevail over my enemies, conquer them and set up a trophy. When he struck down the [?], God was the cause of the victory. And when he waged many wars successfully, set up trophies and captured certain enemy cities together with their men, it was God who made him prevail. That is why he said in song: "The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle." And in the time of Moses too, many such things…

But there is also another war, harder than this one, in which we especially need help from above: when we are drawn up against the opposing powers. To learn that our war is against these, listen to Paul saying: "Our struggle is not against blood and flesh, but against the principalities, against the authorities, against the world-rulers of the darkness of this age." This war is harder because the enemy battalions are of another nature, an invisible one, and because the contest is not about small things but about salvation and destruction. Here one cannot see who is acting, nor learn the time in advance, nor [?] the difficulty of the ground, nor anything else of the kind. For these battalions attack us in the marketplace and at home, while we are playing and taking our ease. So we must be armed at all times. This war knows no truce. It has no heralds, no ambassadors, nothing of that sort; the battle is undeclared. Therefore above all we must be fortified on every side and vigorously fed. The food for this war, and the weapons of such soldiers, is the hearing of the divine Scriptures. Whoever does not enjoy it wastes away with hunger. "For I will send them," he says, "not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord." Here too, then, as in visible wars, there is need of help from above. "For a king is not saved by great power, and a giant will not be saved by the greatness of his strength. A horse is a false hope for safety; by the greatness of its power it will not save." This, at any rate, is how many routed their enemies: prayers went before them and overthrew the enemy battalions. "My mercy and my refuge, my helper and my deliverer." Do you see him again asking to be saved on the ground of God's loving-kindness? Or rather, he hints at something else here. Through these words he shows that he is saying: "I would not have been worthy even of his mercy if he himself had not consented." So it is he who is "my mercy," he says; "I did not earn it by my works." For though it is mercy, it does not come upon everyone indiscriminately: "I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion." It is necessary, then, even if one is to receive mercy, [?] them. [Some manuscripts read: "he hints at a saying full of much wisdom, that not even his." Another reading: [?] "he hints at much wisdom" [?] "for he shows" [?].]

…[the world was not] worthy. But those words concern virtue, and the times when people display it; whereas "What is man?" is said about human nature. And yet nature too is great. It is great, but if you look at the knowledge it has been granted, it falls far short of that. Let the children of the heretics hear this: they rave with great madness, overstepping their own limits, and they suffer from utter ignorance when they claim to know things beyond them. For there can be knowledge in ignorance and ignorance in knowledge. If you like, let us test this on things we can perceive. Tell me: if someone says he can measure the sea and knows how many cupfuls it holds, is he not the one who least knows what the sea is? But the one who says he does not know, and insists that its measure is boundless, is the one who best knows what the sea is. What about God? If someone says, "I have seen God and grasped him with my own eyes," is he not the one who least knows God? He says the invisible is visible, and by trying to add to knowledge he loses even the knowledge that is possible. But if someone says God is invisible and that no one can see him, is he not the one who knows? Again, if one person says God is incomprehensible and another says he is comprehensible, is not the second ignorant and the first the one who knows? Do you not see Paul too taking this road when he says, "We know in part and we prophesy in part"? Consider how much has taken place so that we might learn about God, not what he is in his essence, but that he exists. This is what Paul says: "Whoever approaches God must believe that he exists." All creation proclaims him: "For from the greatness and beauty of created things," it says, "their Maker is seen by analogy." So do the very constitution of man, the honors he has bestowed, the punishments, the benefits, the dispensations, the things foretold through the prophets and the various miracles. After all this the Only-begotten himself came and accomplished that wonderful and awe-inspiring dispensation. And yet there are some who have still not learned clearly. And you say you can grasp by your own reasoning what God is in his essence? "So you do not know God?" someone says. Far from it! I know that he exists, that he loves mankind, that he is good, that he exercises providence, and all the other things the Scriptures have said. But what he is in his essence I do not know. Adam too thought he would discover more, persuaded by the devil, and through this greed he lost even what he had. The same happens to these men, led on by human reasonings and not listening to the words "The Lord gives wisdom, and from his presence come knowledge and understanding." Do they not hear Paul saying, "He revealed it to us through the Spirit," and casting out reasonings? "Demolishing reasonings," he says, "and every lofty thing raised up against the knowledge of God." And another wise man says: "The reasonings of mortals are timid, and their designs are unstable." "What is man, that you have made yourself known to him?" Consider the boundless [?]… [Morel reads: "overstepping their limits, and suffer from ignorance." [?] Savile reads: "the one will be ignorant, the other knowing." [?] "let me then consider the." Next, Savile reads: "I speak of God's worth"; Morel reads: "I speak worthily of God," which is better.]

…of the touch, even if it seems great, falls far short of God's worth. For God does not need to touch the mountains to make them smoke. In fact he does not even need a nod; his counsel and will are enough. Having spoken of man's lowliness, then, he speaks also of God's power, as far as a man can speak of it, since even these words fall far short of that majesty. "Flash forth lightning, and you will scatter them; send out your arrows, and you will throw them into confusion." By lightning and arrows here he does not mean the lightning and arrows we know. Rather, this is what he calls punishments. He uses things already familiar to persuade the scornful and the complacent to tremble, fear and submit. For if no one can bear lightning, though it is not sent as punishment, who will withstand God if he chooses to set his punishing power in motion? God's arrows are famines, plagues, thunderbolts and punishments of every kind. "Send forth your hand from on high; rescue me and deliver me out of many waters, from the hand of alien sons." For God's power is equipped not only to punish but also to save. By "hand" here he means help and alliance. That is why he did not say "Stretch out" but "Send forth": to show this. And if he says "Stretch out" somewhere else, he is again hinting at the same thing. By "waters" he means the disorderly onslaught of the enemy, chaotic and rushing on with great force. That he is not speaking of literal waters is clear from what follows: "From the hand," he says, "of alien sons." By alien sons here he seems to me to mean those who are estranged from the truth. For just as we count the faithful as our own people and our brothers, so we count unbelievers as aliens. It is chiefly by this that we tell our own people from strangers. He is my own who claims the same Father as I do and shares the same table, more than one related to me by birth. This law of kinship is more exact, just as estrangement that comes from opposing beliefs is plainer than estrangement by birth. So do not look at the fact that we live under the same sky and in the same world. I am seeking another kind of fellowship, one above the heavens. There is our citizenship and our life: "For our life," he says, "is hidden with Christ in God." We do not live on earth; we have moved to the capital city above. We have another true light, another homeland, other fellow citizens and other kin. That is why Paul said: "So then you are no longer strangers and sojourners, but fellow citizens with the saints." "How then," someone says, "did Christ say that the Samaritan was a neighbor, even though the gap between them was great?" But he did not say it by the reckoning of nature. So when you have to do good, let every person be near to you. But when the word of truth is being tested, recognize who is your own and who is a stranger. Even if you have a brother of the same father and mother, if he does not share with you according to the law of truth, let him be more barbarous to you than a Scythian. And even if someone is a Scythian or a Sarmatian, if he knows the true doctrines exactly and believes what you yourself believe, let him be closer and nearer to you than the brother born of the same womb as you. Let us tell the barbarian from the one who is not by this test: not by language or by race, but by mind and soul. [Savile reads: "and does not share with you." Next, Savile reads: "even if a Sarmatian." [?]]

…does the things that bring glory and praise to God: for example, when the eye does not look at licentious things; when the hands are stretched out not to rob but to give alms; when the ears are ready to receive psalms and spiritual teaching; when the feet run to church; when the heart does not hatch deceit but [?] love. Then the limbs of the body become a harp and a lyre, and they sing a new song, not with words but with deeds. "To him who gives salvation to kings." For it is not armies, multitudes of soldiers or bodyguards that usually save, but God's help. "Who redeems David his servant." Having spoken of what is common to all, he speaks also of his own case. He did not say "who redeemed" but "who redeems," showing God's continual providence over him. 6. Then he asks again for what he asked before, constantly falling down and pleading to be freed from wicked men. He says: "Rescue me from the evil sword, and deliver me from the hand of alien sons, whose mouth has spoken vanity, and whose right hand is a right hand of injustice. Their sons are like young plants grown tall in their youth." Here he describes worldly prosperity and wealth, and he puts first what comes first: having children vigorous and in their prime, of both sexes. At any rate he added: "Their daughters are beautified, adorned like the likeness of a temple." Along with youth he points to great luxury, and he sketches their headdresses and women's finery, which come from great prosperity. Then he describes wealth again, which seems to come second but perhaps now comes first. He says: "Their storehouses are full, overflowing from one to another." What does "overflowing" mean? Crammed to bursting. The wealth cannot be contained in the storehouses, he means. "Their sheep are prolific, multiplying in their pastures; their oxen are fat." This too was thought no small prosperity. Among the ancients, wealth lay in these things, in herds, flocks and crops, before the softness of the present day was invented. "There is no breach in the hedge, no gap." That is, the farms too enjoy much protection, much care and much diligence. The crops flourish, the hedges stand, and the vineyard is planted and walled round on every side. "No outcry in their streets." Another version has "in their farmsteads." This is another kind of prosperity, one that does not come with every fortune: peace, freedom from fear and security. No one plots against them, no one makes war on them; there is no uproar and no turmoil. "They called blessed the people who have these things. Blessed is the people whose God is the Lord." Do you see the man's virtue? He set out all the wealth and went through it in words, and then added the verdict of the many about it. Yet he himself feels none of the human reactions to these things, nor [does he think them] enviable…

…forever, and to the age of ages. Another version has "For ever without ceasing." This above all is the mark of a devout soul: to be freed from worldly affairs and dedicated to hymns. It would be shameful for a rational human being, more honorable than all visible things, to fall behind creation in giving praise. It would be not only shameful but absurd. And how could it not be absurd, when creation sends up glory to its Master every day and every hour? "For the heavens," it says, "declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands. Day pours forth speech to day, and night declares knowledge to night." The sun and moon, the varied chorus of the stars and the good order of everything else proclaim their own Maker. You are more honorable than all of these. If you not only fail to do this, but also lead a life that brings blasphemy on the God who made you, what pardon could such a person deserve? What defense will he have? He came into being for this very purpose: to please the God who loves mankind and to enjoy the kingdom of the world to come. Yet he takes little account of this, and entangles himself in worldly business and cares. But this man was not like that. Throughout his life he offered praise to God, both in words and in deeds. We owe God a great deal: that he made us when we did not exist; that he made us as we are; that once we were made he sustains us; and that every day he provides for us, both together and individually, secretly and openly, whether we know it or not. What could one say of all the visible things he made for our sake? Their service to us, the forming of the body, the nobility of the soul, his daily dispensation through miracles, through laws and through punishments, his varied and incomprehensible providence, and the crown of all good things: that he did not spare even his Only-begotten for our sake. Then there are the gifts already given through baptism and through the mysteries, and the gifts still to come, those unspeakable good things: the kingdom, the resurrection, and the inheritance full of every blessedness. If anyone lists each of these, he will plunge into an unspeakable sea of benefits and see how much he owes to the God who loves mankind. And we owe him not only for these things, but also for the majesty of his glory and for his pure essence. For on account of this too we owe him praise, blessing, unceasing thanksgiving, worship and constant service. The prophet shows this very thing when he says: "Great is the Lord and greatly to be praised, and there is no end to his greatness." Since he had said, "I will bless and I will praise," he shows that God has no need of our praises or blessings, and that nothing is added to his glory by the acclaim of those who serve him. For his essence is pure and lacks nothing, and it needs nothing else. Those who praise him are the ones who become more glorious. Not through [?]… [Other manuscripts read: "more noble than all these" [?]. Manuscripts read: "worldly, and continually entangles himself in every surge, but not." And so outside [?], in the margin: "entangles himself, but not"; Savile in the margin [?]. Three manuscripts read "will be found"; Morel and Savile read "will plunge."]

"They will speak of the magnificence of the glory of your holiness, and they will recount your wonders." Another translator has: "The beauty of your praise, and the words of your marvels they will recount." Since he had said "power," he shows that it is power beyond all measure. For it did not work imperfectly, nor did it do ordinary things. It went on working wonders and marvels in everything, acting beyond human nature, so that what was done was full of wonder and glory. Think, then, of what happened in Egypt and in Palestine, in the time of Abraham, of Isaac and of Joseph; then again in Egypt under Moses, in the wilderness, after the entry into the land; then in the captivity, under Nebuchadnezzar, at the furnace, among the lions, at the return, in the days of the prophets. All these things proclaimed the strength, the glory and the greatness of the one who did them, and they caused great astonishment and great wonder. "And they will speak of the power of your terrible deeds, and recount your greatness." By this he shows that his strength is complete for both ends, for doing good and for punishing, and that everything he listed contained both. This can be seen not only in what happened at that time but also in creation [470], where the instruments of each, [?] of punishment and of benefit, are many. Among the terrible things are lightning, thunder, thunderbolts, fiery whirlwinds, plagues, snow, hail, blight, frost, scorching heat and floods; among creeping things, serpents, scorpions and snakes; among winged creatures, the locust; and among the lowly creatures, the dog-fly and the caterpillar. These things above all belong to providence, for they turn people back, free them from sloth, wake them from deep sleep, and lead them from stupor to soberness. But his power is complete not only in these things but also in their opposites. That is why, wishing to teach us about these too, after saying, "They will speak of the power of your terrible deeds, and recount your greatness," he added: "They will pour forth the memory of the abundance of your goodness." Another has: "[?] and in your righteousness [?]"; another translator said, "They will extol your mercies." Just as we listed those terrible things, so [?] we must also speak of their opposites. Among the things we see around us, for example, there are the yearly seasons [?], the days, gardens, meadows, flowers of every kind [?], sweet drinking water and useful rain, the birth-pangs of the earth, fruits of every kind, trees of different sorts, gentle winds, the ray of the sun, the lamp of the moon, the varied dance of the stars, the gentleness of night. Among the irrational animals there are sheep, oxen and goats; among wild animals, gazelles, deer, hares and many others; among winged creatures, the Indian birds. And in his works themselves one may see that he does not only punish, but also does much good [?]. [Editorial notes: "Thunder" was missing in Morel [?] ... but it is wrongly read. Two manuscripts have "many others." [?] "those suitable for food," also "Indian." [?]]

[?] of wickedness, and to use the common debt of nature as a medicine, and to bring on them the lightest death, the death by water? The words "to all" can be seen to apply not only to this but to all visible things, to living creatures and to the irrational animals. And if one goes up to the angels themselves and the archangels, he will see great goodness and many compassions, for each of his works enjoys great kindness. Seeing this himself, he added: "Let all your works give thanks to you, O Lord, and let your holy ones bless you." That is: let them give you thanks and send up hymns to you, both those honored with reason and the things that have no voice. For each of the voiceless things was made in such a way that it sends up blessing through its own nature, voiceless though it is, through the people who see it and enjoy it. Those things bless him by their very being, but human beings also by their conduct and [472] by their actions. So he makes this clear by adding, "Let your holy ones bless you." By "holy ones" he means here the saints who fulfil the commandments of God, those whom sin and wickedness cannot reach. "They will speak of the glory of your kingdom." What does "speak of the glory" mean? His freedom from all need, he means, his love for mankind, his care; that he needs nothing from those he rules and yet shows such providence toward them; the inaccessibility of his light, the ineffability of his being, his incomprehensibility. "And they will talk of your dominion": that is, they will sing of your invincible, unconquerable power. This is not because you need these hymns and praises, but for the sake of those who speak them, so that they may also teach others and make them partners in the praise. That is why he added: "To make known to the sons of men your dominion, and the glory of the magnificence of your kingdom." He shows by this that he accepts praises so that others may learn of his dominion. Great, then, is his power, great his glory, great his splendor, great and ineffable. It not only surpasses all speech but defeats every mind. Yet this great and ineffable glory needs people to teach it, because of the folly of the many. The sun is the brightest of the stars, and yet those with diseased eyes do not see its light. In the same way the providence of God is brighter than any sun, but those whose reasoning is perverted and whose ears are stopped need much care before their minds can be opened. 4. So we must keep sounding this teaching in their ears and instilling it. Then, since he had spoken of the glory and magnificence of the kingdom and passed on without explaining it, he takes it up again and says, as far as he could, what that glory is, adding: "Your kingdom is a kingdom of all ages." Not only of the present ages, he means, but also of those to come, for it is endless and boundless, and it alone is eternal. "And your dominion is in every generation and generation." See its endlessness from this too. [?] [Editorial notes: Savile reads "to establish the things of wickedness." Below [?] "not in these" [?] "those ruled" [?] "they will sing"; but Morel reads "they will sing" [variant spelling]. Morel reads "because of the folly"; Savile "because of the ignorance" [?]. Another reads "and with closed ears." Savile reads "in due season."]

[?] everything is set apart and brought forth in different seasons. This above all shows his wisdom: he does not give everything at once, all together, but spreads out the sources of food over the whole year, so that the labor of the farmers [?] has its rest and what is produced does not spoil. So the words "in due season" mean either what we said before, that each thing is allotted its season, or that you give [474] food to those who need and want it. "And how," someone asks, "do the eyes of all hope in you? Yet there are many, those who live in impiety, who say that things exist by chance." Here he is speaking of the nature of the thing itself, as he does elsewhere when he says, "To the young ravens that call upon him," even though the animals have no reason. And again: "Young lions roaring to seize their prey, and to seek their food from God." These too have no reason, and they do not themselves seek. But here again he is speaking of the nature of the thing, for this must be said not from their choice but from the nature of what happens. "You open your hand and fill every living thing with good pleasure." By "hand" he means his activity and his power to provide, teaching you through everything to know that the birth of fruits lies not in the elements but in the providence of God. Or else he said "You open your hand" to show how easily he does it. The people of that time especially had abandoned the cause of all things and worshipped the air and the sun, thinking that these supplied the fruits. So, to lead them up to the principle above, to the cause and Master of these things, he keeps adding these words, showing that everything comes from his hand and that good things flow from his care. 5. Here he says that he "fills with good pleasure," that is, with satisfaction, because he fills each living thing with his will, with what pleases him. For he does not just give food; he gives it according to what is useful for each, according to the desire of each, to the full. What he means is this: you give to the irrational animals and to human beings and to all, as is sweet to each and as pleases each; and you do not only give but fill, so that nothing is lacking. That is why he says, "You fill every living thing with good pleasure." "The Lord is righteous in all his ways, and holy in all his works." By "ways" he means here his dispensations, his providence and his care, through which he shaped all things. For all his works, he says, are praises of him and full of wonders; they give no one a handle against him, even if some rage and rave. So by their nature the works are such that they shine out, gleam, and proclaim the providence, the care, the love for mankind, the righteousness and the holiness of their maker. "The Lord is near to all who call upon him, to all who call upon him in truth." See, here is another part of providence, the chief of all good things. Having spoken of what is given in common to unbelievers as well, food and rain, he speaks also of what is given specially to the faithful [?]. [Editorial notes: [?] "living. How then will they hope in you? he says; of the thing" [?] "to be read truly, as from" [?]. One manuscript has "harm." The repetition "to all who call upon him" is missing [?]. Two manuscripts have "of them was swallowed up, but."]

[?] your [Father] who is in heaven." And again Paul: "Glorify God in your body and in your spirit." And just as in the previous psalm he said, "Every day I will bless you," so here too he says, "I will sing to my God as long as I exist." Then, wanting once more to gain people as partners in the praise, he launches into the story of God's love for mankind, burning and warmed with longing, running round the whole world and gathering everyone into his own choir. For this above all is praise, this above all is glory to God: when one seeks out many who will share in his salvation. "Do not trust in rulers, in sons of men, in whom there is no salvation." Another has: "in one who cannot save." Let those listen to this exhortation and counsel who gape after human patronage, which is perishable and corrupt. What does "in whom there is no salvation" mean? They are not masters even of their own salvation, he means; they cannot even protect themselves. For if death comes, they will lie there more voiceless than stones. That is what he adds: "His breath will go forth, and he will return to his earth. On that day all his thoughts will perish." Another has: "his plans." What he means is this: how will one who cannot protect himself rescue others? Nothing is so precarious and rotten as a hope like that. The nature of things shows it. That is why Paul, speaking about hope in God, said: "And hope does not put us to shame." Human things are not like that; they are weaker than a shadow. Do not tell me that he is a ruler. The ruler has nothing more than the ordinary man; he is subject to the same uncertainty. And if I may say something surprising, it is precisely because he is a ruler that one should not trust him. Such powers stand on a knife-edge. Even if he does not fall, he is quick to anger and uses his power for ingratitude, since he does not expect to be answerable to the one who received the promise [?]. [477] And even if he proves well-disposed, he will be more liable to reversals than private persons, since he is exposed to greater and more numerous plots, and the more plotters he has, the easier he is to overthrow. What else do the bodyguards mean? What do all the guards mean? So if a man, in a well-governed city, cannot feel safe even about his own body, but lives in such anxiety, as if surrounded by enemies, how will he be able to save others? If in time of peace he is more afraid than men at war, how will he set others in safety and rescue them from danger? Many people who could have lived securely on their own found that this very thing, trusting in such men, became a snare to them: when those men fell, they were brought down with them. For others, the guards became traitors. Yet the prophet passes over all these things, since many have escaped them, and puts forward what cannot be disputed: death. For even if everything goes smoothly for you, he says, even if the ruler is kindly and grateful and means to repay you, he ends his life in the middle of his promises and leaves you with empty hopes, because his life is not long enough [?]. [Editorial note: Of these words, in place of "to the one who received the promise" [?] "to the one who received the office" [?] ... where one should read [?] "of those from whom he received the office" [?]; we suspect this to be the reading [?].]

[?] praises those who shine with virtue, saves those who have no protector, and comforts and restores those distressed and grieving because they are orphaned or widowed. Then, since he had said [that the Lord loves] the righteous, he shows that he has helped many for their misfortune alone. Those whom he feeds he feeds because they are hungry, and that is not a matter of virtue. Those in fetters he frees because of their chains; this too is not a matter of virtue but of misfortune. The blind he gives light to because of their blindness; this too is not an achievement but a misfortune. The same is true of being bowed down, of being a stranger, an orphan, a widow. If he cares for those in misfortune, how much more for those who devote themselves to virtue! Since, then, he both can and will, and all his resources are sufficient, and he welcomes virtue and has pity on misfortune, why do you not leave the one who is perishing, weak and mortal, and flee to the one who is strong and invincible, who does not reproach misfortunes but sets them right, who can do whatever he wishes? Notice too how precisely he put the last point. He did not say, "He will destroy sinners," but "their way," that is, their conduct. For he does not turn away from their nature; it is their wickedness he hates. "The Lord will reign for ever, [479] your God, O Zion, from generation to generation." If, then, he reigns always and remains always, there is no room for suspicion. Even if he does not give the reward here, he keeps it for greater things. So let us not be afraid or troubled in our trials if release does not come at once, but leave the time of release to the Lord himself. And if we accomplish some good, let us not demand the reward at once, but again wait for his will, for when he delays, he gives with a greater reward. Let us give thanks for everything and go on praising him. In this way we shall live the present life in great security and obtain the ineffable good things, by the grace and love for mankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and might, with his Father who is without beginning and the life-giving Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.

ON PSALM 146. "Praise the Lord, for a psalm is good." 1. Earlier, in Psalm 144, he said, "Great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised," and discoursed at length about his glory. Here he shows that praising itself is good and that the psalm is the cause of countless blessings. For it draws the mind away from the earth, gives the soul wings, lightens it and lifts it on high. That is why Paul says, "Singing and making melody to the Lord in your hearts." "May praise be sweet to our God." Another has: "Alleluia, for a song to God is good." What does "May praise be sweet to our God" mean? May it be acceptable, he means. Simply singing is not enough to make the praise sweet to God; the singer's life, his prayer and his care are needed too. This psalm seems to me to belong to the time of the return. And [?] [Editorial notes: One manuscript has "helped [them] for [their misfortune] alone." [?] "but even if not for a time here," not badly. Savile has "and the present age."]

That is why he said, "Of his greatness there is no end." And just as his greatness is infinite, so is his understanding. That is why, having said, "Great is our Lord," he added, "And of his understanding there is no number." His knowledge too is wonderful, which is why he said, "Your knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is mighty, I cannot attain to it." And his judgments again are unsearchable, which is why he said, "Your judgments are a great deep." 2. Since, then, he is great and mighty and wise, do not pry into how these things will come about. "The Lord lifts up the meek, but brings sinners down to the ground." So that no fool would say, "What is it to us that he knows the stars precisely?" he tells us that his care for human beings is just as exact. And he did not say, "The Lord helps the meek," but something much greater: "lifts up," as if speaking of a loving father [481]. What does "lifts up" mean? Restores, carries, bears them up. Do you see again that his power is complete for both, to raise the lowly and to bring down the arrogant? And he does not simply bring them down, but to the uttermost, for that is what "to the ground" means. "Begin to the Lord with thanksgiving." Another has: "Recount." Having told of his achievements, he calls them to the hymn again, saying, "Begin to the Lord with thanksgiving," that is, with gratitude and great zeal. "Sing to our God on the harp." Another has: "with the lyre." "To him who covers the heaven with clouds, who prepares rain for the earth." So that none of the senseless would say, "And what are heavenly things to me?" he immediately added human need, showing by what follows why he covers the heaven with clouds. For your sake, he says, so that he may prepare rain for you. And the rain is for your sake, so that it may bring forth grass. See the wisdom of it: he speaks of the universal blessings that he gave to all, silencing them more than enough. For if he shows such lavishness toward unbelievers that he gathers clouds, makes rain [?] and rouses the earth, how much more will he do for you, who were named his own special people? "Who makes grass spring up on the mountains." See the abundance of his providence: not only on arable land but on the mountains too he provides his lavish table, the food of the cattle that were made to serve human beings. That is why he goes on: "Who gives the cattle their food, and the young ravens that call upon him." He speaks again of another generosity, when he provides food not only for the cattle that serve human beings but also for other irrational creatures. "And to the young ravens," he says, "that call upon [him]" [?]. [Editorial notes: One manuscript has "of those senseless people." [?] "was named." [?] In the text of the psalm, "and green herb." Another has "because of the food." One adds "nor having gone astray."]

[?]… by saying, “your God.” For by this word he says all of this: that he has made you his own, that he has made you his heir, and that though he is the common Master of all, he is yours in a special way. That is the first and chief of the blessings. Second, he settled the city in safety. Third, he made its people many. Fourth, he freed from wars and turmoil not only the city but the whole nation. And he did this not once, or twice, or three times, but continually. He did not say, “He who set,” but, “He who sets.” If wars did break out at times, it was not because he abandoned them but because they [?] fell away from him. On his side this work was continual: to wall them in, to keep them safe, and to keep them free of all turmoil and war. Then he names another benefit after that one: good harvests and plenty in the fruits of the earth. Here too he teaches them to credit all of it not to the earth or to the nature of the air but to his providence. What benefit is this? The one he added when he said, “And filling you with the fat of wheat.” Notice that he did not say simply “wheat” but “the fat of wheat,” showing how great the prosperity was. “Fat of wheat” means the richness of the grain. Such are God’s gifts: choice and flourishing. So here he speaks of the finest wheat, and of filling [?] with abundance. To show this he did not say “giving” but “filling you.” “He who sends his word to the earth.” He often moves his discourse from particular things to common ones and back again, and he does so here too. He had said, “Praise your God.” So that none of the foolish among the Jews would think he is the God of the Jews alone, he shows that he is common to the whole world and that his providence reaches everywhere on earth. He leads the discourse from the particular to the common, to providence over all. That is why, having said, “He who sends his word to the earth,” he added, “His word will run swiftly.” He said this to show that God cares not only for our land but for the whole world. By “word” he here means his command, his providential working. Then he presents the ease of it, not only by the name “word” but also by the term “running.” Even this was not enough, and he added speed as well. What he means is this: whatever he commands happens very quickly. He gives commands throughout the world. What does he command? The things that hold our life together, I mean the ordering of the weather, its turnings and its changes. That is why he goes on to say, “Who gives snow like wool, scattering mist like ashes.” Another translator renders this “frozen dew.” [?] … “Casting his ice like morsels. Before the face of his cold, who will stand?” Another says, “Before the face of his heat, who will stand?” “He will send out his word and melt them; he will blow with his wind, and the waters will flow.” Here he sets before me the invincible and boundless nature of his power, that even things that do not exist [?] … [Notes: Other manuscripts read, “is the chief and first.” Others read, “does this.”]

… [casting] ice, but he added, “like morsels.” Here too he seems to me to show the ease and the resourcefulness of the one at work. “He who declares his word to Jacob.” Another translator has “his precise ordinances,” and another “his commands.” “His statutes and his judgments to Israel. He has not dealt so with any other nation.” Another has “likewise.” “And his judgments he has not made known to them.” See how he again moves the discourse from the universal to the particular, to the special privileges of the Jews, because he wants to rouse them to greater zeal. At the start of the psalm he spoke of things perceived by the senses that benefit the body, such as safety, good harvests and peace. Here he raises the discourse to higher things and unfolds the account of the giving of the law. This is the chief kind of benefit: leading away from vice, guiding toward virtue, enlightening the mind. That is why it is said, “What great nation is there that has God drawing near to it, as the Lord our God is in everything for which we call on him?” And David says again, “The Lord does deeds of mercy, and gives justice to all who are wronged. He made known his ways to Moses, his will to the children of Israel.” And Jeremiah says, “This is our God; no other shall be compared with him. He found out the whole way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant, and to Israel whom he loved.” But perhaps someone might ask: if he did not make these things known to the rest of mankind, how can he punish them? That he punishes both those who lived before the law and those who sin anywhere in the world is clear from what Christ says: “The queen of the south will rise up and condemn this generation.” And again: “The men of Nineveh will rise up and condemn this generation.” It was surely said this way because they too must give an account, and some are praised while others are punished. If they had not known what they ought to do, how could they condemn these people? How again could he say, “The blood will be avenged, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah”? And how could he say, “It will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah”? By saying “more tolerable” he shows that they do not escape entirely; they pay a lighter penalty for their sins. And if those who were already punished so severely will pay a penalty again, which of the others will escape? 3. We see that the people of the flood paid the penalty, as did many others, and Cain himself. Paul shows this very thing when he says, “The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and wickedness of those who hold down the truth by their wickedness, because what can be known of God is plain among them. For …” [Notes: “Precise ordinances” [?]; “commands,” Symmachus. [?] Others read, “which is greatest.” [?]]

… to those who have been careless. As far as the literal sense goes, what has been said is enough. But if anyone wants to take the psalm in the higher, spiritual sense as well, we will not refuse to travel this road too, as far as we can. We will not damage the historical sense, God forbid, but will add these things to it for the more diligent. “Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem; praise your God, O Zion.” Paul knows of a Jerusalem above, of which he says, “But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother.” He also knows of Zion as the Church, when he says, “For you have not come to a mountain that can be touched and that burns with fire, to gloom and darkness and storm, but you have come to Zion, the city, and to the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven.” So in the spiritual sense the verse can also be said of her: “Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem; praise your God, O Zion, for he has strengthened the bars of your gates and blessed your children within you.” He walled her in more securely than Jerusalem. He did it not with bars and doors but by fencing her with the cross and with the decree of his own power. By that decree he raised her wall everywhere, when he said, “The gates of Hades will not prevail against her.” 4. At the very beginning all kings, peoples and cities, the armies of demons, the devil’s tyranny itself and countless other things attacked the Church. Yet all of them came apart and perished, while she kept growing and was raised so high that she rose above the heavens themselves. “He has blessed your children within you.” At the beginning he said, “Increase and multiply and fill the earth,” and the word ran through all the earth. In the same way he said afterward, “Go and make disciples of all nations,” and, “This gospel will be preached in the whole world.” And the command reached the very ends of the earth in a brief moment of time. That is why he said, “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.” And again: “When I am lifted up, I will draw all people to myself.” At the beginning many came from one, as their number grew by the law of nature, and so the process moved more slowly. But in the time of the apostles the number grew not by the law of nature but by grace. So at once there were three thousand in one day, then five thousand, then tens of thousands, then the whole world. Born through this fine rebirth, they increased and multiplied and showed by their deeds the blessing they had received. For they were born “not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh,” but of the grace of God. “He who makes your borders peace.” This can be said most properly of the Church. What is more wonderful still, while she was at war she enjoyed peace, and while everyone plotted against her she revelled in security. That is why he said, “My peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you.” “And filling you with the fat of wheat.” This too can be said of the Church … [Notes: [?] “Go.” The words “then five thousand” were missing in Morel.]

… [heave]ns, and let the earth rejoice, for God has had mercy on his people.” And the same prophet again says, “When Israel went out of Egypt, the house of Jacob from a barbarous people, the mountains skipped like rams, and the hills like lambs of the flock.” And elsewhere Isaiah says, “Let the clouds rain righteousness.” They are not able on their own to praise the Master enough, so they go round to everyone and draw them all in to share in the hymn. This prophet does it especially often, as when he says, “And let all the angels of God worship him,” and again, “Mighty in strength, doing his word.” He also proves something else from all this. What is it? That no one among the more foolish should think there are two creators. Creatures differ and are distinct from one another in substance: one creation can be perceived by the senses and the other only by the mind; one is visible and the other invisible; one is full of bodies and the other is bodiless. So that no one would bring in different creators because the works differ, he sets up a single choir and raises one song to God from them all. He says that the same God must be praised both by the creation above and by the creation below, and in this way too he shows that there is one Creator of both. He begins first from above, saying, “Praise him, all his angels; praise him, all his powers.” Another translator has “all his hosts.” He means the cherubim, the seraphim, the dominions, the principalities, the authorities. Rousing everyone to praise the one it loves is the mark of a soul that burns fiercely, of a love on fire. It is the mark of a mind that constantly delights in the thought of God, that is amazed and marvels at his glory, and that is wholly devoted to him. “Praise him, sun and moon; praise him, all you stars and light.” Another has “stars of light.” “Praise him, you heavens of heavens, and you waters above the heavens; let them praise the name of the Lord. For he spoke, and they came to be; he commanded, and they were created. He established them for ever, and for ever and ever.” Another has “He established them to endure eternally.” “He laid down a command, and it will not pass away.” Why did he say only a little about the heavenly powers and quickly leap away from them? Why did he bring the discourse to visible things and dwell on them at length, going through all of them one by one, above and below? Because these were clearer to his hearers at the time, since they could be seen and lay before their eyes. That is why Moses too, when he began the account of creation, said nothing about the things above, small or great. He started from heaven and earth, went on through the sun and moon, plants, swimming creatures and four-footed beasts, and ended the account with man. When he says “heavens of heavens” here, he does not mean many heavens; “heaven of heaven” means the same heaven. In the Hebrew language it is customary to call heaven “heavens,” just as also [?] … or rather three, and if one looks closely, four

[four]: that he made them, that he made them out of nothing, that he made them with ease, and that he holds them together once they are made. Saying “He spoke” shows the ease, just as Paul showed it when he said, “who gives life to the dead and calls the things that are not as though they were.” By the word “calls” he hints at the ease. That God also holds things together once they are made, the prophet shows again when he adds, “He established them for ever, and for ever and ever. He laid down a command, and it will not pass away.” See how here again he points to God’s authority and sovereignty, not only with “established” but also by saying “command.” He shows God’s working in human words. For you, speaking is easy and giving an order is simple. In the same way, for God it is easy to make what did not exist and to hold together what he has made. Or rather it is not merely the same; it is much easier still. It is impossible to convey how surpassingly easily he made these things. What is truly wonderful is not only that he holds them together, or that the laws of nature stand unmoved, but that they have done so for such a boundless span of time. Think how long an age has passed, and nothing that exists has been thrown into confusion. The sea has not flooded the earth, and the sun has not burned up this visible world. Heaven has not been shaken, the boundaries of night and day have not been confused, and neither have the turnings of the seasons or anything else of the kind. Every single thing below and above stands with complete exactness and keeps the limits set for it once and for all at the beginning. So having spoken of the creation above and of the things in heaven, he comes down to the earth. Above, he began from the things beyond the heavens and came down to the heavenly ones. He does the same here, leaping from the heavenly things to the earth. There are some who say that the things in heaven are worthy of God’s creation but find fault with the things on earth, because there are scorpions on it, as they say, and vipers, serpents and the rest of the race of wild beasts, and trees that bear no fruit. As if answering these people, he handles his discourse in a different way. Look at what he does. He passes over the things that all agree are good: sheep and cattle, whose usefulness experience shows, and donkeys, camels and whatever is suited to carrying our goods. He turns his discourse instead to the things that seem useless. He brings forward serpents and the part of the sea that cannot be sailed, and the things that seem to do harm, such as fire, hail, snow and ice. Then come the fruitless trees and the mountains. Again he leaves aside the plains, which are level and suited to farming and to bearing cultivated crops, and moves on to the mountains and hills and the more desolate places, and he mentions all the creeping things. To understand this more clearly, it is worth listening to the words themselves. After saying, “He laid down a command, and it will not pass away,” he added, “Praise the Lord from the earth, [you serpents] …” [?] [Note: One manuscript reads “boundless.”]

… and that by remaining they fill the rank of servants, irrational as they are, and carry out his command with complete obedience. Indeed, a single command has often achieved even things contrary to nature. In the Babylonian furnace the fire was seen both burning and giving cool dew, doing both at once. “Is this, then, worthy of thanksgiving?” someone asks. Very much so. God must be praised alike when he punishes and when he releases from punishment, for both come from his care and both from his goodness. People do the one out of goodness and the other out of wickedness and anger, but God does both out of his love for mankind. So we must praise him alike for placing Adam in paradise and for driving him out. We must be grateful not only for the kingdom but also for Gehenna. He made Gehenna and threatened us with it in order to free us from vice. Think of a physician. We admire him not only when he feeds a patient but also when he squeezes him with hunger; not only when he takes him out into the market but also when he shuts him up indoors; not only when he anoints him but also when he burns and cuts. The things he does are opposites, yet they look to a single end.
