In the same way we must praise God for everything, and all the more because he is God while the physician is a man, and because a physician’s treatments often turn out the opposite of what he intended, while what God does is done with fitting wisdom and care. Hail and fire do not only punish. They have also freed people from punishment, stopped wars and driven back attacking enemies. Do you not know how many wonders were worked through these elements in Egypt, among the Jews, and in our own generation? So great is the power of the one who commands that what he did through angels, those great powers endowed with mind, he often worked through the elements as well. Then, whenever an angel does such things, none of the more foolish would credit them to the angel; they would credit the one who gave the command. Did an angel stop a war? So did hail. Did an angel destroy the firstborn? A storm at sea destroyed an entire people. So give thanks for all things to God, who loves mankind. “Mountains and all hills, fruit trees and all cedars; wild beasts and all cattle, creeping things and winged birds.” See how he lingers on the less useful things: mountains and glens, hills, wild beasts, creeping things and fruitless trees. Fruit-bearing things show their usefulness at once, as do level plains and tame animals. “But what use are wild beasts, creeping things, mountains and fruitless trees?” someone asks. A great deal, and they do much to sustain our life. Mountains, hills and fruitless trees are very useful to us for building [?] … [the beast] has its savagery out in the open, but this one hides his wicked-

-ness behind a mask of gentleness, and so is often hard to guard against. But if you are watchful, neither beast nor man will do you any harm; they will even benefit you greatly. Why do I speak of beasts and men, when even the devil himself did Job no harm at all, and instead gave him the occasion for countless crowns? Why do I speak of beasts and men, when even the elements within you will make you suffer far worse if you are careless? Bile and phlegm will do so, for instance, if you let them get out of hand through some lack of moderation. So a watchful mind is needed everywhere. Carelessness will bring you the greatest harm, but if you are watchful and alert you will reap no small benefit, for everything depends on your own will. What snow, fire and wind are in the universe, phlegm, blood and bile are in the body. These must be managed with the best judgment, so that we draw some benefit from them and are not harmed. And why speak of the body, when the soul too has certain things that become diseases if you let them run to excess, but become helps if they are kept in check? Anger, if you use it when it is needed, becomes a medicine for your salvation; if you use it without measure, it becomes the cause of your ruin. Desire, managed with measure, makes you a father and is useful for having children; but let loose, it often throws you down into fornication and adultery. So do not blame things; in every case blame your own will. If you neglect it, you will be harmed by yourself and destroyed by your own body. But if you take care of it, you will suffer nothing terrible even from demons or from the devil, let alone from wild beasts.

“Kings of the earth and all peoples.” Another translator has “all tribes.” “Rulers and all judges of the earth; young men and maidens.” Another has “chosen ones.” “Old men together with the younger.” Another has “with the young.” “Let them praise the name of the Lord.” Here again he brings up another kind of providence, that of rulers. Paul also sets this out in his Letter to the Romans, where he shows with great understanding that it is the work of God’s wisdom to order this whole world into rulers and ruled. “For he is God’s servant for your good,” he says. Take this away and everything is lost. Even now, when there are rulers and many of them are corrupt, the institution is so needed that great benefit comes from it even when they are badly disposed. So think how much prosperity the human race would have enjoyed if those entrusted with office had handled it well. Shaping the offices was God’s work. That wicked men come to hold them and do not use them as they should is the fault of human wickedness. 5. So he says that we must also offer great thanks to God that there are kings and judges. He cares for good order among people and wants to keep the multitude from being in a state more irrational than the beasts. So he granted offices and kingdoms, much as he granted the skill of the charioteer and the helmsman. And if … [Note: Another manuscript reads “ready.”]

…who has the glory. From now on our part must follow as well, and we too shall enjoy great splendour, by the grace and loving-kindness of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and might for ever and ever. Amen.

[498] On Psalm 149. "Sing to the Lord a new song." 1. In the anagogical sense, the song of the New Covenant is called a new song, for at that time all things became new. The covenant: "I will make with you," it says, "a new covenant." The creation: "If anyone is in Christ," it says, "he is a new creation." Man: "Having put off," it says, "the old man, and having put on the new, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of the one who created him." So because of the new life, and all the other things, it is called the New Covenant, and the prophet now urges us to sing its new song. In the historical sense, it is the song they were to sing over victories, over successes, over trophies, a splendid and remarkable song. "His praise in the assembly of the holy." Do you see how, before words, he looks for thanksgiving expressed through life and deeds, and leads such people into the choir of those who sing hymns? It is not enough to give thanks with words alone unless virtue shown in action goes with it. "His praise in the assembly of the holy." He teaches something else here too. He shows that we must offer our praises together and in complete harmony, for "assembly" is the name for a gathering and a meeting. "Let Israel rejoice in him who made him." He puts the universal benefit before the particular ones, all but urging us by what he adds, and saying: Give thanks to God, because when you did not exist he brought you into being and breathed a soul into you. This too is no small part of his kindness. But here he shows something more. By speaking this way he points not simply to the act of creation but to a special relationship, and he bids Israel give thanks not just because God made him, but because God made him his own people. Do you see how, uniting and joining him to God, he wants him to give thanks not simply, but with pleasure, with gladness, with his mind glowing with warmth? He hinted at all this with the words "Let him rejoice." So he looks for the inner disposition of the one giving thanks: that he be set on fire with longing, roused by love, wholly devoted to the God he is hymning. Elsewhere he showed the same thing when he said, "As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God." And again, "My soul has thirsted for God, the mighty, the living." And again, "My soul has thirsted for you, how many ways my flesh for you, in a desert land, trackless and waterless"; which another translator rendered, "as in a thirsty land." Wanting to portray the disposition and the longing of his soul, he compares it to a thirsty land and to a thirsting deer. [499] And again he shows the same longing in words, saying, "When shall I come and appear before the face of God?" Such are the souls of the saints, like Paul's, which groaned at the delay of its departure from this world [?]… One manuscript: "for this reason also a new life, and all the other things; for this reason it is called the New Covenant." … "In the historical sense." b One manuscript: "of those who hymn him." One manuscript: "seeks." One manuscript: "but also in the display of wonders."

…having worked. "And they shall exult upon their beds." With these added words he shows great security, great relief, great gladness, great pleasure. He says this so that they would know that it was not by their own weapons or their own strength but by God's intervention that all of it happened, and that this help must be drawn down through humility and meekness. "The exaltations of God in their throat, and two-edged swords in their hands, to execute vengeance among the nations, reproofs among the peoples." Here he points to a war waged with dancing, and to the fact that they will prevail by singing and hymning. By "exaltations" he means hymns, psalmody, thanksgivings. That is why another translator rendered "exaltations" as "hymns." "To execute vengeance among the nations, reproofs among the peoples." What does this mean? Since the enemies, who had prevailed all that time, kept taunting them, he promises to refute them through deeds, and to show through their own deeds that it was not God's weakness but their sins that had let the enemy prevail. Indeed, once they had paid a sufficient penalty, the loving God merely nodded, and their affairs underwent an astonishing reversal. And see how overwhelming the victory is. He goes on to say: "To bind their kings with fetters, and their nobles with iron manacles." Do you see the abundance of strength? They did not merely drive the enemy off or push them back; they returned with them as prisoners, displaying God's strength to all. "To execute among them the written judgment." What is a "written judgment"? One that is evident, acknowledged, that cannot be handed over to oblivion. Such are the works [?] of God: by the greatness of the achievements and the overwhelming wonder of the miracles, they reach through all time. Such, he says, will the victory be, and such the trophy, so that it is plain to all, as clear as if written on a pillar and never erased. "This glory is for all his holy ones." What glory is this? To conquer; or rather, not simply to conquer, but to conquer in this way, through God's alliance, through help from above. See how he mentions the holy ones, rousing them to care for their life and for virtue. But it seems to me that he calls not only the victory glory, but also the praise, the melodies and the hymns, teaching through all of this that by hymning God they will clothe themselves in great glory and make themselves more splendid, by the grace [501] and loving-kindness of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and might for ever and ever. Amen.
On Psalm 150. "Praise God in his holy ones." Another translator: "In his holy place." Another: "In his sanctified [?]"
Here he says this either about the people, or about a holy life and holy men. See how he has again closed the book with thanksgiving, teaching us that… One manuscript: "how again here of the."

…let it praise the Lord. Another translator: "breath." He sets every instrument in motion and bids the melody be offered through all of them, warming and rousing their minds. So just as he bade the Jews hymn God with all their instruments, he bids us hymn him with all our members: with the eye, with the tongue, with the hearing, and with the hand. Paul shows this too when he says, "Present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God, which is your spiritual worship." For the eye praises when it does not look at licentious things; the tongue, when it sings psalms; the hearing, when it does not take in wicked songs or accusations against one's neighbour; the mind, when it does not stitch together schemes of deceit but overflows with love; the feet, when they do not run to wickedness but to the carrying out of good works; the hands, when they are stretched out not for robbery, greed and blows, but for almsgiving and the protection of the wronged. Then a person becomes a tuneful lyre, offering God a melody that is wholly harmonious and spiritual. Those instruments were permitted back then for this reason: because of the people's weakness, to blend them together in love and concord, to rouse their minds to do with pleasure what was for their benefit, and because he wished to lead them to great zeal through this kind of delight. For God, devising a remedy for their coarseness, their laziness and their slackness, [?] … for ever and ever. Amen.

On the saying of the prophet David, "Do not fear when a man becomes rich, or when the glory of his house is increased," and on hospitality. 1. It is pleasant for the farmer to draw the plough to clear his field, to cut the furrow, to pull up the thorns, and then to sow the seed with no thorn there to spoil the sowing. But it is far more pleasant for the speaker when he sows divine thoughts into a hearing that is free of tumult. That is why we take up the word with pleasure, because we see that this field has been cleared. Even if we cannot see your minds, your wide-open eyes and your attentive, upraised hearing give me signs of the calm within. I cannot enter into your conscience, but your eyes, fixed and lifted up, give out a voice that says, "There is no tumult within"; or rather, you cry out eagerly, "Sow the seed; we receive whatever you sow, in hope of the harvest, for we have thrust every worldly care out of our minds." [505] That is why I always take up deeper thoughts, confident in the good quality of the field. Scripture looks not only for a wise teacher but also for an intelligent hearer. So I call you blessed, and myself blessed as well. "Blessed," it says, "is he who speaks into the ears of those who listen"; and, "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness." So we shall sow our thoughts among you who have come so eagerly. All the others are now rotting away in marketplaces and worldly cares, while you, rising higher than the earth, receive spiritual thoughts. They serve the slave-woman by tending the flesh, while you adorn and preserve the noble, free soul. Where are you spending your time now, man? In the marketplace. To gather what? Mud and clay. [?] Take ointment from me. Why do you gather money that perishes, avarice the tyrant, offices that perish, an abundance of worldly cares, the… One manuscript: "according to the good quality of the field." b Two manuscripts: "peoples." Another reads "spiritually" instead of "spiritual." Patrologia Graeca 55.

…[when I] see you deceitful, how shall I call you a man and not a [?]? When I see you full of venom, how shall I call you a man and not an asp? When I see you senseless, how shall I call you a man and not a donkey? When [506] I see you committing adultery, how shall I call you a man and not a stallion mad for mares? When I see you disobedient and without understanding, how shall I call you a man and not a stone? You received nobility from God; why do you betray the excellence of your nature? What are you doing? Tell me. Other people have the skill to raise irrational animals, as far as possible, to human nobility. They teach parrots to speak with a human voice and force nature by skill; they make lions tame and lead them through the marketplace. You make the lion, an untamable animal, tame, and yet you make yourself wilder than a wolf? And what is worse, each of the irrational animals has a single defect: the wolf its rapacity, the snake its deceit, the asp its venom. With a wicked man this is not so. Often a man has not just one defect; he becomes rapacious and deceitful and venomous all at once, and gathers the vices of the irrational animals into his own soul. How then shall I call you a man, when you do not have the emblem of kingship, the diadem, or the purple? "Let us make," it says, "man after our image and likeness." Consider after whose image you were made, man, and do not let yourself be dragged down to the worthlessness of the irrational animals. If you saw a king who had thrown off his purple and diadem, was herding together with the soldiers, and was betraying his own rule, what would you call such a king? You too are a man. So do not show me that you have a human soul; show me whether you are a man in your way of thinking. You are ruler of the irrational animals, and have you become a slave of the irrational passions within you? 2. "And how am I to become a man?" someone says. If you master the thoughts of the flesh, those irrational things; if you cast out fornication; if you cast out untimely desire for money; if you cast out that wicked tyrant; if you have made your own ground clean. But how do you become a man? If you come here, where men are fashioned. If I take you as a horse, I make you a man; if I take you as a wolf, I make you a man; if I take you as a snake, I make you a man, not by changing your nature but by transforming your will. But what does he say? "I have children, I run a household, I look after a wife, I am in the grip of poverty, I am busy getting the food I need." These are pretexts and excuses. If I kept you here all the time and did not let you give even a brief moment to outside affairs, you could defend yourself to me and say, "I have children and run a household," and you would be right to say so; or rather, you ought not to say it even then. For while you are occupied here, God is able to arrange all your affairs with greater abundance. But as it is, I compel you to none of this. I do not say, "Take time off every day," but twice a week. What is heavy about that, what is burdensome? Not even the whole day; come to the church for a brief moment. Receive… [?] "a human voice." Below, others read "untamable beast." One manuscript: "with the generals." One manuscript: "that tyranny," not a bad reading. [?] "…affairs, you would say this; or rather you ought never to say this. For God is able."

…the spiritual song. For when envy comes in, and the verse comes in after it, the saying drives the passion away. "Do not fear when a man becomes rich." These are my medicines: they require not money but heaven. I do not treat the body; I heal the soul, and I do not mean only yours, but mine as well. Though I am a teacher, I am a man, subject to our common nature, and I offer a teaching that is common to us all. "Do not fear when a man becomes rich." Take this verse as a treasure and a foundation; take the verse as the root of wealth and plenty. For it is not being rich but not wanting to be rich that is true wealth. Did you understand what was said to you? Whoever wants to be rich needs possessions and money; whoever does not want to be rich always lives in plenty. "Do not fear when a man becomes rich, or when the glory of his house is increased." Do not fear: why, tell me? Since the rich inspire fear, the prophet speaks out life [?]. Why do you fear a man thick with leaves but bare of fruit? Why do you fear a man rooted in bitterness? Why do you fear a man who is always trembling? Why do you fear a man who lives with constant fear? Your slave does not fear you when you are away, but that man carries his master around inside him. Wherever he goes, the love of money follows him; and neighbours, servants, friends, the envious, benefactors — he has them all alike as enemies, for he stirs up great envy. The poor man lives fearing no one, since he is rich only in philosophy and endurance. The rich man, since he lives with greed, is hated by all and goes about in public gatherings as an enemy, flattered to his face but hated in people's thoughts. That this is how things are is clear when the wind comes and strips away the leaves, when a reversal of fortune occurs. Then the pretended friends are found out, then the masks of the flatterers are recognized, then the chorus of hypocrites is exposed, along with the pretence of the drama. Everyone's mouth opens to say, "The vile man, the wicked man, the utterly wicked man!" What are you saying? Weren't you flattering him only yesterday? Weren't you kissing his hands? "That was a mask. The time came, I took off the mask and declared what I really thought." So why, tell me, do you fear someone accused by so many? And what of that? If only he were not his own accuser! I say this, as I have said countless times, not to disparage wealth, but to disparage those who make bad use of a good thing. Money accompanied by good deeds is good. How is it good? [509] If it relieves poverty, if it remedies destitution. Hear what Job says: "I was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame; I was a father to the powerless." Here is wealth, and there was no sin in it, but love of the poor. "My house was open to everyone who came." This is the service wealth can do, wealth not in name but in reality. This wealth is the servant of that other wealth: this one is a name empty of reality, while that one possesses the truth of both name and reality. Which one? The wealth of virtues, of almsgiving. How so? I will tell you. There is a rich man who snatches everyone else's goods, and there is a rich man who gives his own goods to the poor. The one is rich by gathering, the other by spending; and the one sows the earth… Others: "was opened to every man."

…[of one who] loves? Is it the act of someone who loves you, or of someone who hates you? "But you hate me." No, I love you. I have a command from my Master: "Love your enemies." I will not stop trying to heal you. Our Master was being crucified, and he said, "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing." Am I persecuting you? I am driving out your passion. Am I fighting you? I am fighting your wickedness. And do you not think of me as a benefactor? Do you not think of me as a guardian? Do you not think of me as your protector more than anyone else? Who else will speak to you about these things? The magistrate? Nothing of the kind; he speaks about charges and accusations. Your wife? About jewellery and gold. Your son? About his inheritance, the will, his share of the estate. Your servant? About his duties, his slavery, his freedom. Your hangers-on? About banquets, dinners and lunches. The people at the theatre? About shameful laughter and licentious desire. The man in the law courts? About wills, inheritances and freedom, the business he deals in. Where can you hear these things except from me? Everyone fears you, but I despise you. As long as you are like this I despise you, I look down on you, I despise your passion. I cut and you cry out, but I am not afraid of your voice; I long for your salvation, for I am a physician. If you had a wound and called in a physician, and saw him sharpening his knife, would you not say, "Cut, even if it hurts," expecting to be saved by the cutting? Yet you run away from me, though I do not cut you but cleanse your mind with words. And what does the physician do? He often cuts and makes the wound worse; I do not make it worse, but better. There it is nature that is helpless and medicines that lack power; here it is the power of words. The physician does not guarantee your recovery, but I guarantee your salvation. Listen to me. This is why the only-begotten Son of God came down: to lead us up [511] and make us higher than the heavens. I fear one thing only: sin. Let everything else go — wealth, poverty, power, anything at all. I say this, and I will not stop saying it, for I want no one in my flock to perish. What then? Can a rich man be saved? Certainly. Job was rich; Abraham was rich. You have seen his wealth? Look also at his hospitality. You have seen his table? Look also at his kindliness. What then of Abraham? He was rich. Did I argue with you about that? Was Abraham rich? Yes, he was rich. You have seen his wealth? Look also at his way of life. "At midday the Lord appeared to him by the oak of Mamre as he was sitting, and behold, three men. And he rose" (for he did not think it was God who was there; how could he?) "and bowed down, and said: If you have judged me worthy, come into the tent of your [?]." Do you see what the old man was doing at midday? He was not sitting under a roof; he was drawing in strangers and travellers known to him from nowhere, and the rich, noble man rose and bowed down. Setting money aside and leaving behind his house, his wife, his children, his servants — though he had three hundred and eighteen of them — leaving them all, he went out fishing. He spread the net of hospitality, in case a traveller or a stranger should pass by his house. See what the old man does. He does not leave it to a servant, though… Two manuscripts: "and than human things."

…measures of fine flour." A laborious order, a burdensome command: "Knead three measures of fine flour." She did not say, "What is this? Was it on these hopes that I married you, so that you could make me a mill-girl and a baker, a woman with so much wealth? You have three hundred and eighteen servants, and you did not choose to give the order to them; you push me into this service instead?" She said nothing of the kind. She did not even think it. Because she was Abraham's wife, joined to him not only in bodily union but also in a partnership of virtue, he says, "Hurry," and she seizes the command eagerly, for she knew that the fruit of hospitality was bursting forth. "Hurry, knead." He knew how diligent his wife was. Where are the women of today? Let us compare them with Sarah. Do they accept orders like these? Tasks like these? Hold out for me the hand of a woman who loves finery, and you see it gilded on the outside, but holding the fruits of a siege within. Tell me, how many poor people's goods does your hand carry, seized by greed? Hold out your hand for me, show it: what is it clothed in? Greed. Hold out Sarah's hand. What is it clothed in? Hospitality, almsgiving, love, love of the poor. O beautiful right hand! Look at one right hand and at the other. The shape of a right hand is the same, but the difference is great. There, fountains of tears; here, crowns and prizes. I say this so that wives will not seek such things from their husbands, and husbands will not put up with wives who demand them. See Sarah, see the rich woman kneading three measures of fine flour. How great the labor! But she did not feel the labor, because she hoped for the fruit and the gain. "Hurry, knead three measures of fine flour." What are you doing, woman? Making yourself beautiful? To please whom? Your husband? That is a poor pursuit, if this is how you mean to please your husband, if this is how you are eager to please him. How then will you please him? By modesty. And how else will you please him? By gentleness [?], by wisdom, by meekness and love, by concord and harmony. These are your ornaments, woman. These virtues of yours produce concord. Those other ornaments do not make you pleasing; they even make you a burden to your husband. When you say, "Go and grab it and bring it to me," you please him for a little while, but later you have an enemy. And here is how you can tell that it is not your husband you are pleasing: at home you take these things off, and in church you put them on. If you were pleasing your husband, you would wear them at home. But, as I said, you come into church with your hands and neck covered in gold. If Paul comes in, that awesome and beloved man, awesome to sinners and beloved by the devout, he cries out and says just the same: "Women ought to adorn themselves not with gold, not with pearls, not with costly clothing." Then if a pagan Greek comes in and sees those women up there wearing these things, and Paul down here saying these things, will he not say that this is a stage play and a fable? Our faith is not a stage play, even if things happen this way. But the Greek is harmed, and says: "I went into a church of the Christians and heard Paul saying, 'Not with gold, nor with pearls,' and I saw her showing the opposite by what she did." What good is the gold to you, woman? To look beautiful? [Variant readings:] Another manuscript has: "on hopes I was married to you." Others have: "only of bodies." In Savile these words, "Look at one right hand and at the other," are missing. Two manuscripts have: "What are you doing, woman? Making yourself beautiful? Why? So that you can please your husband completely? If this is how you are eager…" Others have: "What are you doing? Making yourself beautiful?" Two manuscripts have: "…that these things are a pretext; for our faith is not a pretext."

[?] …nor should the rich man rejoice because of his wealth. Are you well off? Your wealth is lost unless you bring the fitting wealth out into the open. "Hurry and knead three measures of fine flour." Then he himself ran to the herd and slaughtered a calf. The old man became a runner. The vigor of his flesh did not slacken; his mind was braced by wisdom, and eagerness conquered nature. The master of three hundred and eighteen household servants carried a calf, and he was not weighed down by the burden; his mind was made light by eagerness. The old man had running to do and much service, and the wife had toil and labor. For they welcomed the strangers not only with a generous outlay and a lavish table but also with much ministering and service. They served not through servants but with their own hands and limbs. Then the wife stood by, taking the part of a maidservant, while the strangers reclined at table, unknown to them. I will not stop saying this. They thought these men were just some poor people, but they paid no attention to that, only to the fact that they were receiving strangers. And both of them stood by at that time, harvesting the grape-cluster of hospitality with their goodwill, their wisdom, their service, their welcome, their toil, their ministry, their love, their management, their care, and by leaving nothing undone. And the woman stood by the tree. She used the tree instead of a private room and had the shade of the leaves as her roof, and she was not ashamed to be seen in public. She stood there showing her own modesty and harvesting the fruit of her service. What then did the visitor say? "At this season I will come, and Sarah will have a son." What fruit the table put forth! How beautiful, how quick, how ripe, how dark and perfect the cluster! For that word entered the womb and fashioned the child. Such are the fruits of hospitality. Pay attention to what I am about to say. After this, the child born of the table grew up. When the fruit of hospitality became a man (for that womb did not give birth to him so much as the table did, and above all the word of God), when he had grown and become a man, and it was now time for marriage (pay close attention to what I say), the old man, that blessed Abraham, the patriarch, was about to die. He was living as a sojourner among corrupt women and a most wicked nation, so he called his own servant and said: "The women of the Canaanites here are wicked." What then do you want? "Go to the land where I was born, and bring a wife from there for my son." This is new and astonishing! You know it, and know it very well: when someone wants to get a wife for his son, both the father and the mother negotiate. They go to other people's houses, flattering this one and courting that one. There are many matchmakers, many bridal escorts, promises of money, and every effort by father and mother to negotiate in person. They are not ashamed and do not blush, nor do they leave it to servants. But when a stranger comes, it is: "You go, bring him down, receive him." Abraham did the reverse. When he had to do [?] [Note:] Savile conjectures ἐπενευροῦτο or ἐπενενεύρωτο, but all manuscripts have ἐπενεύρωτο. Morel has ὑποφαίνεται. [?] …but the stranger he [received] himself, and the [matter] of the marriage… [Variant readings:] One manuscript has: "and of all." One has: "the splendor. You say, it has marble…"

[?] …golden [?] of the columns. What is that to his head, filthy with sins? The floor is clean? But the conscience is unclean. The clothes are silk? But the soul is full of rags. The house is rich, but the owner of the house is poor. "When the glory of his house is increased." To show you that the glory belongs to the house and not to the man, I will convict you from your own words. You often go into someone's beautiful house. When you come out, what do you say? "I saw beautiful marble." Do you say, "I saw a beautiful man"? "The columns are wonderful, the windows lovely." Do you say, "The man who lives there is wonderful"? "There's a lot of gold on the ceiling." Do you say, "His almsgiving is great"? "There are many fountains, and great abundance." Do you say, "The owner's generosity is great"? Everything you talk about is the walls, the marble, the fountains, the springs. Again, you see a horse with a golden bridle, and you say, "A fine bridle." Then the praise belongs to the goldsmith. "A wonderful garment." Then the praise belongs to the weaver. "Fine servants." Then the praise belongs to the man who sold them. The owner goes uncrowned, while the things around him enjoy the praise. But when you see a good man, you say: "A good man, fine, gentle, wonderful, merciful, kindly, contrite, always attentive in prayer, always persevering in fasting, always spending his time in church, never parted from divine teaching." These praises are about him; these are crowns. Learn, then, what a man's wealth is and what a house's wealth is, and "Do not be afraid." If you learn to tell wealth apart properly, you will no longer be afraid. Do you see that the man you consider rich is poor and a beggar? "Do not be afraid when a man becomes rich." And to see that this is how things are: if he deceives you here, look at him at the hour of his death. [Variant:] "the praise belongs to the one who toiled."

Delivered after another had spoken first: a homily given at Constantinople in the Great Church, when few had gathered, on "Do not be afraid when a man becomes rich," and on almsgiving.

The fruit of the one who spoke so well was small, but ripe. The string was thin, but the sound was great. The words were few, but the thoughts were rich. He lifted a whole people on wings with his praises and made them more zealous with his commendations. He revealed the one responsible for the harvest, composing hymns to him, and, giving thanks according to the apostle's rule, he ended his discourse in a doxology. If he cleared the table quickly, it was not from poverty but from humility. It was not for lack of more to say that he closed his discourse in silence, but [to leave] to us [the rest] of the teaching [?] … Let us also imitate these, and, freed from the recent

disturbance, the tumult and the waves, let us moor our soul in the reading of the Scriptures as in a calm harbor. The company of the divine Scriptures is a harbor without waves, an unbreakable wall, an unshakable tower, a glory that cannot be taken away, armor that cannot be pierced, an unfading cheerfulness, an unending pleasure, and every good thing one could name. It drives off despondency and preserves cheerfulness. It makes the poor man richer than the wealthy and surrounds the rich with security. It makes the sinner righteous and sets the righteous under safe guard. It uproots the evils that are present and plants the goods that are absent. It drives out wickedness and leads back to virtue. And it does not only lead back to virtue; it roots it firmly and makes it last forever, for it is a spiritual medicine, a divine and ineffable charm that destroys the passions. It pulls up the thorns of sin, makes the field clean, sows the seeds of piety, and brings the fruit to maturity. Let us not neglect such great goods, then, or stay away from the assemblies. Let us run here continually, so that we may be continually healed. Let no one be struck by envy at the sight of a rich man, or be crushed by poverty. Let him learn the true nature of things, pass by the shadows, and hold fast to the truth. A shadow, even if it seems larger than the body, is still only a shadow. In any case it is not larger; it only seems so, and it seems so only when we are farther from the sun's ray. At high noon, when the ray stands directly overhead, the shadow is drawn in from all sides, contracted, and becomes shorter. One can see the same thing in human affairs. As long as someone places himself far from virtue, the affairs of this present life look great. But when he places himself in the very brightest light of the divine Scriptures, then he sees how cheap, how brief, and how worthless these perishable things are. He learns clearly that they are no better than river water, which appears and passes by at the same moment. That is why the prophet, speaking as a philosopher, set out to correct the small-souled and wretched, those who grovel on the ground, gape at the illusion of wealth, and fear and tremble before those who pride themselves on it. He led us away from such anxiety and persuaded us to despise these things as nothing, saying: "Do not be afraid when a man becomes rich, or when the glory of his house is increased. For when he dies he will not take any of it with him." Do you see the precision of his wording and how clear his distinction is? He did not say, "When his glory is increased," but "the glory of his house," showing that a man's glory is one thing and a house's glory another. What, then, is a man's glory, and what is a house's glory? We must know this clearly, so that we do not embrace dreams instead of the truth. The glory of a house is colonnades, walks, a golden ceiling, a floor adorned with mosaic, meadows, gardens, herds of slaves, costly furniture, none of which [belongs] to the man. A man's glory is right faith, zeal according to God, love, meekness, gentleness, in [?] … [Variant readings:] Savile: "of the shadow." Savile: "larger, but then it seems." Savile: "are disposed" (plural). Savile: "of the words." Savile in the margin: "But why do you not love?" Savile in the margin: "[?] you do not love."

…and he talked with a prostitute, was crucified with robbers, and mingled with human beings. But you, enslaved by pride and folly, lose even your humanity? This is the source of our great contempt for almsgiving, our lust for gain, our cruelty and inhumanity. You put a golden bridle on your horse, a golden collar on your servant, gold leaf on stone. You have gilded hides in your house, golden garments, a golden belt, shoes. You load yourself with all these compulsions of wickedness, wanting to fill an insatiable desire and to feed the cruelest of all beasts, avarice. And then you strip orphans and leave widows naked, and you go about as the common enemy of everyone, spinning out a futile labor and running a race that has no good end. What do you want by having your barbarian servant wear gold? What is the gain? What benefit is it to the soul? What profit to the body? What income to the household? It is entirely the opposite: an untimely expense, an outlay full of folly, an occasion for licentiousness, a school of vice, an incitement to a vulgar and dissolute life, the corruption of the soul, a road leading to countless evils. And the beds inlaid with silver and sprinkled with gold, the footstools, the basins made of the same, and all that absurdity: how can they set your life right? How have they made you better, or your wife, or anyone else in the house? Is this not the source of many robbers and burglars? Is this not why servants run away? When they look around and see silver glittering everywhere, the disease of theft is fed in them. If you, a free man who prides himself on his noble birth, are drawn into desire by silver shining in the marketplace, how much more the servant! I say this not to acquit runaway servants and those who commit such crimes of blame, but to urge you not to set before them food for such diseases. "But where shall we put these things?" someone says. "Shall we bury them in the ground?" Far from it! If you will accept my advice, I will tell you a way to make the runaway well-behaved. For wealth is a runaway, leaping today to this man and tomorrow to another. And it is not only a runaway but a maker of runaways, often turning those who guard it into fugitives. How then can this runaway be held? In the opposite way from other runaways. The others stay when they are guarded, but this one flees when guarded and stays when scattered. If this seems a strange thing to say, learn it from farmers. If they shut their grain up in the house and heap it there, they hand it over to moth and worm and lose it. But if they scatter it on the fields, they not only preserve it but increase it. So too with wealth. When it stays in chests, behind doors and bars, or is buried in the ground, it quickly runs away. But if you scatter it into the bellies of the poor, as the farmer scatters grain on the field, not only does it not run away, it grows greater from there. Knowing this, do not entrust it to a servant. Have it held by countless hands: the hands of widows, of orphans, of those maimed in body, of those who live in prison.

[?] …will say: "How many tears built this house! How many orphans were stripped, how many widows wronged, how many deprived of their wages!" So the opposite of what you want happens to you. You wanted to enjoy glory while you lived, but not even after your life has ended are you rid of your accusers. The house carries your name about as if on a bronze pillar, and it leads even those who never saw you alive to pelt you with countless [?]

4. Since this excessive ambition does not bring even this gain, let us flee, beloved, let us flee this disease, and not become more savage than the irrational animals. For them everything is common: land, springs, pastures, mountains, glens, and none has more than another. But you, a human being, the gentlest of creatures, become harsher than a beast, shutting up in a single house the food of countless poor people, often of countless [?]. And yet it is not only nature that we share, but other things far greater than nature. Heaven is common to all, and the sun, the moon, the chorus of stars, the air, the sea, fire, water, earth, life, death, growth, old age, sickness, health, and the need for food and clothing. Spiritual things too are common: this holy table, the Lord's body, the precious blood, the promise of the kingdom, the bath of regeneration, the cleansing of sins, righteousness, sanctification, redemption, the ineffable goods "which eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, and which have not entered the heart of man." Is it not absurd that those who [share] in so many [?] … the power, forever and ever. Amen.

Homily delivered in the Great Week, in which there is also teaching on why it is called Great [?], and on "Praise the Lord, O my soul," and on the jailer in Acts.

1. We have completed the voyage of the fast, and by God's grace we have at last reached the harbor. But let us not grow slack because we have reached the harbor. Let us be all the more zealous, because we have arrived at the end. Helmsmen do the same. When they are about to bring a great merchant ship, loaded with grain and cargo piled high, into the mouth of the harbor, they are anxious and fearful, in case the ship, after the long open seas, strikes some rock there and sinks the whole cargo. In the same way we too must fear and be anxious, so that we do not lose the reward of our labors at the very end. Therefore we must intensify our zeal. Runners do the same: when they see that they are getting near the prizes, they run all the harder. So too athletes, after countless bouts and countless victories, when they draw near to the crowns, rouse themselves all the more and strain their eagerness. Let us also do the same now. For what the harbor is to helmsmen, the prizes to runners, and the crowns to athletes, this present week is to us: the sum of all good things. Now come the bouts for the crowns. That is why we call it Great. It is not because its days are longer than all others, for there are other days that are longer, nor because they are more in number, for there are as many as in other weeks. It is because great deeds were accomplished for us in it by the Master. In this Great Week the long tyranny of the devil was overthrown. Death was quenched. The strong man was bound and his goods were plundered. Sin was abolished and the curse was undone. Paradise was opened, heaven became accessible, and human beings mingled with angels. The dividing wall of the partition was broken down and the barrier was removed. The God of peace made peace between the things above and the things on earth. That is why it is called the Great Week. And as this week is the chief of all the other weeks, so its head is the Great Sabbath: as the head is to the body, so the Sabbath is to the week. That is why many intensify their zeal during it. Some increase their fasting, others their holy vigils, others give more lavish alms. By their zeal for good works and by the intense piety of their lives they [show] the greatness [?] … the word of David, and this; or rather, not even that … [?] bearing witness [to the …] of God. For just as, when the Lord raised Lazarus, all the [?] came out to meet him … [Variant readings:] Savile: "Discourse delivered in the Great Week, in which also [?] … on fasting, and on 'Praise the Lord, O my soul,' and on the jailer spoken of in Acts. It was delivered in the holy and Great Week." One manuscript: "when they wrestle the bout for the crown, then they rouse their [eagerness] all the more." Savile: "For as God has granted a harbor to helmsmen, prizes to runners, and crowns to athletes, so he has granted us the present week."

[?]…of a scribe [?]. This is so that you may learn that the wisdom is spiritual, and that is why it comes with such ease and such speed. When people speak from their own resources, they compose, deliberate, hesitate and take a long time. But there the words gushed out as from a spring, and nothing stood in their way; the flood of thoughts outran the tongue. That is why he said: "My tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe." The streams gush forth below in great abundance, he says, and hence the great swiftness. We have no need of reflection, study or toil. But let us see what he says: "Praise the Lord, O my soul." Let us also sing these words with David today. For even if he is not present in body, he is present in spirit. If you want proof that the righteous are present with us and sing with us, hear what Abraham says to the rich man. When the rich man said, "Send Lazarus, so that my brothers may learn what happens in Hades and set their own lives right," Abraham said to him, "They have Moses and the prophets." Yet Moses and all the prophets had long since died in the body; it was through their writings that the brothers had them. If someone who sets up a lifeless image of a child or a friend thinks the departed person is present, and pictures him through that lifeless image, how much more do we enjoy the company of the saints through the divine Scriptures. We have images not of their bodies but of their souls, for the words they spoke are images of their souls. Do you want to learn that the righteous are alive and present? No one calls the dead as witnesses. But Christ called them witnesses of his own divinity, and before these [?] David himself, to teach you that he is alive. When the Jews were disputing about him, he said to them: "What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?" They said to him, "David's." He said to them, "How then does David, in the Spirit, call him Lord, saying, 'The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand'?" Do you see how David is alive? If he were not alive, Christ would not have called him as a witness to his divinity. And he did not say, "How then did David in the Spirit call him Lord?" but "calls him Lord," to show that David is still present and speaks through his writings. David once sang in psalms, and today we sing with David. He had a lyre with lifeless strings; the Church has a lyre strung with living strings. Our tongues are the strings of the lyre. Each gives out a different sound, but they sound a single, harmonious piety. Women and men, old and young, differ in age, but they do not differ in the singing of hymns. The Spirit blends each one's voice and makes a single melody out of them all. David himself showed this when he called every age and both sexes to this harmony, saying: "Let everything that breathes praise the Lord." "Praise, O my soul…" [?] manuscripts [read] "…gushed out the words…outran the…" [?]. One [manuscript reads] "let us sing in response." One [reads] "relatives." [?] One [reads] [?]. Two manuscripts [read] "of the rhythm" [?].

[?]…power? By singing hymns the three young men quenched the furnace of Babylon. Or rather, they did not quench it. They did something far more wonderful: they trampled the burning flame underfoot like clay. In Paul's case this hymn entered a prison. It loosed his bonds, opened the prison doors, shook the foundations and filled the jailer with fear and great amazement. "At midnight," it says, "Paul and Silas were singing hymns." Then what happened? What? Something altogether new and astonishing: the bonds were loosed, and those in bonds bound those who were free. The nature of bonds is to hold the one bound tightly and keep him in subjection. But now the jailer, a free man, came to the feet of Paul, who was in bonds. The nature of physical bonds is to hold the prisoner, but bonds worn for Christ have such power that they make the free subject to those in chains. The jailer threw them into the inner prison, and from inside they opened the outer doors. He fastened their feet in the stocks, and their fastened feet loosed the hands of others. Then, it says, the jailer fell down before Paul, afraid, trembling, groaning, in anguish and in tears. What on earth has happened? Was it not you who bound him? Was it not you who kept him under guard? And why are you amazed, man, that he opened a prison, when he had received authority to open even the heavens? "Whatever you bind on earth," he says, "will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven." He loosed the bonds of sin; why are you amazed that he looses bonds of iron? He loosed the bonds of demons and set free the souls they held bound; why are you amazed that he released the prisoners' chains? And look at the twofold wonder: he loosed and he also bound. He loosed their bonds, but he bound their hearts, for they did not know they had been set free. He opened and he shut. He opened the prison doors, but he shut the eyes of the prisoners' hearts, so that they did not notice the doors had been opened. Otherwise they might have taken advantage of their freedom and run off. Do you see him both binding and loosing, both opening and shutting?

6. That is why these things happened at night: so that it might all take place quietly, without any disturbance. The apostles did nothing for show or for glory. The chief jailer fell down before him. What then did Paul do? You have seen his miracle; you have seen his astonishing works. Now see his care and his kindness. "He cried out," it says, "and said, 'Do yourself no harm, for we are all here.'" He did not let the man who had cruelly bound him die a cruel death; he bore him no grudge. "For we are all here," he says. See his humility. He did not say, "I worked these wonders," but what? "We are all here." Paul counted himself among the prisoners. When the jailer saw this, he marveled at what had happened, was astounded at the miracle, and gave thanks to God. The jailer [?] truly deserved great care and kindness. He did not think that what had happened was sorcery. Why did he not think so? He had heard them singing hymns to God, and a sorcerer never sings hymns to God. Since he was a jailer, he had taken in many sorcerers, but none of them had ever done such a work. None loosed bonds or showed care [?]. "The one bound": "of those bound, indeed, for Christ." So two [manuscripts]. Two manuscripts [read]: "he himself loosed, and again bound."

[?]…the power of prayer. But when prayer is joined with fasting, it makes the soul stronger. Then our thoughts are thoroughly sober, then the mind is roused, and the soul looks around at all the things above. That is why Scripture has always yoked prayer to fasting. How, and where? "Do not deprive one another," it says, "except perhaps by agreement, so that you may devote yourselves to fasting and prayer." And elsewhere: "This kind does not come out except by prayer and fasting." And elsewhere again: "After they had prayed and fasted," it says, "they laid [their hands] on them…" [?]

5. Do you see that prayer goes with fasting everywhere? For then the lyre sends up a sweeter and more acceptable melody. Its strings are not soaked and slackened by the excess of drunkenness. The reasoning is taut, the mind is awake, the soul is sober. This is how we should approach God and speak with him, alone with the One who is alone. When we have something important to say to friends, we take them aside and talk with them in private. How much more should we do this with God, going into our inner room in deep quiet. And we will certainly obtain everything, provided our request is for what is good for us. Prayer is a great good when it is offered with a thankful and sober mind. And how will it be thankful? If we train ourselves to give thanks to God not only when we receive, but also when we do not get what we ask. For sometimes God gives and sometimes he does not, but he does both for our benefit. So whether you receive or not, you have received by not receiving; whether you succeed or not, you have succeeded by not succeeding. There are times when not receiving what we ask is more profitable than receiving it. If not receiving were not often good for us, he would surely have given every time. But to be refused for our own good is itself success. That is why he often delays our request. He does not want to put us off; by delaying the gift he skillfully draws out our perseverance. Often, once we have received what we asked for, we lose our zeal for prayer. So, wanting to heighten our watchfulness in supplication, he delays the gift. Loving fathers do the same. When their children are careless and run off to childish games, the fathers often keep them close by promising them some great gift. That is why fathers sometimes delay, and sometimes do not give at all. There are also times when we ask for something harmful. Then God, who knows better than we do what is good for us, does not grant our prayers; he arranges what is profitable for us even when we do not know it. And why be surprised that we are not heard, when the same thing happened even to Paul? He too asked many times and did not receive. Not only was he not grieved; he even gave thanks to God. "Three times," he says, "I begged the Lord about this," and "three times" means "many times." If Paul asked many times and did not obtain, how much more must we persevere! But let us see how he responded to not receiving after asking so many times. Not only was he not grieved; he even boasts… One [manuscript reads] "thus we beseech." Two manuscripts [read] "our perseverance." One [reads] "to them." One [reads] "praises." [?] "is about to be reconciled," and soon after, "when you through yourself"; others: "is about to be reconciled," and soon after, "when."

[?]…when you bring a pure mind and sober thoughts, when you do not pray half-heartedly. Many people do just that. Their tongue speaks the words of the prayer, but their soul wanders all over the house, the marketplace and the streets. This is wholly the devil's scheme. He knows that at that moment we can obtain forgiveness of our sins. Wanting to silt up the harbor of prayer against us, he rises up at that very moment and drives our minds away from what is being said, so that we go away having lost rather than gained. Knowing this, then, O man, when you approach God, consider whom you are approaching. The trustworthiness of the one who is about to give you grace is enough to make you sober. Look up to heaven and consider to whom you are speaking. When someone talks with a person raised only a little by human honors, even if he is the most careless of men, he certainly rouses himself and orders his soul to be alert. How much more, if we consider that we are speaking with the Master of the angels, will we find in this reason enough to pay attention to ourselves. But if some other method is needed [?]… Others [read] "the device." Ibid.: others [read] "at the time to converse with God we can [obtain] also forgiveness." Ibid.: others [read] "wishing to make us strike against the very harbor of prayer." One [reads] "send." A little further on, one [reads] "when you approach God." Others [read] "the soul."
